title: Comment from Sacajawea Audubon Society

text:
December 21, 2025

Brian Nesvik
Director U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
1849 C Street, NW
Washington, DC 20240
United States

RE: Docket Numbers: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029

Dear Director Nesvik,

I am writing on behalf of Sea and Sage Audubon Society to urge you to reconsider weakening the Endangered Species Act (ESA) through proposed rules changes, Docket Number: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029: and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044. Sea and Sage Audubon Society is an Orange County, California chapter of the National Audubon Society with nearly 7,000 local members and supporters dedicated to the protection of birds and their habitats.

The proposed changes to the ESA would replace science-based, economically balanced measures for listing, protecting, and recovering endangered species with heavily weighted economic considerations that will put many species at risk. The ESA has been very successful in stabilizing and saving most of the species listed since 1973. Many factors contribute to species becoming endangered, but habitat loss, poisoning, and pollution are among the top, and they are difficult to reverse quickly. And while few species have reached the point of delisting and removal from the list, many species, such as the California Condor, Peregrine Falcon, Bald Eagle, California Pelican, and California Least Tern, are considered stable or have been delisted due to science-based, economically balanced ESA efforts.

The ESA already takes economic considerations into account during all phases, including during the critical habitat designation process. The new proposed changes would undermine the ability to keep endangered populations stable or in recovery. Newly threatened species may not receive adequate protection to keep them from being added to the list, further harming the species that the original 1973 law aims to protect, and potentially creating many financial impacts in the future.

FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029 Removing the blanket 4(d) rule will weaken Section 7 consultations that would delay or reduce critical habitat safeguards, putting species at further risk, and will substantially increase the costs of recovery in the future.
And, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039 redefining Section 4 listing criteria to increase economic considerations will weaken the intent of the I973 law to protect species and balance economic considerations.

FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048 This proposed rule change would give too much emphasis to economic considerations, replacing the protection of threatened and endangered species secondary to factors not considered in the 1973 law.

FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044 Limiting and reducing the importance of species recovery during Section 7 Consultations will alter the FWS's ability to adequately protect species in peril from further harm.

Cumulatively, the proposed rules changes would severely impact the effectiveness of the ESA and contradict the intent of the landmark 1973 law. We urge you to decline these proposed rules changes and to work within the existing ESA framework, which has been very effective and balances science-based protections with adequate economic considerations.

Thank you for your consideration.

Scott Thomas
Vice Chair of Conservation
Sea and Sage Audubon Society

Wyoming Native Plant Society

Re. Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants (50 CFR Part 17; section 4(d) and section 4(b)(2))

December 19, 2025

Dear Madam or Sir,
We maintain that a “blanket rule” is crucial to maintain for newly-listed threatened plant species. It is not good enough to say that the intent to create species-specific rules takes the place of a default rule.

Species-specific rules require staff time. There is an acute shortage of botanical expertise in the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, though significant numbers of Threatened species are plants. This proposed rule would further encumber the Service and mean that newly-listed Threatened plant species would essentially be placed in limbo rather treated with transparency and efficiency.

We are also submitting comments on FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048 and see these proposals as closely related. We urge retaining the phrase “without reference to possible economic or other impacts of such determination” as essential to maintain the intent of the Endangered Species Act. Economic considerations are essential for the public to know, but they are not in listing and delisting decision standards, critical habitat decision standards or Section 7 consultation standards. This is necessary to carry out all different segments of the Endangered Species Act consistent with the extinction-risk focus of decisions under the Act.

As such, we reject the proposed measure to exclude areas from critical habitat designation if they are on federal lands or on other lands with a conservation agreement. This would be a blank check for removing most or all critical habitat designations. In states such as Wyoming, the only places where Threatened and Endangered plant species are protected under the Act is on federal lands, or otherwise where federal actions are involved.

Sincerely,

Bonnie Heidel, Chair

text:
On behalf of 8,204 supporters of the Wildlife Conservation Society, I would like to submit the following comments:

Dear Secretary Burgum:

As a supporter of the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS), I am writing to express my strong opposition to the rules proposed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service that would roll back many of the important protections provided by one of the world’s most successful environmental laws, the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

I am deeply concerned by the erosion of science-based decision-making reflected in these proposed rules. The ESA requires that listing decisions be based solely on the best scientific and commercial data available. Congress’s clear intent at the passage of the ESA was to ensure that decisions were made based on scientific necessity and safeguarded from political considerations that often arise when money is involved.

One rule proposed would allow economic information to be considered in the decision on whether to list or delist a species, a step that is clearly illegal under the ESA. Further, another proposal would make economic impacts a central factor in determining what critical habitat to set aside for species recovery. These proposed rules ignore the original intent of Congress and one of the key reasons the law has been successful—the reliance on science.

One proposed rule includes a rescission of FWS’s blanket 4(d) rule that immediately provides critical protections to species when they are listed as “threatened,” including immediate prohibitions on the killing of or trade in a species. Should this rule be adopted, future listings of species as “threatened” will no longer receive these protections—including protection from killing or trading—without another federal action specifically addressing it. This will significantly reduce the immediate benefits of listing a species as threatened. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule would create a substantial—and unnecessary—burden on FWS to promulgate a species-specific 4(d) rule for every species covered by the ESA under its jurisdiction that is listed as threatened or downlisted from endangered. Given the unprecedented departure of experienced FWS employees this year, the agency’s remaining staff would not have the capacity to prepare individual 4(d) rules each time a new species is listed, leaving dozens of threatened species without protections for potentially years.

For 50 years, the ESA has been one of the most effective tools in any country to protect and recover endangered and threatened species and has demonstrated the United States’ leadership in saving vulnerable species and habitats. As one of the most powerful wildlife laws in the world, the ESA serves as a model for other countries to conserve their species and in key wildlife habitats. I strongly urge the Services to withdraw these egregious proposals and to ensure that the ESA continues to serve its purpose of preventing the decline and extinction of species in need of protection and protecting their habitats which provide critical ecosystem services for all of us.

Thank you for your consideration.

A full list of signatories is in the attached file.

For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,

I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

1. Support a collaborative approach to at-risk species conservation and recovery efforts among federal, tribal, state, and local governments, as well as private landowners and organizations, including the development of interagency guidelines and dedication of adequate funding under Section 6 of the ESA;
2. Support the statutory duties and standards in the Endangered Species Act and actively promote their consistent interpretation to prevent extinctions and recover species;
3. Work to ensure that decisions under the ESA are transparent and based on robust and rigorous analyses of the best scientific data and evidence available, including data provided by states and tribes and peer-reviewed data on current and potential future effects of climate change;
4. Advocate for listing decisions that are based solely on the status of the species in question and oppose listing justifications based on economic and political consideration;
5. Oppose the use of congressional action that subverts established legal and science-based agency processes to affect the listing status or consideration of species under the ESA;
6. Advocate for adequate federal funding and agency staffing to ensure efficiency in ESA listing and recovery planning processes, implementation of recovery actions, and support for at-risk species conservation actions implemented by or in collaboration with states and tribes;
7. Advocate for efficient and transparent rulemaking processes around critical habitat definitions, designation of critical habitat for listed species, and measures to restore,
enhance, manage, and protect occupied and unoccupied critical habitats that are essential to recover endangered and threatened species;
8. Support actions that incentivize and encourage private landowner to contribute to the recovery of listed species and conservation of at-risk species.
title: Comment from Walker, Allison

text:
As a volunteer for threatened and endangered shorebirds on the beaches of New York City I am AGAINST the proposed changes to the ESA. Here's why:

-The blanket 4(d) rule is a proven, science-based tool that gives threatened species immediate protections when they are most at risk.

-Eliminating the blanket rule will delay or weaken protections for newly listed species, putting them in harm’s way during the period when conservation actions are most critical.

-Species-specific rules are not a substitute for broad baseline protections; they are slow, resource-intensive, and increase political pressure from industries seeking exemptions.

-The ESA requires decisions to be based on the best available science, not executive orders aimed at weakening environmental safeguards.

Bottom line: The Fish & Wildlife Service should retain the blanket 4(d) rule to prevent regulatory gaps that could worsen species declines.

text:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to submit a public comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) announced on November 21, 2025 by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, in coordination with the National Marine Fisheries Service.

For more than 50 years, the ESA has served as the cornerstone of wildlife conservation in the United States, earning 84% public support and preventing the extinction of 99% of listed species. Weakening this law through administrative rule changes undermines one of our nation’s most effective and successful environmental protections.

The ESA currently safeguards 743 endangered animal species, ranging from snails to blue whales. Within U.S. jurisdiction alone, 14 species of cetaceans (whales and dolphins) and 5 species of seals and sea lions are listed as endangered. Additionally, species listed as threatened—including the polar bear, Florida manatee, and both southern and northern sea otters—would be significantly impacted by these proposed changes.

These species are already facing unprecedented threats from climate change, habitat loss, pollution, and human activity. Now is not the time to weaken the very protections that have allowed them to survive. Any rule changes that reduce habitat protections, delay critical conservation actions, or elevate economic interests over scientific evidence place these vulnerable species at grave risk.

I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service to withdraw these proposed rule changes and instead recommit to the full strength and intent of the Endangered Species Act. Decisions affecting endangered wildlife must remain grounded in the best available science, transparency, and the long-standing public mandate to prevent extinction.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this comment and for considering the voices of those who value and depend on healthy ecosystems—for wildlife and for future generations.

Sincerely,
Mark and Martha O’Boyle
Carpinteria, Ca 93013
title: Comment from O’Boyle , Mark

text:
Threatened species should be automatically protected from killing, harming, or habitat destruction. The Fish & Wildlife Service should retain the blanket 4(d) rule to prevent regulatory gaps that could worsen species declines. The ESA requires using the best scientific and commercial data available; weakening listing criteria undermines that legal standard.
Species threatened by climate change rely on future-oriented science, narrowing “foreseeable future” restricts the ability to act before collapse.
Recovery often requires habitat beyond the small areas species currently occupy; restricting unoccupied critical habitat contradicts the purpose of the ESA.
Reinstating the 2019 rule moves ESA implementation backward, not forward.
FWS and NMFS should keep the 2024 improvements rather than revert to weaker, outdated language.
The 2020 rule improperly elevated economic and political considerations over the biological needs of species.
Reinstating it contradicts the ESA’s purpose: to conserve ecosystems and recover species, not to reduce protections for industry convenience.
The Service must base exclusions on clear scientific evidence, not speculative economic concerns.
Habitat loss is the primary driver of extinction; weakening critical habitat tools directly harms recovery prospects.
FWS should restore the more balanced 2016 policy or adopt a stronger science-forward framework.

Section 7 consultation is the heart of the ESA; any weakening puts species survival at risk.
Raising the threshold for “reasonably certain to occur” effects will erase legitimate scientific evidence and allow harmful actions to proceed without full review.
The rollback reinstates 2019 rules that courts and scientists criticized as inconsistent with the ESA’s conservation mandate.
Climate impacts, cumulative habitat loss, and landscape-scale consequences must be included in consultations as they are essential to understanding jeopardy.
The rule should be withdrawn; the Service should restore the stronger 2024 protections instead of narrowing them.
title: Comment from Eileen, Tammy

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

To whomever it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.

The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.

I've been working at Mystic Aquarium for 24 years educating guests on the importance of conservation and consider myself a role model advocating for animals. I try and live by our mission of saving aquatic species and empowering communities to save our oceans which is why I'm writing this letter.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Deb Pazzaglia
Assistant Supervisor California sea lions
Mystic Aquarium

text:
I urge you to immediately withdraw the following four proposed regulations that would dismantle the Endangered Species Act and push hundreds of species closer to extinction:

· Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants (FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029) (FWS only)

· Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat (FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039)

· Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat (FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048) (FWS only)

· Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation Regulations (FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044)

These disastrous proposals would gut the Act by making it harder to list and protect imperiled species and easier to destroy the habitat where they make their homes. This isn’t merely tinkering, it’s a radical attack on some of the most important protections for some of our most imperiled animals and plants. If these rules had been in place in the 1970s, the bald eagle and the gray whale might not be around today. If finalized, they will drive hundreds of species closer to extinction.

Rescinding the blanket 4(d) rule would also lead to massive inefficiencies at an agency already struggling to meet its statutory obligations. The Service’s listing program has been chronically underfunded and faces a backlog of more than 400 species awaiting consideration for protection. Adding an additional duty to develop individual rules for newly threatened species will only further burden this already struggling program. Alarmingly, the proposed rule also states that the Service “intends to create species-specific rules for all threatened species currently protected under the ‘blanket rule’ option.”3 In other words, instead of directing scarce staff time and funding toward evaluating imperiled species that remain unprotected, the Service intends to spend what little resources it does have on reexamining — and likely weakening — protections for all 420-plus threatened species. This represents a breathtaking misuse of the agency’s limited resources and all but guarantees more species will be pushed closer to extinction precisely because the Service chose to dismantle a system designed to prevent that outcome.

II. Revisions to Endangered Species Act § 4 Regulations for Listing Species and Designating Critical Habitat

This proposal would fundamentally alter the way the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service evaluate the listing of threatened and endangered species, and it would also substantially limit the circumstances in which the Services could designate critical habitat. If adopted, these changes would undermine the conservation of endangered and threatened species nationwide, weaken their critical habitat protections, and ultimately make recovery of endangered animals and plants far more costly and difficult.4

As an initial matter, the proposal to once again remove the regulatory language in § 424.11 stating that listing determinations must be made “without reference to possible economic or other impacts of such determination” is not a principled reinterpretation of the Act, but the latest turn in a pattern of inconsistent and inadequately justified reversals. After restoring this language in 2024 to protect the scientific integrity Congress expressly required,3 the Services now attempt to resurrect the 2019 approach without explaining why their own recent conclusions are suddenly incorrect. By eliminating the very phrase Congress intended as a firewall against political and economic pressure, the Services invite precisely the interference the Endangered Species Act was designed to prevent. Further, the Services’ failure to justify this renewed departure from the Act’s best available science mandate renders the proposed rule legally indefensible.

The proposed rule would also allow designation of unoccupied areas only where limiting critical habitat to occupied areas would either (1) be inadequate to ensure the conservation of the species or (2) result in less-efficient conservation. While currently occupied areas will often be important to a species’ survival, the ESA does not mandate that they be considered first or treated as categorically superior. IV. Revisions to Endangered Species Act § 4 Regulations for Excluding Areas of Critical Habitat Under Section 4(b)(2)

When Congress amended the ESA in 1982 to specify procedures for designating critical habitat, it provided in section 4(b)(2) that:

The Secretary shall designate critical habitat, and make revisions thereto, under subsection (a)(3). `Please reconsider these proposed changes and withdraw them for the future of our country and of our children.

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service:

I am writing today as a concerned citizen [and, if applicable, a biologist, a teacher, a parent, an outdoor enthusiast, etc.] to express my firm and unequivocal opposition to the proposed regulatory changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act (ESA) of 1973. The ESA is a cornerstone of American environmental law, a testament to our nation's commitment to preserving our natural heritage for future generations. The proposed rulemaking undermines this critical mission and must be withdrawn.

[ARGUMENT 1: ECONOMIC AND SCIENTIFIC INTEGRITY] The proposed changes to the definition of "foreseeable future" and the process for considering economic impacts are a direct assault on the scientific foundation of the ESA. The Act was intentionally designed to make decisions based on the best available scientific data, not on short-term economic projections. Allowing economic considerations to dictate whether a species is listed as endangered is scientifically unsound and creates a dangerous precedent where profit is prioritized over extinction. This will lead to poorly informed decisions that fail to protect species when they have the best chance of recovery.

[ARGUMENT 2: CRITICAL HABITAT PROTECTION] The proposed rules to weaken protections for critical habitat are particularly alarming. Habitat loss is the primary driver of species decline. By making it easier to exclude areas from designation and to weaken the recovery standard for unoccupied habitat, you are removing the very tool species need to recover. This is not just a procedural change; it is a policy decision that sentences countless species to a slow, preventable decline. Protecting habitat is the most effective and cost-efficient long-term strategy for conservation.

[ARGUMENT 3: UNDERMINING RECOVERY AND INTERAGENCY COOPERATION] The ESA's success is built on the principle of interagency consultation, ensuring that all federal actions are reviewed for their potential impact on protected species. The proposed changes to this process would create loopholes, allowing projects to proceed without rigorous, independent review. This undermines the entire collaborative framework of the Act and will inevitably lead to more "incidental take" of species, pushing them closer to the brink of extinction.

[ARGUMENT 4: PUBLIC TRUST AND MORAL OBLIGATION] The Endangered Species Act is one of our nation's most popular environmental laws. It reflects a profound public trust and a moral obligation to act as stewards of our planet's biodiversity. Weakening these regulations betrays that trust. For my children and grandchildren, I want them to inherit a world rich with wildlife, where the call of a gray wolf or the sight of a bald eagle is not just a memory from a textbook but a living reality. These proposed rules jeopardize that legacy.

In conclusion, the Endangered Species Act works. It has prevented the extinction of 99% of the species under its protection. These proposed regulatory changes are a solution in search of a problem, driven by special interests, not sound science or public will. I strongly urge you to withdraw this proposed rulemaking and uphold the strong, science-based protections that the ESA provides.

Thank you for your time and consideration of this critical matter.

text:
I am submitting this comment regarding the proposed revisions to ESA Section 4(d) regulations for threatened species. My comments highlight the importance of timely, appropriately tailored protections for threatened species and the benefits of early interventions that stabilize populations before more intensive, costly actions become necessary.

1.Science-based listings support stability
The ESA’s requirement to rely on “the best scientific and commercial data available” provides a consistent framework for evaluating biological status. Retaining this basis helps avoid uncertainty and litigation. Communities, landowners, and businesses depend on regulatory predictability, so listings should remain grounded in biological evidence rather than economic or political considerations.

Recommendation: Ensure listings rely solely on scientific data for long-term decision-making.

2.Critical habitat supports species and people
Protections maintain watershed health, reduce flood risks, sustain fisheries, and stabilize ecosystems supporting rural economies and recreation. Broadening non-designation or exclusion criteria may weaken these benefits.

Recommendation: Apply a precautionary, science-informed approach to maintain ecological functions supporting human well-being.

3.Comprehensive analysis anticipates risks
Section 7 consultations ensure federal actions consider biological impacts. Narrowing “effects of the action” or “environmental baseline” could limit consideration of cumulative or long-term changes—like altered water flow, wildfire frequency, or shifting species distributions—affecting ecosystems and communities.

Recommendation: Retain definitions allowing agencies to incorporate the best available science on cumulative and long-term effects.

4.Timely protections reduce costs and risks
Immediate protections stabilize populations early, when recovery is more achievable and less expensive. Requiring species-specific 4(d) rules for every threatened listing risks gaps during critical periods.

Recommendation: Maintain a default level of protection to ensure continuity and reduce costlier recovery measures later.

5.Economic impacts must not override recovery
Transparency and statutory consistency build public trust. While economic and social factors matter, they must be balanced with the ESA’s core purpose: preventing extinction and ensuring recovery. Over-reliance on exclusions may undermine ecosystem services such as pollination, erosion control, clean water, and recreation.

Recommendation: Ensure exclusions do not compromise species needs or ecosystem services that support communities.

The ESA has a nearly 50-year record of safeguarding species, supporting sustainable land management, and preserving ecosystems that communities depend on. Revisions should maintain its effectiveness as a science-driven, prevention-oriented tool serving both wildlife and people.

I respectfully urge the agencies to adopt final rules that preserve the ESA’s effectiveness in safeguarding wildlife and environmental systems critical to human communities.
Thank you for considering these comments.

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to voice my firm opposition to the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently being discussed. Each proposal, both individually and collectively, would severely weaken the ESA’s capacity to prevent extinction, aid species recovery, and protect ecosystems that are vital for both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing Default Protections for Threatened Species (Repeal of the Blanket 4(d) Rule)

The ESA is intended to act before species face crisis levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule is based on decades of scientific evidence demonstrating that early, precautionary protections reduce overall recovery costs and prevent further declines. Ending default protections for threatened species would introduce unnecessary delays, require case-by-case rulemaking for protections that are currently automatic, and expose vulnerable species to avoidable harm or killing. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive intent and will result in greater ecological and financial costs in the long run.

2. Making it Harder to List Species by Allowing Economic Considerations and Weakening Future-Threat Analysis

The ESA is explicit that listing decisions must rely solely on the best available scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic considerations—directly or indirectly—would contradict the statutory language, undermine scientific integrity, and risk delaying protections until species are near extinction. Additionally, limiting the use of projected or climate-driven threats disregards current conservation science, which indicates that gradual pressures like habitat loss, warming temperatures, ocean acidification, and shifting ranges heighten species risk long before declines are visible in population counts. Weakening future-threat criteria makes timely listing less likely and raises the likelihood of preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing Critical Habitat Protections and Limiting the Definition of “Harm”

Habitat loss is the primary cause of biodiversity decline globally and in the U.S. Reducing the designation of critical habitat—especially unoccupied or climate-refuge habitats crucial for long-term recovery—directly undermines recovery planning. Similarly, narrowing the definition of “harm” so that habitat degradation no longer qualifies would reverse decades of legal and scientific precedent. Habitat destruction often kills wildlife indirectly, and the law has long recognized this. Weakening these definitions would make inter-agency consultations less effective, increase biological risk, and create inconsistency with the ESA’s recovery mandate.

4. Opening New Loopholes that Allow Agencies or Special Committees to Bypass ESA Protections

Creating or expanding mechanisms that allow agencies to override ESA protections—even when extinction is foreseeable—conflicts with the ESA’s core purpose. These loopholes would incentivize project-by-project exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making away from science-based analysis. This would disproportionately affect wide-ranging and imperiled species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, and could hasten declines in many species already under significant pressure.

The Cumulative Impact of These Proposals

While concerning individually, collectively these rules would:
- Undermine the scientific foundation of the ESA,
- Delay or block protections for species in need,
- Reduce habitat conservation amidst accelerating climate change,
- Heighten extinction risk for both domestic and international species,
- Undermine inter-agency cooperation, and
- Increase long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

text:
I adamantly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

Endangered species need our help now more than ever. Do not roll back these life critical regulations that protect wildlife.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. text:
I respectfully submit this public comment in opposition to the proposed changes to Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations, as outlined in the Department’s press release dated November 19th 2025. I urge the reconsidering changes to the following rules, which undermine longstanding protections that have successfully prevented extinction for hundreds of species.

The proposal to allow economic considerations in listing decisions reverses the ESA’s science-only standard, which has served our nation well for 50 years. Allowing economic costs to influence listings could delay or prevent the protection of species at the edge of extinction.
Species like the bald eagle, whooping crane, and American alligator recovered because they were listed based solely on science, not economic tradeoffs. America would be very different today if our proud and patriotic bird the American Bald eagle was only a memory. On the other hand, 21 species were recently declared extinct because protection came too late, often due to inaction or regulatory delay. (https://www.fws.gov/press-release/2023-10/21-species-delisted-endangered-species-act-due-extinction)

Critical habitat designations are essential for recovery. Species such as the Piping Plover have rebounded from extinction because their habitat received legal protection. Many species also depend on protected areas for safe nesting and breeding, and disruptions can cause immediate and severe harm. Even species that are not currently listed depend on these protections. Even species not in the Endangered Species Act such as the Horned Lark, for example, is experiencing steep declines due to habitat loss and benefits when natural areas are preserved. Weakening the habitat designation process, including allowing exclusions of unoccupied habitat, would remove the very places species need to survive, recover, and adapt to a changing climate.
Threatened Species Protections (50 CFR 17; Section 4(d))
This rule has automatically provided threatened species with protections against harm until a tailored plan can be finalized. For decades, it has helped species like the bald eagle, southern sea otter, and Florida manatee gain immediate safeguards upon listing (FWS, 2019).
Without this automatic protection, newly listed threatened species could be killed, captured, or harassed without legal consequence while they await a species-specific rule. This exposes species to preventable harm during their most vulnerable period.
Critical Habitat Exclusions (50 CFR 17; Section 4(b)(2))
I respectfully submit this public comment in opposition to the proposed changes to Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations, as outlined in the Department’s press release dated November 19th 2025. I urge the reconsidering changes to the following rules, which, if finalized, would undermine longstanding protections for wildlife and habitats that have successfully prevented extinction for hundreds of species.

Habitat loss is the number one driver of extinction. The ESA already allows exclusions, but only when they will not lead to extinction. Broadening this power increases risk to species that already live on the edge. For example, habitat loss contributed to the extinction of the ivory-billed woodpecker, Little Mariana fruit bat, and multiple freshwater mussel species (FWS, 2021) The ESA already allows exclusions, but only when they will not lead to extinction. Broadening this power increases risk to species that already live on the edge.
Interagency Cooperation (50 CFR 402)
I respectfully submit this public comment in opposition to the proposed changes to Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations, as outlined in the Department’s press release dated November 19th 2025. I urge the reconsidering changes to the following rules, which, if finalized, would undermine longstanding protections for wildlife and habitats that have successfully prevented extinction for hundreds of species.

Reinstating outdated definitions of “effects of the action” and “environmental baseline” will severely limit federal agencies' responsibilities to protect listed species during project reviews. Section 7 consultations have prevented many destructive projects or led to mitigations that preserved habitat, protected breeding grounds, or safeguarded water flows for fish. One such success story is of the Florida Panther in which Section 7 was utilized to help steer development of wildlife crossing protecting the species. The changes proposed would allow damaging projects to move forward without full review. Conservationists and legal experts warn that agencies could now “greenlight actions without fully assessing the impact on threatened and endangered species”. Without robust consultation, road projects may lack wildlife crossings, dams may disrupt salmon runs, or development may fragment panther corridors in Florida.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Miller, Therese

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

text:
I am a Nevada resident, an avid hunter, and a frequent user of our public lands. I strongly oppose the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s proposal to remove the “blanket rule” option for protecting newly listed threatened species under section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

Nevada’s public lands—much of which are managed by the Bureau of Land Management and the U.S. Forest Service—support some of the most expansive and ecologically important landscapes in the Lower 48, including sagebrush steppe, high desert basins, mountain ranges, and riparian corridors. These habitats are essential not only for threatened species, but also for cornerstone wildlife such as mule deer, pronghorn, elk, upland birds, and waterfowl that depend on intact ecosystems throughout the year.

As a hunter and public-lands user, I see firsthand how species conservation and habitat protection are inseparable from sound wildlife management. Sagebrush-dependent ecosystems, for example, support species like the greater sage-grouse while also providing critical winter range and migration corridors for mule deer and pronghorn. Weakening baseline protections for threatened species in these shared landscapes risks broader ecosystem degradation that ultimately affects both game and non-game species alike.

The blanket 4(d) rule has long ensured that newly listed threatened species receive immediate and consistent protections while species-specific rules are developed. Eliminating this default safeguard creates unnecessary vulnerability during what can be a prolonged rulemaking period. In arid states like Nevada, where habitat fragmentation, drought, wildfire, invasive species, and development pressures already strain wildlife populations, delays in protection can result in permanent losses.

From a practical standpoint, removing the blanket rule also increases administrative burden and regulatory uncertainty. Requiring individual species-specific rules for every threatened species diverts limited agency resources away from habitat restoration, collaborative conservation, and enforcement—work that is especially critical on Nevada’s vast public lands.

The ESA was designed to be precautionary. Threatened species are, by definition, on a trajectory toward endangerment if meaningful protections are not applied promptly. The blanket 4(d) rule provides a strong conservation baseline while still allowing flexibility where science supports tailored management. Removing this option undermines an effective tool without demonstrating a clear conservation benefit.

As a Nevada hunter who values responsible stewardship of public lands and science-based wildlife management, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule for threatened species. Maintaining strong, timely protections is essential to conserving Nevada’s landscapes, sustaining healthy wildlife populations, and preserving our hunting and outdoor traditions for future generations.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

text:
I strongly support keeping the Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants regulations in place. These protections are essential for conserving biodiversity, maintaining healthy ecosystems, and ensuring that future generations inherit a livable and balanced natural world.
Endangered and threatened species are not just individual plants or animals—they are vital parts of ecosystems that people depend on for clean water, food production, climate stability, and disease control. When a species disappears, it can trigger a chain reaction that harms other wildlife and weakens entire ecosystems. The existing regulations help prevent these losses by protecting habitats, limiting harmful activities, and requiring science-based decision-making.
These regulations are also grounded in strong scientific evidence. Species become endangered due to habitat destruction, pollution, climate change, and overexploitation—often caused or accelerated by human activity. Without enforceable protections, many species would have little chance of recovery. The regulations provide a proven framework that has already helped bring species like the bald eagle and American alligator back from the brink of extinction.
In addition, protecting endangered and threatened species benefits people and local communities. Healthy ecosystems support agriculture, fisheries, tourism, and outdoor recreation, all of which contribute to local and national economies. Weakening or removing these regulations could lead to long-term economic and environmental costs that far outweigh any short-term gains.
Finally, keeping these regulations reflects our ethical responsibility to act as responsible stewards of the planet. Once a species goes extinct, it is gone forever. We have a moral obligation to use our knowledge and resources to prevent irreversible harm and to respect the natural systems that sustain life.
For these reasons, I urge policymakers to maintain and strengthen the regulations pertaining to endangered and threatened wildlife and plants. Protecting these species protects our environment, our communities, and our future.

text:
Public comment
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express my firm opposition to the four proposed modifications to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. Each proposal, individually and collectively, threatens to undermine the ESA's effectiveness in preventing extinctions, aiding species recovery, and conserving ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA was designed to act before species reach critical endangerment. The existing 4(d) rule, supported by decades of science, shows that early protection reduces recovery costs and prevents declines. Removing default protections would delay necessary actions, require case-by-case rulings, and harm vulnerable species unnecessarily, contradicting the ESA's preventive purpose and increasing long-term ecological and financial costs.

2. Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best scientific data available, not economic impacts. Introducing economic factors into the decision process would undermine scientific integrity and delay protections. Additionally, ignoring future threats like climate change would disregard modern conservation science. Weakening these criteria would hinder timely listings and heighten extinction risks.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of "harm"

Habitat loss is a primary driver of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations undermines recovery efforts. Similarly, narrowing "harm" so habitat degradation isn't included would reverse established legal and scientific standards, as habitat destruction indirectly harms wildlife. Weakening these definitions would reduce the effectiveness of inter-agency consultations and compromise the ESA's recovery goals.

4. Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections

Allowing agencies to bypass ESA protections, even with foreseeable extinction outcomes, contradicts the ESA's fundamental purpose. These loopholes would encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and move away from science-based decisions, disproportionately affecting species like Florida panthers and gray wolves that are already under pressure.

Cumulative Impact

Collectively, these proposals would weaken the ESA's scientific foundation, delay protections for vulnerable species, reduce habitat conservation amid climate change, increase extinction risks, undermine inter-agency cooperation, and raise long-term recovery costs.

The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from extinction. It is a key conservation law because it is rooted in science, precaution, and proactive measures. These proposed changes conflict with these principles. In a time of significant biodiversity loss, the U.S. should strengthen, not weaken, its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

Therefore, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes entirely and maintain the current regulatory framework, which is founded on science, legal precedent, and proven success.

Thank you for considering this comment.

I strongly oppose the proposed revisions to 50 CFR Part 17, which would weaken the protections afforded to threatened and endangered species and undermine the core intent of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). These regulations are foundational to the ESA’s effectiveness and have played a critical role in preventing extinction and promoting species recovery for over five decades.

Part 17 provides essential safeguards for species listed as threatened or endangered, including protections against take and habitat destruction. Weakening these provisions—particularly by reducing automatic protections for threatened species or narrowing habitat-related safeguards—exposes imperiled wildlife to increased risk at a time when habitat loss, climate change, and development pressures are accelerating.

Habitat destruction remains the primary driver of species decline. Changes to Part 17 that limit protections for the habitats species depend on directly contradict the science-based purpose of the ESA. Most listed species already occupy only small remnants of their historic range, and further erosion of habitat protections will make recovery far more difficult or impossible.

The ESA requires that decisions regarding species protection be based solely on the best available scientific data. Regulatory changes to 50 CFR Part 17 that prioritize administrative convenience or economic interests over science threaten to politicize a process that must remain objective and evidence-based.

The Endangered Species Act has an extraordinary record of success, preventing extinction for 99 percent of listed species, and it enjoys broad bipartisan public support. Weakening 50 CFR Part 17 is inconsistent with both the law’s intent and the will of the American public.

I urge the agencies to withdraw these proposed revisions and maintain the full strength of 50 CFR Part 17 to ensure that threatened and endangered species—and the habitats they rely on—receive the robust protections necessary for survival and recovery.
title: Comment from Douglass, Lana

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Treloar, Sage

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.
title: Comment from Williams, Adele

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Gaffrey , Michael

text:
Protecting threatened species is not optional—it is a core promise built into the Endangered Species Act, and the blanket rule is essential to upholding Congress’s original intent. Weakening this safeguard would leave already-vulnerable species exposed to avoidable decline. Likewise, the proposed interagency cooperation rule would undermine the very heart of the ESA by shifting its focus from conservation to convenience, allowing commercial interests to overshadow the urgent needs of imperiled wildlife.
Critical habitat is the foundation of species recovery, especially as climate change accelerates habitat loss through drought, fires, shrinking snowpack, and vanishing rivers. Reducing habitat protections or narrowing the definition of “harm” ignores the reality that species cannot rebound without the space and resources to survive. With hundreds of species still waiting for protection—and many having already endured years of delay—now is the time to strengthen safeguards, not weaken them.
Excluding habitat to accommodate profit-driven development disregards both ecological science and public support. Americans overwhelmingly back strong wildlife protections because extinction is permanent; once a species disappears, it is gone forever. To hollow out the ESA is to unravel the biological foundations of a healthy planet. We must defend critical habitat, reject rollbacks, and honor our responsibility to protect the species that depend on us for their very survival.

title: Comment from Strickland , April

text:
Honorable officials,

The Endangered Species Act is the essential tool for stopping the extinction crisis in its tracks. We cannot guarantee species survival and recovery without the strong backstop of a fully protective ESA.  

I oppose any effort by this administration to weaken the Endangered Species Act. The proposed rules are yet another in a series of attacks on imperiled species and the places they live that ignore science and prioritize destruction over conservation. The proposed rules:

***Deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, greater sage grouse, and monarch butterfly could be left unprotected even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings.

***Narrow the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

***Loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

***Violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

***Alter the criteria for designating critical habitat to make it easier to exclude areas from protections by giving more weight to industry claims of economic impact.

With greater threats facing species than ever before, these attempts to weaken the ESA are dangerous.

More than a million of the Earth’s species face the possibility of extinction due to climate change, pollution, habitat loss, and exploitation. Even species that are not yet on the brink will face huge population declines. This extinction crisis is depleting fisheries, wiping out the pollinators that support our food supply, and making our rivers, wetlands, and forests disappear.

Humans are not isolated from the natural environment, and what happens to other creatures affects our existence, too.  

At a time when we must be redoubling our commitment to protect biodiversity and stop extinction, this administration’s proposals are dangerous and will delay the progress we must make to address the alarming rate of extinction our planet now faces.

Respectfully,
Caleb Merendino

Protecting Wildlife: Why the Endangered Species Act MattersEmpty heading
Posted December 15, 2025 by David Jenike
The Endangered Species Act, enacted in 1973, currently serves as the most effective wildlife legislation ever enacted to preserve biodiversity. Species such as the California condor, gray wolf, American alligator, and bald eagle are all here today as a result of this legislation. Here at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, we work to conserve numerous species listed under the Endangered Species Act, including Mexican wolves, Polar bear, sihek, Texas ocelots, and American burying beetles.

One of the most concerning proposals would eliminate the Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule.” This rule automatically provides basic protections for species listed as threatened , such as prohibitions on harming or harassing that wildlife, while species-specific rules are developed.

Without the blanket rule, newly listed species could go months or even years without specific protections, and this delaying of safeguards increases the risk of further population decline.
