Please keep the Endangered Species Act strong and in-place to do what it has been doing since enactment in 1973!
title: Comment from Gianni, Nicole

text:
As an environmental scientist who has worked for three decades to restore habitat for threatened and endangered species. I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposal for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) to remove the rule under the US Endangered Species Act (ESA or the Act) that provides blanket protection for newly-listed threatened species.

Species listed as threatened have reached a high level of population extinction risk because of threats to their populations that need to be addressed as soon as possible. There is often a substantial lag time from when a species is given a threatened designation until when the USFWS is able to do the extensive data collection and reporting to identify threats. This is only going to become longer with recent severe cuts to staffing. While I agree that each species would ideally be considered on a case-by-case basis, this simply is not practical given the backlog of species listings and follow-up documentation such as critical habitat designation and recovery plans. Therefore, if the blanket rule is revoked, it will certainly result in drastic population declines or even extinction of some threatened species while waiting for the necessary documentation of threats. This will have negative effects on humans and other species. I strongly oppose removing the "blanket rule"; this change is not consistent with the purpose of the ESA to maintain population viability of both threatened and endangered species.
title: Comment from Holl, Karen

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Fuchs, Heidi

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Cuyler, Aaron

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Abby

text:

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
December 22, 2025

United States Fish and Wildlife Service

Re: Comments on Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants
Docket Number: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FXES11130900000-256-FF09E23000
RIN: 1018-BI74

I do not support the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) proposal to remove the "blanket rule" option for protecting newly listed threatened species. The proposal to instead create species-specific rules ignores the reality of underfunded conservation staff, capacity, and needs at the U.S. FWS and creates an easy space for political maneuvering that is not in the best interest of the listed species. Simply put, this proposed rule is impractical and easily manipulated.

The proposed rule is impractical because it assumes FWS has the staff, capacity, expertise, and budget to develop species-specific plans. This is counter to the reality that the agency is perennially underfunded, and the present administration's actions to "DOGE" government agencies has gutted their funding, staff, and missions. Creating species-specific plans would require more funding, more staff, more expertise, and more bureaucracy than the "blanket rule" requires. This is not feasible.

The species-specific rule would also be easily manipulated by bad actors who could use public comments and legal challenges as bureaucratic mechanisms to impede and delay necessary species protections. This adds no value to taxpayers, further burdens the process with administrative hurdles, and would not result in more effective conservation outcomes for listed species.

Further, the proposed rule is unnecessary as the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of listed species. This proposed rule does nothing to improve the realistic conservation outcomes for listed species and is clearly an attempt to undermine protection of our natural heritage. The species listed under the Endangered Species Act are not optional. They are critical to the healthy functioning of the unique ecosystems in our country, and it is nonsensical to further imperil them at the same time that wild life makes up less than 4% of the world's biomass and species are going extinct at unprecedented rates.

In summary, I do not support the proposed rule to remove the "blanket rule" for listed species.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed revisions. According to the World Wildlife Fund, "The US Endangered Species Act (ESA) is our nation’s most effective law to protect at-risk species from extinction, with a stellar success rate: 99% of species listed on it have avoided extinction." However, even with the current ESA structure, we are still seeing devastating declines. The proposed revisions will weaken the ESA, and weakening the ESA will only make matters worse.

It is also important to note that the ESA is used as a standard for similar legislation globally. Therefore, the proposed revisions don't just impact the United States and all species that reside within it, but all species globally.

The proposed revisions only take into account short-term economic gain, rather than long-term economic gain. The economy is impacted by a multitude of factors, and our changing climate, as well as the drastic decline in species, are among them. Our economy is going to suffer regardless, but by how much is still up to us. The proposed revisions will make future matters profoundly worse and only speed up economic hardships.

Instead of targeting an astonishingly successful law, efforts should be redirected toward long-term solutions, such as re-evaluating where we get our energy. To "Unleash American Energy," we should look toward the youth and new ideas on how to improve our current energy system, rather than relying on older methods that are limited and set to run out. The youth have the best motivation for creating solutions that actually work and don't have alternative goals; it is their future that is at risk. Many of those who are in power will not have to live with, or get to see, the consequences of their actions. The youth will have to live with the consequences of the actions we take now.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am writing to express my deep concern regarding the ongoing threats to endangered species as outlined in the FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029-0001 document. The protection and conservation of our nation’s endangered species are not only essential for maintaining biodiversity, but they also represent an ethical responsibility we have to future generations. As a concerned citizen and advocate for wildlife, I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to take immediate and robust action to safeguard these species from extinction.

The Importance of Conservation

Endangered species play vital roles in ecosystems, from pollination to pest control, water purification to seed dispersal. The loss of any species creates a ripple effect that can destabilize entire ecosystems, jeopardizing both wildlife and human communities. The ongoing loss of biodiversity is one of the most urgent issues facing the planet, and we must act quickly to prevent further damage.

Specific Species at Risk

[Here, if you know the species or animals being referenced in the document (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029-0001), mention them specifically. For example: "The XYZ turtle, native to the southeastern United States, has seen a drastic decline in its population due to habitat destruction, illegal hunting, and pollution."]

These species, and many others, are critical to maintaining healthy ecosystems. I believe that the proposals and conservation plans mentioned in FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029-0001 must be strengthened to reflect the urgency of this crisis.

Urgent Recommendations

Stronger Habitat Protections: Immediate action should be taken to ensure that the habitats of these endangered species are protected from further degradation. This includes working with local governments, industries, and communities to prevent deforestation, pollution, and other destructive practices.

Increased Funding for Conservation Programs: Adequate funding for research, monitoring, and conservation efforts is essential. The current budget allocated to protecting endangered species is insufficient to meet the growing challenges they face.

Enforcement of Laws and Regulations: The Endangered Species Act and other federal protections must be fully enforced to combat illegal poaching and trafficking of endangered species. Stronger penalties and more rigorous monitoring are necessary to deter harmful activities.

Public Awareness and Education: Engaging communities in conservation efforts and raising awareness about the importance of protecting endangered species is crucial. Through educational programs, media campaigns, and partnerships with local organizations, we can foster a culture of conservation.

A Call to Action

The time to act is now. As one of the most influential agencies in wildlife conservation, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has the power to protect these species before it's too late. I strongly encourage you to prioritize the recommendations and strategies that will lead to the recovery of endangered species listed under FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029-0001.

Thank you for your attention to this urgent matter. I look forward to hearing about the steps the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service will take to ensure the survival of these vital species.

Sincerely,

Kathleen Pease

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

title: Comment from Cote, Ella

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text: I strongly oppose this new rule. This means that wolves will not automatically get full take protections when delisted, meaning states will have more ability to decimate this critical capstone species with poor management decisions including increasing depredation shooting and expanded hunting zones. Revising portions of section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act of 1973 (ESA), to remove the “blanket rule” option for protecting newly listed threatened species would be detrimental to species conservation, including that of the Gray Wolf. Retaining the ESA language as-is would assist in protecting critical species and the environment at large.
title: Comment from Bolden, Joy

text:
As someone who cares deeply about wildlife and the future of our planet, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule that would undermine wildlife protections granted by the Endangered Species Act. This change would go against decades of conservation progress and weaken one of our nation’s most important environmental laws.

I urge you to uphold the mission of the Endangered Species Act and maintain the “blanket rule.” Our wildlife, wild places, and future generations are counting on it.

title: Comment from Rosczyk, Mary Lou

text:
As a third-generation Oregonian who has spent a lifetime learning from and enjoying the outdoors, I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. The United States is exceptional not only because of its people, but because of its extraordinary diversity of landscapes, ecosystems, flora, and fauna. Protecting that natural heritage is a responsibility we owe to future generations.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Why in the world would you manatees? I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

title: Comment from Hannah, Karl

text:
To Whom it May Concern,

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act regulations, specifically the proposed elimination of the blanket 4(d) rule for threatened species (Docket No. FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029). I am an undergraduate student studying international economics in the school of foreign service at Georgetown university. This has afforded me the opportunity to have classes focused towards endangered species management and recovery.

I am writing to raise concerns that eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule will weaken the protections for newly listed threatened species during a critical window for these species’ population, when population declines are often most reversible. Specifically:

Species specific 4(d) rules risk creating delays in protection during early listing stages.
Empirical evidence suggests that early, precautionary protections improve long-term recovery outcomes for threatened species.

The first concern is the loss of immediate protections for threatened species. The proposed rule would eliminate the blanket protections for threatened species and replace them with convoluted specific species rules developed on a case by case basis. While tailoring protections may be the most efficient route if implemented correctly, research suggests that the administrative delay between listing and implementation of species specific regulations expose vulnerable populations to continued habitat loss (Puckett et al., 2016).

Studies of ESA implementation show that the period immediately following listing is one of the most critical for recovery, as populations are often small and declining (Taylor et al., 2005). Without the blanket automatic protections that rule 4(d) provides, the precautionary buffer that ensures a species threat is not exacerbated will disappear whilst tailored rules are developed. Removing this safeguard will increase extinction risk, particularly for species with already limited ranges or rapidly declining populations; this can be seen clearly through the case of the American Horseshoe Crab.

The second major concern is that empirical analysis indicates that species receiving strong protections earlier in the listing process are far more likely to stabilise and/or improve. For example, a comprehensive review by Greenwald et al. (2013) found that delayed and weakened protections were associated with poor conservation outcomes, especially for species affected by habitat protection. This new bill would increase the time it takes to implement species protection, furthering damage to endangered species, and greatly increasing the risk of populations reaching critical levels or going extinct.

Additionally, the National Academies of Sciences emphasises that if there is uncertainty in an ecological system, it warrants precautionary approaches, this is particularly important when species face irreversible thresholds (National Research Council, 2013). The blanket 4(d) rule aligns closely with this principle by ensuring that there are baseline protections until sufficient data and research can be acquired to justify modifications.

Eliminating this rule will therefore conflict with the ESA’s statutory purpose of conserving ecosystems on which endangered and threatened species depend. This almost entirely eliminates the point of having this organisation.

While species-specific management in theory can be an efficient route to managing declining species populations, in practice it often ends up being the least efficient route, economically costing more, but more importantly risking the very chances of a multitude of species survival. Removing automatic protection for threatened species introduces unnecessary risk during a critical conservation window. It is therefore imperative that you retain the blanket 4(d) rule.

Sincerely,
Sia Sakhrani

References

Greenwald, N., Suckling, K., & Hartl, B. (2013). Extinction and the U.S. Endangered Species Act. PeerJ, 1, e126.
https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.126
National Research Council. (2013). Endangered and threatened species recovery programs: Assessing the role of science and adaptive management. National Academies Press.
https://nap.nationalacademies.org/catalog/18392
Puckett, E. E., Kesler, D. C., & Greenwald, D. N. (2016). Taxa, petitioning agency, and lawsuits affect time spent awaiting listing under the US Endangered Species Act. Biological Conservation. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocon.2016.07.005
Taylor, M. F. J., Suckling, K. F., & Rachlinski, J. J. (2005). The effectiveness of the Endangered Species Act: A quantitative analysis. BioScience, 55(4), 360–367.
https://doi.org/10.1641/0006-3568(2005)055[0360:TEOTES]2.0.CO;2

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

As a little girl, I found a monarch chrysalis and watched it hatch into a butterfly. I worry that if this revision goes through, my five-year-old niece will never have the same chance, because no more monarchs will be left. Once they're gone, we can't get them back, and this revision makes that all the more likely.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to firmly oppose the four proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. Each proposal, whether considered independently or together, would severely undermine the ESA's role in averting extinction, aiding species recovery, and safeguarding ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Eliminating Default Protections for Threatened Species (Repeal of the 4(d) Rule)

The ESA was created to act before species reach critical levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule is based on decades of scientific evidence demonstrating that early protective measures reduce recovery costs and prevent further declines. Removing such protections would cause unnecessary delays, mandate case-by-case rulemaking for protections that are currently automatic, and leave vulnerable species exposed to preventable harm. This goes against the ESA’s preventive aim and will lead to higher ecological and financial costs over time.

2. Introducing Economic Considerations and Weakening Future-Threat Analysis in Species Listing

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best available scientific data, not economic impacts. Factoring in economic considerations would contradict statutory language, undermine scientific integrity, and risk delaying protections until species are critically endangered. Furthermore, limiting the consideration of projected threats, such as climate change, ignores current conservation science, which indicates that pressures like habitat loss and climate shifts heighten species risk long before population declines are evident. Weakening future-threat criteria reduces the likelihood of timely listing and increases the chance of avoidable extinctions.

3. Reducing Critical Habitat Protections and Altering the Definition of “Harm”

Habitat loss is a leading cause of biodiversity decline globally and nationally. Curtailing the designation of critical habitat, especially unoccupied or climate-refuge areas crucial for long-term recovery, directly undermines recovery efforts. Similarly, narrowing the “harm” definition to exclude habitat degradation would overturn years of legal and scientific standards. Habitat destruction indirectly harms wildlife, which has long been recognized by law. Weakening these definitions would hinder inter-agency consultations, elevate biological risks, and conflict with the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. Creating Loopholes Allowing Agencies to Bypass ESA Protections

Establishing or expanding measures that allow agencies to override ESA protections, even when extinction is foreseeable, contradicts the ESA’s primary mission. These loopholes would encourage exemptions on a project-by-project basis, reduce transparency, and shift decisions away from science-based analysis. This would disproportionately impact wide-ranging and threatened species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, potentially accelerating declines in many already pressured species.

⸻

Combined Impact of These Proposals

Taken together, these proposals would:
• Weaken the scientific foundation of the ESA,
• Delay or obstruct protections for species in need,
• Reduce habitat conservation during a time of accelerating climate change,
• Increase extinction risk for both domestic and international species,
• Undermine inter-agency cooperation,
• Raise long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from extinction and stands as one of conservation’s most successful laws due to its foundation in science, precaution, and proactive measures. These proposed changes conflict with those principles.

In this era of significant global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should strengthen, not weaken, its most effective wildlife protection statute.

⸻

Request

Based on the reasons provided, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed changes entirely and maintain the current regulatory framework, which is supported by science, legal precedent, and decades of successful enactment.

text:
Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted, Chloe Radd

text:
I am a biologist and concerned US citizen and voter, writing to strongly oppose the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s proposed 2025 rule revising the so-called “blanket rule” that extends Endangered Species Act (ESA) protections to threatened species. Think of the key species that have already been protected: the bald eagle--our national symbol--the California condor, and many more.

The blanket rule has long been one of the most effective and efficient tools for conserving wildlife at risk of extinction. By automatically applying core ESA protections to newly listed threatened species—unless tailored exceptions are clearly justified—the rule provides immediate safeguards at the most critical moment in a species’ decline. The proposed change would dismantle this proven framework and replace it with a slower, weaker, and more discretionary system that leaves threatened species vulnerable to harm.

Threatened species, by definition, are on a trajectory toward endangerment. Delaying or withholding protections until species-specific rules are developed ignores ecological reality and invites further decline. In addition, with staff at regulatory agencies already stripped down by this administration, the process would be even slower. Many species cannot withstand years of regulatory gaps while bespoke 4(d) rules are drafted, litigated, or delayed. The proposed change would institutionalize these gaps and increase the likelihood that threatened species will become endangered—directly contradicting the ESA’s preventive purpose.

The ESA is one of the world’s most effective conservation laws, and it has protected 99% of the species listed under it. Our nation’s species are part of our national heritage and should be protected for future generations. This rule, plus the gutting of staff and budget at US Fish and Wildlife Service and other conservation agencies, is an attempt to allow our nation’s valuable natural resources to be plundered by already-wealthy corporations. In essence, it is selling off our future to the wealthy few.

The proposal also undermines the ESA’s science-based foundation. Conservation biology overwhelmingly demonstrates that early, comprehensive protection is far more effective and less costly than emergency measures after populations collapse. Weakening the blanket rule prioritizes administrative convenience and political discretion over the best available science and sound conservation outcomes.
In addition, the proposed change reduces regulatory clarity and public accountability. The blanket rule provides clear, predictable protections for species, land managers, and the public. Replacing it with ad hoc, species-by-species determinations increases uncertainty, invites inconsistency, and heightens the risk of political interference in decisions that should be guided by science and statutory mandate.

At a time of accelerating biodiversity loss, habitat destruction, and climate change, weakening protections for threatened species is both irresponsible and contrary to Congress’s clear intent in enacting the ESA: to conserve species before they reach the brink of extinction.
For these reasons, I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to withdraw the proposed 2025 change to the blanket rule and retain strong, default ESA protections for threatened species.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
Sincerely,
Carol Blaney, MA Botany, MS Resource Interpretation
United States

My name is Janet Raddatz from Plymouth, WI. I am retired from the food industry with a background in biology and microbiology. In retirement I am a WI Master Naturalist and active in many citizen science projects related to birds and other wildlife.
I am opposed to the proposed changes in Section 4(d), related to the “blanket rule”. This piece of the regulation provides broad protections against hunting and commercialization of threatened species. The current regulation already allows for species-specific regulations to be created.
Rescinding the “blanket rule” could push more species to extinction due to the delay to create species-specific regulations and ultimately requiring more time, resources, and funds to bring a species back from the brink of extinction. Listed species are currently experiencing a more prolonged listing process caused by budgetary constraints. Funding for the ESA has not kept pace with species listing and inadequate funding increases time to listing (Puckett, Kesler, & Greenwald, 2016). Do not make this process take even longer by requiring threatened species to each have a specific regulation.
The “blanket rule” focuses on preventing threatened species becoming endangered. Research consistently shows that proactive, early protection of threatened species is significantly more cost-effective and successful than reactive, emergency measures - Drechsler et al. (2011) and Eberhand et al. 2022.
Additionally, tailored rulemaking is a large burden that takes time and resources. With this administration’s focus on government efficiency, it makes no sense to require a more complex, time consuming, and costly process.
Again, I am opposed to the overall weakening of one of our strongest laws for preventing species extinction. The ESA is credited with saving 99% of the species it protects, as cited by the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service.
Diverse ecosystems are more resistant to changes like climate change, disease outbreaks, and natural disasters. Loss of diversity results in higher costs to humans due to the loss of the ecosystem services that are lost as species go extinct. Keep the ESA strong for the long-term health of humans and all life on earth.

text:
To whom it may concern,

I’m writing to strongly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. These changes would severely weaken the ESA's ability to prevent extinctions, aid in species recovery, and protect critical ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA aims to act before species reach critical levels. The 4(d) rule is based on decades of scientific evidence showing that early protections lower recovery costs and prevent declines. Removing these protections would lead to unnecessary delays, needing individual rulemaking, and would expose vulnerable species to avoidable harm. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive goals and will incur greater ecological and financial costs over time.

2. Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic factors would undermine scientific objectivity and delay necessary protections. Limiting the consideration of future threats disregards current conservation science, which acknowledges that issues like habitat loss and climate change threaten species long before population declines become evident. Weakening these criteria makes timely protection less probable and increases the risk of preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is the leading driver of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations undermines recovery efforts, while narrowing the definition of “harm” would undo years of legal and scientific precedent. Habitat destruction often indirectly harms wildlife, a fact long recognized by the law. Weakening these definitions would reduce the effectiveness of inter-agency consultations and increase biological risks.

4. Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections

Creating loopholes for agencies to bypass ESA protections contradicts the ESA’s purpose. These would encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and move decision-making away from science-based analysis, disproportionately impacting species like the Florida panther and gray wolves.

The cumulative impact of these proposals

Collectively, these changes would:
• weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation,
• delay or block necessary protections,
• reduce habitat conservation,
• increase extinction risk,
• undermine inter-agency cooperation,
• and raise long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has historically prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct, proving its effectiveness through science, precaution, and early action. These proposals conflict with those principles.

In a time of global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should strengthen—not weaken—its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

For these reasons, I urge the withdrawal of all four proposed rule changes and retaining the current regulatory framework, grounded in science and successful implementation.

Thank you for taking the time to read this comment.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and urge you to oppose any attempts to weaken and dismantle it.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Gulbranson, Andrea

text:
As a Floridian who loves her state, and all of the endangered and precious animals living in it, I am against the proposed revisions to Section 4 of the Endangered Species Act.

These changes would weaken how species are listed and how critical habitat is protected, putting already vulnerable wildlife at even greater risk.

Species like the West Indian manatee depend on healthy habitats, especially seagrass meadows, for food and survival. Manatees have already experienced severe population losses due to declining water quality, habitat destruction, and seagrass die-offs, including the recent mass starvation events in Florida, where more than 1,100 manatees died in a single year.

Weakening ESA protections now ignores clear scientific evidence and undermines one of our most important tools for preventing extinction.
The proposed rule would make it easier to delay or deny habitat protections by narrowing how
"foreseeable future" and "occupied habitat" are defined, even when those areas are biologically essential. Seasonal feeding grounds, migration corridors, and warm-water refuges could be excluded, leaving them vulnerable to development, pollution, and degradation.

Protecting manatees also means protecting the seagrass ecosystems that support clean water, fisheries, and coastal resilience for people. The systems are all connected, and what we do to Wildlife eventually affects us.

I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service to reject this proposal and uphold the Endangered Species Act's science-based mission to conserve wildlife and the habitats we all depend on. Thank you.

text:
Public Comments Processing Attn: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044 U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service MS: PRB/3W 5275 Leesburg Pike Falls Church, VA 22041-3803
Re: Support for ESA Regulatory Reforms to Restore Balance and Respect Local Rights
To the Secretary of the Interior and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service:
My name is Lisa Mott, and I am writing to you from Siskiyou County, California. Our county is ground zero for the conflict between federal regulation and rural livelihoods. We live daily with the consequences of an Endangered Species Act (ESA) that has drifted far from its original intent, morphing into a tool for controlling land and water at the expense of the people who steward it.
I am writing to express my strong support for the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations. These changes are a breath of fresh air. They signal a return to common sense, lawful governance, and a recognition that human communities are part of the environment, not an enemy to be removed from it.
Restoring the "Environmental Baseline" (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044)
For too long, federal agencies have treated every consultation as an opportunity to rewrite history. They act as if our farms, ranches, and infrastructure are new "impacts" that must be mitigated, rather than the established baseline of our community.
Respecting Existing Rights: I strongly endorse the proposal to clarify that the Environmental Baseline includes ongoing, non-discretionary activities and existing infrastructure. Our water rights and our presence on this land predate the ESA. We should not be forced to justify our existence in every new biological opinion. This change protects our property rights and restores the proper scope of federal review.
Prioritizing Reality Over Models
In Siskiyou County, we see the river and the land every day. We know when the fish are running and when the creeks are dry. Yet, we are constantly regulated by computer models from distant offices that contradict what we see with our own eyes.
Empirical Data: I support the move to prioritize empirical, on-the-ground data over theoretical modeling. If a model says a fish needs water in a place where nature never put it, the model is wrong, not the farmer. We need a regulatory system that values local knowledge and physical reality over outcome-oriented science.
Counting the Cost (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048)
The federal government has a moral obligation to consider the human cost of its actions.
Economic Impacts: I applaud the proposal to mandate the consideration of economic impacts when designating Critical Habitat. When you designate vast swathes of our county as critical habitat, you aren't just drawing lines on a map; you are devaluing property, restricting land use, and strangling our local economy. It is time for the Service to weigh these costs honestly and to use its discretion to exclude areas where the economic damage outweighs the conservation benefit.
Conclusion
The people of Siskiyou County are tired of being treated as collateral damage in a federal regulatory experiment. We want healthy forests and rivers, but we also want a vibrant economy and a future for our children. These proposed rules offer a path to balance. They respect the law, they respect science, and most importantly, they respect the people who live here.
I urge you to finalize these rules immediately.
Sincerely,
Lisa Mott Siskiyou County, California

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed changes that would eliminate the long-standing policy of providing threatened species with the same protections as endangered species unless and until a species-specific rule is finalized.

For decades, the blanket 4(d) rule has been one of the most effective and efficient tools under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). It ensures that newly listed threatened species receive immediate, meaningful protection at the moment they are recognized as being at risk. This policy reflects the scientific reality that species listed as “threatened” are often already in serious decline and can quickly become endangered without swift action.

Removing this automatic protection would create a dangerous gap between listing a species as threatened and the development of a species-specific rule. During this gap, threatened species would be left vulnerable to habitat destruction, exploitation, and other harmful activities that the ESA was specifically designed to prevent. Developing species-specific rules can take years, and many species simply do not have the time to wait.

Eliminating immediate protections means:

*Threatened species could be legally harmed, captured, or killed.

*Critical habitat could be degraded or destroyed with little to no restriction.

*Conservation efforts would be delayed precisely when action is most urgent.

*Agencies would face increased administrative burdens while species face increased risk of extinction.

The blanket rule is not an overreach; it is a commonsense safeguard. It provides clarity, consistency, and efficiency, while ensuring that conservation keeps pace with biological reality rather than bureaucratic timelines. Weakening this protection undermines the purpose of the ESA and places already vulnerable species at even greater risk.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of the most successful conservation laws in the world because it prioritizes prevention and timely action. Rolling back the blanket 4(d) rule would reverse decades of progress and jeopardize countless species that depend on immediate protection to survive.

Species-specific rules are not a substitute for broad baseline protections; they are slow resource intensive and increase political pressure from industries seeking exemptions.

The ESA requires decisions to be based on the best available science, not executive orders aimed at weakening environmental safeguards.

I urge you to reject this proposed change and maintain full, automatic protections for threatened species. Our nation’s wildlife cannot afford delays, loopholes, or weakened safeguards.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment and for considering the long-term consequences of this decision.

text:
I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposal by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service to narrow the definition of “harm” under the Endangered Species Act (ESA), thereby removing protections for wildlife from habitat destruction.

For decades, the ESA has correctly recognized that “harm” includes significant habitat modification or degradation that kills or injures wildlife by impairing essential behaviors such as breeding, feeding, or sheltering. This interpretation has been essential to the success of the Act and to the survival of numerous species whose decline is driven primarily by habitat loss rather than direct killing.

Eliminating habitat destruction from the definition of “harm” would severely weaken the ESA’s effectiveness. Activities such as gillnetting, overfishing, seabed blasting and mining, logging, wetland drainage, and coastal and inland development could proceed even when they foreseeably degrade or eliminate the ecosystems endangered species depend upon. Protecting species without protecting their habitats is biologically unsound and contrary to the intent of the law.

This proposal also raises serious concerns about intergenerational responsibility. Young people are frequently urged by political leaders to invest in the future - by building families, contributing to society, and supporting long-term economic stability. If we are expected to make those commitments, we must also be able to offer future generations a meaningful perspective: one in which they inherit functioning ecosystems, intact wildlife populations, and a natural world worth experiencing, not landscapes depleted and polluted beyond recovery.

The Endangered Species Act has long represented a societal promise that we will not sacrifice irreplaceable species and ecosystems for short-term gain. Weakening the definition of “harm” breaks that promise and shifts the consequences of today’s decisions onto those who will have no say in them.

I urge the Services to withdraw this proposal and retain the long-standing, science-based definition of “harm” that includes habitat destruction. Preserving ecosystems is not an optional addition to species protection—it is the foundation of it.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment and for considering the long-term public interest in this rulemaking.

Respectfully, Elina

title: Comment from Bodner, Kelly

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.
