title: Comment from Plants, Sophie

text:
I respectfully oppose the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s proposal to remove the section 4(d) “blanket rule” for newly listed threatened species under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

The ESA was designed as a preventive conservation statute, intended to protect species before they reach the point of extinction. The 4(d) blanket rule provides immediate, baseline protections for threatened species at a critical stage of decline, consistent with Congress’s intent to conserve both imperiled species and the ecosystems upon which they depend (16 U.S.C. § 1531(b)).

Eliminating the blanket rule would delay protections while species-specific rules are developed, increasing biological risk during a period when populations are especially vulnerable. Scientific evidence consistently shows that even short-term increases in habitat loss, disturbance, or mortality can push small or declining populations past recovery thresholds.

The blanket rule also ensures consistent protection against “take,” including harm through habitat modification—widely recognized as the primary driver of species decline. Replacing this default protection with species-specific rules risks inconsistent, weakened, or delayed habitat safeguards, contrary to the best available science. As a conservation biologist, delaying protections causes massive alarm for biodiversity and species protections. With potentially thousands of species being lost annually, we are already in a crisis and the rescinding of the blanket rule will only exasperate this crisis causing irrevocable harm to our plant and human health.

Additionally, removing the blanket rule would increase administrative burden, regulatory uncertainty, and litigation risk, diverting limited agency resources away from recovery planning and implementation. The Service has not demonstrated that this change would improve conservation outcomes; evidence instead suggests that earlier and stronger protections reduce the likelihood that threatened species will require endangered listing.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to withdraw this proposal and retain the 4(d) blanket rule as an essential, science-based safeguard for threatened species.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

As a concerned citizen, I oppose the proposed rule changes listed in FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029.

While reading through the summary, I came across several concerning statements that lead me to believe these proposed changes are not in the best interests of Americans or our wildlife. The blanket rule requires a species listed as threatened receive immediately section 9 prohibitions. The proposed rule change lists two reasons for why the blanket rule should be removed: 1. implementation of a species specific set of protections 2. “a tailored approach reduces burdens on the Service and regulated entities alike”. This EO “directed all departments and agencies to review agency actions that impose an undue burden on the identification, development, or use of domestic energy resources, and, as appropriate and consistent with applicable law, consider suspending, revising, or rescinding agency actions that conflict with this national objective.” By using this specific EO to uphold the proposed rule changes listed in the summary, I am led to believe that the changes are not made for better protections of wildlife, but rather for the protections of corporate interests.

Protections must be put in place for threatened and endangered species expeditiously. These proposed rule changes would cause unnecessary delays in protections, causing potentially furthering destruction of the species. Therefore, I reject this proposed rule change entirely.

Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
MP

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I am firmly against the proposal to remove the longstanding blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. This rule has crucially extended key protections to threatened species right from their listing, unless specific rules were crafted for them. Eliminating this safeguard will lead to significant delays in providing necessary conservation measures, directly opposing the precautionary aims of the ESA.

Congress created the “endangered” and “threatened” categories to enable early intervention, not to postpone protections until the situation becomes dire. The blanket rule is an effective and scientifically valid approach that prevents threats from escalating as tailored management plans are developed. Without this rule, newly threatened species will be left vulnerable, increasing the risk of them moving toward endangered status or extinction.

Furthermore, there is no evidence that the blanket rule causes regulatory issues inconsistent with the ESA or APA. In fact, removing it will increase administrative burdens by requiring numerous species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying critical protections.

For these reasons, I strongly urge the Service to maintain the blanket 4(d) rule, ensuring timely and scientific protection for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Budzynski, Douglas

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

text: As a citizen of the United States of America, I am making a public comment on the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act of 1973.  I do not agree with proposed change by the current federal administration to the E.S.A. concerning threatened species protections. I do not agree that the "blanket rule" should be eliminated. I do not agree that species-specific rules, tailored to each species under threat of extinction, should be required to include species living in critical habitats in the protections offered by the E.S.A. Although the proposed change would only apply to species added in the future to the protected classes under the E.S.A., current critical habitat destruction as seen in the death of warm-water coral reefs by rising water temperatures, gives ample evidence of the need for "blanket rules" to protect all species dependent on critical habitats for survival. It does not make rationale sense to create undue burden for already resource-constrained government employees to create species-specific rules. The current federal administration has made significant budget cuts to agencies that protect and manage wildlife and their habitats, like the National Park Agency. The addition of labor and cost-intensive legislative hurdles will critically impair government employees from performing their jobs and ensuring the E.S.A. is implemented effectively. This proposed revision to the E.S.A. would be an unfair roadblock to the continued work which has created measurable increases in endangered species populations. Difficult-to-access critical habitats, i.e. certain bodies of water and forests, make locating and identifying species highly improbable for workers implementing E.S.A. standards. Species need protection under the E.S.A. from environmental factors that destroy habitat, such as oil drilling and mining operations. The proposed legislation makes it easier to pollute habitats which will kill many species, by focusing on loopholes found in species-specific protections. title: Comment from Lutz, Natalie

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

Although I am not familiar with every legal term in the proposed rule, the core issue is clear: weakening or “deregulating” the Endangered Species Act (ESA) undermines the very purpose for which it was enacted. The ESA was designed to prevent the irreversible loss of species and to ensure that federal actions do not push vulnerable wildlife closer to extinction. That purpose has not changed, and the need for strong protections remains as urgent as ever.

Decades of research demonstrate that the ESA’s existing consultation and critical habitat requirements are effective. A quantitative analysis published in *BioScience* found that species with designated critical habitat for at least two years were **more than twice as likely to show improving population trends** compared to species without such protections. Additional reviews of ESA implementation show that many listed species experience measurable recovery when the law’s safeguards are fully applied, underscoring the importance of maintaining strong regulatory standards.

Weakening consultation requirements would reduce accountability, increase the risk of harm to already‑vulnerable species, and contradict the statute’s intent as established by Congress. The evidence consistently shows that strong, science‑based oversight is essential for species recovery.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw the proposed rule and maintain the current consultation standards to ensure continued compliance with the ESA and to uphold the expectations of the American public.

Sincerely,

Tina L. Turner

The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.
Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.
The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.
title: Comment from Randolph, Gail

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposed rule "FWS-HQ-2025-0044 ESA Proposals Regarding Interagency Consultation". My comments are based upon my formal training in Wildlife Biology at the University of Montana, where I received undergraduate and graduate degrees in Wildlife Biology. My comments are also based upon my 41 years of professional positions in wildlife research and management, with 37 of those years spent as a professional Wildlife Biologist and Tribal Wildlife Program Manager on the 1.33 million-acre Flathead Indian Reservation in western Montana. IN that capacity, I worked closely with the U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) on a wide variety of issues related to listing of Threatened and Endangered Species conservation.

This proposed regulation would remove the "blanket rule" that provides the same protections for Threatened Species as for Endangered Species under the Endangered Species Act (ESA), including the prohibition of "take", as defined by the ESA for all future listings. I oppose this revision because it is not based upon any scientific evaluation and is not consistent with the ESA. The USFWS already has a substantial backlog of species listing needs that are precluded by funding and staffing issues. The costs of delayed listing and proper conservation is extinction. Estimates of 650 species extinctions because of late conservation measures have been cited by the National Wildlife Federation. Removing the blanket rule for threatened species delays essential protections due to a bad assumption that species analysis will be adequate for conservation needs. The delays that this will cost will very certainly cause additional extinctions. This effort is a blatant effort to pander to economic interests at the expense of the very conservation mission that the USWS is tasked with. This proposed regulation does nothing to support conservation of threatened or endangered species or the habitat that they rely on for their existence. It also fails to provide any assurance of any modicum of transparency in the rationale or the steps that the USFWS might take with regard to any listing or the agency's management efforts in staving off extinction of species that rightfully should be considered for Endangered Species status. I repeat that this proposal fails to be consistent with the intent of the ESA, and taken in conjunction with the other three proposed revision of ESA regulations currently under consideration (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039 and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048), these actions will undoubtedly lead to serious and irrecoverable declines in the status of rare species, in the long-term viability of those species, and the very likely extinction of many of those species.

I strongly oppose this revision, and I respectfully request that it be dropped for consideration.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Capstick, Hilary

text:
I strongly oppose proposals to weaken the Endangered Species Act by excluding habitat damage from the definition of “take” and by incorporating financial considerations into listing and protection decisions.

Habitat loss and degradation are the primary drivers of species decline and extinction worldwide. In the United States, the vast majority of species listed under the Endangered Species Act are threatened not primarily by direct killing, but by the destruction, fragmentation, or degradation of the habitats they require to survive and reproduce. Treating habitat damage as separate from harm to species ignores decades of ecological science and undermines the biological reality that species cannot persist without suitable habitat.

Redefining “take” to exclude habitat destruction would significantly weaken the Act’s core protective mechanism. It would allow activities that eliminate breeding grounds, migration corridors, food sources, and shelter to proceed unchecked, even when the foreseeable outcome is population decline or local extinction. This approach creates a loophole that permits indirect but inevitable harm while claiming compliance with the law’s intent.

I am also deeply concerned about proposals to factor financial or economic analysis into decisions about whether a species warrants protection. The Endangered Species Act was intentionally designed to be science-based. Its purpose is to prevent extinction, not to weigh the short-term economic convenience of human activities against a species’ right to exist. Introducing financial considerations at this stage shifts the Act away from objective biological assessment and toward subjective, politically influenced decision-making.

Short-term economic calculations consistently underestimate long-term costs. Healthy ecosystems provide essential services including clean water, pollination, flood mitigation, soil stability, and climate resilience. The loss of species and habitats ultimately imposes far greater economic and social costs than proactive conservation ever does. Once species are gone and ecosystems are degraded, restoration is often impossible.

Weakening habitat protections and prioritizing near-term financial interests represents poor stewardship of our shared natural heritage. It transfers irreversible environmental damage to future generations, who will bear the consequences without having had a voice in these decisions. Conservation laws exist precisely because markets and short-term incentives fail to account for long-term ecological stability.

The Endangered Species Act has been one of the most effective conservation tools in the world, preventing the extinction of the vast majority of species listed under it. Its success is rooted in its clear, science-driven mandate. Diluting that mandate by ignoring habitat loss and prioritizing economic considerations will erode its effectiveness and accelerate biodiversity loss at a time when ecosystems are already under unprecedented stress.

I urge decision-makers to uphold the original intent of the Endangered Species Act by maintaining strong habitat protections, preserving a science-based decision framework, and rejecting changes that would lead to short-sighted outcomes with irreversible environmental consequences.

title: Comment from Meissner , Jamie

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.
The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.
title: Comment from Dewar, Alyson

text:
The ESA’s success depends on early, consistent protection. The longstanding “blanket rule” for threatened species ensures immediate safeguards unless science supports a tailored alternative. This approach minimizes regulatory delay and economic uncertainty.

Approximately 99% of listed species have avoided extinction under the ESA (USFWS), a stark contrast with global trends, where monitored vertebrate wildlife populations have declined by nearly 70% since 1970 (WWF, Living Planet Report 2024). Delays in protection increase the likelihood that species decline further, requiring more expensive recovery efforts or resulting in permanent loss of ecosystem services.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule introduces gaps in protection while species-specific rules are developed, increasing biological risk and regulatory unpredictability. From an economic perspective, this creates uncertainty for landowners, agencies, and industries by prolonging unresolved conservation status and increasing litigation risk.

Retaining the blanket 4(d) rule provides clarity, consistency, and cost control while allowing flexibility where science supports it. I urge the Service to preserve this framework.

I oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. title: Comment from Davis, Virginia

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Baker, Donna

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

title: Comment from Scheib, John

text:
The proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act present important considerations, as they may impact on the law's original objectives. These modifications could potentially increase the risks faced by threatened and endangered wildlife, potentially making them more susceptible to extinction. It is essential to evaluate the possible consequences of modifying existing protections for vulnerable species. Only about 15% of the known species in the United States have been studied in sufficient detail to determine whether or not they are imperiled. The four proposals outlined in this amendment intend to repeal well-established conservation regulations that have proven effective and have enjoyed significant American Citizen support over time.

Eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" raises concerns about the potential decline of threatened species populations. This rule serves as a critical conservation mechanism within the Endangered Species Act (ESA), providing a clear legal framework that has proven effective in promoting species recovery. Currently, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has the authority to create specific special rules for each listed species, allowing for tailored management and exemptions as needed. Without the blanket 4(d) rule, the agency would face increased challenges, as it would be required to develop individual 4(d) rules for each threatened species, thereby complicating compliance with ESA regulations. The proposed changes will bring more burden to the agency (USFWS) that has loss tremendous amount of staff and funding.
Proposed changes to regulations on critical habitats may impact how the U.S. lists endangered species and designates their vital habitats. Under the new rule, some habitats on federal lands could lose protection if development is deemed more beneficial. This could lead to increased energy, transportation, grazing, logging, and other commercial activities in areas essential for the survival of threatened species. As we face ongoing habitat loss from development, pollution, and climate change, this regulation poses a serious threat to many species that exist only in small remnants of their historic ranges, raising concerns about the recovery of at-risk species.
Introducing economic factors in species listing decisions undermines the ESA's core principle of based purely on scientific and commercial data. This shift could lead to inappropriate cost-benefit analyses, politicizing a process that should remain strictly science-based.
The effort to streamline the interagency consultation process with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service could undermine their vital role in assessing the impacts of development on endangered species. This push is misleading; in effect, it may mean that federal agencies responsible for enforcing the Endangered Species Act will have minimal, if any, say in evaluating the potential harm a project could inflict on listed species.
Recent revisions proposed in the Endangered Species Act (ESA) mirror troubling policies from the initial Trump administration, undermining effective wildlife conservation and defying public opinion. Since its inception, 99 percent of species protected under the ESA have avoided extinction, underscoring its vital role. A 2025 national poll found that over 80 percent of Americans from various political backgrounds support the ESA, emphasizing the importance of protecting endangered species for future generations.
Currently, a significant number of imperiled species are found in only tiny remnants of their historical habitats, which were once vast and thriving. Despite the decades that have passed since the Endangered Species Act (ESA) was established, the urgency for effective species protection remains as critical as ever. In fact, the escalating posed by urban development and the impacts of climate change heighten the need for robust implementation and diligent enforcement of the ESA. Now, more than at any other point in time, we must prioritize the preservation of our vulnerable wildlife and their ecosystems.
I urge the appropriate agencies and this federal administration to reconsider and retract these proposed regulatory changes. It is crucial for the well-being of America's endangered wildlife and the essential habitats they rely on for survival. These adjustments pose significant threats to the delicate balance of our ecosystems, potentially exacerbating the decline of vulnerable species and disrupting the intricate relationships within their habitats. Protecting these natural environments is not only vital for the species that inhabit them but also is the natural capital for the current U.S. Citizens and future generations as well as for the overall health of our planet.

title: Comment from Gage, kyle

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. Protecting Wildlife: Why the Endangered Species Act MattersEmpty heading
Posted December 15, 2025 by David Jenike
The Endangered Species Act, enacted in 1973, currently serves as the most effective wildlife legislation ever enacted to preserve biodiversity. Species such as the California condor, gray wolf, American alligator, and bald eagle are all here today as a result of this legislation. Here at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, we work to conserve numerous species listed under the Endangered Species Act, including Mexican wolves, Polar bear, sihek, Texas ocelots, and American burying beetles.

One of the most concerning proposals would eliminate the Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule.” This rule automatically provides basic protections for species listed as threatened , such as prohibitions on harming or harassing that wildlife, while species-specific rules are developed.

Without the blanket rule, newly listed species could go months or even years without specific protections, and this delaying of safeguards increases the risk of further population decline.

Public input matters. You can make your voice heard by submitting a comment opposing the removal of the blanket rule. Submit a Public Comment by Monday, December 22nd

Use the sample message below or create your own. Even a short comment makes a difference! When we share why we care about wildlife and wild places, we help decision-makers understand the impact of these changes.

As someone who cares deeply about wildlife and the future of our planet, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule that would undermine wildlife protections granted by the Endangered Species Act. This change would go against decades of conservation progress and weaken one of our nation’s most important environmental laws.

The “blanket rule” gives essential baseline protection to threatened species until species-specific safeguards can be established. Removing the “blanket rule” may make them more vulnerable to extinction, in opposition to the intent of this legislation.

I urge you to uphold the mission of the Endangered Species Act and maintain the “blanket rule.” Our wildlife, wild places, and future generations are counting on it.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Salinas, Meredith

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) is a profoundly successful tool at achieving the bipartisan goal of preventing extinction of wildlife, fish and plant species and the destruction of their habitats. Akin to an emergency room, the ESA is an effective response to ecological crises that aids species on their road to recovery. That success, however, is predicated on strong implementing regulations. The four proposed changes to those regulations would undermine the law's efficacy. Each must be rejected.

I oppose any and all efforts to weaken the Endangered Species Act and urge you to withdraw the proposed rule changes. The proposed rules:

Deprive species newly listed as “threatened” with extinction of protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take,” even when that take is amongst the greatest drivers of the species' decline. This makes no sense. We must address each of the threats that are causing imperilment.

Fail to protect important habitat that was historically occupied but is currently unoccupied by narrowing the definition of critical habitat. Protecting historical habitat is often vital to the recovery of imperiled species. The goal of the ESA is to get species out of the proverbial emergency room, which inherently necessitates increasing populations and restoring species to historic range. Failing to protect historically occupied habitat fundamentally undermines the effectiveness of the law. Holistic approaches to species recovery is essential in the face of climate change impacts to habitat.

Reduce cooperation between and amongst agencies tasked with implementing the ESA. This change would make it easier for agencies to green light destructive extractive proposals even when doing so will clearly further imperil listed species. Again, this proposed change undermines the letter and intent of the ESA.

Allow consideration of economics in decisions of whether to protect species the science clearly shows are at risk of extinction, in direct violation of the ESA. The ESA clearly states that preventing extinction is the priority, and the Supreme Court has agreed. This regulatory change flips that on its head and allows short term potential lost profits to trump species safeguards.

Each of these proposed changes undermines the letter and intent of the ESA, a law passed with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed by a Republican President who stated upon doing so: “[T]his legislation provides the Federal Government with needed authority to protect an irreplaceable part of our national heritage—threatened wildlife. Nothing is more priceless and more worthy of preservation than the rich array of animal life with which our country has been blessed. This important measure grants the Government both the authority to make early identification of endangered species and the means to act quickly and thoroughly to save them from extinction.” - President Nixon.

It is a betrayal of this legacy to undermine the efficacy of the law by making these ill advised regulatory changes. We all should be proud of the effectiveness of the ESA. Take for example, the bald eagle, our national bird and symbol of the USA - without the ESA's protections, we likely would have lost this iconic species. Now, Americans across the country are able to see bald eagles flying free.

As we confront the dual biodiversity-loss and climate crises, weakening the ESA is not only short sighted, it is dangerous. Protecting species and their habitats benefits humans as well - the law safeguards forest habitats that clean the air, watersheds and wetlands that filter drinking water for millions of Americans, pollinators that support our food supply, and estuaries that mitigate flooding. Humans are not isolated from the impacts of increasingly severe weather events and damaged ecosystems that are the symptoms of a rapidly changing climate.

Please rescind the four proposed rules (docket numbers: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048-0001, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029-0001, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044-0001, and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039-0001) undermining the Endangered Species Act for the benefit of wildlife, fish, plants and humans alike.

Sincerely,
Michelle Casey

Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text: Removing the blanket rule is a clear attack on living organisms and shows this administration does not respect the living. So many species will be put at risk without the blanket rule as they will now be susceptible to unregulated hunting, harm, and habitat destruction. This rule change will irreparably destroy our planet, leading to humanitarian and economic disaster. Without a healthy and biodiverse planet, humans cannot survive. We rely on other species for our air, food, clean water, building materials, etc. By removing the blanket rule, we will be on the fast-track to destroying society. For an administration so concerned about the economy, they make changes that will harm the economy in the short and long-term.
title: Comment from Edmondson, Asha

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text: Please do not get rid of the Endangered Species Act - we need to do all we can to protect these animals!
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:
Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.
Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.
Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.
Respectfully submitted,
title: Comment from gale, jennifer

text: Please do not allow the EPA blanket rule. It has helped to protect and preserve so many of our endangered species. We should not be declaring a war on protecting endangered species!!
title: Comment from Brimm, David

text:
I have a degree in Zoology and have worked in the field and teaching college biology since the 90s. An Executive Order titled “Unleashing American Energy,” that directs all departments and agencies to "review agency actions that impose an undue burden on the identification, development, or use of domestic energy resources, and, as appropriate and consistent with applicable law, consider suspending, revising, or rescinding agency actions that conflict with this national objective” is blatantly stating its real purpose. The EPA was started in 1970 to protect the environment. The Fish and Wildlife Service is supposed to protect wildlife and plants. That is why these departments were created, and for good reason. Human activity focused on profit does not care about the health or safety of the planet and its inhabitants, and this became painfully clear by the 60s, when pollution became a global crisis. Air, water, and land were so polluted that people, plants, and animals were sickened and dying because of the loss of habitat and the disregard for the what remained. Laws and departments were put in place with the purpose of tackling the issues of clean air, clean water, and healthy environments. The relatively clean air and water that we enjoy today are a result of decades of hard work by thousands of regular people, government employees, and other public servants.

A proposed rule such as this one is attempting to make changes in current regulations that would allow the “unleashing of American energy” by opening up opportunities for logging, mining, and drilling in what has been protected lands, or to relax pollution standards so these activities can take place. When considering the prospects of making money, it’s important to remember that healthy ecosystems provide an estimated 150 TRILLION dollars in "services" every year, for free. They provide flood and polllution control; keep our air and water clean; control our climate; provide recreation/tourism and economic support for the local businesses that come with that recreation/tourism; give us the oxygen we breathe; allow for pollination of food plants (with wild bees accounting for 190 billion dollars alone); increased property value; and that's just off the top of my head. These "services" are priceless, truly- we can't survive without them. Disrupting the health of our ecosystems any more than we have already threatens our health and well-being, leading to greater environmental and medical crises.

Do not pass this proposed rule. It’s short-sighted and will cause more problems in the future that will take additional decades to address, if they even can be. Once you destroy an ecosystem, it may or may not be able to be remediated, and it definitely takes a long time. Let’s not go backwards- wasn’t it bad enough in the 60s? We will be much better off by conserving the land and species that we have now, and restoring degraded land than we will by chipping away at the hard-won, long fought-for protections that we have right now. Profits and money-making are less important than the health of our only planet.

Sincerely,
Marni Fylling-Ellison
