title: Comment from Swango, Kathleen

text:
I strongly disapprove of the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act and further disapprove of the proposed exceptions to enforcing the act based on economic considerations. Nothing in this proposed rule document proves that ESA compliance poses an "undue burden" on the energy industry or developers. Indeed, according to an analysis posted by Bariteco within the past month, the top 20 mining companies in the United States are showing profits in the tens and hundreds of millions, and billions, of dollars. And while an article published this past October on CNBC's website describes the oil industry as needing to reduce costs to protect shareholders' payouts, this lag is coming in contrast with the "monster profits" of previous years ("Big Oil forced to confront some tough choices as ‘monster profits’ fade into memory"). The data out there does not suggest these are downtrodden industries in need of cuts in order to survive and thrive, particularly at the expense of our ever-more-vulnerable environment. In fact, I would argue that because these are industries that use more of the earth's resources than other industries, they have an ethical duty to give back more. And because they utilize more resources, they have more capacity for destruction, whether intentional or no. So how, exactly, is it an "undue burden" to require said industries to devise and enact practices responsible to vulnerable wildlife, when they already have a recent history of record profits and potential to destroy ecosystems beyond repair? From where I stand, it is absolutely not a burden, let alone an undue one.

I would argue that environmental health is an investment rather than a burden. Human life, both rich and poor, depends upon biodiversity in flora and fauna. Once upon a time, back in 2022, the U. S. Department of State recognized the worldwide crisis in biodiversity-- "The global decline of nature represents an existential threat to livelihoods, food systems, and health"-- and produced a comprehensive plan to help tackle the problem. It is a shame we have fallen so far away from those priorities and into a space where the Trump administration deregulates pesticides, disperses the independent wing of the EPA that researches the effects of chemicals, proposes declassifying essential wetlands, handles 'climate change alarmism' by removing access to scientific research, etc., and now this. Narrowing the scope of the Endangered Species Act and proposing exceptions for abiding by it will absolutely exacerbate the biodiversity crisis. Leaving "threatened" species without protection while the U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service takes years to establish individual guidelines leaves said species on the path to extinction and likely other species newly vulnerable. That is a pattern that will continue. Additionally, tossing aside considerations for habitat historically occupied by threatened and endangered species gives said species fewer places to grow in their numbers-- an ideal and goal of the ESA. Habitat loss is a main driver for species extinction. As extreme weather events become more common and alter landscapes, habitat protection becomes more-- not less-- important. Honestly, this proposal is disappointing. After everything we have witnessed in declining nature in recent decades, I should, here in the year of Our Lord 2025, be commenting on a document that seeks to strengthen the ESA, not weaken it.
title: Comment from Davis, Katherine

text:
I am OPPOSED TO the proposed revisions of the ESA. Having worked with species of greatest conservation need for 30 years, I see the proposed changes effectively gutting the intention and efficacy of the ESA. Trying to protect endangered species without protecting their habitats, including adjacent suitable yet unoccupied habitats and those that serve to connect occupied habitats, will sadly be a lost cause. In light of climate change, larger buffers and more flexibility to protect suitable habitats are needed. While making allowances for economic and national security considerations seems, at face value, to be logical exceptions to the rule, we have already seen the current administration stretch and abuse these types of considerations. Allowing exclusions on federal land is just a way of bulldozing a path to destroy protected land that belong to US citizens. Eliminating recovery as a justification for delisting cripples the very purpose of the ESA.
I ask that the USFWS and the Dept. of the Interior reject the proposed revisions and instead continue to protect our native wildlife as mandated by the ESA.
title: Comment from Colt, Tammy

text:
I vehemently oppose the rule changes for threatened species protection under 50 CFR part 17; section 4(d). This change relies on the assumption that different species in our ecosystem are disconnected from each other and inherently unaffected by changes to other species. That is unequivocally false. The blanket rule has been instrumental in fast-tracking the protection of threatened species all across the United States. Scientific research (Taylor et al., 2005) shows that immediate protections for a species upon listing heavily reduces the risk of extinction for said species. So what could be the possible reason for removing this rule? Furthermore, it is well known that habitat loss and climate change significantly heighten the vulnerability of threatened species, and the blanket rule is key in helping to defend against these environmental disasters.
I hope that these changes are not made permanent, but rather changes are made that strengthen existing regulations and protect our environment.

Martin F. J. Taylor, Kieran F. Suckling, Jeffrey J. Rachlinski, The Effectiveness of the
Endangered Species Act: A Quantitative Analysis, BioScience, Volume 55, Issue 4, April
2005, Pages 360–367,

text: Please don’t do anything that would weaken our current Endangered Species Act including the blanket rule which offers protections for newly threatened species until specific rules for them can be developed and enacted. These threatened species are like canaries in a coal mine and need our protection as they warn us of possible harm or threats to our environment. Do not let human choices lead to their endangerment or possible destruction. Thank you for your sincere concern and consideration.
title: Comment from Biery, Donna

text:
I write to strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design. These long delays could result in species extinction, contrary to the entire point of the ESA.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction. The best time to support species recovery is early, before species crater on the cusp of extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections. This is not efficiency, and it is not good for species recovery, the regulated community, or agency staff alike.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species, as required by the text of the statute.
title: Comment from Auerbach, Adam

text: The current blanket rule coverage for threatened species protections are barely adequate. There has been absolutely no evidence provided by this administration to justify removing current minimal protections. This rule change is without scientific support, not in the best interest of the American public, nor is it conducive to local economies. Leave blanket rules in place to provide these minimal protective measures to threatened species.

Quoting WWF new article, Washington, DC (October 9, 2024) -"There has been a catastrophic 73% decline in the average size of monitored wildlife populations* in just 50 years (1970-2020), according to World Wildlife Fund‘s (WWF) Living Planet Report 2024. The report warns that parts of our planet are approaching dangerous tipping points driven by the combination of nature loss and climate change which pose grave threats to humanity.

The Living Planet Index, provided by the Zoological Society of London (ZSL), tracks almost 35,000 vertebrate populations of 5,495 species from 1970-2020. The steepest decline is in freshwater populations (85%), followed by terrestrial (69%) and then marine (56%).

Habitat loss and degradation and overharvesting, driven primarily by our global food system are the dominant threats to wildlife populations around the world, followed by invasive species, disease and climate change."

Given that habitat loss is the primary driver in this massive loss of wildlife already underway, we need to be protecting MORE habitat, not creating impossible loopholes and criteria that developers can use to destroy more habitat, and make it more difficult for species to be listed and protected. In an interconnected ecosystem, it's unwise/self-defeating to destroy the life support system on which one's society depends, aside from the general morality of the issue. If we are "stewards" of this planet, then we have a responsibility to care for and protect life, not destroy it as it suites us for profit. The economic considerations should not be a factor in this case because there is an inherent flaw in the economic calculations- that is that they assume that infinite growth is possible and desirable in a finite and fragile planet. Seeking and striving for balance is sustainable, smash, grab and hoard is not. We have a responsibility to future generations as well. Our wildlife is precious and so is the land- let's start acting and legislating that way. I have a degree in Environmental Studies and one in Anthropology, and the disaster of climate change is a clear and present danger, as is the loss of biodiversity. I believe those in charge are well aware, but foolishly place more value on short term gains. That needs to end, and the people are realizing it. What is "unduly burdensome" is trying to explain to children why their leaders aren't looking out for their interests, and watching the animals you love suffer and disappear for greed, or trying to survive on an unhealthy, increasingly poisoned planet. 99% of species protected by the ESA are still living and with us- it works, and it could be better and stronger still. Let's start doing the right thing for a change, valuing and protecting what is precious and innocent instead of exploiting it? Thank you for your attention to this matter.

text:
I am writing to firmly oppose all four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations.
4. Opening new loopholes allowing agencies to bypass ESA protections

Creating mechanisms for agencies to override ESA protections contradicts the ESA’s purpose. These loopholes incentivize exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decision-making from scientific to project-based analysis. This would disproportionately affect species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, accelerating their decline.

The cumulative impact of these proposals would weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation, delay or block species protections, reduce habitat conservation, increase extinction risks, undermine cooperation, and raise recovery costs for taxpayers. title: Comment from Z, Veronica

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act, as I have worked to conserve the country's rarest wildlife for 40 years. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage. It works, when we want it to work and allow it to work.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on few and overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically based on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process. Do economic analysis but keep it separate from the decision on which species are listed.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including not designating unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA. The ESA is an elegant law that is well written and litigation has clarified many aspects of that law. Section 7 does not need to be weakened.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Because of my serious concern for manatees, I ask you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

I am against these proposed regulations because they would destroy the available protections to manatees and all other vulnerable species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Lauren

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
My name is Dr. Reilly Jackson and I am a wildlife research biologist that has trained and worked in the US for over ten years. I have worked on numerous studies focused on actions to support the recovery of Threatened and Endangered species listed under the Endangered Species Act (ESSA). Today, I am writing to express my opposition to the federal government’s proposal to rescind the “blanket rule” within the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

This proposed change is at odds with the current best available science. The “blanket rule” currently provides Threatened species with the baseline protections afforded Endangered species, at a time when immediate protections are needed before species-specific rules can be developed. The “blanket rule” requires that Threatened species are protected from “take” which includes activities that degrade habitat or directly injure or kill individuals, both of which are major events that negatively impact the ability for species to recover (Fahrig 1997; Hanski 2011; Fardila et al. 2017; Chase el al. 2020, Smith-Hicks and Morrison 2021). Until the FWS develops a rule to quickly generate specific 4d regulations for recently listed Threatened species, the “blanket rule” is required to ensure that Threatened species do not move closer to extinction until they can be thoroughly assessed. Currently, the FWS does not have the time, funds, or capacity to quickly generate rules for Threatened species following the best available science given the recent staffing reductions incited by the Trump Administration. You can either have a work force that is fully staffed and funded to create rules quickly, or remove initial blanket protections. You cannot have both without opening the federal government to hundreds of potential lawsuits.

Cheers,
Reilly Jackson

Sources cited:

Chase, J. M., Blowes, S. A., Knight, T. M., Gerstner, K., & May, F. (2020). Ecosystem decay exacerbates biodiversity loss with habitat loss. Nature, 584(7820), 238-243.

Fahrig, L. (1997). Relative effects of habitat loss and fragmentation on population extinction. The Journal of wildlife management, 603-610.

Fardila, D., Kelly, L. T., Moore, J. L., & McCarthy, M. A. (2017). A systematic review reveals changes in where and how we have studied habitat loss and fragmentation over 20 years. Biological Conservation, 212, 130-138.

Hanski, I. (2011). Habitat loss, the dynamics of biodiversity, and a perspective on conservation. Ambio, 40(3), 248-255

Smith-Hicks, K.N., & Morrison, M. (2021). Factors Associated with Listing Decisions under the U.S. Endangered
Species Act. Environmental Management.

text:
I am writing to specifically address FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029 (Section 4(d)), which proposes the elimination of the "blanket rule" used by the Fish and Wildlife Service in forming plans to protect species. The proposal seeks to tailor the species protection plans specifically to each species to ensure that those that do not require certain protections are not unnecessarily restricted. In theory, this seems like a good idea. No solution works for every problem, and different species have different conservation needs. I fear, however, that in practice this change would be used to justify the stripping of protections from certain species without considering their importance in the context of the food web. The decline of a species population that the Fish and Wildlife Service deems healthy could have negative effects that resound through trophic levels, affecting endangered species. The idea of trophic levels, articulated by Robert Paine with an experiment on starfish in the Pacific Northwest, showed the significance of species at every level of the food chain. When the predatory Pisaster ochraceus was removed from tidal pools, the pools' biodiversity reduced drastically (https://nautil.us/the-ecologist-who-threw-starfish-235831/). This lent concrete evidence to the Green World Hypothesis, which introduced the idea of top-down or predator driven population control, and also showed that the decline of certain species can have adverse and unknown effects on the populations of other species in their ecosystems. I see the failure to address the complexities of conservation efforts as a significant oversight of this proposal,
The most apparent issue to me in this proposal is that conservation efforts will inevitably take a hit from the relaxing of the blanket rule. A Langhammer et. al meta-analysis on the positive impacts of conservation concluded that, "it will require substantially scaled-up funding and commitment for implementation of demonstrably effective conservation interventions—a real transformational change—which in turn depends on increased political will and investment" (https://www-science-org.proxy.library.georgetown.edu/doi/10.1126/science.adj6598). It seems that this proposal will accomplish the opposite, disinvesting from key protections for ecosystems. Although it may mean less funding is required, I believe it will hamstring the Fish and Wildlife Service's conservation efforts and have detrimental long-term effects on the ecological health and biodiversity of environments under the care of United States. If the Fish and Wildlife Service chooses to pursue this policy change, I would advise that it carefully consider each case, accounting for both a species' individual needs and the broader implications on other species with which it interacts. I also urge the Fish and Wildlife Service to reevaluate whether this measure will truly help the agency achieve its conservation goals, or if it is a political move to appease the current administration.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I strongly oppose the proposed revisions to Section 4 of the Endangered Species Act. text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Brittany Andrias

Raimondo to situations that are not analogous.

There is no justification for these revisions of the Endangered Species Act. They act against recovery of species by reducing protection of critical habitat and promote commercial and economic considerations over science.

The reason the US imports oil is because many refineries are old and configured for specific grades of oil not produced in the US. Increasing production will not make the US oil and gas independent or significantly lower the cost of gasoline. Demand for oil fluctuates and influences prices. Renewable solar and wind energy are cheaper to produce than fossil fuels and cause much less environmental damage. Recently, renewable energy supplied more than half of the United States’ electricity generation for an entire month.

Do not implement these proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from D, Anja

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Walker, Jennifer

text:
Dear Sirs,
As someone residing in California and frequently witnessing the repercussions of habitat loss, I am deeply concerned about the potential weakening of protections for endangered species. I firmly believe in the importance of science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in our country.
The Endangered Species Act stands as a testament to the effectiveness of a system that prioritizes science and the public interest over political pressure or economic influence. It empowers science to guide us in understanding the needs of species for survival, while values play a crucial role in determining whether we choose to protect them. However, the proposed changes to the rule would shift decision-making away from both science and values, potentially jeopardizing the survival of imperiled species.
One significant concern is the proposed classification rule (Section 4), which aims to remove automatic protections from newly listed species. This move places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even commence. Newly listed species could be left unprotected while recovery efforts are delayed, exacerbating their vulnerability.
Another concern lies in the proposed 4(d) rule (Section 4(d)), which seeks to eliminate the blanket rule for threatened species. This change would result in inconsistent protections and delays in recovery for imperiled wildlife, especially at a time when they require the fullest protection possible.
Furthermore, the proposed exclusion rule (Section 4(b)(2)) narrows the criteria for critical habitat exclusions. This could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, posing a threat to ecosystem health. If economic interests are given precedence over essential habitat, entire ecosystems, not just individual species, are at risk.
Lastly, the proposed consultation rule (Section 7) limits federal review of agency actions. This limitation would facilitate the progress of destructive projects without fully assessing their impacts on endangered wildlife.

In light of these concerns, it is crucial to emphasize the importance of the democratic process and accountability in environmental conservation. Federal oversight serves as a vital check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily influenced by industry interests. These rollbacks reduce public accountability, especially at a time when a significant portion of the American population supports stronger environmental conservation protections.
A democratic, science-based process requires transparency and meaningful review to ensure that the best interests of endangered species are prioritized.
I strongly urge the agency to rescind these proposed rules and uphold the ESA’s robust, science-based protections.
Please prioritize strengthening, rather than weakening, federal safeguards to ensure that states and industry are held accountable for protecting endangered wildlife.
I respectfully request that you adhere to the ESA’s original intent: to prevent extinction and guarantee that future generations will inherit thriving and resilient ecosystems.

PLEASE STOP THIS BILL FROM PASSING!!
Stephanie Holzner, Ph.D.

title: Comment from Blakely, Natasha

text:
Public Comment (Oppose weakening; strengthen the ESA)

To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service:

I’m submitting this comment regarding FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039 to strongly oppose any weakening of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge the Service to maintain and strengthen its full protections.

The ESA remains one of our nation’s most effective, science-based conservation laws. It protects wildlife before extinction becomes inevitable, and it protects the habitat and ecological processes species need to survive and recover. Weakening the ESA shifts costs onto the public, future landowners, and future taxpayers—while increasing the risk of irreversible biodiversity loss.

I urge the Service to reject changes that reduce protections, including anything that would:
•Narrow or weaken the definition of “harm” or “take,” or make enforcement harder in practice
•Undercut critical habitat designations or make them optional, delayed, or overly restricted
•Create broad exemptions that weaken Section 7 consultation (the federal duty to avoid jeopardy and adverse modification)
•Allow political or economic pressure to override best available science in listing, delisting, or recovery decisions
•Reduce consideration of cumulative impacts (habitat fragmentation, development pressure, water withdrawals, pollution, invasive species, and climate-driven stressors)

Instead, the Service should strengthen implementation by:
1.Keeping decisions grounded in best available science and transparent, peer-informed analysis
2.Protecting habitat up front (because preventing habitat loss is cheaper and more effective than trying to rebuild populations later)
3.Ensuring consistent, enforceable standards across regions so protections do not depend on where a species lives
4.Improving recovery planning with measurable benchmarks, clear timelines, and robust monitoring
5.Investing in proactive conservation and partnerships (landowner incentives, habitat connectivity, watershed restoration), while maintaining strong backstop protections when voluntary measures aren’t enough
6.Strengthening capacity for timely consultation and permitting by adequately staffing field offices—so projects can move forward without sacrificing species survival

The ESA is not just about protecting individual species—it’s about protecting the natural systems that support clean water, healthy soils, flood protection, fisheries, outdoor recreation, and local economies. Once species and habitats are gone, we don’t get them back.

Please maintain the ESA’s full intent and authority and reject any proposal that weakens protections for listed species or their habitat. I respectfully urge the Service to move in the opposite direction: strengthen habitat safeguards, improve recovery outcomes, and ensure the Act remains durable, enforceable, and science-driven.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Sincerely,
Chris

As a supporter of wildlife conservation, I oppose this proposed rule change and urge the agency to withdraw it.

The "blanket rule" provides a uniform baseline of protections for threatened species. Rescinding this rule and promulgating species-specific rules for every newly listed threatened species will introduce inconsistency, confusion, and unnecessary complexity for landowners and agencies who must follow these regulations. Also, the additional labor required to develop species-specific rules instead of automatically applying the blanket rules will strain already limited resources.

Otherwise, a delay in issuing the species-specific protection rules would mean that threatened species would go without any protections for that time, hindering their recovery and potentially furthering their decline.
title: Comment from Garrett, Zoe

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

To whomever it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to
urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.
The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium
works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine
wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through
education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation
programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and
coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these
remarkable species.

Working as an aquarium instructor, I see firsthand how different species spark joy in the hearts of children of all ages, inspiring kids to help their communities and grow in their understanding of the world around them. The thought of future children only knowing these species as parts of the past, is not only a major disservice to them, but also a startling look into what would happen if the protections under the ESA are weakened. Protecting wildlife protects us and our connection to our planet. We are not separate from these ecosystems, and a failure to protect species and their habitats will echo in our lives.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for
delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation
requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken
safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase
stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic
Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving
these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and
for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the
ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Jennifer Vela
Instructor, Mystic Aquarium

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,

I am writing to formally oppose the proposed removal of the “blanket rule” that automatically extends core Endangered Species Act protections to newly listed threatened species.

As a freshman in college, I just completed an intensive ten-week course in fish and wildlife conservation. I recognize that my knowledge is small compared to the federal, state, and local biologists who work under chronic underfunding to maintain ecological balance for food production, public use, and biodiversity. That is precisely why I believe we should rely on proven, science-based safeguards rather than weaken them.
Threatened species exist at a critical tipping point (they are the step before endangered). Removing default protections while waiting for species-specific rules introduces unnecessary delays during the most vulnerable stage of decline. In ecological terms, population losses are not linear—small disruptions can push a species past recovery thresholds. Habitat loss, fragmentation, and disturbance do not pause while regulatory details are finalized.

The Endangered Species Act has a strong track record. Since 1973, over 93 percent of ESA-listed species have stable or increasing populations. Fifty-six species have been downlisted from endangered to threatened, and the U.S. Dept. of Interior says 54 species are no longer on the list due to recovery! These successes occurred under a framework that prioritized precaution, not regulatory gaps. Weakening protections at the threatened stage risks reversing decades of progress and forcing species back into endangered status.

Fish illustrate this risk clearly. Fish are currently the taxonomic group most threatened with extinction in the United States. Salmon, including Chinook salmon in the Columbia River Basin, depend on intact freshwater habitat long before they ever reach the ocean. Disturbances across entire watersheds—habitat loss due to development, road building, nonintentional logging —affect water temperature, sediment, and flow. These impacts accumulate silently and quickly. A delay in protections is not neutral; it actively increases extinction risk.
This proposal also undermines the Public Trust Doctrine, a foundational legal principle established by the Supreme Court in 1841. Wildlife is not owned by private interests; it is held in trust by the government for present and future generations. Removing automatic protections shifts risk away from short-term economic actors and onto the public—especially future Americans who will inherit diminished ecosystems.

I also learned that we are living through a sixth mass extinction event, driven largely by habitat loss. Species cannot adapt or reproduce fast enough when protections are weakened during periods of environmental stress. Precaution is not anti-progress; it is responsible stewardship.

History shows that extinction is not a hypothetical risk. More than 99 percent of all species that have ever lived on Earth are now extinct. Of the roughly one percent of species still alive today, scientists have formally identified only about 1.2 to 1.8 million—leaving an estimated 86 percent of land species and 91 percent of marine species still undocumented. In other words, we are making permanent decisions about species we barely understand or don’t even know. Weakening protections at the threatened stage risks repeating an “oops” moment in human history—acting too late and realizing only afterward what has been lost. The Endangered Species Act exists to ensure we act as stewards, not predators, in our relationship with the natural world.
Aldo Leopold, known as the father of wildlife management, argued that conservation is not opposed to progress, but a different form of progress—one rooted in ethics and restraint rather than short-term efficiency. Removing the blanket rule moves us backward from that ethic. He also said conservation succeeds only when people truly want it and support it through their collective will, not merely through laws or economic incentives, ultimately resting on the ethical will of society. The public response to this and other ESA proposals suggests that such will is not lacking. What is often scarce is not concern, but the time allowed for it to be expressed.

I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule for threatened species. It provides continuity, clarity, and protection at the exact moment species need it most.

Respectfully,
Jennifer Puccio

text:
I am writing to support keeping the blanket 4(d) rule of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) because it currently provides immediate, automatic protections for threatened species during their most vulnerable period. The proposed rule would let economic interests override science-based decisions about endangered species protection.

Delaying protections is unacceptable and it puts the lives of endangered and threatened species at risk. Species recovery and climate resilience would be weakened.
Decades of conservation gains for endangered and threatened species could be reversed.

More than 99% of species listed under the ESA have been saved or are on the path to recovery. Bald eagles, gray whales, and more have been brought back from the edge of extinction because of the ESA.

All species have an intrinsic value and should be protected. It is necessary to protect those parts of the Earth that are still in their natural state.

Humans are just one of several million species yet their activities, especially animal farming and agriculture, take up over 50% of the land area of the Earth, whereas all the other species are left with the remainder, which is getting smaller as humans continue to take land

Although species have been going extinct ever since life on Earth appeared hundreds of millions of years ago, human activities are causing them to happen hundreds of times faster than they would go extinct due to natural causes.

I lived in Australia from 1970 to 1992. Since I do not wish to be part of a country in which the large-scale destruction of natural habitats, logging of forests and extermination of native animals continue to take place and which is the result of genocide against First Nations Peoples, I returned to my country of origin, Croatia, and encourage others to do the same. Please keep the native species of the United States of America protected by not weakening the Endangered Species Act.
title: Comment from Validzic, Simon

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Joe Goldufsky, Joe

text:
RETAIN THE BLANKET 4d rule.
GROUND THINGS IN SCIENCE.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am vehemently opposed to any of the proposed rule changes to the Endangered Species Act. Section 4d: blanket rule protects threatened species by giving them the same level of protection as endangered species. The blanket rule protections prevent "take" of listed species which including harming, hunting, wounding, killing, and trapping these species. By ending blanket protections, then threatened species could only get protection status when species-specific rules are created. The blanket rule is important for threatened species for immediate protection. It would take too long to wait for species-specific rules to be implemented. By the time that they are created and implemented, a lot of damage will have already been done to the different threatened species. Whereas with the blanket protection, those threatened species will already be protected. The blanket rule will ensure that threatened species won't fall victim to regulatory gaps or influence of special-interest groups.

Proposed Rule: Section 7: Interagency consultation: Section 7 is very crucial since it makes certain that other federal agencies don't undermine endangered or threatened species or hurt critical habitat. It requires agencies to consult with USFWS and National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) before carrying out any action that could jeopardize species’ survival and recovery and destroy or degrade critical habitat. The new proposed rules for Section 7 would limit the consultation process. It could also hurt the imperiled species and the critical habitat that imperiled species depend on. The changes to Section 7 would make it more difficult for USFWS and NMFS to prove that actions requested by other federal agencies would negatively impact listed species and critical habitat. This would exclude many indirect, cumulative, or climate-driven effects from being considered. Section 7 is vital to ensure that other agencies don't further harm wildlife through actions such as oil drilling, mining and logging. The Section 7 consultation process has been instrumental to the Act’s remarkable success in preventing the extinction of imperiled animals and plants; 99% of species listed under the Act survive today.

Proposed Rule: Section 4(b)(2): Critical Habitat exclusion rule- Inherent in the success of the Act, is the condition that economic costs not be a factor in deciding whether to protect an animal. The changes to the proposed rule for Section 4(b)(2) puts economic costs of whether to save a species or not. The new regulations call for greater emphasis on economic impact analysis, despite the law forbidding anything except science from influencing a listing decision. Science and species conservation, not politics or money interests, should steer the designation of critical habitat. Habitat loss is the main cause of extinction. This rule would weaken key habitat protection tools and drive more species towards extinction.

Proposed Rule: 50 CFR Part 424: Listing and Critical Habitat Rules: This rule would narrow the interpretation of listing requirements, and make it harder to list species as endangered or threatened and easier to delist a species. These changes would make it more challenging to grant Endangered Species Act protections for species that are impacted by climate change, drought, disease, and other effects. True endangered species conservation requires forward-thinking and future projections. Removing the ability to list species by narrowing the scope of “foreseeable future” hinders our ability to proactively save species before they hover on the brink of extinction. True recovery looks at all areas a species did roam, and could roam in the future – not just where they’re currently found.

The key to saving wildlife that are threatened and endangered is through prevention, which is through the Endangered Species Act. There is a 99% success rate in protecting at risk species from extinction. By protecting the critical habitat areas where threatened and endangered animals live, we are saving the species since habitat loss is the main threat to all species. It is immoral and inexcusable to sacrifice threatened and endangered species so that other agencies can plunder the natural resources of the land for economic gain and greed. By protecting critical habitat, we are saving the wildlife for everyone and for future generations. Whereas if we allow certain agencies to make a profit for timber, for oil, and for drilling at the cost of threatened and endangered animals' lives, only a few will profit and the rest of us will suffer. It is easier to save species through prevention by preventing other agencies from harming the critical habit than it is to allow the destruction to occur. Once the damage is done, it will push these protected species closing to the brink of extinction. It will make it harder to revive their numbers and it will take too much time and bureaucracy to implement species-specific rules.

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act (I used to work as an Endangered Species Biologist for the Federal government). It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

I urge you to uphold the intent of the Endangered Species Act and maintain the “blanket rule.” Protecting wildlife is not a political issue—it is a matter of responsibility, faith, and leaving a worthy inheritance for future generations.
