text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,

text:
Rebuttal: the government must provide stronger protection for endangered species

The recent proposals to revise the Endangered Species Act reduce protection for plants and animals instead of strengthening it. This is unacceptable in the middle of a global biodiversity crisis. The government must do more, not less, to protect species and their habitats.

Key points of the rebuttal

1. Protection for species must not be weakened
The new rules aim to remove automatic protections for “threatened” species. As a result, many species would no longer receive immediate protection once they are listed. This causes delays and increases the risk of extinction.

2. Economic interests must not set the standard
The proposal allows economic impact to be considered when designating critical habitat. This undermines the core purpose of the law, preventing extinction. Habitat protection must take priority over short term economic interests.

3. Climate change and habitat loss demand action, not retreat
Many species decline because of climate change and habitat loss. In some cases, climate threats are excluded as a basis for protection. This harms species that are already under pressure from changing climate conditions.

4. Waiting for species specific rules costs lives
The proposals require species specific rules instead of automatic protections. This approach delays action. For many species, delay means irreversible loss.

5. Public support for strong protection is clear
Scientists, conservation groups, and the public warn that these proposals weaken the law and increase extinction risk. Public consultation shows broad support for strong and effective protection of vulnerable species.

Conclusion
The government must stop lowering protection standards. It should instead:

• Restore automatic protection for threatened species.
• Put ecological science first, not economic pressure.
• Protect and restore critical habitats.
• Anticipate climate change impacts when granting protection.

Strong regulations give vulnerable species time to recover. Healthy ecosystems matter to people too.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Protecting Wildlife: Why the Endangered Species Act MattersEmpty heading
Posted December 15, 2025 by David Jenike
The Endangered Species Act, enacted in 1973, currently serves as the most effective wildlife legislation ever enacted to preserve biodiversity. Species such as the California condor, gray wolf, American alligator, and bald eagle are all here today as a result of this legislation. Here at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, we work to conserve numerous species listed under the Endangered Species Act, including Mexican wolves, Polar bear, sihek, Texas ocelots, and American burying beetles.

One of the most concerning proposals would eliminate the Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule.” This rule automatically provides basic protections for species listed as threatened , such as prohibitions on harming or harassing that wildlife, while species-specific rules are developed.

Without the blanket rule, newly listed species could go months or even years without specific protections, and this delaying of safeguards increases the risk of further population decline.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. title: Comment from Engel, Joan

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Dorer, Michael

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Judi Garnsey Andrews

Protecting Wildlife: Why the Endangered Species Act MattersEmpty heading
Posted December 15, 2025 by David Jenike
The Endangered Species Act, enacted in 1973, currently serves as the most effective wildlife legislation ever enacted to preserve biodiversity. Species such as the California condor, gray wolf, American alligator, and bald eagle are all here today as a result of this legislation. Here at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, we work to conserve numerous species listed under the Endangered Species Act, including Mexican wolves, Polar bear, sihek, Texas ocelots, and American burying beetles.

One of the most concerning proposals would eliminate the Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule.” This rule automatically provides basic protections for species listed as threatened , such as prohibitions on harming or harassing that wildlife, while species-specific rules are developed.

Without the blanket rule, newly listed species could go months or even years without specific protections, and this delaying of safeguards increases the risk of further population decline.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species. Human beings exist in a plant based ecology. Species diversity among plants is critical for all plants and thus for humans. We must respect the delicacy of plants which form the food web for all creatures.

text:
I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the blanket rule, which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The blanket rule is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

Protecting Wildlife: Why the Endangered Species Act MattersEmpty heading
Posted December 15, 2025 by David Jenike
The Endangered Species Act, enacted in 1973, currently serves as the most effective wildlife legislation ever enacted to preserve biodiversity. Species such as the California condor, gray wolf, American alligator, and bald eagle are all here today as a result of this legislation. Here at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, we work to conserve numerous species listed under the Endangered Species Act, including Mexican wolves, Polar bear, sihek, Texas ocelots, and American burying beetles.

One of the most concerning proposals would eliminate the Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule.” This rule automatically provides basic protections for species listed as threatened , such as prohibitions on harming or harassing that wildlife, while species-specific rules are developed.

Without the blanket rule, newly listed species could go months or even years without specific protections, and this delaying of safeguards increases the risk of further population decline.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

Protecting Wildlife: Why the Endangered Species Act MattersEmpty heading
Posted December 15, 2025 by David Jenike
The Endangered Species Act, enacted in 1973, currently serves as the most effective wildlife legislation ever enacted to preserve biodiversity. Species such as the California condor, gray wolf, American alligator, and bald eagle are all here today as a result of this legislation. Here at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, we work to conserve numerous species listed under the Endangered Species Act, including Mexican wolves, Polar bear, sihek, Texas ocelots, and American burying beetles.

One of the most concerning proposals would eliminate the Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule.” This rule automatically provides basic protections for species listed as threatened , such as prohibitions on harming or harassing that wildlife, while species-specific rules are developed.

Without the blanket rule, newly listed species could go months or even years without specific protections, and this delaying of safeguards increases the risk of further population decline.

(3) As proposed, removing the blanket 4(d) rule risks leaving many threatened species without protections and without any timelines or requirements for putting them in place. Furthermore, it will likely increase conflicts, which cost staff time and money for the federal government and the regulated community, while reducing conservation incentives for the species. Eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline and need to be listed as endangered, thus triggering additional restrictions on the regulated community.

The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements. This would be a waste of my taxpayer dollars.

(5) As the USFWS described in a FAQ publication about the 4(d) Rule clarification in 2024: “[I]t is more straightforward and transparent to have species-specific 4(d) rules in one place in the Code of Federal Regulations and “blanket rule” protections described in another, as the Service had done for 40 years before September 26, 2019. This approach will result in less confusion, less duplication of regulatory text in the Code of Federal Regulations, a lower risk of error in transposing regulatory text, and reduced administrative costs associated with developing and publishing a rule in the Federal Register and Code of Federal Regulations. Reinstating the “blanket rule” option also ensures there is never a lapse in threatened species protections. If the Service does not promulgate a species-specific 4(d) rule at the time of listing, the “blanket rule” protections will be in place to provide for the conservation of that threatened species. The Service is simply providing a streamlined option for protecting threatened species in situations in which they do not promulgate species-specific 4(d) rules.”

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
The F&WS thinks that the current definition of "harm" is too confusing. Quite the contrary, The definition of “harm” is the target of the Services’ proposed changes. In attempting to justify the change, the Services argue that the current definition of “harm,” which includes habitat modification, “runs contrary to the best meaning of the statutory term ‘take.’”[8] They argue that “‘the question that matters’ is whether ‘the statute authorizes the challenged agency action.’  In other words, does the agency’s regulation match the single, best meaning of the statute?”[9]

Upon its inception, the ESA was envisioned to protect the habitats of threatened and endangered species, stating, in no uncertain terms, that “[t]he purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species,” and to implement various wildlife and ecological protection treatises and conventions.[10]

The Services’ proposal does not provide an alternative definition for “harm.” Rather, the new regulatory scheme would remove the word’s nesting definition, relying solely on the statutory definition of “take.” In practice, this would likely narrow the scope of regulation to the intentional harm of a specific animal(s) in the species, rather than the broader harms of incidental habitat destruction to the holistic ecosystems and connected communities. Thus, parties seeking to engage in projects or developments that would “only” harm a species’ habitat, rather than the animal itself, need not apply for permits under the ESA. For example, imagine a condominium developer buying land that houses a grey wolf den. Because the developer would likely not intentionally trap or kill the grey wolves, even though they may bulldoze the wolves’ den, the developer would likely escape regulatory oversight under this newly proposed ESA.

By removing the definition of “harm,” the Services’ would thus render the Act effectively toothless and fail the Act’s intended purpose, its champions, and the species it protects.[11]

text:
At the outset, the Court made abundantly clear that Loper Bright does not “call into question prior cases that relied on the Chevron framework.”[21] Indeed, the Court eliminated the possibility of this type of legal distortion, clarifying explicitly that “[m]ere reliance on Chevron cannot constitute a ‘special justification’ for overruling such a holding.”[22] This is a stronger instruction than the Services recognize when they present Loper Bright as holding that “prior cases that relied on the Chevron framework . . . are still subject to statutory stare decisis.”[23] Rather, the Court actually articulated that mere invocation of Chevron does not call into question the Court’s ruling at all. The Services do not address this higher burden.
Despite the Services’ sweeping statements alluding to such a conclusion, the Court, in evaluating the definition of harm thirty years ago, went well beyond Chevron deference in upholding the definition. In doing so, the Court conducted a comprehensive examination of the purpose of the ESA, its legislative history, and the ordinary meaning of the word.

To be sure, the Court begins its decision in Sweet Home not by saying that the Secretary’s regulatory definition of “harm” is merely acceptable under Chevron. Rather, the Court begins by concluding “[t]he Act provides three reasons for preferring the Secretary’s interpretation.”[24] Preferring—not accepting, not permitting. This first sentence alone knocks the wind out of the Services’ sails.

The Court then continues to articulate these reasons, succinctly and clearly, in the remainder of the syllabus:

First, the ordinary meaning of ‘harm’ naturally encompasses habitat modification that results in actual injury or death to members of an endangered or threatened species. … Second, the ESA’s broad purpose of providing comprehensive protection for endangered and threatened species supports the reasonableness of the Secretary’s definition. … Third, the fact that Congress in 1982 authorized the Secretary to issue permits for takings that § 9(a)(1)(B) would otherwise prohibit, ‘if such taking is incidental to, and not for the purpose of, the carrying out of an otherwise lawful activity,’ § 10(a)(1)(B), strongly suggests that Congress understood § 9 to prohibit indirect as well as deliberate takings.[25]
Reading the syllabus alone renders the Services’ characterization that “Sweet Home held only that the existing regulation is a permissible reading of the ESA, not the only possible such reading” plainly false.[26]Under Loper Bright, which expressly prohibits this type of legal distortion, the Act’s current regulatory definition must stand.

text:
I. Loper Bright Does Not Justify, Let Alone Necessitate, this Change

At the outset of their proposed rulemaking, the Services claim that the Court’s decision in Loper Bright necessitates removing the regulatory definition of harm. To address this argument, a quick background of the three major cases here (Sweet Home, Chevron, and Loper Bright) is needed. After the ESA was passed in 1975, the Supreme Court heard a challenge to the regulatory definition of “harm” in Babbitt v. Sweet Home.[12] The Court upheld the regulatory definition of “harm,” in part relying on the Chevron doctrine,[13] which instructed courts to exercise deference to a federal agency’s interpretation of a statute in cases where the statutory language is ambiguous and the agency’s interpretation is reasonable. In Sweet Home, the Court applied Chevron, reasoning that it need not determine whether the definition of “take” compelled the agency definition of “harm” that included incidental habitat modification or degradation.[14] Rather, the Court reasoned that Chevron deference compelled the Court to uphold the definition as reasonable.[15] The Court, however, also engaged in its own analysis of the definition of harm, discussed further below.

Last year, the Supreme Court heard and ruled on Loper Bright,[16] deciding to overturn the longstanding Chevron doctrine. In its holding, the Court reasoned that the Administrative Procedure Act requires courts to exercise independent judgment in deciding whether an agency has acted within its statutory authority—an about-face from Chevron deference. The Services argue this holding compels the change in the ESA.

Specifically, the Services argue that Loper Bright requires regulatory rulemaking to be aligned with the single best reading of the statute, and that the definition of harm does not comport with this standard, as discussed further above.[17] The Services then address Loper Bright’s instruction to preserve stare decisis[18] and assert that their proposed rescission of the definition is still correct, as “under the then-prevailing Chevron framework, Sweet Home held only that the existing regulation is a permissible reading of the ESA, not the only possible such reading.”[19] Thus, the Services argue, “[o]ur rescission of the regulation definition on the ground that it does not reflect the best reading of the statutory text thus would not only effectuate the executive branch’s obligation to ‘take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed,’  but would also be fully consistent with Sweet Home.”[20]

This is an incorrect reading of several Supreme Court holdings.

Species like the West Indian manatee depend on healthy habitats, especially seagrass meadows, for food and survival. Manatees have already experienced severe population losses due to declining water quality, habitat destruction, and seagrass die-offs, including the recent mass starvation events in Florida, where more than 1,100 manatees died in a single year.
Weakening ESA protections now ignores clear scientific evidence and undermines one of our most important tools for preventing extinction.
The proposed rule would make it easier to delay or deny habitat protections by narrowing how "foreseeable future" and
"occupied habitat" are defined, even when those areas are biologically essential.
Seasonal feeding grounds, migration corridors, and warm-water refuges could be excluded, leaving them vulnerable to development, pollution, and degradation.
Protecting manatees also means protecting the seagrass ecosystems that support clean water, fisheries, and coastal resilience for people. I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service to reject this proposal and uphold the Endangered Species Act's science-based mission to conserve wildlife and the habitats we all depend on
title: Comment from Leto, Celia

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Even if the Services’ reading of the Court’s legal posture was accurate, reading the Act in its entirety makes clear that Congress intended to preserve habitats as well as their inhabitants. In the ESA, Congress repeatedly emphasized the importance of endangered species’ habitats—demonstrating clear congressional understanding of the ecological need to preserve habitats for the success of the species.
The Act, in Section 5, authorizes the Secretary to, in cooperation with the States, acquire land to aid in preserving such species.[29] To avoid any doubt of Congress’s intentional weight on habitat protection, Section 7 requires federal agencies to ensure that none of their activities, including the granting of licenses and permits, will jeopardize the continued existence of endangered species “or result in the destruction or adverse modification of habitat of such species which is determined by the Secretary . . . to be critical.”[30]

These provisions, though broad, cannot alone protect the habitats endangered and threatened species rely on; they are only effective against harmful actions that have yet to occur. Section 9 (Prohibited Acts) contains the teeth for regulating harmful acts already occurring—and relies on the nesting definitions of “take” and “harm.”[31] Specifically, Section 9 reads: (1) Except as provided in sections 6(g)(2) and 10 of this Act, with respect to any endangered species of fish or wildlife listed pursuant to section 4 of this Act it is unlawful for any person subject to the jurisdiction of the United States to—

…

(B) take any such species within the United States or the territorial sea of the United States.[32]

With nesting definitions, Section 9 broadly prohibits harming any species or its habitat.

Indeed, “take,” according to those drafting the Act, “is defined . . . in the broadest possible manner to include every conceivable way in which a person can ‘take’ or attempt to ‘take’ any fish or wildlife.”[33] There can be no doubt as to congressional intent: the ESA was drafted in intentionally broad terms to account for all possible harms and methods of protecting the Nation’s most vulnerable species.

text:
In a final attempt to justify the proposed narrowing of the Act, the Services adopt the canon of interpretation noscitur a sociis, which translates to “known by its associates.”[50] Roughly, the canon suggests that, in interpreting a word, the reader should define the ambiguous term in the way that would most align with the other terms in the list. Applying noscitur a sociis in this instance may suggest, as the Services claim, that the current definition of “harm” is too broad in comparison to its company in the remainder of the definition of “take.”[51] This conclusion is not supported by the literal meaning of the words, nor by the canon itself.

At the outset, reliance on noscitur a sociis is improper when the list of words does not have a clear set of criteria, such as here. Contrary to Justice Scalia’s framing of the list in his Sweet Home dissent, the definition of take does not include only narrow, direct words.[52] Rather, “the term ‘harm’ is accompanied by an assortment of words ranging from the precise and narrow ‘shoot’ to the vague and expansive ‘harass.’ ‘Harm’ is not a single elastic word among many ironclad ones but an ambiguous term surrounded by other ambiguous terms.”[53]

Additionally, there is no ground for the argument that the definition of “take” would otherwise require intent or purpose. Should a reader so find, they would be ignoring Section 11’s express provisions that a “knowing[]” action is enough to violate the Act.[54] Several of the words that accompany “harm” in the Section 3 definition of “take,” especially “harass,” “pursue,” “wound,” and “kill,” refer to actions or effects that do not require direct applications of force.[55] Thus, there is no reason to find that “harm” in this setting would necessitate intentional or direct action. Indeed, the dictionary definition of “harm” does not include the words “directly” nor “intentionally,” nor does it suggest that only direct or intentional action that leads to injury constitutes “harm.”[56] The FWS already agrees with this categorization, though, having articulated in 1981 that “harm” is not limited to “direct physical injury to an individual member of the wildlife species”—a categorization that stood for 44 years.[57]

Protecting Wildlife: Why the Endangered Species Act MattersEmpty heading
Posted December 15, 2025 by David Jenike
The Endangered Species Act, enacted in 1973, currently serves as the most effective wildlife legislation ever enacted to preserve biodiversity. Species such as the California condor, gray wolf, American alligator, and bald eagle are all here today as a result of this legislation. Here at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, we work to conserve numerous species listed under the Endangered Species Act, including Mexican wolves, Polar bear, sihek, Texas ocelots, and American burying beetles.

One of the most concerning proposals would eliminate the Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule.” This rule automatically provides basic protections for species listed as threatened , such as prohibitions on harming or harassing that wildlife, while species-specific rules are developed.

Without the blanket rule, newly listed species could go months or even years without specific protections, and this delaying of safeguards increases the risk of further population decline.

The blanket 4(d) rule is one of the fastest and most effective tools the Endangered Species Act provides to protect threatened species when they need it most. Eliminating it strips away immediate safeguards at the exact moment species are first listed and most vulnerable.

Without the blanket 4(d) rule, threatened species will no longer receive automatic protection from killing, harm, or habitat destruction! Instead, they will be forced to wait for individual, species-specific 4(d) rules. This is a very slow and resource heavy process. During that delay, very real harm can and will occur.

This change creates dangerous regulatory gaps just after listing, when populations are often small, declining, and on the brink. This is a critical time for conservation!

The proposal is not driven by science or conservation need. It traces directly back to efforts to roll back ESA protections in response to executive orders aimed at reducing perceived burdens on industry. That is not how extinction prevention should be decided.

The ESA requires decisions based on the best available science, not politics! The Fish and Wildlife Service must retain the blanket 4(d) rule to ensure threatened species receive immediate, meaningful protection and are not sacrificed to regulatory delay.
title: Comment from Lambert, Rachel

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Blanton, Cricket

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Kandy, A.J.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.
