text:
To Whom it May Concern,

I’m writing because I’m troubled by this proposal and what it could mean for the living world we’re responsible for caring for.

I was taught, both in church and in everyday life that we don’t truly own the Earth. “The earth is the Lord’s, and everything in it” (Psalm 24:1). That idea has stayed with me over the years. It reminds me that we are caretakers, not owners, and that looking after what we’ve been given is part of our responsibility. The Endangered Species Act offers a practical, secular way to live out those values by protecting life that cannot protect itself. We should not be weakening those protections at a time when so many plants and animals are already struggling.

Genesis tells us that people were placed in the garden “to work it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). I’ve always understood that word “keep” to mean protect, not neglect. When safeguards for threatened species are reduced, it feels like we’re stepping away from a God-given responsibility.

The Bible also reminds us that care for animals is a measure of our character: “The righteous care for the needs of their animals, but the kindest acts of the wicked are cruel.” (Proverbs 12:10). That doesn’t mean perfection, but to shirk this responsibility is wickedness.

Once a species is gone, it’s gone for good. That’s a heavy thing to carry, and I worry about what kind of legacy we’re leaving behind. I believe we should be erring on the side of care, humility, and caution, not rolling back protections that took decades to build.

I urge you to reconsider this proposal and choose a path that reflects responsibility and respect for the gift of creation.

Thank you for your consideration,
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am submitting this comment in strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act that would eliminate the blanket 4(d) rule for threatened species.

These changes are unduly harsh, short-sighted, and fundamentally out of step with the realities facing wildlife today. At a time when species are declining due to habitat loss, climate change, and human activity, weakening protections for threatened species is not just irresponsible, it is indefensible.

The blanket 4(d) rule exists because delay causes harm. Removing automatic protections and replacing them with slow, species-by-species rulemaking creates predictable gaps in protection during the very window when intervention is most effective. This is not a technical adjustment. It is a choice to tolerate greater risk of extinction.

Weakening protections for threatened species sends a clear message that extinction is an acceptable outcome as long as it happens slowly and out of public view.

The Endangered Species Act was never meant to wait until species are on the brink of disappearance before acting. text:
Growing up, traveling across the US to see the natural beauty of this country was a family tradition we did each year. Driving and camping in many of our National Parks gave me and my sister the chance to see stunning wildlife, and served as an incredible opportunity to learn not only about our world but our place within it. I will never forget seeing my first grizzly in Yellowstone, watching southern sea otters swimming with their pups off the California coast, and spying for bats in Mammoth Cave. These and many others are core memories, that shaped not only my childhood, but me as a person to my core. I learned and lived through these animals, and loved these experiences deeply as a child, and still love the memories as an adult. These experiences grew both my love of nature, and a sincere appreciation for the sacred wildlife of our country. My deep respect and admiration for our nation’s remarkable wildlife that grew from my childhood has stayed with me through adulthood.

In March, after many hardships, my husband and I welcomed our first child into the world, a son named Jack. He is now 9 months old, and his amazement at the simple things, like a spatula or the TV remote, do make us laugh. But it’s also what we live for now - watching our child’s world and experiences grow, and seeing the beauty he sees in the world through his little eyes.

As he grows up, I am so excited to expand his world and give him new experiences. More than anything, I’m excited to introduce him to the traditions of my childhood, and travel with him across our beautiful nation, visiting its national parks and seeing the wildlife that abounds. I cannot wait to experience his first bald eagle, or sea turtle, or monarch butterfly with him, and watch his awe and amazement at the beauty of our nation’s wildlife. To see these animals again, but through his eyes like it’s the very first time, is, in a way, a small miracle, and something we will cherish for a lifetime. Creating these core memories with my own child, and helping him grow and learn through these experiences, is so incredibly important to us.

But without protections in place for our nation’s beloved wildlife, I fear we may never get these beautiful opportunities with our child. It deeply saddens me to think my son may never experience the awesome sight of a polar bear, or the majesty of a diving humpback whale, or the fun of spotting monk seals on the beach. These animals deserve protections, not simply for the enjoyment and education of my son, but because these animals deserve to exist, and they help to create the very fabric of our diverse and beautiful nation.

As someone who cares deeply about wildlife and the future of our planet, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule that would undermine wildlife protections granted by the Endangered Species Act. This change would go against decades of conservation progress and weaken one of our nation’s most important environmental laws.

The “blanket rule” gives essential baseline protection to threatened species until species-specific safeguards can be established. Removing the “blanket rule” may make them more vulnerable to extinction, in opposition to the intent of this legislation.

I urge you to uphold the mission of the Endangered Species Act and maintain the “blanket rule.” Our wildlife, wild places, and future generations are counting on it.

Please do not throw out or ignore my comment. I am a wildlife professional, and I am appalled that we are forced to once again protect the ESA from our administration.

This rule has automatically provided threatened species with protections against harm until a tailored plan can be finalized. For decades, it has helped species like the piping plover, southern sea otter, and Florida manatee gain immediate safeguards upon listing (FWS, 2019).

We cannot afford to lose more than we have already lost.

text:
Howdy,

My name is Elisa and I am a mother to a beautiful and profoundly deaf 7 month old baby.

I am also a former teacher, university faculty administrator, and swim coach living in Las Vegas, Nevada. I do not live in a casino (yet).

I was born in Utah to a mother from rural Idaho (Sweet, for those that are lucky enough to know) and a father from the now-ashen Pasadena California. My husband is from Chicago (no really- from the South Loop!) and we met at the University of Oregon (go ducks).

After college I worked as a Road Trip Tour Guide between cities and national parks for international travelers, driving the van, cooking the dinners, and setting up camp. Since then, after many miles and misadventures, I have been to all 50 states.

All of my life, I have been on the road between some pretty special places- mountains, deserts, beaches, swamps, woods, lakes, and plains, with cities gleaming like wristwatches all across them.

I’ve been lucky to see many of God’s creatures, big and small-

a mother grizzly and her cub coming off
the mountain and onto the road right next to us in Alaska

an enormous tarantula crossing the road in West Texas

a manatee and her baby next to a random dock in the Florida Keys

a minuscule pupfish in a tiny spring-fed pond in Death Valley National Park

a rat the size of a house cat in the subways of New York

so many enormous goofy looking moose in Maine, and in Utah, and in Idaho

a cotton tailed rabbit under the El in Chicago

the tail end of a bobcat in the mountains of California

A chukar on the volcanic rocks of Haleakala National Park

An absolutely gorgeous rattle snake and a big fat chuckwalla fighting on while on my way to the local hot spring

a condor soaring in the sky above Zion National Park

A burrowing owl coughing up an ow pellet in the middle of my local construction zone

the tiniest iridescent purple of a Costa’s Hummingbird out my window.

Like many of us, and most especially children, I find that there is no greater reverence for the earth, my place in the universe, and the glory of God than glimpsing an animal in its all wildness on this great American land.

As I mentioned, my son is deaf. He will heavily rely on his sight to learn about and engage with the world.

How can I teach him about stewardship, responsibility, and respect of leaving a place better than you found it?

How can I teach him that he is a small yet vital part of this country, this world, this life?

How can I teach him, in the words of the late Rachel Carson, that those who dwell among the beauty and mysteries of the earth are never alone, or weary of life?

How can I teach him the things my parents taught me about the circle of life, about the absolute sacred magic of wild creatures in this wild world?

How can I teach him

when they are gone?

Thank you,

Elisa Marcheschi Hickey

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) is one of the most effective environmental laws ever enacted, grounded in the simple but vital principle that once a species is lost, it is gone forever. The Act provides a science-based framework to prevent extinction, protect critical habitats, and promote recovery before loss becomes irreversible. Its success is measurable: iconic species such as the bald eagle, gray wolf, and American alligator have rebounded precisely because protections were strong, enforceable, and prioritized ecological reality over short-term convenience. Weakening or removing these protections would undermine decades of proven conservation progress.

Beyond safeguarding individual species, the ESA protects entire ecosystems that humans depend on for clean water, food security, climate resilience, and economic stability. Healthy ecosystems reduce flood risk, support agriculture and fisheries, and buffer communities from climate extremes. When species decline, it is often an early warning sign of deeper environmental harm that will ultimately affect people. Allowing protections to be stripped away ignores this interconnectedness and shifts costs—environmental, economic, and public health—onto future generations.

Finally, the ESA reflects a moral and ethical responsibility to act as stewards of the natural world. Extinction caused by human activity is not inevitable; it is a choice. Maintaining strong protections affirms that economic development and conservation are not mutually exclusive, but must be balanced thoughtfully and responsibly. Rolling back the ESA would prioritize short-term gains over long-term survival—of species, ecosystems, and the benefits they provide to society as a whole.

text:
Dear Mr. Nesvik,

Point Blue Conservation Science (Point Blue) strongly opposes the four recently proposed rule changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations governing listing, threatened species protections, interagency cooperation, and critical habitat determinations and exclusions. Collectively, the proposals would weaken ESA protections and undermine species recovery and long-term conservation by reducing reliance on the best available science and increasing risk to imperiled species and habitats. The history and science are clear: protections under the ESA — especially immediate protections for newly listed species and early designation of critical habitat (both occupied and unoccupied) — are foundational to species’ survival and recovery, and conservation action under the ESA has prevented extinction for more than 99% of listed species (U.S. Department of the Interior 2016, Greenwald et al. 2019).

Point Blue is a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization with the mission to advance the conservation of birds, other wildlife, and ecosystems through science, partnerships, and outreach. Founded in 1965 as Point Reyes Bird Observatory, we have deep expertise in conducting biological and ecological scientific research for over 60 years. Point Blue staff have published over 1,000 peer-reviewed papers in scientific journals. Our research has covered a wide range of topics including bird population trends and demography (Ballard et al. 2003, Gardali et al. 2000), the effects of drought on shorebirds (Barbaree et al. 2020), foraging behavior of penguins (Lescröel et al. 2020), the impacts of environmental variables on survival of western snowy plover individuals (Stenzel et al. 2023), and specifically the importance of habitat for wildlife (Wintle et al. 2019, Shuford et al. 2019, Saracco et al. 2022, Seher et al. 2022, Iverson et al. 2023), including protected habitat (Dettling et al. 2021).

The proposed rule changes reduce agency reliance on the best available science to make important decisions about establishing protections for threatened and endangered species, weakening protections for wildlife. Given shifting environmental changes, there is currently an increased need to take a more conservative and precautionary approach to protecting endangered species. Scientific evidence supports the value of early and broad protections for listed species. Specifically, research has found that species listed for longer periods of time and species with designated critical habitat are more likely to show improvements and less likely to decline (Taylor et al. 2005).

As a well-respected and recognized expert in science related to wildlife conservation, Point Blue has published a wide range of research that consistently demonstrates the importance of habitat for threatened and endangered species as well as the importance of utilizing the best available science to inform conservation management and action. We respectfully urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rule changes and instead retain (or strengthen) the existing standards. Failure to do so would represent a step backward for biodiversity protection and put countless imperiled species at greater risk.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Sincerely,

Rose Snyder, Director of Community Engagement
Point Blue Conservation Science

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act regulations published on November 21, 2025.
The Endangered Species Act has been remarkably successful, preventing extinction for 99% of listed species and enabling recoveries such as the bald eagle and humpback whale. These proposed changes—particularly those limiting consideration of future threats like climate change in listing decisions, restricting critical habitat designations (including unoccupied areas essential for recovery), and altering interagency consultation processes—would undermine the Act's science-based approach and jeopardize vulnerable marine mammals, including several seal species.
Many seals, such as the endangered Hawaiian monk seal, bearded seal (threatened due to sea ice loss), and ringed seal (threatened), rely heavily on intact habitats like sea ice, coastal haul-outs, and foraging areas that are increasingly impacted by climate change, coastal development, and human activities. Weakening protections for critical habitat and future threats would hinder recovery efforts and increase extinction risks for these species, which are already facing significant challenges.
I urge the Services to withdraw these proposed rules and retain the current regulations that prioritize the best available science and proactive conservation. Strong implementation of the ESA is essential to protect America's wildlife heritage for future generations.
Thank you for considering my comments.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed removal of "blanket rules" and the proposed requirement of economic considerations under Section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act. I am a public lands wildlife biologist and I conduct Section 7 activities as a regular part of my job.
First, economic considerations will result in a false analysis. It is relatively simple to prepare a metric for number of jobs, salaries of jobs, and number of times money cycles in an economy. Yet, it is not possible to determine a metric for the economic benefit of the ecosystem services provided by a species listed under the Act. For example, pollination services of a listed bird, bat, or insect; clearly has qualitative economic benefit, yet it would be difficult to provide a quantitative metric. Please consider a second example: A listed species may contain within it a biochemical that can cure cancer. If this fact is unknown, an economic value analysis is impossible. Yet, even if the fact is known, the economic value analysis is still difficult. Finally, each species has an intrinsic, moral, and ethical value to its existence that is not measurable. In summary, economic considerations have no place here.
This second part of my comment is related to the proposed removal of "blanket rules." The "blanket rules" automatically provided valuable protections to threatened species that endangered species already possessed. These protections stated that is was illegal to take, import, export, sell, or transport species. In many situations, the removal of these protections could easily result in a threatened species becoming necessary for endangered status! The Administration is suggesting that species-specific 4(d) rules can provide these protections. Yet, on the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's own website, the Service states that maintaining the "blanket rules" reduces the costs of preparing and publishing specific 4(d) rules in the federal register, prevents a lapse in species protections, provides important species protections, and streamlines species protections. Please refer to this website for more information: https://www.fws.gov/node/267756. Clearly, the "blanket rules" are valuable in protecting species and are justified by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.
Thank you!

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
If the blanket rule is removed, it will deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species of automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, such as the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly, could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes their listings. This delay would expose vulnerable species to preventable harm during the period when they are most at risk.

My field experience with the federally endangered Karner blue butterfly, the declining monarch butterfly, and multiple bumblebee species underscores the consequences of withholding timely protections. These species rely on highly specific and increasingly fragmented habitats. Karner blues depend entirely on wild lupine, monarchs require milkweed for breeding and larval development, and bumblebees rely on diverse native flowering plants throughout the growing season. Even short gaps in protection can result in habitat degradation or loss that these species cannot recover from.

I urge you to withdraw this proposal. Delaying protections for threatened species leaves them vulnerable to becoming endangered, and in many cases, pushes already declining populations closer to irreversible loss.

text:
I strongly disagree with the proposal to eliminate the blanket 4(d) rule for threatened species!! This change is deeply troubling. The blanket 4(d) rule has long provided a basic level of protection for species that are already struggling to survive. Replacing it with tailored, species-by-species rules creates dangerous gaps at exactly the moment when these animals and plants need certainty and care, not delay.

Threatened species are not “safe.” They are often only one step away from becoming endangered, and that line can be crossed quickly. Waiting to design individualized protections means real harm can happen in the meantime; habitat can be destroyed, populations can decline, and recovery can become impossible. Once a species is gone, there is no second chance! This proposal also seems to assume that agencies will always have the time and resources to act quickly and perfectly. In reality, limited staffing, funding constraints, and legal challenges mean tailored rules may come too late. The blanket 4(d) rule exists precisely to prevent that kind of failure.

At its core, the Endangered Species Act is about preventing extinction, not reacting to it after the damage is done. Weakening automatic protections sends the message that we are willing to take risks with wildlife that cannot afford them and cannot speak for themselves. I care deeply about protecting our natural world, not just for today, but for future generations. I urge the agency to keep the blanket rule in place and to maintain strong, precautionary protections for all threatened species before it is too late. I stand with countless others who love and respect this planet along with all those who inhabit it. How many more innocents must be sacrificed in the name of profit and greed?

text:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The ESA has been one of the most effective conservation laws in the world precisely because it is precautionary, science-based, and focused on preventing irreversible harm to species and ecosystems.
Protecting endangered species matters deeply to me because extinction is irreversible, and laws like the ESA are among the few tools society has that place long-term ecological responsibility above short-term gain.
The proposed changes risk weakening these core protections at a time when biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation are accelerating. Once a species is pushed beyond a recovery threshold, legal or economic efficiencies become irrelevant—the loss is permanent. The ESA was explicitly designed to act before such tipping points are reached, even where scientific uncertainty remains.
Several aspects of the proposal are particularly concerning:
Erosion of precautionary decision-making.
The ESA’s strength lies in requiring protective action when credible risk is identified, not when absolute certainty is achieved. Weakening this standard increases the probability of irreversible extinction events.
Reduced protection for habitat and recovery.
Species do not survive in isolation. Any narrowing of habitat protections or recovery-focused interpretation undermines the biological reality that species persistence depends on intact, functioning ecosystems.
Increased discretion at the expense of science.
The ESA was intentionally structured to insulate species protection from short-term political or economic pressures. Shifting the balance away from independent scientific assessment risks decisions that favour expedience over long-term ecological stability.
It is also important to recognise that the ESA has consistently enjoyed strong, bipartisan public support over many decades. Its durability reflects a widely shared understanding that preventing extinction and protecting ecosystems are core societal responsibilities, not niche or partisan concerns. Weakening the Act risks undermining both its conservation effectiveness and its public legitimacy.
The ESA is not merely a regulatory tool—it is a safeguard against irreversible loss. Its success should not be measured by how easily it accommodates development, but by how effectively it prevents extinction and enables recovery. Weakening its protections now will externalise costs to future generations who will inherit diminished ecosystems and fewer options for recovery.
I urge you to withdraw or substantially revise the proposed changes and to reaffirm the original intent of the ESA: to protect imperilled species and the ecosystems upon which they depend, using the best available science and a precautionary approach.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this critical issue.
Sincerely,
Andy Hope, London, England

title: Comment from Richardson, Kyle

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.

We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.
title: Comment from Jeremy, DeAnn

text: Please don’t change the rules. Endangered species need more protection, not less.
title: Comment from D, J

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.
title: Comment from Matthews, Jamie

text:
I am submitting this comment because biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter deeply to me. Science can tell us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both.

* Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4):Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
* Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)):Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
* Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)):Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
* Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7):Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.
Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests.

Please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so states and industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife

title: Comment from Corsaro, Amir

text:
I appreciate the opportunity to submit comments on the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act regulations. These questions are of profound importance, as they directly influence how we protect the imperiled species entrusted to our care and how we fulfill our responsibilities as stewards of the land. I thank the Department for considering public input as you work to shape regulations that will guide the conservation of our nation’s natural heritage.

I submit this comment in support of a balanced, stewardship-centered approach to managing threatened species under the Endangered Species Act—one that reflects both our moral responsibility to care for the natural world and our practical obligation to pass on healthy lands and waters to future generations.

The Endangered Species Act is rooted in a simple truth: we are stewards of the land, not its owners alone. The forests, rivers, wildlife, and fisheries that sustain us are an inheritance we hold in trust. How we manage threatened species today will shape the ecological and economic options available to our children and grandchildren.

A graduated approach reflects common sense and care

I support a graduated protection framework in which newly listed threatened species receive temporary baseline protections for a defined period (such as 18–24 months), followed by species-specific, tailored protections developed through careful scientific and public review.

This approach recognizes that when a species is first listed, it is often at a point of real vulnerability. Immediate baseline protections help prevent irreversible loss while agencies do the necessary work to craft thoughtful, targeted rules. This is not overreach—it is prudence.

Periodic review reflects humility and accountability

Tailored protections should not be frozen in time. Conditions change, threats evolve, and conservation efforts sometimes succeed. For this reason, I strongly support periodic review of tailored 4(d) protections, ideally coordinated with existing five-year status reviews.

Regular review:

- Ensures protections remain aligned with real-world conditions
- Allows flexibility where recovery has occurred
- Strengthens trust that regulations are guided by evidence, not inertia

Stewardship requires not only action, but ongoing attention and care.

Weak protections often cause deeper economic harm

Experience has shown that delayed or insufficient protections frequently lead to worse economic outcomes over time.

The Klamath River salmon fishery is a clear example. Years of inadequate ecosystem protection contributed to salmon declines that devastated commercial, recreational, and tribal fisheries. These losses were felt not just by conservationists, but by families, small businesses, and entire communities. Recent restoration efforts—including dam removal and habitat protection—are now restoring salmon runs and renewing economic opportunity. This recovery demonstrates that conservation, when done right, supports livelihoods rather than undermining them.

A second example is the bald eagle, once pushed to the brink by habitat loss and pesticide use. Strong, science-based protections under the ESA allowed populations to recover to the point where the species was successfully delisted. Today, bald eagles support tourism, recreation, and a shared sense of national pride. This success story reminds us that firm protections, applied thoughtfully, can lead to both ecological and economic renewal.

Stewardship is an investment, not a burden

Healthy ecosystems provide benefits that far exceed their short-term regulatory costs—clean water, flood control, fisheries, recreation, and resilience in the face of climate change. When protections are too weak or too slow, the eventual costs of collapse, emergency intervention, and lost opportunity are far greater.

A framework that combines temporary baseline protections, tailored long-term rules, and periodic review honors both the spirit and the practical wisdom of the Endangered Species Act. It affirms that caring for the land is not an obstacle to prosperity, but a foundation for it.

Thank you for considering these comments and for your continued efforts to ensure that the Endangered Species Act reflects our shared values, responsibilities, and hope for the future.

title: Comment from Baughman, Molly

text:
I respectfully oppose the proposed rule “Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants” (Federal Register Document No. 2025 20552). The rule would eliminate the long-standing blanket 4(d) rule, which currently provides newly listed threatened species with immediate baseline protections.

Removing the blanket rule will leave threatened species unprotected during the period before species specific 4(d) rules are written, which can take YEARS. During this gap, species already identified as at risk would remain vulnerable to habitat loss, exploitation, and other threats. The Federal Register summary acknowledges that the service intends to create species specific rules for all threatened species, but crafting these rules is time and resource intensive. This delay undermines the ESA’s purpose to conserve species and the ecosystems upon which they depend.

Scientific evidence shows that many species decline rapidly once they reach threatened status, and timely intervention is critical to preventing further endangerment. The blanket 4(d) rule ensures that protections are not postponed during administrative processes. Eliminating it increases extinction risk for vulnerable species without providing corresponding conservation benefits.

For these reasons, I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule.

Thank you for considering this comment.
title: Comment from deFeijter, Enya

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.
title: Comment from Parks, Leslie

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Impact fwd llc

text: I am writing to voice my strong opposition to the proposed rule that would remove the blanket 4(d) protections for endangered species in the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The Service has not adequately demonstrated that the blanket rule creates regularly burdens and in fact, fails to acknowledge that the removal of the blanket rule will in fact create more workload for the agency. The Blanket Rule provides a set of regulations that are broadly applicable and can be enacted before species are on the brink of extinction. The Blanket Rule lies at the scientific heart of the ESA’s purpose of creating protections before it’s too late. I am a biologist and I hold a PhD in biology. I work with animals protected under the ESA including leatherback, Kemp’s ridley, loggerhead, and green sea turtles. Without the Blanket Rule, conservationists like myself would be stuck in an endless loop of administrative delays while trying to achieve species-specific protections. The Blanket rule circumvents this and allows us to extend essential safeguards automatically to threatened species. Removing this rule has no scientific basis and is against what conservation science recommends, and its removal increases the risk that populations of threatened species, like sea turtles, will further decline. The Blanket Rule is a a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA, and as such, I urge you to strengthen it, not weaken it.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am submitting this comment in opposition to the proposed changes to threatened species protections under Docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029.
Removing automatic protections for species listed as “threatened” creates a dangerous gap at precisely the point when conservation action is most effective. Without default safeguards, protections become discretionary and delayed, increasing the likelihood that species will continue declining until emergency endangered listing becomes necessary.
The longstanding “blanket rule” provided clarity, consistency, and timely protection grounded in science. Replacing it with case-by-case determinations introduces uncertainty and increases the risk that threatened species will be functionally unprotected.
The ESA was designed to prevent extinction, not respond only after recovery becomes far more costly or impossible. I urge the Service to maintain automatic baseline protections for threatened species.
title: Comment from Chancey, Erin

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) is one of the world’s most effective conservation laws, and because of this law, 99% of species listed have been saved from extinction. However, four recently proposed ESA regulations will eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species. These regressive proposed rules degrade many processes in the ESA, including how species are listed, designating critical habitat needed for species' survival, and damaging the integrity of the interagency consultation process. Manatees are particularly sensitive to these changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs, and their current listing as “threatened” under the ESA.

I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,

Andrea Feldman

text:
The Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida (the “Tribe”) submits this comment in response to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service (collectively, the “Services”) proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (“ESA”) implementing regulations published in the Federal Register on November 21, 2025, Docket Nos. FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039; FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044; FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029; FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

The Tribe has been at home in the Everglades since time immemorial. It maintains deep cultural and spiritual connections to the land, water, and wildlife of the region. Numerous species protected under the ESA—including the Florida panther (Puma concolor coryi), the wood stork (Mycteria americana), and the Everglade snail kite (Rostrhamus sociabilis plumbeus)—are culturally significant to the Tribe and play an important role in the ecosystems that encompass the Tribe’s lands and waters. The proposed regulatory changes would significantly weaken protections for these species and their habitats, contrary to the ESA’s statutory purpose and the federal government’s trust responsibilities to Tribal Nations. The Tribe therefore opposes their implementation for numerous reasons, detailed below.

First, the proposal to eliminate the longstanding “blanket rule” protections for threatened species under ESA Section 4(d) would delay or deny essential safeguards for species listed as threatened under the ESA. Requiring species-specific rules before ESA protections may apply to species listed as threatened creates regulatory gaps, during which development or other federal actions may proceed without precautionary, science-based safeguards. For Tribal communities, such delays risk harming culturally important species and the ecosystems they rely on.

Second, several of the proposed revisions introduce new limitations that discourage or preclude critical habitat designation. For example, the proposed addition to 50 C.F.R. § 424.12(1)(ii), allowing the Secretary to forgo designation where threats to habitat “stem solely from causes that cannot be addressed through management actions resulting from consultations under section 7(a)(2),” risks creating a broad exemption to critical habitat designation for actions that do not trigger section 7 consultation. If an action does not require section 7 consultation (because it is not solely tied to a federal agency, require federal authorization, or receive federal funds), important critical habitat designations will not be made, increasing the risk that listed species’ habitat, and therefore the species themselves, will be negatively impacted, in areas prone to development like south Florida. It is the Tribe’s opinion that this phrase be entirely omitted from the provision.

Third, the proposed revisions to 50 C.F.R. § 424.12(b)(2) governing designation of unoccupied critical habitat constrain the Secretary’s ability to protect listed species in ways inconsistent with the ESA’s Congressional mandate. The requirement that the Secretary determine with “reasonable certainty” that an unoccupied area will contribute to species conservation introduces a level of confidence that is unachievable in prospective conservation decisions. Species recovery often depends on protecting habitat before it is occupied, particularly in dynamic ecosystems such as the Everglades. Replacing a precautionary, science-informed approach with a de facto requirement for near certainty risks excluding areas that are essential for long-term species survival and adaptation. It is the Tribe’s opinion that “reasonable certainty” be exchanged with “likelihood.”

Fourth, these proposed regulatory changes collectively shift ESA implementation away from its preventative and recovery-oriented purpose and toward a framework that prioritizes economic and development interests. As written, the proposed regulations increase the likelihood that large-scale land use and energy development will proceed at the expense of imperiled species and Tribal interests. At a time of accelerating biodiversity loss, they weaken science-based species protections and increase the risk of irreversible harm to species and ecosystems that are culturally and spiritually significant to the Tribe, rather than strengthen them.

The Tribe respectfully requests that the Services withdraw or substantially revise its proposed regulation revisions, remove provisions that unduly restrict critical habitat designation, elevate conservation considerations rather than economic interests, and preserve science-based decision-making in ESA implementation.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Domingo-Horne, Rose

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

I am writing to express my concern that corporate interests are driving efforts to weaken the Endangered Species Act.
