title: Comment from Enneking, Stacey

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Rhea Manaattisisko

title: Comment from Huffine, Josh

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
respectfully submit this comment to express my opposition to the proposed revision that would eliminate the longstanding “blanket rule” protections for newly listed threatened species under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). This proposal would remove automatic baseline protections and require species-specific rules to be developed for each threatened species. 
The blanket rule has been an important tool to ensure that species listed as threatened receive immediate, consistent protections. Removing it creates delays and uncertainty at a time when species already face escalating threats from habitat loss, climate change, pollution, and other stressors. Many conservation advocates and scientists note that delaying protections, even for short periods, can allow vulnerable populations to decline further, undermining the preventative intent of the ESA. 
Strong habitat and species protections under the ESA benefit not only wildlife but also human communities through clean water, climate regulation, and ecosystem services that support agriculture, recreation, and long-term economic stability. Weakening these protections in favor of short-term economic considerations will not serve the American public or biodiversity well over the long term. 
I urge the Fish and Wildlife Service to retain the blanket protections for threatened species and ensure that ESA regulations remain science-based, preventative, and effective at conserving imperiled wildlife.
Thank you for considering my comments.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Posted December 15, 2025 by David Jenike
The Endangered Species Act, enacted in 1973, currently serves as the most effective wildlife legislation ever enacted to preserve biodiversity. Species such as the California condor, gray wolf, American alligator, and bald eagle are all here today as a result of this legislation. Here at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, we work to conserve numerous species listed under the Endangered Species Act, including Mexican wolves, Polar bear, sihek, Texas ocelots, and American burying beetles.

One of the most concerning proposals would eliminate the Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule.” This rule automatically provides basic protections for species listed as threatened , such as prohibitions on harming or harassing that wildlife, while species-specific rules are developed.

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029) to rescind the "blanket 4(d) rule" protections for species listed as threatened under the ESA. The proposed removal of automatic "take" prohibitions for threatened species is a dangerous step backward that undermines the primary purpose of the ESA: to prevent extinction and facilitate recovery. I urge the Service to withdraw this proposal based on the following concerns:

1. Creation of Protection Gaps. By rescinding the blanket rule, newly listed threatened species will be left without any legal protection against being killed, harmed, or harassed during the time it takes the Service to finalize a species-specific rule. Historically, these rules can take years to develop, leaving species at risk during their most critical window for recovery.

2. Increased Risk of Extinction. Threatened species are, by definition, likely to become endangered in the foreseeable future. Withdrawing the default standard of protection shifts the burden onto the agency to justify protections on a case-by-case basis, rather than keeping the focus on the biological needs of the species.

3. Inefficiency and Regulatory Uncertainty. Replacing a clear federal standard with a patchwork of species-specific rules creates confusion for landowners and industry. A lack of immediate standards will lead to increased litigation and delays, harming both the economy and the environment.

4. Misalignment with Scientific Conservation. Effective conservation relies on the precautionary principle. Removing baseline protections before a species-specific plan is in place is biologically reckless. It prioritizes administrative convenience over the scientific necessity of safeguarding biodiversity.

5. Prioritizing Political Directives Over Science. This proposal is explicitly framed as a response to Executive Order 14154, which directs agencies to prioritize energy production and economic deregulation. However, Executive Orders are political instruments, not scientific ones. Section 4 of the ESA mandates that listing and protection decisions must be based solely on the best scientific and commercial data available. By allowing a political mandate for "unleashing energy" to dictate the removal of protective standards, the Service is abdicating its statutory duty to prioritize the biological reality of species survival over political and industrial interests.

The Fish and Wildlife Service should be strengthening the ESA, not dismantling it. I strongly request that the Service maintain the blanket 4(d) rule and ensure that all threatened species receive the immediate, science-based protection they require.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this important matter.
Sincerely,
Elizabeth Silveman

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Kraynik, Andrew

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Lonneman, Claire

text:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed revisions to the regulations governing listing endangered and threatened species and designating critical habitat (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0030).

I submit these comments as an ecologist trained at the New York Botanical Garden, holding professional certificates in both Botany and as an Urban Naturalist. My daily work in Van Cortlandt Park and Central Park provides me with a front-row view of the fragility of biodiversity and the absolute necessity of robust federal protections. In my professional experience, once habitat is lost or a species' decline reaches a tipping point, "efficiency" and "economic considerations" cannot reverse the biological damage.

I urge the Service to withdraw these revisions based on the following concerns:
1. Illegally Inserting Economics into Science-Based Decisions
The proposal to remove language prohibiting the consideration of economic impacts during listing determinations is a direct violation of the ESA. Section 4 mandates that listing decisions be based solely on the best available scientific data. As a botanist, I know that a plant’s risk of extinction is determined by soil health, pollinators, and climate—not by the potential profitability of the land it occupies.

2. Undermining Climate Resilience and Habitat Recovery
The proposed "two-step" process for designating unoccupied critical habitat is devastating for recovery efforts. In urban ecosystems like those in New York City, we see firsthand how species rely on fragmented corridors and "unoccupied" spaces for migration and resilience. By restricting habitat protections to only where a species currently exists, the Service is ignoring the biological reality of climate-driven migration.

3. Narrowing the Definition of the "Foreseeable Future"
The proposed change to the definition of "foreseeable future" ignores long-range ecological modeling. In the field of botany, we must look decades ahead to understand how shifts in temperature and water tables will impact species survival. To limit protections only to what is "reasonably likely" in the short term is to ignore the primary threats of the 21st century.

4. Executive Orders Are Not Scientific Evidence
These revisions are framed as a response to Executive Order 14154 and Executive Order 14219. As a scientist, I must emphasize that Executive Orders are political instruments, not peer-reviewed data. The ESA’s success depends on its immunity to political shifts; allowing a mandate for "energy production" to dictate the threshold for extinction is an abdication of the Service’s scientific and statutory duty.

5. Creating Barriers to Full Recovery
The goal of the ESA is to return species to self-sustaining populations. Removing "recovery" as a specific consideration for delisting is short-sighted and scientifically unsound. It risks "yo-yo" listings where species are removed from the list prematurely, only to face immediate decline again.

My work in NYC’s most iconic parks has taught me that once we compromise on the science of conservation, we lose the very foundation of our natural heritage. I strongly urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain the current, science-based standards for listing and habitat protection.
Thank you for your time and for considering these professional comments.
Sincerely,

Elizabeth Silverman
title: Comment from Silverman, Elizabeth Betsy

text:
As someone who cares deeply about wildlife and the future of our planet, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule that would undermine wildlife protections granted by the Endangered Species Act. This change would go against decades of conservation progress and weaken one of our nation’s most important environmental laws.

The “blanket rule” gives essential baseline protection to threatened species until species-specific safeguards can be established. Removing the “blanket rule” may make them more vulnerable to extinction, in opposition to the intent of this legislation.

I urge you to uphold the mission of the Endangered Species Act and maintain the “blanket rule.” Our wildlife, wild places, and future generations are counting on it.

title: Comment from Lock, Josephine

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Angel Valkolilja

This allows for time for more targeted understanding and appropriate policy to be developed and implemented. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.  It is important that immediate action be taken and then adjustments can be made rather than waiting and then crafting a plan.
title: Comment from Gregg, Peter

text:
As someone who cares deeply about wildlife and the future of our planet, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule that would undermine wildlife protections granted by the Endangered Species Act. This change would go against decades of conservation progress and weaken one of our nation’s most important environmental laws.

The “blanket rule” gives essential baseline protection to threatened species until species-specific safeguards can be established. Removing the “blanket rule” may make them more vulnerable to extinction, in opposition to the intent of this legislation.

I urge you to uphold the mission of the Endangered Species Act and maintain the “blanket rule.” Our wildlife, wild places, and future generations are counting on it.
title: Comment from Trentman, Sarah

text:
One of the proposed revisions to Endangered Species Act regulations would overturn the 4(d) rule, removing blanket protections for threatened species. I am writing to express my staunch opposition to this proposal, which is all but guaranteed to delay critical protections and push threatened species to the brink of endangerment.

As you know, the “blanket rule” established under the ESA automatically prohibits all threatened species from being killed, harmed, trapped, or traded. But under the proposed rule, protection would no longer be the default. Agencies would instead be required to produce species-specific rules to establish protections, making the process of listing even one threatened species an incredibly time-intensive one.

Rather than making it increasingly difficult to establish essential protections, we should be preserving the regulations that are helping threatened species recover. Please stand up for American wildlife by leaving these blanket protections in place.

Thank you.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Basham, April

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.
title: Comment from Basom, Kathleen

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Feldman, Tim

text:
I am writing in opposition of the proposed changes to the "Blanket Rule" within the Endangered Species Act (ESA). As both a member of an environmental regulatory agency in the state of Florida and a member of the public concerned with the increasingly rapid changes to Earth's biosphere, the proposed changes deeply shake my confidence in the Federal commitment to protecting and preserving endangered species. Beyond that, my work and that of my coworkers for the state of Florida's unique and sensitive environments is threatened by the proposed changes.

In particular, the proposed removal of the "Blanket Rule" would handicap the ability of the Agency to fulfill the intent of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The proposal claims that species-specific rules are more effective in long term conservation, which is true, but the presence of the "Blanket Rule" does not prevent the implementation of species-specific rules. The "Blanket Rule" is a first line of defense, a guarantee that newly threatened species are immediately protected.

Repealing the "Blanket Rule" would result in newly identified threatened species waiting months or even years for species-specific rules to be implemented before they receive the protection they need. The speed of mass extinctions and impacts to our climate grow more rapid by the day, and under the proposed rule many specifies may die out or become unrecoverable before rules can be implemented to protect them. The "Blanket Rule" is essential for the ESA to respond to a rapidly changing world in pursuit of it's statutory purpose. Removing it is in opposition to everything the ESA stands for.

I urge the Administration to rescind the proposed revisions to the ESA. Over it's lifetime, the ESA has saved many species from extinction. To weaken it now, when threats to endangered species are only growing more significant, is to abandon the core obligation of the ESA.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

Interagency Consultation (Section 7) Rule (2025-20551)

I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.

We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.
title: Comment from Ellington, Paige

text:
I submit this comment to oppose the proposed rescission of the blanket 4(d) rule that has provided essential protections for threatened species for more than four decades.

Congress established both "endangered" and "threatened" categories to allow protective measures before species decline becomes severe. A species is "threatened" when it is "likely to become an endangered species within the foreseeable future" (16 U.S.C. § 1532(20)). This reflects Congressional recognition that waiting until a species is on the brink of extinction is biologically and economically foolish. Early intervention is more effective and less costly than emergency measures. The blanket 4(d) rule implements this intent by ensuring threatened species receive meaningful protections promptly upon listing, while the agency develops species-specific management measures as needed. Eliminating this rule creates a protection gap precisely when intervention is most valuable—before species reach crisis levels.

The proposed rescission will leave newly threatened species unprotected for months or years while species-specific 4(d) rules undergo development, review, and adoption. During this period, the very threats that prompted listing will continue unabated. For species facing habitat destruction or overexploitation, such delays can be catastrophic. The blanket rule is not merely administratively efficient—it is biologically essential. Species decline is not linear. Populations can remain stable and then collapse rapidly when critical thresholds are crossed. Allee effects reduce reproductive success at low density. Loss of genetic diversity reduces adaptive capacity. Fragmentation isolates populations. These dynamics mean the period between "threatened" and "endangered" can be brief, and opportunities for intervention can close quickly.

There is no evidence of disproportionate burden. The agency has provided no compelling evidence that the blanket 4(d) rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA's purposes. The protections it affords are precisely those Congress determined appropriate for species at risk. If particular activities are compatible with conservation of specific threatened species, the agency retains full authority to adopt species-specific rules authorizing those activities. The blanket rule does not prevent tailored approaches; it ensures baseline protection in the interim. Conversely, the proposed rescission will dramatically increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific rules—resources that could otherwise be directed toward on-the-ground conservation.

Ecosystem functions cannot wait. Many threatened species perform ecosystem functions disproportionately important relative to their abundance. Native bees pollinate wildflowers and agricultural crops—population declines compromise pollination across entire landscapes. Freshwater mussels filter water and provide habitat structure—their decline degrades water quality and disrupts aquatic food webs. Bat species control agricultural pests—their decline leads to increased pesticide use with attendant environmental consequences. When we delay protection for threatened species, we risk the ecological stability of systems they inhabit. These systems provide services human communities depend upon: clean water, pest control, pollination, nutrient cycling, and climate regulation.

The proposed rescission will delay critical protections, increase administrative burden, and undermine the ESA's preventive approach. I urge the Service to retain the blanket rule and reaffirm that threatened species warrant prompt and meaningful protection. The distinction between "threatened" and "endangered" was never meant to be a distinction between species that deserve protection and those that do not. It was meant to enable earlier, more effective intervention. When we act early, we have more options, greater likelihood of success, and lower costs. When we delay, we court failure.

The species we list as threatened are warning lights telling us that systems we depend upon are under stress. Responding to those warnings promptly is not regulatory excess—it is basic prudence. We owe it to future generations to maintain landscapes where eagles still soar, where salmon still run, where the quiet buzz of pollinators still fills summer meadows. The blanket 4(d) rule is a small but essential tool in honoring that obligation.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,

text:
Rule 0029-0001, regarding: Blanket Rule for threatened species

I strongly urge you to withdraw this proposed rule, as it runs directly counter to Congress’s original intention for the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Should this proposed rule be implemented, it would further weaken the ESA, very likely resulting in pushing already threatened species further along on their route to extinction. Delaying protections for species that are already threatened with extinction is exactly the wrong thing to do if the goal is to protect those species. With all of the many threats that so many species are encountering in recent years, including the climate crisis and habitat loss, any delay in meaningful protections allows the species to drift, or be pushed, ever closer to the point of no return. These delays are not what threatened species need. They need to be protected, and as quickly as possible.

The failure of the Trump Administration to see that in prioritizing corporate profits over a healthy and sustainable environment, it actually reduces America’s national security. Without a healthy and sustainable environment, which is inseparable from a healthy biodiversity, this country can never be secure, as we, and future generations, are all absolutely dependent upon this environment for our survival. Any further destruction of our environment ultimately threatens our national security. Beyond that, it is simply immoral to allow other species to be pushed by humans into extinction. Other species have as much right to exist as do humans.

For these reasons, I very strongly urge you to withdraw this proposed rule. Thank you for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Russell Wray

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

text:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Crone, Megan

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I submit this comment in opposition to the proposed rule that would remove the blanket rule option for protecting threatened species under Section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act. I have professional experience implementing the ESA, including service with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service working on Endangered Species Act and CITES matters. I currently lead a nature technology company focused on nature-based risk analytics.

The proposed rule would eliminate the automatic extension of endangered species protections to threatened species, requiring instead species-specific 4(d) rules for each. This change would leave newly listed threatened species vulnerable during the rulemaking process.

Section 4(d) authorizes regulations necessary for threatened species conservation. The blanket rule has provided immediate protections since shortly after the ESA's enactment in 1973, aligning with congressional intent to prevent extinction. TVA v. Hill, 437 U.S. 153 (1978), confirmed Congress intended to halt extinction trends "whatever the cost." Removing automatic protections without statutory mandate undermines this purpose.

Under FCC v. Fox Television Stations, 556 U.S. 502 (2009), and DHS v. Regents, 140 S. Ct. 1891 (2020), agencies reversing policy must provide good reasons and address reliance interests. This rule overturns a decades-old regulatory approach without new evidence, ignoring recovery programs that rely on prompt protections for threatened species.

The blanket rule enables timely conservation by ensuring no gap exists between listing and protection. Requiring species-specific rules for all newly listed threatened species could expose them to harm during an accelerating extinction crisis, particularly given current agency staffing and resource constraints.

Executive Order 14154's premise lacks empirical backing. Protections for threatened species support conservation outcomes. The 2022 National Survey of Fishing, Hunting, and Wildlife-Associated Recreation estimates wildlife-related recreation contributes approximately $395 billion annually to the U.S. economy.

I urge the Service to withdraw this proposed rule.
