text:
As a person who cares deeply about the connection between nature and the modern world, I believe that it is not our duty to destroy all that the natural world has to offer in an effort to make room for new advancements. We could begin by addressing the concerns that many people have about the proposed changes to section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act. It is both illogical and unethical to remove the “blanket rule” for all newly listed threatened species for many reasons, some of which are mentioned here.

1: This rule will increase the likelihood of “threatened” species becoming “endangered” sooner.

Removing the “blanket rule” for all threatened species means these species will only be protected by species-specific rules that would be assigned if deemed necessary. The problem with this approach is that it will both take more time for threatened species to get the protection that they need and create more room for error in this process. The US Fish and Wildlife Services agency mentions that creating a specific rule for each species increases the possibility of confusion and duplication of rules, which is more time consuming and less effective than simply giving all threatened species support. This lack of effort and efficiency could lead to more species listed as endangered, with the ESA as their last chance to make a comeback and thrive in the wild. With more species listed as endangered, more time and resources would be put into the protection of these species.

If the implication of this act takes a toll on the existing threatened or endangered species, it could possibly lead to destructive consequences on both the natural and modern world. The NOAA mentions that one extinction has the power to throw off balance in an entire ecosystem. For example, keystone species are the center of a habitat, and their decline or disappearance could destroy the balance of an ecosystem and everything living in it. The US Fish and Wildlife Services remind us that chemicals discovered in the wild have provided solutions to over ¼ of medical conditions prescribed each year. As well as this, wildlife tourism - for example, whale watching - has positively impacted the US economy in recent years. Aside from that, people also find great beauty and peace in nature and all that wildlife has to offer. The death or decline of these species would have countless influences on America as we know it.

2: The energy and financial cost of implementing species-specific rules will be greater than that of the preventative “blanket rule”.

Stripping the protective cushion that threatened species have now means the implementation of species-specific rules if deemed necessary. Constructing a specialized rule for each threatened species could make saving a species more costly according to Eric Holst, the Associate Vice President of Working Lands at the Environmental Defense Fund. As well as this, the US Fish and Wildlife Services say that providing each threatened species with a preventative cushion is easier and more cost-effective than “emergency care” for an endangered species that was previously neglected or not given preventative care to the necessary extent.

Many people believe that the “Blanket act” is a burden on energy companies because they have to be mindful about harming the habitats of not only endangered species but also threatened species. This could possibly lead to costly drawbacks in the production of these industries. Though preventative acts may seem irritating to companies wishing to expand, the negative economic impacts of removing preventative measures for many species are still feasible.

Nonetheless, I strongly believe that America’s top priorities should not be limited to those that increase the economic position of the country. We should learn to coexist with nature and respect the intricate balance of living things that we are so fortunate to be a part of.
title: Comment from Taheri, Mia

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

Comment on Blanket 4(d) Rule Removal (2025-20552)

I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

The blanket rule follows Ben Franklin's well founded logic that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. Acting early to help secure species' protection will ultimately make the process of ensuring their recovery quicker and easier. Removing the blanket protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. At that point, the decline may be unrecoverable, which seems to be the intent behind this proposed changed and the other, similar rule changes under comment currently. The blanket rule is an efficient mechanism based on scientific research. It prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted, allowing those plans to be developed correctly, without rushing. Without the blanket rule, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, where they are on the edge between a status where they could recover on their own with a little shielding or a status where they need significantly more help. The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Meacham, Timothy

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
In the 51 years since its passage, the Endangered Species Act has prevented the extinctions of 99% of its listed species, making it very successful. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the federal government to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Hicks, Jane

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Dear Sir or Madam:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to any effort to cancel or weaken the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The ESA is one of the most effective environmental protection laws in the United States, and it plays a critical role in preserving biodiversity, protecting ecosystems, and safeguarding the natural heritage that future generations depend on.

First, the Endangered Species Act is essential for preventing extinction. Species loss is irreversible, and once a species disappears, it cannot be recovered. The ESA has successfully prevented the extinction of hundreds of species by requiring science-based decision-making and timely conservation actions. Protecting endangered species is not only an ethical responsibility, but also a practical one, as healthy ecosystems support clean water, pollination, food systems, and climate stability.

Second, the ESA benefits people as well as wildlife. Many ecosystems protected under the Act help prevent flooding, reduce erosion, improve air and water quality, and support local economies through recreation, tourism, and fishing. Weakening or canceling the ESA would place these benefits at risk and could result in higher long-term economic and environmental costs.

Third, the ESA relies on scientific evidence rather than short-term political or economic pressures. This ensures that decisions are made using the best available data, which is critical when addressing complex environmental challenges. Removing these protections would undermine science-based policy and leave vulnerable species and habitats unprotected.

Finally, future generations deserve the opportunity to experience the same natural diversity that exists today. Canceling the Endangered Species Act would shift the burden of environmental damage onto those who have no voice in today’s decisions. Protecting endangered species reflects long-term responsibility, stewardship, and respect for life.
For these reasons, I urge you to maintain and fully enforce the Endangered Species Act. It remains a vital law for environmental protection, scientific integrity, and the well-being of both current and future generations.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this public comment and for considering my perspective.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

title: Comment from Hamilton , Carly

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

text:
Dear Members of Congress,

I am writing to express concern regarding the proposed rule FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, which revises regulations governing Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants under the Endangered Species Act of 1973 (ESA). In particular, changes to Section 4(d) that eliminate the long-standing “blanket rule” for threatened species would weaken conservation protections and pose serious risks to the recovery of Gray Wolves and other imperiled species nationwide.

The Section 4(d) blanket rule has historically provided automatic protections for newly listed threatened species by extending the unauthorized take prohibitions of Section 9. This approach prevents gaps in protection during vulnerable periods and ensures consistent, science-based safeguards while species-specific management rules are developed. Removing this provision would result in less predictable and less protective conservation outcomes.

For Gray Wolves, these changes would mean that upon delisting or reclassification, they would no longer automatically receive full take protections. This shift would grant states greater discretion in management decisions, including increased depredation-related shooting, expanded hunting zones, and more aggressive population control measures. Such flexibility, absent baseline federal protections, increases the risk of overexploitation, fragmented recovery, and population declines driven by short-term pressures rather than long-term ecological sustainability.

Gray Wolves remain vulnerable in much of their historical range and require coordinated, precautionary management to maintain stable, connected populations. The removal of default take protections increases the likelihood of inconsistent state-level regulations, which can undermine recovery efforts and complicate future relisting if populations decline.

The broader implications of this proposed rule extend to many other threatened species that rely on Section 4(d) protections to avoid extinction. Species such as the Mexican gray wolf, red wolf, Florida panther, grizzly bear, wolverine, manatee, sea turtles, and numerous bird and fish species have benefited from the blanket rule by receiving immediate protection from take while recovery planning proceeds. Weakening this framework increases the likelihood of regulatory gaps that expose species to harm during critical recovery phases.

The success of the Endangered Species Act has been rooted in its precautionary approach and its reliance on science-based, enforceable protections. Eliminating the Section 4(d) blanket rule departs from this foundation and risks reversing decades of conservation progress by allowing avoidable harm to threatened species.

I respectfully urge Congress to oppose changes to Section 4(d) that reduce baseline protections for threatened species. Maintaining automatic take protections is essential to ensuring consistent, effective conservation for Gray Wolves and the many other species that depend on the Endangered Species Act for survival and recovery.

Thank you for your consideration and for your continued commitment to evidence-based wildlife conservation.

This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:

title: Comment from Catt, Savannah

title: Comment from Hudson, Ben

text:
Dear Officials of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,

I am writing to formally oppose the proposed change to Section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act that would eliminate the blanket rule protections for threatened species, including wolves.

Wolves are a keystone species, meaning their presence is critical to maintaining healthy, balanced ecosystems. Their role in regulating prey populations—such as deer and elk—prevents overgrazing, protects plant diversity, and supports the health of waterways, forests, and countless other species. The removal or weakening of protections for wolves does not simply affect one species; it disrupts an entire ecological web that depends on their presence.

Threatened species rely heavily on the existing blanket 4(d) rule for immediate and meaningful protection. Eliminating this safeguard would expose wolves to increased risk during the often lengthy process of developing species-specific rules. These delays create dangerous regulatory gaps during which populations can decline rapidly, sometimes irreversibly. Wolves, in particular, have already faced decades of persecution and remain vulnerable to habitat loss, illegal killing, and political pressure.

While species-specific rules are an important long-term tool, they require substantial time, resources, and scientific review. Until those rules are finalized, the blanket 4(d) protections serve as a vital safety net—ensuring that threatened species are not subjected to harm, harassment, or exploitation simply due to administrative delays.

Broad baseline protections also help insulate wildlife conservation from special-interest influence. Without them, management decisions risk prioritizing short-term political or economic interests over sound science and long-term ecological stability. The Endangered Species Act was created to prevent exactly this kind of outcome.

On a personal level, I love wolves not only for their beauty and intelligence, but for what they represent—resilience, family bonds, balance, and the wildness that still remains in our world. Wolves belong on this landscape, not just in history books or photographs. I want future generations to grow up knowing that wolves still roam our forests, still play their vital role in nature, and still inspire the same sense of awe and respect that they inspire in me today. Protecting wolves now is a responsibility we owe to those future generations, so they can inherit a world that values coexistence over eradication.

Weakening protections for wolves ignores decades of scientific evidence demonstrating their ecological importance and undermines the very purpose of the Endangered Species Act: to prevent extinction before it is too late. Once a species is lost or pushed beyond recovery, no regulation can undo that damage.

I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule protections for threatened species and to continue prioritizing science-based, precautionary conservation measures. Wolves—and the ecosystems they support—deserve proactive protection, not reactive regret.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this important matter.

title: Comment from Baughman, Katy

text:
Comment on Listing & Critical Habitat Designation Rule (2025-20549)

I’m writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed revisions to the regulations governing species listing and critical habitat designation under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

The proposed revisions flagrantly exceed the agency’s authority in a way that is entirely impermissible. Congress could not have been clearer when it directed the Secretary to make listing determinations “solely on the basis of the best scientific and commercial data available” (16 U.S.C. § 1533(b)(1)(A)). The statute does not leave room for policy preferences, economic balancing, or administrative discretion on this question. It is a mandatory, unqualified instruction. The Supreme Court has repeatedly stated that when Congress speaks with this level of clarity, agencies are bound by that command. They do not have license to revisit or dilute it.

The proposed rule attempts to do exactly that. By introducing economic considerations into the listing process, considerations Congress expressly excluded, the agency is asserting a power it does not possess. This is not a matter of interpretation or gap-filling; it is a direct contradiction of the statutory text. An agency may not override Congress because it prefers a different policy outcome, nor may it recast a prohibited factor as a permissible one through regulatory language. Doing so would effectively amend the statute by regulation, something no agency has the authority to do.

Additionally, the proposed narrowing of critical habitat designations is inconsistent with both the statutory text and longstanding judicial interpretation. Critical habitat must include both occupied and unoccupied areas essential for conservation and recovery. By imposing new constraints on unoccupied habitat, including requirements that effectively preclude designating future climate-suitable habitat, the rule undermines the recovery mandate at the heart of the ESA. The Supreme Court has affirmed that “conservation” means recovery, not mere survival. Any rule that prevents the Service from designating habitat needed for recovery is contrary to law.

The ESA is a statute whose commands are specific. The agency does not have discretion to disregard them. These proposed revisions are in defiance of the law and should be rescinded.

text:
I care about science-informed wildlife conservation and work in wildlife advocacy to protect imperiled species before they reach the brink of extinction. The ESA is a critical law that protects species in need of conservation in the U.S., and the 4(d) rule is a key provision of this law.

The blanket 4(d) rule has been one of the most effective tools under the Endangered Species Act for nearly four decades. By extending core protections to threatened species while allowing for tailored exceptions where appropriate, it has helped prevent further decline and support recovery in a wide range of species.

Rescinding the blanket 4(d) rule would leave newly listed threatened species with little to no protection during a critical window, increasing the likelihood of continued harm while species-specific rules are delayed or weakened by political pressure. This change would incentivize classifying species as “threatened” rather than “endangered” in order to reduce regulatory obligations, undermining the integrity of the listing process.

At a time of accelerating biodiversity loss and climate disruption, threatened species need more protection, not less. Weakening the 4(d) rule reverses decades of conservation progress and introduces unnecessary risk and inconsistency into wildlife management.

I strongly urge the Service to withdraw this proposal and retain the blanket 4(d) rule, continuing the proven approach of providing immediate baseline protections while allowing case-by-case flexibility grounded in science.
title: Comment from Culbertson, Mandy

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular. When making decisions under the ESA, I urge the FWS to remember the Act’s purpose: to conserve endangered and threatened species and their ecosystems. Conservation of wildlife and their habitat should be at the forefront of every decision regarding the ESA and supported by the best available science, not overshadowed by the economic benefits of exploiting our most threatened and imperiled wildlife and ecosystems.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements. Recent and likely future cuts to funding and personnel within the agency puts a greater strain on the agency to adequately evaluate conservation needs and effectively implement species-specific rules. Therefore, the “blanket 4(d) rule” should remain.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Upon signing the Endangered Species Act, President Nixon was quoted as saying, "Nothing is more priceless and more worthy of preservation than the rich array of animal life with which our country has been blessed." Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
To whomever it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.

The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.

I have worked as a volunteer for 17 years in Mystic Aquarium’s Animal Rescue Program, which has been rescuing, rehabilitating and releasing sick, injured and stranded marine animals along the Northeastern coastline since 1975. Every year, our team responds to animals harmed by threats that the ESA was designed to mitigate: entanglement in fishing gear, vessel strikes, habitat degradation, pollution, and climate driven events such as cold stunning. These incidents are not rare anomalies, but are daily realities. Many of the animals we treat are members of populations that remain extremely vulnerable, with slow reproductive rates and long recovery timelines. Even small regulatory shifts can have outsized impacts on their survival.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Laura Wyeth
Mystic Aquarium Animal Rescue Program Volunteer
title: Comment from Wyeth, Laura

text:
Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):
Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully,
Conserve for a tomorrow.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I understand the desire behind this proposal. Conservatives are rightly skeptical of one-size-fits-all federal rules, and the idea of tailoring protections species-by-species sounds like common sense. In theory, it promises precision, flexibility, and less unnecessary regulation.

But in practice, removing the blanket rule would likely create more bureaucracy, more uncertainty, and more federal control, not less—and those costs would fall hardest on landowners, rural communities, and states.

Here’s why this matters.

First, the blanket rule currently provides clarity and predictability. Everyone—landowners, farmers, ranchers, hunters, developers, and states—knows what the baseline protections are the moment a species is listed as threatened. Removing it replaces a clear rule with a long waiting period where decisions depend on future agency action. That uncertainty is poison for private property owners trying to plan land use, investment, or conservation efforts.

Second, species-specific rules sound local, but they actually centralize power in Washington. Instead of a known default standard written into regulation, every threatened species becomes subject to case-by-case rulemaking by federal officials. That means more discretion for unelected bureaucrats, more lobbying by special interests, and more opportunity for inconsistent or politically motivated decisions—exactly the kind of government overreach conservatives have opposed for decades.

Third, this approach invites lawsuits, which conservatives know all too well. When protections aren’t clearly defined up front, activist groups step in and sue to force stricter rules. The result is not freedom—it’s judges and lawyers shaping land-use policy instead of Congress, states, or local communities. Ironically, weakening the blanket rule may hand more power to the very environmental litigation industry conservatives distrust.

Fourth, it discourages voluntary conservation by landowners. When people don’t know what rules will apply in the future, the rational response is to avoid attracting attention altogether. That can lead to habitat destruction before species are listed, a phenomenon known as “shoot, shovel, and shut up.” The blanket rule reduces that fear by setting expectations early and evenly.

Finally, this risks undermining the original conservative strength of the Endangered Species Act: conservation through stability, not chaos. The Act worked best when it created clear incentives, predictable rules, and respect for private stewardship. Constantly rewriting protections species by species erodes trust and turns conservation into a moving target.

If the goal is less red tape, more local involvement, and stronger property rights, this proposal may achieve the opposite. It replaces a known rule with bureaucratic delay, invites court battles, and shifts power further away from states and landowners.

Conservatives have always believed in conserving America’s natural heritage—not through endless federal micromanagement, but through clear rules, accountability, and respect for those who live and work on the land. This proposal risks losing all three.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from P, Lauren

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

The Endangered Species Act is one of the most successful and scientifically grounded conservation laws in U.S. history. The proposed changes would undermine these foundations.

•Narrow or complicate the designation and protection of critical habitat, even when habitat loss is a primary driver of extinction;
•Reduce the effectiveness and accountability of interagency consultation under Section 7;
•Introduce unnecessary ambiguity that benefits short-term development interests over long-term species recovery.

Weakening ESA regulations will increase extinction risk, shift costs to states and taxpayers, and invite further litigation rather than providing regulatory certainty.

Congress designed the ESA to err on the side of preventing irreversible harm. These proposed changes move in the opposite direction and are inconsistent with the statute’s purpose, scientific consensus, and public interest.

I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to withdraw these proposals in full and maintain robust, science-driven ESA regulations that prioritize species recovery and habitat protection.

This lead to the establishment of the EPA and the Clean Water Act, but decades later we are just now seeing the return of species such as beavers, otters, bald eagles and fishers to the region. With this history in mind, I am concerned about weakening protections for imperiled species.

The Endangered Species Act works because it centers science and the public interest—not political pressure or economic influence.
Science can tell us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both.
The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality. Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests. We've seen this in action this year with Florida's trophy bear hunt despite the lack of genetic diversity in its small bear population and with the targeted killings of wolves including critically endangered Mexican Grey Wolf Pups who were key for their genetic diversity, at the behest of ranchers despite science showing that non-lethal methods are more effective and not being utilized at all.

I am concerned about the following issues:
Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.

These rollbacks reduce public accountability at a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections.
A democratic, science-based process requires transparency and meaningful review. I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections. Please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so states and industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife. I ask you to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.
title: Comment from Severance, Sarah

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Garrard, Bryan

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted.

There is no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

I urge that the blanket rule be kept in place.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed legislation and any related actions that would weaken the Endangered Species Act.
The Endangered Species Act has functioned for more than fifty years as a science-based safeguard against extinction. Altering its core processes, particularly the scientific consultation framework, undermines the integrity of decisions meant to protect species already facing severe ecological pressure. Replacing evidence-driven evaluation with political or economic considerations puts both wildlife and ecosystems at unnecessary risk.

Slowing the listing of imperiled species while accelerating the removal of protections contradicts the purpose of the Act. Recovery from endangerment is not linear, and premature delisting increases the likelihood of population collapse rather than long-term stability. These changes favor speed over accuracy and weaken accountability.

Transferring management authority to states while species remain federally listed is also deeply concerning. Wildlife does not conform to state boundaries, and inconsistent protections create gaps that exploitation can easily exploit. Federal oversight exists precisely because national coordination is essential for effective conservation.

These proposals come at a time when federal agencies responsible for implementing the Endangered Species Act are already experiencing significant staffing and resource reductions. Weakening the law while simultaneously reducing enforcement capacity compounds the threat and increases the likelihood of irreversible harm.

The Endangered Species Act has prevented extinction for the vast majority of species under its protection and has helped preserve ecosystems that provide clean water, agricultural stability, and climate resilience. It is one of the most effective and publicly supported environmental laws in the United States, with broad bipartisan approval.

I urge the government to reject any legislation or regulatory changes that erode the scientific foundation, enforcement strength, or national scope of the Endangered Species Act. Protecting imperiled species and their habitats is not optional, it is a responsibility to current and future generations.

It is difficult to view these changes as anything other than an intentional weakening of a law that has worked. The Endangered Species Act is not failing; it is being deliberately undermined to accommodate short-term interests that benefit from fewer limits and less oversight. Calling this process “reform” does not change the reality that it reduces protections, sidelines science, and shifts risk onto species that already have no margin left.

title: Comment from coniglio, b

text:
I am a systems ecologist, social science and sustainable development scholar, educator, and I vote. The ESA is really about whole systems, not just individual species. I have studied causative links between degradation of critical ecological systems upon which humans are directly dependent and migration, civil war, and interstate war. It’s not always obvious how the health of a species or an event fits into long-term processes. But we do know. Popular examples are wolves reintroduced to Yosemite that led to several management problems being alleviated, or places where fishermen have informed agency to co-manage locally endangered fish or shellfish with agency and scientific support. Those actions don’t happen without strong Federal protections that initiate study, and facilitate discussion and democratic or consensus-based processes.

Weakening protections for newly-protected species, eliminating blanket protections, changing critical habitat designations, and limiting federal review run counter to public oversight and participation. Weakening regulations does not support processes that support ecosystem-based function. Weakening regulation most often hands power over to the biggest wallet and the loudest voice. And it leads to economic and political instability more surely than a short-term economic gain. Chemically intensive agriculture, the acid rain crisis in the 1970s and 1980s, hydropower impacts on fisheries, etc. all are connected to large unanticipated systemic impacts – symptoms of which are endangered species and from which the ESA and implementation processes were devloped. Regulations function to slow things down to allow for dialogue and study, and decentralize power to include all those affected.

I understand the small government argument. We know that in fact often the federal level is the last line of defense against local corruption or industry influence, and the best source of current research and support for collaborative processes. “Streamlining” or reducing regulatory costs for industry is not a scientific, whole-system, multi-generational view. We have no obligation to expedite business profits. We do have an obligation to provide clean water, clean air, healthy food and functioning ecosystems that provide those things to our and to future generations. Many civil and interstate wars and the fall of empires are linked to failure of those systems to meet local needs. It is in the best interest of the public to maintain the ESA as is or strengthen it, and to consider ecological and social sciences and their ability to explain and predict factors of societal health and stability that economics cannot. Development decisions must be made with scientific and public review, and democratic accountability regardless of industry or economists concerns about efficiency. Remediation, restoration, and extinction are not efficient, and the costs never fall directly on those who caused the harm. The ESA is the public’s defense against having to pay for expensive, unanticipated, systemic outcomes linked to why species become endangered. We must protect this law in the public interest by withdrawing the proposed changes.
title: Comment from Stone, A.M.

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,

I am writing today to express my strong opposition to the administration’s proposal to eliminate the "blanket 4(d) rule," which currently provides automatic protections to species listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

The ESA is our nation's most effective tool for preventing extinction, and the blanket 4(d) rule is a cornerstone of that success for the following reasons:

Immediate Protection is Critical: The blanket 4(d) rule serves as a proven, science-based safety net. It ensures that when a species is identified as being at risk, it receives immediate protections. Removing this baseline ensures that newly listed species will face a "regulatory gap" during their most vulnerable period while specific rules are being negotiated.
Inefficiency and Political Pressure: Transitioning to exclusively species-specific rules is a slow and resource-intensive process. This shift would likely delay conservation actions and open the door for increased political and industrial pressure to grant exemptions that are not based on biological necessity.
Adherence to Best Available Science: The ESA mandates that listing and protection decisions be based solely on the best available scientific data. Weakening these safeguards through executive changes undermines the scientific integrity of the Act and prioritizes short-term administrative goals over the long-term survival of American wildlife.

I urge the Fish and Wildlife Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule. Maintaining broad baseline protections is essential to prevent further species decline and to ensure that our ecosystems remain resilient for future generations.

Sincerely,

Dhamar Garcia
title: Comment from Garcia, Dhamar

text:
I’m writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed revisions to the regulations governing species listing and critical habitat designation under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). With respect to the Listing & Critical Habitat Designation Rule (2025-20549), the proposed revisions flagrantly exceed the agency’s authority in a way that is entirely impermissible. Congress could not have been clearer when it directed the Secretary to make listing determinations “solely on the basis of the best scientific and commercial data available” (16 U.S.C. § 1533(b)(1)(A)). The statute does not leave room for policy preferences, economic balancing, or administrative discretion on this question. It is a mandatory, unqualified instruction. The Supreme Court has repeatedly stated that when Congress speaks with this level of clarity, agencies are bound by that command. They do not have license to revisit or dilute it.

The proposed rule attempts to do exactly that. By introducing economic considerations into the listing process, considerations Congress expressly excluded, the agency is asserting a power it does not possess. This is not a matter of interpretation or gap-filling; it is a direct contradiction of the statutory text. An agency may not override Congress because it prefers a different policy outcome, nor may it recast a prohibited factor as a permissible one through regulatory language. Doing so would effectively amend the statute by regulation, something no agency has the authority to do.

Additionally, the proposed narrowing of critical habitat designations is inconsistent with both the statutory text and longstanding judicial interpretation. Critical habitat must include both occupied and unoccupied areas essential for conservation and recovery. By imposing new constraints on unoccupied habitat, including requirements that effectively preclude designating future climate-suitable habitat, the rule undermines the recovery mandate at the heart of the ESA. The Supreme Court has affirmed that “conservation” means recovery, not mere survival. Any rule that prevents the Service from designating habitat needed for recovery is contrary to law.

The ESA is a statute whose commands are specific. The agency does not have discretion to disregard them. These proposed revisions are in defiance of the law and should be rescinded.
title: Comment from Brown, Tim

text:
I am submitting this comment to express my strong opposition to this proposed rule. Threatened species depend on the blanket 4(d) rule as their first and most reliable layer of protection. Until species‑specific rules are drafted — a process that can take years — the blanket rule prevents these species from falling into regulatory gaps or becoming vulnerable to pressure from special interest groups.

Removing or weakening the blanket 4(d) rule strips away the broad, science‑based baseline protections that keep threatened species from sliding closer to extinction. It provides immediate, consistent safeguards across regions and agencies, and without it, many species would be left exposed at the exact moment they are most at risk.

As someone who cares deeply about the health of our environment and the future of our wildlife, I believe this proposal moves in the wrong direction. Once a species is gone, it is gone forever. The agency should be strengthening protections, not dismantling the foundational tools that keep species alive. Thank you for considering my perspective.
