text:
Founded in 1936, The Wildlife Society is an international network of over 11,000 leaders in wildlife science, management and conservation who are dedicated to excellence in wildlife stewardship. The mission of The Wildlife Society is to empower wildlife professionals to advance conservation through science, community, and professional excellence. As a professional scientific and educational organization, The Wildlife Society refrains from advocacy where it cannot ground its views on science. 

The Arizona Chapter of The Wildlife Society (AZTWS) was established in 1968 and is dedicated to promoting sound management and conservation of Arizona’s wildlife resources. Membership is open to all professionals, students and laypersons interested in wildlife research, management, education, and administration. Our chapter works to maintain communication among wildlife professionals, encourage communication between those professionals and the public, support continuing education through grants, hold workshops and regional meetings, encourage student involvement in the wildlife profession, and actively participate in shaping management and conservation policy through letters, public statements and resolutions.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) have announced four proposed rule changes that will narrow the definitions of critical habitat, alter criteria for listing or delisting a species, and change regulations with regard to Section 7 under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). We, the AZTWS, are committed to ensuring that decisions under the Act remain transparent, grounded in rigorous scientific analysis—including data from states, tribes, and peer-reviewed climate research—and free from economic or political influence. We further advocate for adequate federal funding and staffing to support efficient listing and recovery processes, collaborative conservation actions, and transparent rulemaking that strengthens the protection, restoration, and management of critical habitats essential to the recovery of endangered and threatened species.

The USFWS and NOAA are proposing to remove the “blanket rule” option for protecting newly listed threatened species pursuant to section 4(d) of the Act. The USFWS intends to create species-specific rules for all threatened species currently protected under the “blanket rule” option. Until such species-specific rules are promulgated, threatened species that receive protections under the “blanket rule” option will continue to receive those protections. The purpose of the “blanket rule” is to provide immediate protection, streamline the listing process, and avoid delays in conservation for vulnerable species. Further, the "blanket rule” applies the same strong protections (similar to endangered species) automatically to all newly listed threatened species. Although the USFWS can issue customized rules, keeping the “blanket rule” saves time and resources especially considering the decreased USFWS federal workforce. In other words, the “blanket rule” reduces the burden on USFWS, which has limited funds, by avoiding the need to create unique rules for every species. Lastly, having the option of relying on the “blanket rule” and the option of species-specific customized rules provides the best option for the conservation of species being listed as threatened. AZTWS requests that the interim application of endangered-level protections (§17.31) remains in place until a species-specific rule is finalized or that the USFWS otherwise maintains the application of the blanket 4(d) rule.

Thank you for your considerations to our comments on the USFWS four proposed rule changes.

Regards,

Holly Hicks, President

Arizona Chapter of The Wildlife Society

text:
I’m deeply concerned by the proposed rollbacks to the Endangered Species Act—these changes threaten the very foundation of wildlife recovery in my home state of Washington. Rather than weakening protections, we should strengthen the ESA, which has already proven critical to our region’s ecological and economic well-being.

Recovery of Salmon, Steelhead, and Bull Trout
Federal ESA protections, in partnership with state grants, have funded habitat restoration projects across Washington—like the $50 million+ in grants awarded in 2024 to restore riparian zones, reduce sedimentation, and improve fish habitat for salmon, steelhead, and bull trout. In August 2024, a court ordered removal of the century-old Electron Dam on the Puyallup River, citing ESA violations. This win will reopen critical spawning habitat for Chinook salmon, steelhead, and bull trout. [rco.wa.gov] [earthjustice.org]

Forest Protection Plans & Riparian Conservation
Through an innovative 50-year Habitat Conservation Plan—endorsed by USFWS and NOAA Fisheries—roughly 2.6 million acres of working forest in Washington have implemented streamside buffers, protecting ESA-listed species while allowing sustainable forestry. This plan exemplifies how federal-state-private cooperation can succeed. [wfpa.org]

Protection of Iconic Wildlife
ESA safeguards have enabled recovery efforts for gray wolves, southern resident orcas, western pond turtles, Canada lynx, and Pacific martens across Washington. Weakening the Act’s habitat or “blanket” protections risks undoing decades of progress. [cascadepbs.org], [seattlemag.com]

Efficiency and Outcomes
Contrary to criticism of bureaucratic slowdowns, the ESA’s Section 7 consultations in Washington typically conclude within two weeks, and formal consultations within about 60 days—far briefer than critics suggest.

The proposed regulatory changes—reducing “blanket” protection for threatened species, narrowing critical habitat designation, and injecting economic considerations into listings—would significantly erode these proven recovery outcomes and complicate coordinated federal-state efforts. [cascadepbs.org], [wildlife.org]

Washington has already witnessed the tangible benefits of a robust ESA. Weakening it now risks reversing restoration of salmon runs, rebuilding wildlife corridors, and strengthening forest conservation. We cannot afford to degrade the science-based framework that has kept species from extinction, revitalized ecosystems, and supported our communities.

Preserving and reinforcing—not dismantling—ESA protections is essential to safeguarding Washington’s natural heritage and ensuring continued recovery for the species that define our region.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Re: Public Comment on Proposed Revisions to 50 CFR Part 17 (Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants)
Docket No.: FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039

Dear Administrative Record:

I submit this comment in my personal capacity as a concerned citizen regarding the proposed revisions to 50 CFR Part 17, which governs the scope of protections afforded to species listed as endangered or threatened under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

Part 17 gives practical effect to the ESA’s substantive protections. Changes to this part do not merely clarify process; they determine whether listed species receive timely, enforceable safeguards against take, habitat degradation, and other threats. For that reason, revisions to Part 17 warrant particularly careful scrutiny.

My comments focus on two closely related concerns: (1) the elimination of the longstanding “blanket” 4(d) rule for threatened species, and (2) the resulting shift away from precautionary, uniform protections toward a more fragmented and delayed regulatory approach.

1. Eliminating the Blanket 4(d) Rule Risks Immediate and Irreversible Harm to Threatened Species

For decades, the Services have applied a default rule extending take prohibitions to threatened species unless and until a species-specific rule is adopted. This approach has provided immediate baseline protection while preserving the Services’ discretion to tailor measures where appropriate.

The proposed revisions would abandon this framework in favor of case-by-case, species-specific 4(d) rules, with no default protections in place during the interim. As a practical matter, this change creates a real risk of regulatory gaps at precisely the moment when newly listed species are most vulnerable.

Listing decisions reflect a scientific determination that a species faces a meaningful risk of extinction. Removing automatic protections following that determination undermines the Act’s preventive design and shifts the burden of uncertainty onto the species rather than onto regulated actors.

2. Species-Specific 4(d) Rules Should Supplement - Not Replace - Baseline Protections

The ESA authorizes tailored 4(d) rules for threatened species where doing so is “necessary and advisable” for conservation. That authority was never intended to function as a deregulatory default.

A system that requires the Services to affirmatively justify protections species by species, while allowing take in the absence of a finalized rule, risks turning 4(d) from a conservation tool into a bottleneck. Limited agency resources, competing priorities, and administrative delay can all translate into lost protections on the ground.

Uniform baseline safeguards, coupled with carefully justified exceptions, better align with the ESA’s structure and purpose than an approach that begins with permissiveness and relies on later corrective action.

3. The Proposed Changes Weaken Regulatory Predictability Rather Than Strengthen It

The stated rationale for revising Part 17 includes improving regulatory certainty. Ironically, eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule may have the opposite effect.

A predictable, uniform baseline provides clarity to landowners, project proponents, and conservation practitioners alike. By contrast, a patchwork of species-specific rules - issued on uneven timelines and with varying scopes - introduces uncertainty and invites inconsistent outcomes.

True regulatory certainty flows from clear, durable standards that apply consistently unless a reasoned and transparent exception is warranted.

Conclusion

50 CFR Part 17 operationalizes the ESA’s core promise: that once a species is recognized as at risk, meaningful protections follow. I urge the Services to retain a precautionary framework that provides immediate baseline safeguards for threatened species while preserving the flexibility to craft species-specific rules that enhance, rather than delay, conservation.

Weakening default protections in the name of flexibility risks sacrificing species to administrative delay. The ESA was designed to err on the side of life, not convenience. Part 17 should continue to reflect that judgment.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this comment.
title: Comment from Brushwood, Charles

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) is important because it protects the living systems that keep ecosystems—and ultimately people—alive. At its core, the ESA recognizes that species are not isolated; plants and animals are part of interconnected webs. When one species disappears, the effects ripple outward, destabilizing ecosystems that provide clean water, fertile soil, pollination, flood control, and climate resilience.

The ESA also exists because extinction is permanent. Once a species is gone, there is no way to bring it back. The law creates a safeguard against short-term economic or political pressures that can lead to irreversible loss. By requiring scientific evidence and long-term planning, the ESA ensures that decisions about land and development consider consequences beyond immediate profit.

Importantly, the ESA has a proven track record. Iconic species such as the bald eagle, gray wolf, and American alligator were brought back from the brink because of its protections. These recoveries show that conservation works when given legal backing and time.

Beyond ecology, the ESA reflects ethical responsibility. Humans have accelerated extinction rates through habitat destruction, pollution, and climate change. The law acknowledges a moral obligation to prevent harm where possible and to act as stewards rather than exploiters of the natural world.

Finally, the ESA benefits people directly. Healthy ecosystems support agriculture, fisheries, medicine, and outdoor recreation, all of which contribute to local economies and public well-being. Protecting endangered species is not a luxury—it is an investment in environmental stability, economic resilience, and the survival of future generations.

In short, we need the Endangered Species Act because protecting biodiversity protects everything else that depends on it—including us.

text:
I am submitting this public comment to express my opposition to any revisions within the proposed rule Endangered and Threatened Species: Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants that would weaken, delay, or narrow protections for species listed under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

The ESA is one of the most effective environmental laws ever enacted, responsible for preventing extinction and supporting the recovery of hundreds of species across the United States. Its success depends on clear, enforceable protections for endangered and threatened wildlife and plants based on the best available scientific and commercial data. Any changes that reduce these protections undermine the core purpose of the Act.

I am particularly concerned about provisions that:
•Reduce automatic protections for threatened species
•Increase discretionary exemptions or carve-outs that allow harm before recovery is achieved
•Delay protective measures until populations are critically depleted
•Devalue habitat protection for plants and non-charismatic species
•Prioritize short-term economic or administrative convenience over scientific evidence

Threatened species are, by definition, on a trajectory toward endangerment without intervention. Weakening safeguards at this stage makes recovery more difficult, more costly, and in some cases impossible. Preventative protection is far more effective—and far less expensive—than emergency intervention after population collapse.

Plants and wildlife form the foundation of healthy ecosystems. Native plant species stabilize soils, regulate water systems, support pollinators, and sustain food webs that wildlife and humans depend on. When protections for plants or animals are weakened, entire ecosystems unravel, leading to cascading environmental and economic impacts.

At a time of accelerating climate change, habitat fragmentation, and biodiversity loss, the nation should be strengthening protections for endangered and threatened species—not eroding them. The ESA was designed to act as a science-based safety net for species under pressure, and its integrity must be preserved.

I urge you to reject any revisions that weaken protections for endangered and threatened wildlife and plants and to uphold the full intent and authority of the Endangered Species Act.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this comment and for considering the long-term public interest and ecological health of our shared lands and waters.

Respectfully,
Michaela Purvines

title: Comment from Whitehead, Matt

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,

I am writing to submit a public comment on the proposed rule identified as FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, concerning revisions to the inter-agency cooperation regulations under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act.

I appreciate the opportunity to comment and recognize the importance of efficient, clear regulatory processes. However, I am deeply concerned that the proposed changes, as written, risk weakening the practical protections the Endangered Species Act is intended to provide to imperiled wildlife and their habitats.

Concerns Regarding Narrowed Scope of Analysis

Section 7 consultation has long served as one of the ESA’s most critical safeguards by requiring federal agencies to evaluate whether their actions may jeopardize listed species or adversely modify critical habitat. The proposed revisions appear to narrow how agencies define and analyze:

“Effects of the action”

The environmental baseline

Indirect, cumulative, and long-term impacts

From a scientific and ecological perspective, these factors are often inseparable from species decline. Habitat fragmentation, climate-driven range shifts, increased human access, and incremental development pressures rarely act in isolation. Limiting the scope of analysis risks overlooking the very conditions that place species at risk of extinction.

Implications for Wolves and Other Wide-Ranging Species

Species such as the gray wolf, Mexican wolf, and red wolf depend on large, connected landscapes and long-term habitat stability. Federal actions affecting land use, infrastructure, grazing, energy development, or access corridors can have significant indirect and cumulative effects on these species—even when no single action appears catastrophic on its own.

By narrowing the consultation framework, the proposed rule could make it more difficult to fully evaluate how federal actions contribute to habitat degradation, population isolation, or increased human-wildlife conflict. This would undermine recovery efforts for species that already face multiple overlapping threats.

Alignment With the Purpose of the ESA

Congress enacted the Endangered Species Act with a clear intent: to prevent extinction and promote recovery using the best available science. Courts have repeatedly recognized that the ESA is meant to be precautionary and protective in nature. Regulatory changes that constrain scientific analysis or exclude known drivers of species decline run counter to both the letter and spirit of the law.

Efficiency and clarity in consultation are important goals, but they should not come at the expense of meaningful environmental review or long-term conservation outcomes.

Requested Action

I respectfully urge the Services to:

Retain a broad, science-based interpretation of “effects of the action” that includes indirect and cumulative impacts.

Ensure the environmental baseline reflects real-world ecological conditions affecting listed species.

Avoid regulatory changes that would reduce the ability of Section 7 consultations to identify and prevent jeopardy to species or adverse modification of critical habitat.

Reconsider or revise portions of the proposed rule that would weaken the practical protections afforded under the ESA.

Thank you for considering my comment and for the important work you do to conserve our nation’s wildlife heritage. I urge you to ensure that any final rule strengthens—rather than diminishes—the Endangered Species Act’s effectiveness for present and future generations.

Respectfully submitted,

Anthony Milhorn
Christiansburg, VA
title: Comment from Milhorn, Anthony

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am writing to express deep concern about the proposed revisions to the regulations governing protections for threatened wildlife and plants under the Endangered Species Act. The proposal to eliminate the long-standing “blanket rule” that automatically provides protections to all species classified as threatened would weaken essential safeguards for animals and plants that are already vulnerable to extinction.

The Endangered Species Act was designed to prevent species from slipping toward extinction and to create a pathway for genuine recovery. Automatically applying core protections to threatened species has been a cornerstone of this approach. When the blanket rule is removed, protections become contingent on developing and finalizing individual rules for each species. Drafting species-specific rules takes years, requires extensive scientific analysis and agency resources, and inevitably delays protections at the very time when species are most fragile. These delays are not theoretical. They translate directly into habitat loss, increased mortality, and reduced chances for recovery. Protecting wildlife should not be treated as an optional add-on that waits on lengthy bureaucratic steps when lives are at stake.

The blanket rule also has the benefit of transparency and predictability. Scientists, landowners, local communities, and conservation partners know from the moment a species is listed as threatened that key protections are in place. Removing this automatic bar leaves stakeholders unsure of what standards apply and opens the door for inconsistent protections that vary from species to species without clear scientific justification.

Threatened species face the same root causes of decline that endanger species do, such as habitat destruction, climate change, pollution, and invasive competitors. Vulnerable does not mean “less deserving.” It means species on a downward trajectory that require immediate, consistent protections to prevent them from becoming endangered in the first place. The “blanket rule” embodies the preventative intent of the Act by ensuring that protections begin without delay and remain in force while recovery planning progresses.

I respectfully urge the Fish and Wildlife Service to maintain the automatic application of core protections for threatened species rather than replacing them with a fragmented, discretionary process that delays conservation and increases risk of irreversible loss. The future of countless species depends on strong, consistent protections that act quickly when science shows they are needed. Thank you for considering this comment.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,

Alexis Ware

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Knickrehm, Courtney

text:
I object to the proposed rule changes.
These changes are not minor technical adjustments or routine administrative cleanups. They represent a fundamental shift in how the federal government interprets and applies the law that has, for more than fifty years, stood between countless species and extinction.Since its passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act has operated on a simple but powerful premise: when a species is at risk of disappearing forever, decisions about its fate should be guided by the best available science, not political convenience or short-term economic pressure.The law has prevented the extinction of roughly 99 percent of the species placed under its protection and has driven some of the most celebrated conservation recoveries in American history.One of the most consequential changes would dismantle the long-standing “blanket 4(d) rule,” which automatically extends key protections to species listed as threatened. Under the current system, newly listed threatened species receive safeguards similar to endangered species unless the Fish and Wildlife Service deliberately crafts a tailored rule.Removing that default flips the logic of protection, forcing conservationists to argue for safeguards species by species, often while populations continue to decline. In a time when climate change and habitat loss are accelerating, delay can be fatal.Other proposed revisions would narrow how critical habitat is designated and considered, making it easier for federal agencies to approve projects that degrade or fragment the very places species need to survive and recover.Habitat loss is already the single greatest driver of extinction, yet these rules would make it more difficult to protect unoccupied but ecologically essential areas—precisely the landscapes species may need as climate conditions shift. This approach treats conservation as a static exercise, ignoring the reality that wildlife must move, adapt, and expand to survive in a rapidly changing world.Equally troubling are changes to the interagency consultation process, the mechanism that requires federal agencies to ensure their actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed revisions would weaken consultation standards, reduce accountability, and make it easier for agencies to conclude that harmful projects pose no meaningful risk.This is not an abstract concern. From roads and pipelines to dams, mines, and timber sales, countless federal actions hinge on these consultations. Weakening them increases the likelihood that irreversible harm will be approved with minimal scrutiny. Again, I object to this proposed rule revision and others that would irrevocably endanger the process by which biodiversity is supported and ensured.

It also removes requirements for mitigation or offsets when federal agencies cause unavoidable harm to species or habitat. Both of these proposed regulations weaken the Endangered Species Act.

FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048 expands the circumstances under which areas may be excluded from critical habitat for economic or national security reasons.

FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029 eliminates the default full protections (“blanket rule”) for newly listed threatened species. Instead, USFWS would create species-specific 4(d) rules for each threatened listing - a slower and more resource-intensive process that will significantly increase species listing times and delay protections for many species.  The proposed rule increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based. Trying to compare economic benefits to the threat of species extinction is of dubious value. Who derives these economic benefits? How sustainable are these economic benefits? Economic benefits are often ephemeral. Extinction is forever.

Since the onset of the industrial revolution in the late 1700s extinction rates are at least 50 times (perhaps 1000 times) greater than the background extinction rate through geologic time. Humans are driving species to extinction without understanding what it is we are destroying.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled plants and wildlife.
title: Comment from Shaner, Greg

text:
Personal Public Comment Opposing the Proposed Changes to the Endangered Species Act

A letter to the government and public servants elected to represent the health and safety of its constituents, including the biodiversity upon which we all depend.

For more than five decades, the Endangered Species Act has stood as one of America’s most effective tools for preventing extinctions. Its strength lies in a commitment to clear, science-based decision-making and an understanding that safeguarding at-risk species is a matter of national importance. The proposed revisions would erode the Act’s foundational principles. By introducing uncertainty, weakening longstanding protections, and narrowing the pathways through which vulnerable species receive attention and support, these changes would make it harder for species to persist and recover.

I oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA), published on November 21, 2025. I am are deeply concerned about the cumulative impacts the proposed changes would have on the conservation of imperiled species and their habitats.

The proposed revisions mirror changes introduced in 2019 that were ultimately withdrawn because they undermined the ESA’s purpose. Then, and now, the proposed measures run afoul of scientific expertise and legal precedent – and go against strong public, bipartisan support for a robust, science-driven ESA that preserves our shared natural heritage.

1. Economic considerations should not Influence listing decisions. The proposed changes to ESA regulations would permit economic assessments to be considered alongside scientific analysis for listing decisions, weakening a core principle of the law.

2. The proposed interpretation of “foreseeable future” would undermine protections for species affected by long-term threats. Previous efforts to narrow the definition of “foreseeable future” were broadly criticized by scientists and conservation practitioners. Doing so would limit the ability of agencies to consider long-term threats such as climate change and habitat fragmentation, placing species—particularly invertebrates with small ranges or climate-sensitive life cycles—at heightened risk. For example, the endangered Poweshiek skipperling (Oarisma poweshiek) occupies less than 5% of its former range. Conservation of this species requires a long-term view that accounts for how processes like climate change might reduce the viability of its small, geographically isolated populations into the future.

The cumulative effect of the proposed rules would disproportionately harm invertebrates, migratory species, and niche specific species. The proposed rules would create additional barriers for listing and recovery, making it even harder to protect invertebrate species before declines become irreversible. For example, the changes would make it more difficult to designate critical habitat, particularly in areas not currently occupied by a species— including former range and future climatic refugia. For a species like the endangered rusty patched bumble bee—once widespread in the eastern U.S. but now reduced to small, scattered populations— connecting formerly occupied habitat to maintain genetic diversity is essential.

Counter to the ESA’s purpose, the proposal also broadens when agencies may decline to designate critical habitat, prioritizing short-term development interests over long-term conservation needs. Economic considerations are already permitted during the critical habitat designation process. The proposed changes are unnecessary and undermine agencies’ ability to safeguard habitats essential for recovery.

The ESA's current framework already allows for efficiency, flexibility, and science-based decision-making. The agencies have the necessary tools to tailor protections, evaluate the significance of threats, and promote cooperative conservation without weakening standards. Many of the proposed changes seem unnecessary and would likely create confusion, invite more legal challenges, and weaken public confidence in how species are protected.

The ESA is an essential safeguard at a time when biodiversity loss is accelerating. Weakening the Act’s regulatory foundation would have long-lasting consequences for wildlife, ecosystems, and the human communities that depend on them. For the reasons summarized in this letter, I respectfully request that the relevant U.S. agencies (FWS, DOI, NOAA, DOC) withdraw all proposed revisions. I urge the agencies to maintain the core principles that have guided ESA implementation for decades and to uphold the Act’s high standards, which have a proven track record of preventing extinctions.

Thank you for your consideration.
title: Comment from Murphy, Emily

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Richthammer, Cindy

text:
I strongly oppose any effort to weaken the Endangered Species Act. The ESA is one of the most effective conservation laws in the world and remains a critical safeguard against the ongoing extinction crisis. Diluting its protections is not a minor regulatory change. It is a decision to allow preventable extinctions to occur.

The proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, including FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044 and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048, represent a disturbing pattern of attacks on imperiled species and the habitats they depend on. They ignore well-established science, undermine decades of conservation progress, and prioritize short-term economic interests over the survival of plants and animals that cannot advocate for themselves.

The proposed rules would:

***Deny newly listed threatened species automatic protection from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take,” leaving species such as the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, greater sage grouse, and monarch butterfly exposed even after they are officially recognized as at risk of extinction.

***Narrow the definition of “critical habitat” by excluding unoccupied but historic habitat. These areas are often essential for recovery, especially as climate change and habitat loss make current ranges increasingly unviable.

***Weaken federal agency accountability, making it easier to approve destructive activities like logging, mining, and drilling even when those actions place protected species in direct harm’s way.

***Most troubling, the proposed rules would inject “economic considerations” into decisions about whether species and their habitats deserve protection. This approach fundamentally distorts the purpose of the ESA. The Act was intentionally designed to be science-based and precautionary, not a cost-benefit analysis where extinction can be justified because protecting wildlife might interfere with development or reduce profits. Allowing economics to override biological reality is not pragmatic. It is morally and legally indefensible.

***Alter critical habitat designation standards to make it easier to exclude areas from protection based on industry claims of economic impact, further stacking the deck against species already struggling to survive.

At a time when more than one million species face the risk of extinction globally, weakening the ESA is reckless and dangerous. Biodiversity loss threatens food security, clean water, ecosystem stability, and the health of human communities. We are not separate from the natural world, and sacrificing species and ecosystems for short-term economic gain ultimately harms us all.

This is a moment that demands stronger protections, not rollbacks. I urge the administration to withdraw these proposed rule changes and uphold the Endangered Species Act as Congress intended, guided by science, focused on recovery, and committed to preventing extinction rather than negotiating its price.

text: As a child of the 1970s and learning about the necessity of protecting animals and their habitats, I urge you to strengthen ecological conservation and protection. Please put the survival of this planet above financial gains for limited individuals.

text:
This rule has automatically provided threatened species with protections against harm until a tailored plan can be finalized. For decades, it has helped species like the piping plover, southern sea otter, and Florida manatee gain immediate safeguards upon listing (FWS, 2019).
Without this automatic protection, newly listed threatened species could be killed, captured, or harassed without legal consequence while they await a species-specific rule. This exposes species to preventable harm during their most vulnerable period.
Habitat loss is the number one driver of extinction. The ESA already allows exclusions, but only when they will not lead to extinction. Broadening this power increases risk to species that already live on the edge. For example, habitat loss contributed to the extinction of the ivory-billed woodpecker, Little Mariana fruit bat, and multiple freshwater mussel species (FWS, 2021)
title: Comment from Tarquinio, Matthew

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.
Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.
The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.
For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.
title: Comment from Nuñez, Jackie

text:
If you care about the economy, level of habitable land, general human wellbeing, etc, you will not pass this.

I appeal to you in this way: this is not about saving species for the sake of saving species. This is about saving species because they benefit us. Their benefit to their ecosystems is, in turn, benefit to us as humans.

Let's look at the wolves in Yellowstone. Wolves were once eradicated from Yellowstone. In their absence, their main prey source, elk, became overpopulated and overgrazed. The overgrazing caused soil to become unstable and fall into/change the course of/pollute rivers. Overgrazing took away habitat for other animals like insects, which pollinate crops, for one. With no grass for grasshoppers to eat, there are no grasshoppers for mice to eat, and no mice for coyotes to eat, and so on. With no coyotes to keep the mouse population in check and no habitat for mice, they invade our homes. When wolves were reintroduced, the ecosystem rebalanced itself. Also, Yellowstone draws in millions as a tourist attraction every year, including just for the wolves themselves.

Saving the wolves of Yellowstone, in turn, not only improved the ecosystem, but also fixed habitats and made them more beautiful and thus more appealing to come to from far away. Wolves and bison both live there, both endangered, and draw in tourists to see these rare animals. Books, games, documentaries, and more all have been born from Yellowstone, generating more money.

This is just one example using charismatic fauna. Endangered plants can be keeping soil in place to combat eroding shorelines. Even insects are important. Every single organism is important and every single organism benefits its ecosystem in some way (including mosquitos). We are at the mercy of the ecosystem; if we allow it to be destroyed, it will destroy us as a consequence. Hunting wolves to extinction led to pollution and unstable soil, both of which directly impact humans.
Repealing the ESA shows that you know nothing about the world we share and you act brashly with no thought for future generations or that you care about what you propose. To propose such a change, you should be deeply informed about the topic in question which it is clear that you aren't because, if you were, you would not have proposed it in the first place.

So, I implore you, even if you have no value for biodiversity, consider the socioeconomic impact, environmental damage, and how endangered animals benefit us as humans.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act because they weaken the law’s foundational purpose and place already vulnerable species at even greater risk of extinction. Collectively, the four proposed rules (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) dismantle long-standing conservation measures that have demonstrated both effectiveness and broad public support.

First, removing the blanket 4(d) rule for threatened species would substantially increase the likelihood of further population declines. This rule has long served as a clear, efficient, and legally sound mechanism for extending baseline protections while still allowing the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to tailor species-specific exceptions when appropriate. Eliminating it would not only reduce protections but would also create additional administrative burdens by requiring the agency to draft individual 4(d) rules for every newly listed threatened species.

Second, the proposed changes to critical habitat regulations would significantly weaken both the listing process and habitat designation. Allowing federal lands to be excluded from critical habitat protections based on economic considerations would prioritize short-term development interests—such as energy projects, grazing, and logging—over the ecological needs of imperiled species. At a time when many listed species occupy only small remnants of their historical range, narrowing the scope of critical habitat designation would further compromise their ability to survive and recover in the face of ongoing habitat loss, pollution, and climate change.

Third, introducing economic factors into decisions about whether to list a species undermines a core principle of the ESA: that listing determinations must be based solely on the best available scientific and commercial data. This shift invites political and economic pressure into what has historically been a science-driven process, weakening the credibility and effectiveness of species protections.

Fourth, weakening interagency consultation requirements threatens to erode meaningful oversight of federal actions that may affect listed species. Efforts framed as “streamlining” consultation risk sidelining the expertise of wildlife agencies and reducing their role in evaluating and minimizing project-related impacts on threatened and endangered species.

Taken together, these proposals revive approaches that previously sought to limit the scope and effectiveness of the ESA. Such changes are inconsistent with the law’s proven success and with public support for wildlife conservation. Since its passage, the ESA has prevented the extinction of the vast majority of species under its protection, and public polling continues to show strong bipartisan support for the law.

The challenges facing imperiled species have not diminished over time. On the contrary, increasing development pressures and accelerating climate impacts make strong, science-based implementation of the ESA more critical than ever. For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw these proposed regulatory changes and uphold the Endangered Species Act’s essential role in conserving America’s wildlife and the habitats upon which they depend.

text:
I'm outraged to learn that the Trump administration is trying to dismantle our most successful conservation law: the Endangered Species Act.

Since its passage in 1973, this landmark act has prevented the extinction of roughly 300 species — and more than 99% of the species under its care have been saved or are on their way to recovery. This incredible law has also protected millions of acres of forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans.

The proposed rollbacks will be devastating if finalized. They'll strip vital protections from our nation's most vulnerable species and pave the way for widespread habitat destruction — all in the name of profiteers, polluters, and special interests.

The Endangered Species Act works, and it has for decades. It’s the reason bald eagles, alligators, gray whales, and other iconic species are still around today. We should work to *strengthen* the Act — not weaken it.

I stand with most Americans in supporting the Endangered Species Act and the strong protections it provides to the United States’ most endangered animals and plants. I strongly oppose rollbacks to the Act and urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries to stop this attempt to dismantle it by withdrawing the administration's destructive proposals immediately.

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from porcino, nancy

text:
I'm completely outraged to learn that the Trump administration is trying to dismantle our most successful conservation law: the Endangered Species Act.

Since its passage in 1973, this landmark act has prevented the extinction of roughly 300 species — and more than 99% of the species under its care have been saved or are on their way to recovery. This incredible law has also protected millions of acres of forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans.

The proposed rollbacks will be devastating if finalized. They'll strip vital protections from our nation's most vulnerable species and pave the way for widespread habitat destruction — all in the name of profiteers, polluters, and special interests.

The Endangered Species Act works, and it has for decades. It’s the reason bald eagles, alligators, gray whales, and other iconic species are still around today. We should work to *strengthen* the Act — not weaken it.

I stand with most Americans in supporting the Endangered Species Act and the strong protections it provides to the United States’ most endangered animals and plants. I strongly oppose rollbacks to the Act and urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries to stop this attempt to dismantle it by withdrawing the administration's destructive proposals immediately.

title: Comment from Heidler, Brittany

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Hoey, Clara

text:
As someone who cares deeply about wildlife and the future of our planet, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule that would undermine wildlife protections granted by the Endangered Species Act. This change would go against decades of conservation progress and weaken one of our nation’s most important environmental laws.

The “blanket rule” gives essential baseline protection to threatened species until species-specific safeguards can be established. Removing the “blanket rule” may make them more vulnerable to extinction, in opposition to the intent of this legislation.

I urge you to uphold the mission of the Endangered Species Act and maintain the “blanket rule.” Our wildlife, wild places, and future generations are counting on it.
title: Comment from Kelley , Patrick

text:
The blanket 4(d) rule is a proven, science-based tool that gives threatened species immediate protections when they are most at risk.

Eliminating the blanket rule will delay or weaken protections for newly listed species, putting them in harm’s way during the period when conservation actions are most critical.

Species-specific rules are not a substitute for broad baseline protections; they are slow, resource-intensive, and increase political pressure from industries seeking exemptions.

The ESA requires decisions to be based on the best available science, not executive orders aimed at weakening environmental safeguards.

The Fish & Wildlife Service should retain the blanket 4(d) rule to prevent regulatory gaps that could worsen species declines.

text:
The blanket 4(d) rule is one of the quickest and most effective tools for giving threatened species immediate protection, because it gives newly listed threatened species the same protections as endangered species unless a species-specific rule is written. When a species has been identified as threatened, time is often of the essence. If the factors contributing to the threat are allowed to continue, a species identified as threatened may not survive long enough for recovery efforts to be put in place and take effect. That's why I'm vehemently opposed to the proposed removal of the blanket 4(d) rule in its entirety.

The blanket 4(d) rule is a proven, science-based tool that provides threatened species immediate protections when they are most at risk. By eliminating the blanket rule, protections for newly listed species will be delayed or weakened, subjecting them to harm during the period when conservation actions are most critical.

Replacing the blanket 4(d) rule with species-specific rules is a very ineffective method of protecting threatened species. Because they are slow, resource-intensive, and increase economic/political pressure from industries seeking exemptions, species-specific rules are not a valid substitute for broad baseline protections.
.
Executive orders aimed at weakening environmental safeguards are not useful in protecting threatened species and should not be the basis for rule changes such as what's being proposed. Rather, the ESA requires decisions to be based on the best available science because that is the most effective basis for protection and eventual restoration of threatened species. Rather than basing decisions on executive orders that weaken protections, ESA mandates such decisions to be based on the best available science. The ESA is established law enacted by Congress and should not be weakened by proposals of this type.
In summary, the Fish & Wildlife Service should retain the blanket 4(d) rule to prevent political pressure and regulatory gaps that could worsen the decline of threatened species.

text:
I am against the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.
Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.
Eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.
For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.
As a retired federal natural resource specialist, I support the existing law, which preserves our natural values. Do not make these proposed changes; future generations will suffer!
