First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I'm writing today to ask our government to oppose any efforts to weaken the Endangered Species Act. This landmark law has protected Hawaiian monk seals, Guadalupe fur seals, southern sea otters, manatees, wolves, and other animals and their ecosystems for more than 50 years. The proposed changes would seriously undermine these protections and threaten decades of progress. The change proposed in this threatened species "blanket rule" would weaken species listing criteria by limiting use of the best scientific data available, which is the opposite of the intent of the ESA.  I urge you to withdraw this proposal.  Our government and lawmakers should turn to the scientists and biologists that have devoted their careers and lives to understanding the needs of our keystone species and let them lead in guiding regulations to set policy that protects their habitat and ensures their survival for decades to come. We are in a pivotal time, where weakening these policies seriously risks degrading the natural environment and genetic diversity of the world our children will inherit from us. This is an oversight that can't be tolerated.

title: Comment from Krebs, Merilee

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) was passed and enacted in 1973 because “ordinary” citizens, legislators and the executive branch finally realized that we humans were needlessly driving other species to extinction due to the amount and type of economic activity and wide-spread ignorance about our impacts on other species and their habitats and ecosystems.

The ESA is considered strong compared with similar laws in other countries. It is strongly reliant on scientific evidence and incorporating scientific findings as they become available. Its basic purpose is to prevent us from driving other species to extinction. Therefore, potential effects of listing on the economy are not to be considered. The ESA has facilitated the recovery of many species and to-date, prevented the extinction of many more. At the same time, some species have gone extinct since passage of the ESA. Other species remain listed and face increasing threats to habitat loss, exacerbated by effects of climate change. Those effects are not well-understood, even as scientific research is continually improving our understanding.

Bottom line- this is no time to be weakening legal protections for listed species. However, the four rule changes proposed will weaken the ESA and its ability to protect other species.

Do not eliminate the “blanket 4d rule”.

The existing rule already allows USFWS to develop species-specific rules. Eliminating the rule places greater burdens on an agency which the administration has already severely downsized and crippled.

Under those conditions, it is not clear how the agency can possibly develop meaningful science-based species-specific rules in a sufficiently short time to protect listed species.

Changing the rule will likely lead to fewer species listed as “endangered” and instead as “threatened”. An endangered listing is protective in the sense that it is less subject to agency manipulation under political pressure.

text:
Endangered Species Act comment
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) was passed with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by a Republican president. It has been successful in preventing extinction of many animals important for our national legacy, including the American bald eagle.

Protecting endangered species helps keep the natural systems we depend on working properly. Plants and animals are connected in ways that support clean water, healthy soil, reliable pollination, and stable wildlife populations. These connections stretch across all types of landscapes, from farmland and forests to deserts, mountains, and coastlines. When these natural systems are functioning well, they benefit communities, agriculture, outdoor recreation, and local economies.

Endangered and threatened species have led to medical innovation and advances. For instance, the Gila Monster’s venom led to the development of GLP-1 diabetes/weight loss drugs. Chemicals from the rosy periwinkle have dramatically increased the survival rates for children with leukemia and are used to treat Hodgkin lymphoma. A substance found in the Pacific Yew tree is now used to treat ovarian, breast, and lung cancers. These examples illustrate how the loss of a species can mean the permanent loss of unique biological compounds and research opportunities. Once a species is extinct, its potential contributions to medicine and public health are gone forever, which is precisely the type of irreversible harm the Endangered Species Act was designed to prevent.

Endangered species often act as early warning signs. When a species begins to disappear, it can signal deeper problems affecting land, water, and other wildlife. For example, the sharp decline of the monarch butterfly—an important pollinator in the United States—points to broader challenges facing prairie lands that many farmers and communities rely on. Addressing these issues early helps prevent larger and more costly problems down the road.

The ESA helps safeguard these essential natural resources, which are critical for human safety and economic stability. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, wildlife-related recreation—including hunting, fishing, and wildlife watching—supports hundreds of billions of dollars in economic activity and millions of jobs nationwide, all of which depend on healthy fish and wildlife populations.

Weakening the Endangered Species Act could increase risks to public health and economic stability. The loss of species can disrupt natural processes that support pollination, food production, and other essential services. It can also eliminate opportunities for discovering medical compounds, including potential treatments for serious illnesses. Protecting species helps safeguard these resources, which are important for food security, public well-being, and the nation’s long-term economic interests.

Habitat loss, habitat degradation, and pollution are the most significant driving forces of extinction today. For the best chance at adapting to changes in their environment, plants and animals need robust populations and room to migrate. Depleting their populations and hemming them in contributes to species loss. Policies that weaken the ESA risk accelerating these pressures rather than addressing them.

I support the Endangered Species Act and the strong protections it provides for the nation’s most at-risk plants and animals. I oppose efforts to weaken the Act and urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries to withdraw the proposed changes. The focus should remain on maintaining and improving the effectiveness of the Act, rather than reducing its protections.

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I'm outraged to learn that the Trump administration is trying to dismantle our most successful conservation law: the Endangered Species Act.

Since its passage in 1973, this landmark act has prevented the extinction of roughly 300 species — and more than 99% of the species under its care have been saved or are on their way to recovery. This incredible law has also protected millions of acres of forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans.

The proposed rollbacks will be devastating if finalized. They'll strip vital protections from our nation's most vulnerable species and pave the way for widespread habitat destruction — all in the name of profiteers, polluters, and special interests.

The Endangered Species Act works, and it has for decades. It’s the reason bald eagles, alligators, gray whales, and other iconic species are still around today. We should work to *strengthen* the Act — not weaken it.

I stand with most Americans in supporting the Endangered Species Act and the strong protections it provides to the United States’ most endangered animals and plants. I strongly oppose rollbacks to the Act and urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries to stop this attempt to dismantle it by withdrawing the administration's destructive proposals immediately.
title: Comment from Behnke , Caitlyn

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Warren Gross
title: Comment from Gross, Warren

text:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to any efforts to weaken or alter the Endangered Species Act (ESA). For more than fifty years, the ESA has served as one of the most effective conservation laws in the United States, protecting vulnerable species and preserving the ecosystems upon which both wildlife and people depend.
The ESA is grounded in sound science and long-term stewardship. It recognizes that once a species is lost, it cannot be recovered. Altering the Act to prioritize short-term economic or political interests over ecological integrity risks irreversible damage to biodiversity, natural resources, and environmental stability. Healthy ecosystems provide essential services—clean air and water, pollination, flood control, and climate resilience—that benefit communities and economies nationwide.
Weakening protections for endangered and threatened species also undermines the precautionary principle that has guided responsible environmental policy. The current framework ensures decisions are based on the best available science rather than shifting political or commercial pressures. Any dilution of these standards increases the likelihood of extinction, ecosystem collapse, and costly remediation efforts in the future.
Additionally, the Endangered Species Act has demonstrated that conservation and economic development are not mutually exclusive. Many recovery efforts have succeeded while allowing responsible land use and innovation. Rather than altering the Act to reduce protections, resources should be directed toward improving implementation, funding recovery programs, and fostering collaboration among stakeholders.
For these reasons, I urge you to oppose any changes that would weaken the Endangered Species Act. Protecting our nation’s wildlife heritage is not only an environmental responsibility, but a moral obligation to future generations.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely, Michelle

title: Comment from Cruz, Elizabeth

text:
I am writing to express my deep concern about the proposed changes to how the US Fish and Wildlife Service administers protections for threatened species under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). These changes would have direct and harmful consequences for the ecosystems and communities where I live.
Under the current ESA framework, species listed as threatened automatically receive nearly all of the same protections afforded to endangered species, with only limited exceptions. This longstanding approach ensures that vulnerable species receive immediate, baseline safeguards against harm, giving them the best possible chance to stabilize and recover before their populations decline further.
The proposed rule would reverse this protective default. Instead of automatically extending these essential safeguards, ever newly listed threatened species would require a separate, species-specific rule under section 4(d) to determine what protections they receive, if any. This shift would make the exception the norm. It would also introduce significant delays, uncertainty, and inconsistency to a process that is already time-sensitive for species in dire need.
Species-specific rules take time to develop and cannot reliably provide the comprehensive protections that threatened species need. During these delays, species would remain vulnerable to harassment, habitat degradation, and other forms of harm that the ESA is designed to prevent. For ecosystems like those in my region of the Texas Hill Country, where species are tightly interconnected, these gaps in protection would have cascading effects on water quality, habitat stability, and overall ecological health.
The proposed changes could directly affect efforts to secure protections for imperiled salamander species in Central Texas, including the Pedernales River Springs Salamander and the Lipan Salamander. If these species were listed as threatened rather than endangered under the new rule, they would no longer be guaranteed timely or adequate protections. Given how sensitive these salamanders are to groundwater quality, spring flow, and habitat disturbance, any delay in safeguards could have irreversible consequences for the species and the health of aquifer-fed ecosystems that our local communities depend on.
For these reasons, I urge the Fish and Wildlife Service to maintain the current default protections for threatened species. The ESA has been successful for decades precisely because it provides swift, science-based protections at the moment a species is recognized as being at risk. Weakening that foundation would undermine recovery efforts, jeopardize vulnerable species, and harm the ecosystems that sustain both wildlife and people.
title: Comment from Bjornson, Kirsten

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

Wildlife letter:

Good evening! I am submitting a comment because I am troubled by the potential harm this could do to the creatures we share this world with. They cannot obliterate our population and we owe them the same respect. The United States is a series of beautiful, unique and extremely complex ecosystems and environments. Why in the world are we proposing changes that could endanger that which makes this country unique? I care about a scientifically informed approach to protecting our ecosystems. The proposed changes come from a distinctly industry focused perspective. This shifts decision making away from the public who will actually live to suffer from these changes. In fact the ESA has been effective because it has been informed and strongly regulated by the government, the public, and expert scientific opinion. The ESA become weaker and those who benefit from that are a microbe compared to those who suffer. The consultation rule proposal (Section 7) appears to weaken federal reviews for projects that could irreversibly damage American ecosystems. Anyone who wants that is an idiot or uncaring of our critters, and neither should be anywhere near our ecosystems. Our federal oversights on the ESA are sometimes all we have to keep greedy companies in check as they turn priceless life into a few dollars. We ought to be increasing these protections for those animals who cannot protect themselves and these environments which will never again regrow in our lifetimes. Humans will survive, these unique American Animals like the Hellbender will die. Is it not God’s will that humanity take care of his creations? We’re watching, us who see life instead of profit. I ask these proposed changes be withdrawn and the ESA left intact as is unless more protections for wildlife are actually being considered. Strong, scientific, protections and comprehensive and meaningful federal review of these protections are a public demand. Let us ensure the safety of those environments not just for us but for all and all to come. Please don’t kill my hellbender buddies and all the other animals these changes would endanger.

title: Comment from Rome, Heather

text:
I am writing to you to oppose FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029. This proposal would weaken protections for endangered and newly listed species by eliminating automatic safeguards and forcing case-by-case political fights over whether a species deserves protection; it would narrow the definition of critical habitat, excluding areas species need to recover as climate change accelerates; it would allow economic and corporate impacts to outweigh scientific evidence in listing decisions; and limit the scope of federal review so agencies can more easily greenlight harmful projects like logging, mining and drilling, when they place wildlife in harm’s way. We depend on this ecosystem and biodiversity. Growing up in South Florida, I witnessed firsthand the habitat loss causing more animals to venture into (recent) housing developments and get killed. I also witnessed more wildlife getting hit by cars. There’s also been more hunting of animals without any protections. I now live in New York State and I’m witnessing the same issues. Native Wildlife forced from their habitats for the growing housing and industry developments. Plants and trees uprooted and cut down which then also devastates insect survival and reproduction. These species are already threatened and some are on the brink of extinction. Surely with this passed they will be pushed to extinction and those who have made a comeback will be vulnerable once again. We need to protect all of our wildlife and native plant species because our own survival depends on it. Everything is connected in the ecosystem and if one keystone species is wiped out then we all suffer. The Endangered Species Act works because it centers science and the public interest—not political pressure or economic influence. I care about collaboration and governments working together with agencies and communities to protect wildlife and their habitats so we can coexist together. Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide. And removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed. Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife. Most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections. I want the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections.
Please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so states and industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife. I ask you to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems. Thank you!

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. text:
I am opposed to the proposed changes, and any changes that would weaken, limit, or undermine the Endangered Species Act or its enactment. A vast majority of Americans want a strong Endangered Species Act, want it strongly enacted, and fully funded. The proposed removal of Section 4(d) Blanket Rule would reduce protections for threatened animals and plants that are listed in the future, and therefore is counter to the intent of the ESA and the will of the majority of Americans.

Removing the blanket 4(d) rule would weaken protection for threatened species and encourage further political interference in the recovery process. By automatically applying the same prohibitions against “take” as given to endangered species (making it illegal to kill, injure, harm, or harass threatened animals), and rescinding or restricting protections when and where advisable, this regulation has helped move threatened species towards recovery for nearly 40 years. If the 4(d) rule is rescinded, I am concerned that newly listed threatened species will be afforded little to no protection. I am also concerned that political or corporate pressure may lead to more “threatened” designation of species that are truly “endangered” in order to facilitate industry and other development interests by removing requirements to minimize harm to threatened species. I urge the Services to retain the blanket 4(d) rule and maintain the existing practice of creating special rules on a case by case basis where more specific or tailored protections are needed based on scientific data. This interpretation resembles some earlier, unsuccessful legislative proposals, including the 2004 “Sound Science for Endangered Species Act Planning Act” (H.R. 1662) that sought to limit the use of predictive models in listing decisions. Such approaches directly contradict recommendations from the National Research Council’s report entitled “Science and the Endangered Species Act,” which recommended greater use of predictive modeling techniques such as population viability analysis in decision-making. In the wolverine decision, the FWS characterized the evidence of threats from loss of snow cover as “speculative,” imposing a higher level of proof for climate-driven threats. A federal court overturned this decision, concluding that “No greater level of certainty is needed to see the writing on the wall for this snow-dependent species standing squarely in the path of global climate change.” Codifying this approach through the proposed definition of “foreseeable future” would risk denying protections to many species due to perceived uncertainty. As the Court emphasized, the ESA requires “action at the earliest possible, defensible point in time to protect against the loss of biodiversity within our reach as a nation.” I urge the USFWS to withdraw the proposed definition of foreseeable future and develop one consistent with the precautionary intent of the Endangered Species Act and the best available climate science.

In addition, if enacted this would require each species to have its own rules set, and with the current administration’s staffing and funding reductions, the proposed changes would certainly result in a delay and backlog of protection decisions.
Natural solutions can combat flooding, aquifer depletion, pest control, water filtration, air filtration, soil regeneration and cleaning, and carbon sequestration far better and far far cheaper than human-based solutions can. We have to protect and invest in the species and habitats that generate this ecological capital - or the security, welfare, and wealth of all Americans will suffer. A strong ESA works to achieve that goal, and these proposed changes seem to run counter to it.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. text:
Hey Fish and Wildlife folks, I am writing as a California resident who spends significant time along our state's coastline and in the Lake Tahoe Basin. These landscapes have shaped my understanding of how fragile and interconnected our natural systems are, and I am deeply troubled by the proposed weakening of Endangered Species Act protections.
In coastal California, I've witnessed the delicate balance that supports species like the snowy plover and California least tern. At Lake Tahoe, I've seen firsthand how even small changes in habitat can ripple through an ecosystem. The clarity of that alpine lake depends on intact watersheds and healthy forests that provide refuge for species like the Sierra Nevada yellow-legged frog and countless others.
The current proposal to remove automatic protections for newly listed species is particularly concerning. When a species reaches the point of requiring ESA listing, immediate action is critical—not bureaucratic delays that could allow further decline during the most vulnerable period.
Similarly, eliminating consistent baseline protections for threatened species invites a patchwork approach that could leave wildlife unprotected in precisely the places where they're struggling most. The coastal and alpine environments I care about don't recognize administrative boundaries, and our protections shouldn't either.
I'm also concerned about changes that would expand the ability to exclude critical habitat based on economic considerations. Both the California coast and the Tahoe Basin face intense development pressure. Allowing economic interests to override habitat science would undermine the ecosystems that sustain not only endangered species but also the recreational opportunities and natural heritage that define these regions.
Weakening federal consultation requirements would further reduce accountability for projects that could harm imperiled wildlife. In California, where we've seen the consequences of habitat fragmentation and water management conflicts, strong federal oversight provides essential safeguards that complement state efforts.
I urge you to withdraw these proposed rule changes and maintain the ESA's foundation in biological science and comprehensive protection. The Act has succeeded because it prioritizes recovery over convenience. These proposed changes would reverse that priority at exactly the wrong moment in our biodiversity crisis.

The ESA provides critical federal oversight to an assessment process that select industries would otherwise weaken, but this oversight is necessary to protect America's iconic wild species.

The proposed rule changes threaten democratic processes by reducing public accountability and transparent science. text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.
The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.
Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.
I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species

text:
Subject: OPPOSITION to Proposed Revisions to ESA Regulations (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039)

To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service:

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act regulations announced on November 19, 2025. Specifically, I object to the rescission of the “Blanket Rule” under Section 4(d) and the re-introduction of economic considerations into listing decisions.

1. Restore the Blanket Rule: Removing the automatic protections for “Threatened” species creates a dangerous gap in enforcement. For species like the Tope Shark, which is currently awaiting listing decisions, this change means they could be listed as threatened but remain legally unprotected from harvest for years while species-specific rules are drafted. This delay could lead to functionally extinct populations before a single protection is enforced.

2. Science Over Profit: The ESA was designed to base extinction decisions solely on science. Re-introducing economic impact assessments into the listing and critical habitat designation process inevitably prioritizes short-term industry profits over long-term biodiversity. For highly migratory species like the Oceanic Whitetip Shark and Scalloped Hammerhead, protecting critical habitat is often inconvenient for commercial fisheries. That inconvenience is not a valid reason to allow a species to go extinct.

3. Lessons from Success: The recovery of the Eastern North Pacific (California) Gray Whale and Southern Sea Otter proves that strict, automatic protections work. The ESA has saved 99% of species listed under fifty years since the ESA was enacted. The California Gray whale population numbered only a few thousand when it was listed in 1973. The rebuilding of the population- up to 27,000 in 2016 led to the delisting of the whale in a great success story. However, a lack of food and other threats have put this whale back into peril, underscoring the need for vigilance. Weakening the ESA would ensures that other threatened species will not share in the success story shared by plants and animals protected in the past.

I urge you to withdraw these proposals and maintain the automatic protections that have prevented the extinction of 99% of listed species. I am deeply upset by the proposed changes and what they will mean for the survival of our diverse wildlife. I want my son to live in a country that protects our unique species, ensuring that future generations will be able to know these special plants and animals.

Sincerely,
Erin Loury
Santa Cruz, CA

I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Neilson, A.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I am writing to oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. I am an underwater photographer who works in both marine and freshwater environments, and I derive part of my income as well as a deep sense of purpose from healthy, functioning ecosystems. Through my work, I have spent years observing California’s kelp forests, headwater streams, and remote coastal and freshwater habitats. These are places whose survival often depends on strong federal protections when other pressures would otherwise push them toward collapse.
I have seen firsthand how fragile these systems already are. Kelp forests are declining under the combined stress of warming waters, altered food webs, and cumulative human impacts. Headwater freshwater ecosystems are especially vulnerable. Though often out of sight, they are critical to downstream rivers, fisheries, and communities. These are exactly the kinds of places the Endangered Species Act was designed to protect when short term economic interests threaten long term ecological health.
The proposed rule changes would undermine that purpose. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule for threatened species weakens protections at the stage when they matter most. Recovery depends on early and consistent safeguards. Forcing case by case determinations opens the door to delay, inconsistency, and political influence that the ESA was intended to prevent.
Similarly, narrowing the criteria for critical habitat exclusions under Section 4(b)(2) risks allowing economic considerations to outweigh the protection of essential habitat. A species cannot be protected without protecting the environment it depends on. When habitat is compromised, recovery becomes impossible, and the damage extends beyond individual species to entire ecosystems.
Limiting federal consultation under Section 7 further erodes accountability. Federal oversight is often the only effective check on state wildlife governance systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests. Reducing the scope of review makes it easier for harmful projects to proceed without fully assessing their impacts on imperiled wildlife and the ecosystems that support them.
Taken together, these changes would hollow out the Endangered Species Act and leave it unable to meet its core mission. At a time of accelerating biodiversity loss and climate driven ecosystem stress, weakening one of our most effective conservation laws is a serious mistake.
I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and uphold the intent of the Endangered Species Act. Please maintain strong, science based federal protections so future generations inherit living, resilient ecosystems rather than a record of preventable loss.

title: Comment from Scholvin, Joan

text:
Docket Number FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029

I urge you to withdraw the proposed rule change that would remove the "blanket rule" option.

I do support listing decisions and critical habitat designations based on the status of the species in question, as supported by best-available scientific knowledge. However, species-specific rules, while necessary for long-term recovery of the species, require significant time and energy to be created. Due to chronic underfunding and exacerbated by the recent large-scale firings by DOGE, FWS has neither sufficient qualified staff nor the resources to prepare species-specific rules in a timely manner.

Quantitative data illustrate this point. Based on evaluation of 40 years of records, Puckett et al 2016 found that species waited a median 12.1 years between first consideration and ESA listing. These process times exceed ESA deadlines, which are two years when initiated from a third party. Such delays can perpetuate population declines and hinder recovery efforts. [Puckett, Kesler, Greenwald (2016). "Taxa, petitioning agency, and lawsuits affect time spent awaiting listing under the US Endangered Species Act," Biological Conservation, 201: 220-229.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocon.2016.07.005]

Removing the blanket rule option would weaken protections for species listed as threatened, and leave them subject to ongoing “take” including killing and disturbance. The blanket rule provides needed protections until species-specific rules are drafted. Broad baseline protections such as that provided by the blanket rule option minimize the danger that species fall prey to regulatory gaps or the influence of special-interest groups.
title: Comment from Fabryka-Martin, June

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species because these actions are the opposite of the clear intent of the Endangered Species Act. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design. The blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing. Withholding any protections while the cumbersome and oft-delayed species specific rules are developed would allow harm to progress and increase the likelihood that threatened species become extinct
Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.
The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.
For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.
title: Comment from Albrecht, Steve

text:
submitting this comment because biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter deeply to me. As a resident of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, I regularly see the effects of habitat loss and environmental degradation, and I am concerned about proposals that would weaken protections for imperiled species. I strongly value science-informed stewardship of our nation’s wildlife.

The Endangered Species Act is effective because it centers scientific evidence and the public interest rather than political pressure or short-term economic influence. Science tells us what species need to survive; our values determine whether we act on that knowledge. These proposed changes move decision-making away from both by allowing industry considerations to outweigh biological need and scientific reality.

Several aspects of the proposal are deeply concerning. Removing automatic protections for newly listed species would leave vulnerable wildlife exposed at the very moment protection is most critical. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule for threatened species would result in inconsistent protections and delay recovery. Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions risks allowing economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening entire ecosystems. Limiting federal consultation and review would further reduce oversight and allow damaging projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered species.

Federal oversight is often the only meaningful check on state wildlife systems already shaped by industry influence. Weakening these safeguards reduces transparency and public accountability at a time when Americans overwhelmingly support stronger conservation protections.

I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the Endangered Species Act’s strong, science-based protections. Please uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit resilient, thriving ecosystems.

title: Comment from Rynearson, Kaity

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Novak, Casey

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed removal of the blanket rule that automatically extends key Endangered Species Act protections to newly listed threatened species. This rule has long ensured that species receive immediate protection from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited take once they are listed.

Eliminating this safeguard would leave newly listed threatened species vulnerable for years while species specific rules are developed. During that gap, populations could experience irreversible harm. Species currently proposed for listing, including the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly, are already facing serious and well documented threats. Delaying protections after a listing decision is finalized directly undermines the purpose of the Endangered Species Act.

The strength of the Act lies in its ability to provide timely and effective protection when species are determined to be at risk. Removing automatic protections weakens conservation outcomes, increases uncertainty, and creates unnecessary risk for species that can least afford further decline.

I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to retain the blanket rule and ensure that all newly listed threatened species receive immediate and meaningful protections consistent with the intent of the Endangered Species Act.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this comment.

I strongly urge you to not finalize proposed rules under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will reduce the ability to conserve and recover vulnerable birds and other wildlife, and increase uncertainty for the public.

Third, changes to critical habitat designations, such as those around unoccupied habitat, will keep wildlife experts from addressing the needs and threats impacting species.

Again, I urge you to reject these proposals that would weaken the implementation of the ESA and its ability to serve as a vital tool to recover our country's imperiled birds.

text:
Please accept the attached submission of 427 public comments in response to several proposed regulatory changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA), including proposed revisions to ESA Sections 4(b), 4(d), 4, and 7.

While many of these comments share similar language and concerns, each represents an individual comment submitted by a distinct member of the public. Several comments are further customized and personalized. Although these comments are transmitted together for administrative convenience, they should be reviewed, counted, and considered as individual public comments and not as a single consolidated submission.

Collectively, these comments express strong opposition to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s and National Marine Fisheries Service’s proposed revisions to the ESA. For more than fifty years, the ESA has been one of our nation’s most effective conservation laws, preventing the extinction of 99 percent of listed species. It is not broken. The proposed rules would undermine this success by elevating speculative or industry-driven economic considerations over the best available science and the survival and recovery of imperiled species.

Across the attached comments, individuals raise serious concerns that the proposed changes would:

Encourage the exclusion of critical habitat based on speculative or industry-provided economic information, contrary to the ESA’s science-based mandate and longstanding legal precedent;
Weaken listing decisions by improperly treating economic impacts as “commercial data,” despite decades of agency practice and court rulings to the contrary;
Delay or deny essential protections for newly listed threatened species by eliminating automatic take prohibitions under Section 4(d);
Narrow the scope of Section 7 consultations by restricting consideration of cumulative, foreseeable, and baseline impacts that are often decisive for species survival;
Limit recognition of climate-driven risks by unduly constraining the concept of the “foreseeable future”;
Undermine protections for distinct populations and recovery efforts by narrowing interpretations of “species” and restricting critical habitat to currently occupied areas.

As reflected in these comments, such changes would place already vulnerable species at heightened risk, including northern spotted owls, northwestern pond turtles, salmon and steelhead populations, wolverines, and wolves. In states like Oregon, where species face compounding pressures from habitat loss, climate change, and drought, the consequences of these revisions would be immediate and lasting.

The ESA’s strength lies in its consistent, science-based application and its clear focus on preventing extinction and promoting recovery. The attached commenters urge the Services to withdraw these proposals and to uphold the ESA’s longstanding, legally sound protections for wildlife and the ecosystems upon which they depend.

text:
As a citizen of the United States, I take tremendous pride in our unique, awe-inspiring native wildlife species. These species are an integral part of my state and national identity, both for me and many others. The Endangered Species Act is a critical piece of legislation that has a proven track record of success for ensuring the protection of these species both for current citizens of the U.S. and for posterity, having prevented an estimated 291 species’ extinction and saved an estimated 99% of listed species (Greenwald et al. 2019 “Extinction and the U.S. Endangered Species Act”). The success of the Endangered Species Act has been seen in population recoveries of species such as the red-cockaded woodpecker (Dryobates borealis, downlisted to Threatened in 2024) and the Kirtland’s warbler (Setophaga kirtlandii, delisted in 2019), and this Act is recognized internationally as a premier example of effective biodiversity conservation legislation.
I am commenting in regards to the proposed changes to Section 4(d) as outlined in FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029, and I ask the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to NOT enact these changes and to instead retain the 2024 regulations.
One crucial aspect that has contributed to the Endangered Species Act’s success are providing prompt protections and recovery plans for all listed species (see Martin et al. 2005 “The Effectiveness of the Endangered Species Act: A Quantitative Analysis”). Removing the blanket protections afforded to threatened species and forcing each species to have protections evaluated on a case by case basis would create unnecessary delays in the creation of recovery plans for these species. These delays will mean critical population and habitat losses, pushing these species closer to needing endangered status rather than closer to delisting, as is the goal of the act. Additionally, requiring species-specific rules will overburden the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service biologists and staff charged with creating them, many of whom are already operating with reduced staff capacity. Retaining the current framework and allowing for blanket protections for threatened species allows for a more rapid assessment and response that enables on the ground conservation to be enacted in a timely manner.
In summary, the proposed changes would hinder the Endangered Species Act’s proven effectiveness and ultimately, lead to population declines of our beloved native species. Keep the Endangered Species Act strong and keep the tools to protect nature in the hands of the communities who live among and care for these rare, native species.

text:
I submit this comment in support of maintaining the Endangered Species Act as a strong, science-based statute and retaining regulatory interpretations that faithfully carry out Congress’s intent.

Section 4 of the Act is foundational. Listing, delisting, and critical habitat determinations control whether any of the Act’s substantive protections apply. For that reason, the standards governing these decisions matter. Congress was explicit that listing determinations must be based solely on the best scientific and commercial data available. That directive reflects a deliberate choice to insulate extinction decisions from short-term economic or political pressures. Regulatory interpretations that narrow or weaken this framework risk undermining the core structure of the Act.

The ESA was enacted because extinction is permanent. Once a species is lost, there is no corrective action that can undo that outcome. Section 4 operates as a front-end safeguard against irreversible harm by requiring decisions to be grounded in evidence and long-term consequences rather than immediate convenience.

Habitat protection is central to this framework. Congress identified habitat destruction as a primary driver of species decline and required designation of critical habitat to the maximum extent prudent and determinable. Critical habitat is one of the Act’s primary conservation tools. It directs federal agencies to consider how their actions affect the physical and biological features necessary for a species’ survival and recovery. Weakening or minimizing this tool undercuts the Act’s conservation purpose.

The Act’s effectiveness is well established. Species such as the bald eagle, gray wolf, and American alligator recovered because listing and habitat protections were applied consistently and over time. These outcomes show that the ESA functions as intended when its standards remain clear and grounded in science.

The ESA also reflects a basic responsibility. Human activity has accelerated extinction through development, pollution, and climate change. The Act represents a policy judgment that the federal government has a role in preventing avoidable loss where the causes are known and within human control.

Maintaining a strong ESA also benefits people directly. Healthy ecosystems support agriculture, fisheries, water quality, recreation, and local economies. Conservation under the Act is not abstract. It is tied to long-term environmental stability and public welfare.

For these reasons, I support maintaining ESA regulations that preserve science-based decision-making and fully implement the Act’s conservation purposes. The Endangered Species Act has endured because it works. It should continue to be applied in a manner consistent with its text, structure, and intent.

text:
I’m writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed revisions to the regulations governing species listing and critical habitat designation under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).
The proposed revisions flagrantly exceed the agency’s authority in a way that is entirely impermissible. Congress could not have been clearer when it directed the Secretary to make listing determinations “solely on the basis of the best scientific and commercial data available” (16 U.S.C. § 1533(b)(1)(A)). The statute does not leave room for policy preferences, economic balancing, or administrative discretion on this question. It is a mandatory, unqualified instruction. The Supreme Court has repeatedly stated that when Congress speaks with this level of clarity, agencies are bound by that command. They do not have license to revisit or dilute it.
The proposed rule attempts to do exactly that. By introducing economic considerations into the listing process, considerations Congress expressly excluded, the agency is asserting a power it does not possess. This is not a matter of interpretation or gap-filling; it is a direct contradiction of the statutory text. An agency may not override Congress because it prefers a different policy outcome, nor may it recast a prohibited factor as a permissible one through regulatory language. Doing so would effectively amend the statute by regulation, something no agency has the authority to do.
Additionally, the proposed narrowing of critical habitat designations is inconsistent with both the statutory text and longstanding judicial interpretation. Critical habitat must include both occupied and unoccupied areas essential for conservation and recovery. By imposing new constraints on unoccupied habitat, including requirements that effectively preclude designating future climate-suitable habitat, the rule undermines the recovery mandate at the heart of the ESA. The Supreme Court has affirmed that “conservation” means recovery, not mere survival. Any rule that prevents the Service from designating habitat needed for recovery is contrary to law.
The ESA is a statute whose commands are specific. The agency does not have discretion to disregard them. These proposed revisions are in defiance of the law and should be rescinded.
