text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

I am writing out of deep concern for the future of manatees to urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):
•Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039
•Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029
•Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044
•Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048

I strongly oppose these proposed regulations because they would significantly weaken the protections available to manatees and countless other imperiled species at a time when those protections are more necessary than ever.

I have had the privilege of traveling to Florida and experiencing manatees in person - an experience that was the highlight of my entire year. Seeing these gentle, curious animals in their natural habitat made clear to me what is at stake when we talk about conservation policy. I am now the adoptive parent of two manatees, a commitment that reflects not only personal affection, but a belief that we have a responsibility to protect species whose survival depends on thoughtful, science-based regulation.

Manatees are a powerful example of why the ESA matters. Since their federal listing in 1967, manatee populations have increased, largely due to ESA-driven protections. At the same time, their threats have intensified. The 2020–2022 Unusual Mortality Event, which claimed the lives of more than 1,200 manatees due to starvation from seagrass loss, demonstrated how precarious their recovery remains. More than 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm-water outfalls from power plants to survive winter months, and as these facilities transition away from warm-water discharges, manatees urgently need alternative protected winter habitat. Additional ongoing threats- from watercraft strikes to water control structures - continue to injure and kill manatees each year. One of my adopted manatees, Paddy Doyle, was killed from a boat strike this year. When I had to tell my 9-year-old godson that our manatee - who was otherwise healthy - had been killed by a boat, he cried so hard that it tore my heart open. I cannot begin to imagine the grief it will cause when more manatees die if they lose these protections.

These realities underscore why it is essential to maintain or strengthen ESA regulations, not weaken them. Proposed changes such as eliminating the “blanket 4(d)” rule for threatened species would leave animals like the Florida manatee vulnerable to killing, harassment, and other harmful activities. Further, increasing barriers to designating critical habitat and allowing economic considerations to override biological necessity would deny species the protections they need to survive and recover.

Manatees are Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of local economies through wildlife tourism. More importantly, they are sentient, long-lived animals whose survival depends on our willingness to prioritize conservation over short-term convenience. Weakening the ESA now would place manatees at even greater risk during a period when forward-looking, adaptive conservation is urgently required.

I respectfully urge you to withdraw these proposed regulations and uphold the foundational protections of the Endangered Species Act. The future of manatees- and countless other species - depends on it.

Respectfully submitted,
Mishelle McCall
title: Comment from McCall, Mishelle

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the longstanding “blanket 4(d) protections” for threatened species.

Section 4(d) of the ESA directs the Secretary to issue *protective regulations that are “necessary and advisable to provide for the conservation” of species listed as threatened. Without such a rule, threatened species do not automatically receive the substantive protections afforded to endangered species under Section 9, including prohibitions on take, possession, or other harmful activities. ￼

For decades, the “blanket 4(d) rule” ensured that key protections—such as prohibitions on take—automatically applied to newly listed threatened species unless a narrower species-specific rule was promulgated. This automatic, science-based baseline was critical to prevent immediate harm to vulnerable species during their most precarious period of decline.

Eliminating the blanket rule introduces delays and uncertainty in extending essential protections. Species newly listed as threatened could go without protective regulations for months or even years while tailored rules are developed—a period when they are most at risk of further decline. Broad ecological and population studies show that early intervention and preventative protections can significantly reduce extinction risk; delaying such protections would be inconsistent with the ESA’s precautionary and conservation mandates. The Service has provided no evidence that the blanket rule imposes undue regulatory costs but has proposed to remove it despite clear ecological risk. ￼

The blanket rule historically helped ensure coherence between threatened and endangered species protections and prevented regulatory gaps. Rescinding it diminishes species safeguards without demonstrating necessary and advisable conservation benefits, and this deficiency undermines the ESA’s purpose to proactively conserve species before they become critically imperiled. I urge you to rescind the proposed rule.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Mallegol-Hansen, Jessica

text:
Species richness and healthy ecosystems are deeply and profoundly connected to human well-being in both a physical and emotional capacity, which is why I adamantly and vehemently OPPOSE all four proposed rules changes designed to weaken the Endangered Species Act. The ESA has helped to protect habitat that is enjoyed by all from hunters and nature enthusiasts to tourism industry and more.
Healthy, biodiverse ecosystems provide essential services such as clean air, clean water, pollination of crops, and natural disease regulation. For example, diverse ecosystems can reduce the spread of infectious diseases by limiting the dominance of disease-carrying species (often called the “dilution effect”), which directly benefits human health. Studies also show that people exposed to greener, more biologically diverse environments experience lower stress, improved mood, and reduced risks of anxiety and depression. Biodiversity-rich green spaces are linked to better psychological restoration than less diverse or degraded environments. This is why every species habitat we threaten with human development or industrial activity without the strictest protections in place impacts our own state of wellbeing. Protecting species also personally goes far beyond my own benefit as a human-being because I view the natural world as inherently valuable, independent of what benefits it brings to me, and I am certainly not alone. Most Americans are in support of stronger environmental protection and wildlife conservation measures.

All of this combined and more is why it is incredibly crucial to protect and uphold, even strengthen the ESA, especially in the era in which we now find ourselves. The scales have always been tipped well-against the natural world’s favor as species and their natural habitats don’t have the power of human industrial lobbyists, corporate money and extraction interests on their side, in fact those entities tend to all to often be in exact opposition and constant conflict with our environmental and ecological world. Look at any map showing the scale of habitat fragmentation and loss in our country over time. It’s only getting worse.
These proposed rules should be withdrawn to prevent weakening the Endangered Species Act and to keep its protections firmly based on science.
•Please withdrawal Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species puts vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery can begin. These species may remain unprotected while recovery plans are delayed.
•Please withdrawal Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Removing the standard protections for threatened species would lead to uneven safeguards and slow recovery, even though these species need strong protection now.
•Please withdrawal Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing the rules for excluding critical habitat could let economic concerns outweigh habitat protection, putting ecosystems at risk—not just individual species.
•Please withdrawal Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Reducing federal review would allow harmful projects to move forward without fully considering their impact on endangered wildlife.
These proposed rule changes are not grounded in sound science, ecology, or a fair democratic process. Limiting public comment to just 30 days—timed right before the holidays—undermines meaningful public participation on changes of enormous consequence. After more than 30 years witnessing the devastation caused by habitat loss in my home region, I know how difficult it already is to protect wildlife. Weakening transparency and review only pushes us further in the wrong direction. I strongly oppose all four proposals, which together would dismantle the most effective law we have to protect wild species and wild places. Attacking the Endangered Species Act runs directly counter to the public interest. What is at stake is irreversible: once species and ecosystems are lost, they are gone forever. The ESA works. It should be upheld and strengthened—not weakened. Thank you.

title: Comment from Brown , Aidan

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

Greetings, I am a concerned citizen regarding this proposed revision. While I don’t have any official experience in regard to wildlife management or any degrees or certifications in this field, I certainly can make up for that in terms of my knowledge and passion regarding wildlife conservation and ecological science as a whole. That being said, I understand the importance proper conservation and regulation has on our society and the health of our species as a whole. Everything I have stated leads me to strongly oppose the revision to section 4(d) proposing to remove the “blanket rule”. It seems to me that the blanket rule has been crucial in providing a necessary buffer for any new threatened species to guarantee they get whatever protections they need as soon as possible by deeming them to require the same care as endangered species without consideration of economic impacts. On paper, this may seem like too many protections to guarantee to every new threatened species or a waste of potential profits, but the benefit of protecting threatened species with the best care is worth it. According to the Institute for Environmental Research and Education, which is a nonprofit organization that uses fact-based evidence to help with environmental policy making, a healthy environment is absolutely required for economic growth due to the benefits gained from needing to spend less money on natural disasters, for example, and the potential for new jobs that increased ecology management could have. Those are just two crucial reasons to always consider the environmental impacts before economics. If this seems unrelated, it is not, since nature is a closed system; the harm caused by fewer protections on the threatened species will ripple to more natural disasters, which turn into economic damage. One must also consider the public disapproval these measures have due to the importance the environment and biodiversity have to the public’s well-being. In conclusion, due to the reasons I have listed and many more left out, I think these revisions will cause more harm than good and, quite frankly, should be left as they are. Any alternative recommendations I have include simply increasing wildlife and ecological protections to increase jobs if that is a concern, and leaving the current rules as they are, since they do a sufficient job.
​
Citations: Team, I. (2025, June 30). Why is the environment important?. The Institute for Environmental Research and Education. https://iere.org/why-is-environment-important/

text:

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am writing to express my firm opposition to any attempts to weaken the Endangered Species Act (ESA) as it currently stands, including through eliminating the ESA's "blanket 4(d) rule." This rule provides essential protection for populations of threatened species who are not yet but likely to be determined endangered at a future date. Its elimination would significantly and unacceptably increase the risk that these populations would decline even more precipitously. Providing equal protection for both threatened and endangered species is a critical part of the huge success of the ESA. Furthermore, the rule as it currently stands ALREADY allows USFWS to issue special rules for each listed species, so its removal is entirely unwarranted on these grounds.

In reality, eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule outright would place a much greater burden on the agency, forcing it to issue specific 4(d) rules for each and every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements. For the sake of a fully-functioning Endangered Species Act in service of our country's irreplaceable array of unique and diverse species, all of whom are a vital part of our heritage as Americans, I urge you to retract this and any other proposed regulatory changes like it.

text:
As someone who grew up in rural Iowa, spending a lot of my childhood playing in the local woods and backroads, I have seen over the course of my life as nature has lost it’s lustre. I no longer see the summer lightning bugs, I know that the populations of bees (Vital to our ecosystems) have been lessening and suffering.

Through my schooling, our teachers in environmental sciences, nature and just general sciences as early as elementary talked about how important biodiversity are to maintaining a healthy ecosystem. The world around us is our most precious resource, not for monetary reasons, not for what we can take from it, but from the beauty and life it brings us. I can’t say I know a lot of folks in my area that want to see the local woodlands turned into empty space or, worse, another slot of flattened land waiting for some plant or warehouse or data center to be plopped down. I can’t imagine folks elsewhere in the country look forward to such a thing either, unless they are directly profiting from it, and folks like that are the very few.

And part of the protections of such areas comes directly from federal protections, and this proposal as well as others I am commenting on, will put the lands of our forefathers at risk of destruction solely to benefit a few.

We cannot remove automatic protections because it would obviously leave open time that species go without protection.

Removal of blanket protection also leads to issues of delays and inconsistency.

And limiting federal review, and narrowing the criteria for habitat exclusions, both open the door for opaque actions and corruption if our wildlands are going to be put at less importance than what some businessman things they can wring out of it. These things need to be approached scientifically and carefully.

People want stronger conservation protection, we love our home and country, and we don’t want our land carved up and our wildlife lost because someone in some office wants to work around the protections to see a profit sooner.

I want my government to value science and our homeland, so nature can recover and so those who come after can have a chance to have the sort of childhood I did.
title: Comment from Vote, Allen

text:
I strongly support retaining the blanket 4(d) rule because it has been essential for providing immediate protections to newly listed threatened species since 1978. This rule ensures that species are safeguarded against threats such as take, sale, and transport while species-specific rules are developed. If the blanket rule is rescinded, I am deeply concerned about how the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) will guarantee timely protections without delaying the listing process. Until a viable alternative is in place, I believe the blanket rule should remain. In my view, increasing staff and funding is critical to meet the workload demands of species-specific rulemaking.

Although species-specific rules are ultimately preferable, I oppose the proposed regulatory change. Specifically, I object to inserting “…that were added to the List of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife at §17.11(h) on or prior to [EFFECTIVE DATE OF THE FINAL RULE]” into CFR §17.31 Prohibitions and urge that this proposal be rescinded.

I also request that economic impacts be removed from consideration when determining species-specific rules (§17.31(d)). The Endangered Species Act was created to prevent extinction and promote recovery, and economic factors should not override these objectives. If economic considerations remain, I believe USFWS must provide transparency about how recovery goals will be achieved within those constraints.
While consistency between USFWS and NMFS is admirable, I do not believe it justifies eliminating the blanket rule. If consistency is the goal, NMFS should adopt the blanket rule rather than USFWS removing it.

Finally, if USFWS moves forward with rescinding the blanket rule, I urge the agency to prepare an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) under NEPA. Removing these protections will have significant cumulative impacts, including delayed listings and species being listed as threatened without any protections in place. Under these scenarios, take of species and habitat degradation may continue unchecked, reducing recovery prospects and increasing the likelihood of extinction. Additionally, requiring case-by-case rulemaking will further burden an already overstretched agency, slowing the listing process and putting more species at risk.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on these proposed changes. I appreciate your consideration and strongly urge USFWS to maintain the blanket rule until a practical alternative is implemented.

title: Comment from Bilderback, Marcia

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed Section 4(d) (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029): Threatened Species Protections: the proposed changes to Section 4(d) would end or weaken automatic protections for threatened species, turning what is now a strong default safeguard into a flexible, often politically influenced, case-by-case framework. For Wolves that are listed as threatened or down listed from endangered to threatened, this would open the door to recreational hunting, trapping, & expanded lethal control long before populations are biologically secure. Gray Wolves face extreme pressures across the West in WY, MT, & Idaho some of the most aggressive hunting & trapping regimes in the U.S., with year round killing, unlimited quotas, night hunting & bounty-style reimbursements. Such pressure fragments packs, removes lead Wolves, weakens genetic integrity, & increases susceptibility to disease events such as manage & distemper. Western Wolves are not recovered. WA state recently declined to send Wolves to CO due to it's own declining numbers & unanswered questions about population stability. Oregon suffers from chronic poaching crisis. CA has only around 70 Wolves w high pup mortality. CO's reintroduction has stalled & NV only receives occasional dispersers. In the Great Lakes the region supports some of the largest remaining Wolf populations in the lower 48, but they are not immune to over harvest or high kill numbers. Wisconsin's February 2021 spring hunt demonstrated how quickly a population can be heavily reduced when management is politically driven & not grounded in science. Current science shows effective population sizes should be above N=500, perhaps N=1,000 to maintain connectivity, genetic resilience. MN does not meet that standard so connectivity with Wisconsin Wolves is critical & removing or lessening protections of Wolves in these states for this reason alone jeopardizes genetic health These populations require strong ESA Protections, not regulatory weakening.

Stripping automatic protections for threatened species would expose Grizzlies to sport hunting and hostile state management. Under the current ESA framework, Grizzlies are protected from intentional "harm", harassment, killing or other "take" without very limited exemptions. These protections help keep human-caused deaths at a lower level. Weakening ESA protections would allow lethal removal of bears in conflict areas, i.e. livestock predation, property damage. Hunting policies against Grizzlies & expanded lethal controls under state jurisdiction will ensue without strong federal oversight. Removing or weakening ESA prohibitions increases the likelihood that bears killed outside of strict scientific or safety exemptions will go unregulated, raising mortality rates beyond sustainable thresholds.

Without federal safeguards key habitats will not be conserved & degradation, fragmentation of critical Grizzly habitats will accelerate due to development or conversion of Grizzly habitats. Grizzlies need large, connected landscapes to maintain viable populations. Disrupted habitat connectivity would follow, an immediate danger for Grizzlies. Rolling back key safeguards, management authority would shift toward states bringing less stringent protections for Grizzlies & varying enforcement capabilities & legal frameworks. History shows that when ESA protections were removed for Grizzlies in Yellowstone region in 2017, it opened the door to planned hunts, reduced federal enforcement, which will, if protections are lessened, threaten recovery gains. Populations in the Cabinet-Yaak and Selkirk have low resiliency & limited redundancy compared to stronger population in the GYE or NC Divide. Their long term recovery & survival still depends upon federal oversight, proactive conservations measure that ESA provides & protections provide frameworks for addressing cumulative stressors, including from climate change. Without robust federal protections, climate related impacts & large scale threats may go unmitigated.
Grizzlies remain functionally endangered across the lower 48 while often described as "recovered" Grizzlies occupy less than 6% of their historic range, down from an estimated 50,000 pre-settlement bears to~2,000 today scattered across fragmented recovery zones. The ESA's statutory definition of recovery ~ a species no longer at risk of extinction across a significant portion of it's range ~ has not been met.

The states where Gray Wolves were delisted have continually shown a systematic extirpation agenda and if Grizzlies were to lose their threatened ESA status and the ESA weakened by the four proposed regulatory changes Grizzlies would be in profound danger as their recoveries are unfinished and only in the GYE & NCDE have populations the appearance of stability at around 1,000-1,100 bears each. But, these populations remain genetically isolated, with no confirmed female-connectivity between ecosystems, no linkages to smaller, more fragile populations.
title: Comment from Hersey, Rene

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

As a citizen with deep commitments to the preservation of biodiversity and healthy ecosystems, I write in opposition to the FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029 (Section 4(d): threatened species protections) proposed rule change to the Endangered Species Act, which would eliminate the blanket rule for threatened species and result in both inconsistent protections and delays in recovery for imperiled wildlife.

I urge the agency to withdraw this proposed rule change in order to help preserve the environment for our generation and especially for future ones.

The proposed changes in this rule would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality. title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
The Service states in its proposal that removal of the "blanket rule" will "reduce burdens on the Service and regulatory entities alike and allows for the Service to better protect threatened species." However, the Service's assessment seems only to account for regulatory actions such as permitting requirements and conservation actions that would arise after a species has been designated as threatened or endangered. The Service does not provide an assessment of the staff, time, and monetary burden of developing new regulations on a case-by-case basis for new threatened or endangered species. Species-specific regulations are an important to their conservation, but such regulations require time and effort to develop before they can be implemented. This time and effort is likely to outweigh any time and effort benefits that may be accrued after regulations are in place.

The stated goal of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) is to protect both species that are threatened with extinction or are critically endangered, and the habitats on which they depend. Threatened and endangered species, by definition, are already declining, and may be declining rapidly. The time required to develop and implement species-by-species regulations threatens the species in question with further declines in their population size before protections are enacted, which in turn makes recovery of the species more difficult. The blanket rule allows for immediate basic protections to attempt to halt further decline of the species, providing time for species-specific regulations to be evaluated and implemented.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Loesch, Sarah

text:
The Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule” automatically gives newly listed threatened species the same baseline protections as endangered species while the USFWS identifies species-specific safeguards. This proposed change will eliminate the “blanket rule,” which means species that could be listed in the future—like the northwestern pond turtle—may lose the standard protections vital to their recovery.

Use this sample message or write your own.
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Torget, Marie

text:
The 1982 amendment of the Endangered Species Act (Act) confirmed that listing of a species pursuant to the Act is to be "solely" based on the best scientific and commercial data available. The H.Rept. 97-835, which was adopted by the Senate, made it clear that the principal purpose of the amendments to the Act was:
"...to ensure that decisions in every phase of the process pertaining to the listing or delisting of species are based solely upon biological criteria
and to prevent non-biological considerations from affecting such decisions."
Economic factors are clearly non-biological considerations. Involving economic impacts when establishing strict regulations for the conservation of Threatened species, even if only considerations, illegally introduces non-biological factors in the overall listing decisions of a species.

Chapter 3 of The Codex of the Endangered Species Act, Volume II: The Next Fifty Years:
"Unlocking the Full Power of
Section 4(d) to Facilitate Collaboration
and Greater Species Recovery" by
David Willms, J.D., which is cited by a number of Congressional reports (i.e., HR 118-879, Committee on Natural Resources Serial # 119-14), states:
"There is evidence that the mere threat of litigation can negatively impact a listed species,
and even unlisted species. Social science research supports the idea that if a party’s economic interests are threatened, they will modify habitat to the detriment of listed species."

Therefore, any thoughts, considerations, reflections, and/or musings of economic impacts regarding any listing consideration of Threatened species would be a strict violation of ESA Section 4(b)(1)(A) and the will of Congress.
title: Comment from Rubinoff, Jay

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Anderson, Weston

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Stimpson, Lisa

text:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. My perspective comes from experience in animal science, wildlife rehabilitation, field research, and rescue work, where delayed protections often mean the difference between recovery and non-reversible decline.

For decades, the blanket 4(d) rule has ensured timely and consistent safeguards by extending core ESA protections to threatened species immediately upon listing. In practice, this early intervention is critical. In rehabilitation/research settings, I have seen that species are often listed only after substantial population declines have occurred. Removing automatic protections during this vulnerable window would allow additional harm to accumulate when species are least resilient.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule contradicts the ESA’s precautionary purpose and its intent to prevent threatened species from slipping into endangered status. Wildlife declines are not sudden events; they are gradual processes driven by habitat loss, disturbance, and cumulative stressors. Delaying protections until species-specific rules are finalized ignores ecological reality and undermines conservation.

The Service provides no evidence that the blanket 4(d) rule creates undue regulatory burden, while its removal would clearly increase administrative delays and uncertainty. From a practical standpoint, this shift would divert limited conservation resources away from on-the-ground recovery and toward prolonged rulemaking, increasing the risk of further imperilment.

Based on my experience working directly with wildlife and using conservation science in real-world contexts, I believe rescinding the blanket 4(d) protections would weaken the ESA at a critical stage in species conservation. This rule should be retained to ensure timely, science-based, and effective protection for threatened species.

text:
I am adamantly opposed to any attempts to weaken the Endangered Species Act (ESA) as it currently stands, including through eliminating the ESA's "blanket 4(d) rule." This rule provides essential protection for populations of threatened species who are not yet but likely to be determined endangered at a future date. Its elimination would significantly and unacceptably increase the risk that these populations would decline even more precipitously. Providing equal protection for both threatened and endangered species is a critical part of the huge success of the ESA. Furthermore, the rule in its current state already allows USFWS to issue special rules for each listed species, so its removal is entirely unwarranted on these grounds.

In reality, eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule outright would place a much greater burden on the agency because it would then be forced to issue specific 4(d) rules for each and every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements. For the sake of a fully-functioning Endangered Species Act in service of our country's irreplaceable array of unique and diverse species, all of whom are a vital part of our heritage as Americans, I urge you to retract this and any other proposed regulatory changes like it.
title: Comment from Adams, Suzanne

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent and undermines the original intent of Congress to advance science-based conservation.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. Introducing ambiguity in the definition of “recovery” raises serious concerns about the premature removal of protections for threatened and endangered species. If applied loosely, at risk species could lose ESA protection before populations are truly stable and resilient. The proposed rule also shortens the time horizon for assessing threats, limiting USFWS’ ability to account for long-term or emerging risks like habitat loss or climate change. Together, these changes could lead to delisting decisions that ignore cumulative and dynamic threats, undermining decades of recovery efforts and accelerating species decline, contrary to the ESA’s purpose.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
All my life I have cared about wildlife, and as I have grown, I see caring about wildlife is central to the future of our children and planet. I urge you to pull this proposed change to the blanket rule that would undermine wildlife protections granted by the Endangered Species Act. This change would go against decades of conservation progress and weaken one of our nation’s most important environmental laws, without which we would have lost the Golden Eagle, the grey wolf, the Condor, and many other important and iconic species that were once "threatened" but received the necessary coverage while their numbers declined until these protections kicked in and allowed for some recovery. Several other species are in that same place and they deserve the same level of protection, and we cannot afford any further backsliding of other species either still in peril or tenuously beginning their recovery.https://www.snexplores.org/article/has-endangered-species-act-saved-species-from-extinction#:~:text=American%20burying%20beetles%20are%20North,no%20longer%20considered%20even%20threatened.

The blanket 4(d) rule is a proven, science-based tool that gives threatened species immediate protections when they are most at risk. Waiting for later will not yield anything but an even harder road to recovery, if at all possible if their habitat is destroyed. Provable recovery by bald eagles, peregrine falcons, grey wolves, brown pelicans, American alligator, grey whale, whooping cranes, humpback whales, sea otters, grizzly bears, and several other species were saved because of these rules. https://www.doi.gov/blog/endangered-species-act-celebrating-50-years-success-wildlife-conservation

Furthermore, the blanket 4(d) rule is particularly important as it prevented skyrocketing expenses and increased difficulties associated with the conservation efforts needed to save an endangered species once its numbers became critically low (endangered status). Protecting threatened species allows for better returns on investment in both cost savings and species savings.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule will delay or weaken protections for newly listed species, putting them in harm’s way during the period when conservation actions are most critical. Again, when a species is threatened is when they should get protection, not when they are past threatened and on to endangered - the difficulties are multiplied the longer we wait, and the likelihood of success diminishes, and the overall costs from litigation through to on the ground conservation explode - especially when taking into consideration the other proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act.

Species-specific rules, while necessary for long-term recovery of the species, require significant time and energy to be created so the blanket 4(d) rule is necessary to provide needed protections until species-specific rules are drafted. However, species-specific rules are not a substitute for broad baseline protections; they are slow, resource-intensive, and increase political pressure from industries seeking exemptions. This is a divide and conquer approach, and while no one wants industries to fail, we do not have the right to force a threatened species even closer to extinction or render them extinct - we have options, and this baseline blanket 4(d) rule protection for both threatened and already classified endangered species is the best pathway until such time as more targeted approaches can be meticulously researched and based on the best available science, not executive orders aimed at weakening environmental safeguards - and being based on the best available science is the mandate already within the ESA.

Especially taking into consideration the DOGE cuts to the necessary scientists with field experience and conservationists with on the job experience, and to the climate scientists monitoring the very environments this rule is to protect, we will need even more time to develop these specific rules, leaving protected and threatened species alike vulnerable to collapse. The long-term development of species-specific rules is neither the reason or is now the time to rescind the blanket 4(d) rule.

Finally, broad baseline protections like the blanket 4(d) rule ensure that species don’t fall prey to regulatory gaps or the influence of special-interest groups, which sadly is a threat to particular species based on their location or proximity.

I urge you to uphold the mission of the Endangered Species Act and maintain the blanket 4(d) rule. Our wildlife, wild places, and future generations are counting on it

text:
The Endangered Species Act should not be altered as the government now proposes. The new regulations are absurd and lopsided in favor of one time profits, without sufficient guard rails.

Here is the essential problem with the proposed changes: Imagine if the ESA were applied to humans - would the government say that it is illegal to kill a person, but permissible to starve them to death?

By allowing the destruction of a wild animals’ habitat the government is approving starvation for the creatures who depend on that habitat. Saying they can move is likewise erroneous: if all the impacted creatures all go to the same habitat- they will over graze, damage the habitat because there are too many of them - and then their population will collapse.

The proposed rule reads like it was written by a landlord from Queens. A guy who is unaware of actual, functional life, who thinks species are disposable without consequences. This is not true.

Imagine that a habitable earth is a 747 airplane. The rivets holding the plane together are all the plants and animals and microscopic beings and insects. Imagine that each species that goes extinct is like a rivet popping off the 747. A few rivets and the plane can still fly. But finally there will comd a point when the structure of the 747 will not withstand losing another rivet. So the government must ask itself: which will be the last species that goes extinct for economic gain causes the last river to fly off, that delivers our mutual destruction?

Don’t roll the dice for some fat cat’s bank account. This is massively stupid.

There is no scientific justification for this rule change.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
As a country, we need to stop this political back-and-forth on issues that should be bipartisan, such as Endangered Species. Americans largely agree to the premise of ESA – the “what” is to invoke actions, regardless of political party or administrative boundaries, and set into place effective methods to preserve species that meet the T&E criteria. The American Bald Eagle is that classic success story, and it is classically bi-partisan, invoking great pride in our country as a symbol of Democracy.

The administration and subsequently the Secretary of the Interior and Commerce need to dig deeper into this flip-flopping of rule-making [2016, 2019, 2020, 2024, 2025]. It is a waste of time between administrations, and it is not accomplishing the ultimate Congressional Intent (located in the Legislative History) as made by passing the ESA of 1973. The law is only 20 pages; it is not for us to re-interpret 50+ years later the intent of those who wrote it at that time, but to go back to the Legislative History and ensure that their intent is being followed. That law is the law of the land until Congress, not the current administration, changes that. This game of back and forth is neither effective nor is it productive for the stated intent of ESA. We ask that the Secretaries make an honest effort to meet the intent of those Congressmen and women in 1973 to do the right thing. Moving forward as proposed, places great risk on losing critical cogs and wheels that will put species at risk of extinction.

We have grave concerns about the removal of the “blanket rule.” These concerns include:
1.Increased workload and capacity issues: Developing these individual plans for each newly listed species will/is highly likely to significantly increase the workload for the FWS, which is already facing capacity challenges as a result of the actions taken by DOGE earlier this year on an agency already below capacity. This raises concerns about the agency's ability to effectively implement and enforce the proposed regulation change.
2.Potential for delays in protection: The transition to species-specific rules could lead to delays in the implementation of necessary protections for newly listed threatened species, potentially putting them at greater risk during the interim period. An interim period that is undefined and therefore could extend for years to decades, and places the species at potential risk of a trajectory toward extinction. Habitat loss and “take” are key vectors toward that extinction trajectory.
3.Legal and Regulatory uncertainty: The proposed changes may lead to increased litigation and regulatory uncertainty as stakeholders may challenge the new approach, similar to past challenges against the blanket rule.
4.Economic considerations: The proposal allows for economic impacts to be considered when developing species-specific rules, which could lead to conflicts between conservation goals and economic interests, potentially undermining the effectiveness of ESA.

We recognize that there may be those who suggest that there are potential benefits to the removal of the “blanket rule,” such as tailored conservation efforts to the species, flexibility in regulation leading to more effective conservation strategies, and public involvement in species-specific rules. We actually believe these perceived benefits exist under the “blanket rule” as well. The “blanket rule” has allowed and currently allows the agency to work on specific threats to a species while buying time to complete a more comprehensive recovery strategy. Removal of the “blanket rule” creates a large gap of valuable time and effort that is likely to be irretrievable (such as habitat degradation and “take”), which will put species on a direct line toward extinction.

We respect that there are incredibly smart people who can re-evaluate this action and develop a legitimate proposal that works to meet all. Meaning that we need to stop this partisan back-and-forth and develop meaningful changes that will meet the intent of ESA. The proposed rule change must not go forward at this time. A better solution through bipartisan solution-making needs to occur.

Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
As a conservative who believes in responsible stewardship of our natural resources, I am strongly opposed to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that would weaken protections for at-risk species. The ESA has been a roaring success, protecting listed species from extinction and maintaining our uniquely American heritage.

The loss of wildlife has direct and practical consequences. Declines in marine life, including fish, shellfish, marine mammals, and reef-dependent species, threaten commercial and recreational fisheries, coastal jobs, and food security. Healthy oceans depend on intact ecosystems, and once marine species are pushed past recovery, the economic and ecological losses are permanent.

The decline of pollinators such as bees and butterflies poses serious risks to agriculture and ranching. Pollinators are essential to crop production and food supply stability. Their loss increases costs for farmers, reduces yields, and undermines rural economies.

Birds and mammals also play critical roles in maintaining balanced ecosystems, controlling pests, dispersing seeds, and supporting healthy forests and rangelands. Their disappearance signals broader ecosystem failure that ultimately harms landowners, hunters, anglers, and outdoor traditions that many conservatives value.

The Endangered Species Act reflects core conservative principles: reliance on sound science, long-term thinking, and accountability in managing irreplaceable resources. Allowing species to decline beyond recovery in the name of short-term gain is neither prudent nor responsible.

I urge policymakers to reject changes that weaken the Endangered Species Act and instead focus on improving its implementation through science-based decision-making, cooperation with landowners and resource users, and practical conservation measures that support both wildlife and working communities. Protecting America’s wildlife is not a partisan issue, it is a duty to every American now and in the future and to the livelihoods that depend on healthy ecosystems.
title: Comment from Cook, Fran

text:
I am writing as a concerned citizen to express strong opposition to the proposed reduction in federal protections under the Endangered Species Act.
The ecological role of wolves is among the best-studied and most dramatic examples of a keystone predator in North American ecosystems. Their presence or absence produces cascading effects that influence the health of entire landscapes.
Key scientifically documented benefits of wolf presence include:
* Regulation of large herbivore populations (especially elk and deer), preventing chronic overgrazing and allowing vegetation recovery
* Increased plant diversity and height in riparian areas, leading to improved streambank stability
* Higher water tables and improved stream conditions in some systems (most famously documented in Yellowstone National Park)
* Increased biodiversity of songbirds, amphibians, beavers, and other species that benefit from healthier vegetation and wetland conditions
* Reduction of overabundant mesopredators (coyotes) in some ecosystems, benefiting smaller native species
* Important nutrient cycling through carcass distribution across landscapes
* Behavioral effects on prey that reduce browsing pressure even in areas where wolves are not immediately present (“the ecology of fear”)
These trophic cascade effects are not theoretical. Decades of peer-reviewed research—particularly from Yellowstone, but also from other systems in Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, and internationally—have repeatedly demonstrated that the removal or severe reduction of wolves frequently leads to:
* Degraded riparian ecosystems
* Reduced biodiversity
* Increased soil erosion
* Poorer water quality
* Higher incidence of chronic wasting disease in some deer/elk herds due to lack of selective predation
* Economic costs associated with degraded range conditions and increased need for artificial management of ungulates
Reversing or significantly weakening wolf protections at this time risks unraveling many of the ecological gains achieved over the past 25–30 years in areas where wolves have been successfully restored. These gains represent some of the most significant and well-documented conservation success stories in modern American history.
While I recognize that wolf-livestock conflicts create real economic and emotional hardship for some ranchers, the scientific evidence strongly indicates that well-funded, well-implemented non-lethal coexistence tools (range riders, fladry, guard dogs, fencing, carcass removal, range riding, etc.) combined with targeted, surgically precise lethal control of chronically depredating individuals remain far more effective and ecologically sustainable than broad population reductions or complete removal of federal protections.
I respectfully urge you to maintain or strengthen, rather than weaken, federal and/or state protections for gray wolves, recognizing their irreplaceable role as apex predators and keystone species. The long-term ecological, economic, and cultural costs of once again eliminating or drastically reducing wolf populations will almost certainly outweigh the short-term benefits.
Thank you for your time and consideration of this critically important issue. I would appreciate any response outlining how the proposed changes will be reconciled with the extensive body of scientific evidence regarding the ecological importance of wolves.

Sincerely,
Kyle Younkin
Medina County Resident

Provable recovery by bald eagles, peregrine falcons, grey wolves, brown pelicans, American alligator, grey whale, whooping cranes, humpback whales, sea otters, grizzly bears, and several other species were saved because of these rules. https://www.doi.gov/blog/endangered-species-act-celebrating-50-years-success-wildlife-conservation

Furthermore, the blanket 4(d) rule is particularly important as it prevented skyrocketing expenses and increased difficulties associated with the conservation efforts needed to save an endangered species once its numbers became critically low (endangered status). Protecting threatened species allows for better returns on investment in both cost savings and species savings.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule will delay or weaken protections for newly listed species, putting them in harm’s way during the period when conservation actions are most critical. Again, when a species is threatened is when they should get protection, not when they are past threatened and on to endangered - the difficulties are multiplied the longer we wait, and the likelihood of success diminishes, and the overall costs from litigation through to on the ground conservation explode - especially when taking into consideration the other proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act.

Species-specific rules, while necessary for long-term recovery of the species, require significant time and energy to be created so the blanket 4(d) rule is necessary to provide needed protections until species-specific rules are drafted. However, species-specific rules are not a substitute for broad baseline protections; they are slow, resource-intensive, and increase political pressure from industries seeking exemptions. This is a divide and conquer approach, and while no one wants industries to fail, we do not have the right to force a threatened species even closer to extinction or render them extinct - we have options, and this baseline blanket 4(d) rule protection for both threatened and already classified endangered species is the best pathway until such time as more targeted approaches can be meticulously researched and based on the best available science, not executive orders aimed at weakening environmental safeguards - and being based on the best available science is the mandate already within the ESA.

Especially taking into consideration the DOGE cuts to the necessary scientists with field experience and conservationists with on the job experience, and to the climate scientists monitoring the very environments this rule is to protect, we will need even more time to develop these specific rules, leaving protected and threatened species alike vulnerable to collapse. The long-term development of species-specific rules is neither the reason or is now the time to rescind the blanket 4(d) rule.
