title: Comment from Jensen, Laura

text:
I oppose the elimination of the blanket 4(d) rule.

For one thing, the delay in administering classification of species (plants and animals both) that we've seen happen as the application moves through the process can and likely will result in harm to a species that would have initially qualified as "threatened" but due to the time lag has now entered an even more perilous condition, due to logging, grazing, mining, etc. Thus the species has indeed become endangered, and yet would be (eventually) listed only as "threatened", causing further harm and habitat loss to the point that recovery would be difficult or even impossible.

There is no justification that I can see that would create benefit in any manner that outweighs the risk of losing our country's rich and diverse abundance of species, many found nowhere else on earth, the rightful heritage of the public, especially the next generations. The species that are facing the stresors of habitat loss, climate instability, over harvesting, etc. are increasing in numbers as the stressors themselves grow greater every day. We cannot sustain our own quality of life if we diminish the full web of life itself; we are intimately interconnected with insect life (many of our native bees, for example, are responsible for much of our food), trees that help maintain our hydrological cycles, etc. The health of our rivers depends upon the health of the life forms that live in them or prevent damage to them; the same for the predators that keep other species in check and prevent deer from overpopulation and overgrazing and further habitat destruction; the same for countless species that depend upon organisms in the soil (and vice versa) so that we don't lose that intricate balance that protects our topsoil. In other words, we fail to see the full picture if we only choose certain species for protection and ignore the ecology that depends upon them and that they in turn depend upon.

I write this with the understanding that we as a species need an intact ecosystem ourselves in order to survive the global changes to our life support systems. As storms grow more powerful, droughts and floods increase, pollution spreads, overpopulation continues along with hunger and poverty and disease, we depend upon the survival and health of the rest of the life forms that sustain us.

If we weaken what protections we have, and turn away from a policy that has served us better, depending only on individual 4(d) rules, we and those species become more vulnerable, especially since the process will likely become more vulnerable to corporate influence. title: Comment from Beasley Bailey, Shannon

text:
I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed revisions to regulations governing threatened species under the Endangered Species Act (ESA), which would eliminate the longstanding “blanket” 4(d) rule and require species-specific protections to be developed individually. The best available science clearly demonstrates that delaying or weakening protections for threatened species increases extinction risk and undermines recovery. Peer-reviewed analyses of ESA performance consistently demonstrate that species benefit most from early and continuous legal protections. Taylor et al. (2005) found that species listed for longer periods under the ESA are significantly more likely to show stable or improving population trends, highlighting the importance of immediate protections upon listing. Removing automatic 4(d) protections creates a gap during which threatened species may continue to decline while awaiting species-specific rules. Conservation biology literature emphasizes that delay itself is biologically consequential. Small populations are highly vulnerable to demographic stochasticity, environmental variability, and genetic erosion. Studies show that delayed conservation action results in lower recovery potential and higher extinction probability (Brook et al. 2008). Automatic 4(d) protections serve as a scientifically justified precautionary measure to prevent such losses during the earliest, most vulnerable stages of protection. Habitat loss and degradation are the dominant threats facing imperiled species globally and within the United States (Wilcove et al. 1998). Automatic 4(d) protections help immediately limit harmful activities such as take, habitat destruction, and degradation. Eliminating these default protections allows ongoing habitat loss to continue unchecked during regulatory delays — directly contradicting decades of empirical evidence identifying habitat loss as the leading cause of extinction. More recent analyses confirm that species receiving core ESA tools — including take prohibitions and recovery planning — are significantly more likely to show improving population trends. Greenwald et al. (2019) found that most listed species are stable or improving, and that declines often reflect insufficient or delayed implementation, not over-protection. Species-specific 4(d) rules often take years to develop due to administrative complexity, limited agency resources, and political pressure. During this period, threatened species may experience continued population declines, habitat fragmentation, and loss of genetic diversity, all of which reduce long-term recovery potential (Traill et al. 2010). From a scientific standpoint, this regulatory gap is indefensible. The scientific record is clear: early, automatic, and consistent protections reduce extinction risk and improve recovery outcomes. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule for threatened species would delay conservation action, expose vulnerable populations to continued harm, and weaken one of the ESA’s most effective precautionary tools.

For these reasons, I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule and ensure that threatened species receive immediate protections grounded in the best available science, consistent with the ESA’s purpose of preventing extinction and promoting recovery.

title: Comment from Lamm, Kimberly

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from O'Rourke, Susan

text:
I am submitting this comment because I care deeply about the health of our environment, which includes healthy ecosystems and biodiversity. I care about science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country, and want to see my government continue to uphold the Endangered Species Act.

The ESA works because it centers science and the public interest. This and other proposed changes to the ESA would allow private economic interests to outweigh scientific reality and the public interest. I have the following concerns with the rule changes currently being proposed:
-The Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4) would remove automatic protections from newly listed species. It takes time to write species-specific rules and for recovery efforts to begin to have an impact. The blanket rule provides critical immediate protections to newly listed species so that they are not killed or subjected to further habitat destruction before recovery efforts can begin.
-The proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)) narrows the criteria for critical habitat exclusions and could allow economic interests to override needed habitat protection. Failure to protect essential habitat puts entire ecosystems at risk, not only individual species. Proposed changes that would narrow how “foreseeable future” is interpreted when determining species listing would also hamper the Department’s ability to take into consideration the impacts of climate change on species, undermining the scientific basis of rules. Science tells us that climate change is happening and we know how ecosystems are change and will continue to change as global warming continues, so it is critical that we take those facts into account when determining how to protect ecosystems and species into the future.
-The proposed consultation rule (Section 7) would limit interagency review and consultation, threatening what should be a science-based process that fully assesses the potential impacts of federal projects on endangered wildlife before a project can proceed. A democratic, science-based process requires meaningful review and transparency, which this proposed rule would undermine. Section 7 is the backbone of the ESA, which ensures that federal agencies do not approve projects that would destroy critical habitat or harm threatened or endangered species.

I grew up visiting family in Maine every summer, and I remember when I was younger how seeing a bald eagle flying over the lake was a rare joy. Happily we see multiple eagles every year now, but it still feels like a gift every time. The recovery of bald eagles in the United States is a success story of the Endangered Species Act, and limiting the use of DDT enabled these birds and others to recover without lasting harm to our economy. Without the protections of the ESA, eagles could be extinct, and the symbol of our country could be just a symbol. I now live in the Pacific Northwest, where many species of salmon are threatened or endangered under the ESA. Salmon are a keystone species, essential to the health of whole ecosystems—feeding animals as diverse as eagles, ravens, wolves, and bears, and bringing nutrients back to the forests that provide multiple benefits to our communities from recreational opportunities to spiritual connection to carbon sequestration. Salmon are incredibly important for the health of ecosystems in our region and culturally significant to many Americans who live here, and it is essential that they continue to be protected over the long term through the ESA.

I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections. Please act in the interest of the American people by upholding the intent of the Endangered Species Act to prevent extinctions and ensure future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.
title: Comment from Watson, Amanda

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes in this docket that would weaken how species are evaluated for listing, uplisting, and continued protection under the Endangered Species Act. These changes risk undermining the scientific integrity of the listing process and would make it more difficult for imperiled species, including Southern Resident killer whales, to receive and retain the protections they need to survive and recover.

The ESA requires that listing decisions be based solely on the best available scientific and commercial data. This standard is critical because endangered species decisions must be grounded in biology, ecology, and population dynamics... not speculation, short-term trends, or economic convenience. Any changes that allow agencies to downplay known threats, rely on uncertain future actions, or reinterpret risk more narrowly would erode this foundation.

For Southern Resident killer whales, population vulnerability cannot be assessed through simplistic metrics or short-term fluctuations. This population is small, socially complex, and subject to compounding stressors, including chronic prey limitation, acoustic disturbance, toxic contamination, and climate-driven ecosystem changes. These threats interact in ways that amplify risk and suppress recovery, even during periods when births occur or deaths temporarily decline. A weakened listing framework that discounts cumulative and long-term threats would fail to capture the true extinction risk faced by this population.

The proposed rule appears to invite greater discretion in how agencies characterize threats, weigh uncertainty, or interpret the likelihood of future harm. This is deeply concerning. Scientific uncertainty should never be used as a justification for reducing protections when the consequences of being wrong are irreversible. The ESA is intentionally precautionary because waiting for absolute certainty has historically resulted in extinction.

Additionally, any move to treat conservation efforts, voluntary measures, or speculative future actions as justification for limiting or avoiding protections undermines accountability. Southern Resident killer whales have been subject to decades of recovery planning, yet key threats particularly prey availability and underwater noise remain unresolved. Promising future improvements cannot substitute for enforceable protections today.

Weakening listing standards also risks politicizing the ESA by shifting decisions away from objective science and toward subjective interpretation. This would erode public trust, invite increased litigation, and destabilize conservation planning for species already on the brink. The existing framework has been repeatedly upheld by courts and remains essential for transparent, defensible decision-making.

I urge the agency to reject the proposed changes in this docket and to maintain rigorous, science-based listing criteria that fully account for cumulative, long-term, and interacting threats. For species like Southern Resident killer whales, anything less places recovery out of reach and increases the risk of extinction under the guise of regulatory reform.

Thank you for considering this comment and for upholding the scientific standards that make the ESA effective.

text:
As a concerned citizen, I strongly oppose the proposed rule to change the long-standing definition of “harm” under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The current definition, supported by sound science and legal interpretation, appropriately recognizes that habitat modification and destruction can cause harm to threatened and endangered species. Excluding habitat modification from the definition of harm could drastically weaken one of the ESA’s most effective and widely used protections. Without question, this change could threaten the survival and recovery of endangered species, and could inadvertently fast track many species onto the list. Species we cannot afford to lose. Additionally, the recovery of listed species could become much more difficult and costly as more essential habitat could be impacted or lost. Protecting habitat is essential to avoid future ESA listings.

There is long-standing scientific documentation that habitat destruction, fragmentation, and degradation are the leading cause of species declines in the US and globally. It is not only over-harvesting or direct impacts to individual plants and animals that result in the decline of a species. The greatest threats – the degradation and loss of their habitat, critical feeding, sheltering, breeding, and/or nesting grounds – bring species to the brink of extinction. Furthermore, the current interpretation of the definition of harm, to include impacts to habitats, has been utilized by the USFWS for decades. This interpretation has even been upheld in a case before the US Supreme Court.

In Illinois, the survival of federally endangered species, like the Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus), over a dozen mussel species, the Indiana (Myotis sodalis) and Northern Long-Eared Bat (Myotis septentrionalis), and the Rusty Patched Bumble Bee (Bombus affinis), are dependent on the ESA protections offered to these species, including protections to the habitats on which they depend. title: Comment from Voeun, Luna

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I ask you to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I respectfully urge the rejection of the proposed Endangered Species Act regulatory changes as someone who values both conservation and responsible economic stewardship,

The intent of the Endangered Species Act is to prioritize the survival of species. While economic goals are understandable, the cumulative effect of these proposed changes risks weakening the ESA’s most cost-effective function: preventing irreversible loss before it becomes expensive, disruptive, and unavoidable. The Act’s strength has always been its focus on preventing extinctions before they occur — a goal grounded in sound science and an understanding that healthy ecosystems provide essential services: clean water, clean air, pollination, flood control, soil stability, outdoor tourism, cultural resiliency, land conservation, and many more. These services support hunting, fishing, recreation, ranching, and farming — industries that contribute substantially to rural economies and Republican constituencies. All of these are American ideals, the envy of the rest of the world and they are entirely dependent on protecting ecosystems which is impossible if we don’t stop the loss of species that is already occurring even with existing safeguards.

The move away from baseline protections for threatened species in favor of species-specific rules ignores a basic reality: species do not live in isolation. Wildlife depends on shared habitat, food webs, and migration corridors. Protecting one species while allowing the surrounding ecosystem to be degraded is ineffective and ultimately wasteful.

From a land-management and business standpoint, this also creates a confusing patchwork of rules. Landowners and industries benefit from clear, consistent standards, not constantly shifting, species-by-species requirements. Removing early protections increases the likelihood that threatened species become endangered—triggering stricter regulations, higher costs, and longer recovery timelines. Weakening early safeguards doesn’t reduce regulation; it guarantees more of it later.

Conservatives have long understood that conservation is about stewardship, not ideology. Theodore Roosevelt and generations of hunters, farmers, and landowners recognized that protecting land and wildlife protects property values, local economies, and national strength.
Short-term regulatory relief may benefit a few interests today, but the long-term costs of degraded land, lost wildlife, and emergency recovery efforts will fall on taxpayers, landowners, and future generations. A strong, science-based ESA remains one of the most fiscally responsible tools we have.

Over 84% of all Americans support the Endangered Species Act and are in favor of preventing species extinctions above all else. Please do what is right for all Americans (not just a few) and DO NOT adopt ANY of the proposed changes to the ESA.

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,

I am writing as a concerned citizen to voice my unwavering opposition to the proposed rule changes under docket FWS HQ ES 2025 0029 0001. This proposal represents a fundamental dismantling of the safety net that has protected our nations threatened species for decades. By seeking to eliminate the blanket rule, the Service is choosing to replace a proven and efficient system with a fragmented approach that prioritizes administrative delay and industrial convenience over the survival of our natural heritage.

The blanket rule has long served as an essential default. It ensures that the moment a species is recognized as threatened, it receives the same fundamental protections against harm as those classified as endangered, unless a specific rule says otherwise. It is a proactive stance that acknowledges a simple biological truth: when a species is in decline, we do not have the luxury of time. Yet, this proposal seeks to strip away that default. Under the new framework, every newly listed threatened species would be left in a state of legal limbo while the Service slowly moves through the bureaucratic process of drafting individual rules. We are talking about months or even years where vulnerable animals and plants could be left without the protections they need to prevent them from slipping further toward the brink of extinction.

The justification provided for this change is a thin veil for a policy that serves corporate interests at the expense of the public trust. To claim that we need more flexibility to avoid unnecessary restrictions is to ignore the reality of the biodiversity crisis we are currently facing. We are losing species at a rate hundreds of times higher than the natural background level. In such a crisis, the burden of proof should be on those who wish to harm a species, not on the scientists trying to save it. By removing the blanket rule, you are shifting that burden. You are creating a system where protections are the exception rather than the rule, and where every specific protection must be fought for against a tide of political and industrial pressure.

There is a hard fact at the center of this proposal: extinction is permanent. Once a species is gone, no amount of regulatory predictability can ever bring it back. The Endangered Species Act was designed to be a visionary law that placed the value of life above the short term gains of commerce. This proposal subverts that vision. It treats the protection of our environment as a hurdle to be cleared rather than a sacred duty to be upheld. The move toward species specific rules is not an improvement in efficiency; it is an invitation for lobbying and political interference. It allows powerful interests to pick apart protections piece by piece until the law is nothing more than a hollow shell.

I am particularly disturbed by the timing of these changes. Our wildlife needs more protection, not less. We need a government that acts as a steward of the land, not one that seeks to expedite its exploitation. The legacy of the Endangered Species Act is found in the recovery of the bald eagle and the grizzly bear. These successes happened because the law had teeth and because we chose to act decisively. This proposal would pull those teeth. It would replace a strong and unified front with a series of weak rules that are far easier for industries to bypass.

Furthermore, the administrative burden this change places on the Service itself is nonsensical. Why would you require overstretched staff to draft hundreds of individual rules when a single blanket rule has worked effectively for years? The answer is clear: the goal is to slow down the process of conservation until it is too late to make a difference. It is a strategy of attrition where the biological needs of a species are secondary to the timelines of development.

As a citizen, I find it deeply immoral to put a price tag on the existence of a species. When we lose the monarch butterfly or the rusty patched bumble bee, we lose a part of ourselves. We lose the clean water and the natural beauty that define our country. This proposal is a betrayal of the generations of Americans who will inherit the silence of a world where we chose profit over life. I urge you in the strongest possible terms to withdraw this proposal. Maintain the blanket rule. Keep the safety net intact. Do not let your legacy be the one that presided over the managed decline of our nations wildlife. Our children deserve a world that is still wild and capable of sustaining the variety of life that makes this planet home.

Respectfully,

A Concerned Citizen

OPPOSITION to Proposed Revisions to ESA Regulations (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039)

To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service:

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act regulations announced on November 19, 2025. Specifically, I object to the rescission of the “Blanket Rule” under Section 4(d) and the re-introduction of economic considerations into listing decisions.

1. Restore the Blanket Rule: Removing the automatic protections for “Threatened” species creates a dangerous gap in enforcement. For species like the Tope Shark, which is currently awaiting listing decisions, this change means they could be listed as threatened but remain legally unprotected from harvest for years while species-specific rules are drafted. This delay could lead to functionally extinct populations before a single protection is enforced.

2. Science Over Profit: The ESA was designed to base extinction decisions solely on science. Re-introducing economic impact assessments into the listing and critical habitat designation process inevitably prioritizes short-term industry profits over long-term biodiversity. For highly migratory species like the Oceanic Whitetip Shark and Scalloped Hammerhead, protecting critical habitat is often inconvenient for commercial fisheries. That inconvenience is not a valid reason to allow a species to go extinct.

3. Lessons from Success: The recovery of the Eastern North Pacific (California) Gray Whale and Southern Sea Otter proves that strict, automatic protections work. The ESA has saved 99% of species listed under fifty years since the ESA was enacted. The California Gray whale population numbered only a few thousand when it was listed in 1973. The rebuilding of the population- up to 27,000 in 2016 led to the delisting of the whale in a great success story. However, a lack of food and other threats have put this whale back into peril, underscoring the need for vigilance. Weakening the ESA would ensures that other threatened species will not share in the success story shared by plants and animals protected in the past.

I urge you to withdraw these proposals and maintain the automatic protections that have prevented the extinction of 99% of listed species.

Sincerely, Tara Beckman [Eagle, ID]

title: Comment from Brophy, Georgie

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Carper, Erin

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

Interagency Consultation (Section 7) Rule (2025-20551)

I oppose the proposed revisions to the interagency consultation regulations under ESA section 7. Effective consultation is essential to ensuring that federal actions do not jeopardize listed species or destroy critical habitat. The proposed changes would significantly weaken this process.

By narrowing key definitions — including the “environmental baseline” and the standard for effects “reasonably certain to occur” — the rule risks allowing agencies to overlook cumulative, indirect, and climate-driven impacts that are well-documented in ecological literature. For many species, particularly those experiencing habitat fragmentation or climate stress, these indirect effects are among the primary drivers of decline. Excluding them from consideration is inconsistent with both the ESA’s purpose and the “best available science” standard.

The removal of offsetting measures, which have long been an important tool for reducing harm when incidental take cannot be avoided, further undermines conservation outcomes. Offsetting requirements are not substitutes for avoidance, but they are essential for ensuring that unavoidable impacts do not cumulatively weaken populations over time.

The ESA requires a “conservation” mandate that promotes recovery, not simply survival. These revisions move consultation away from that statutory requirement. I urge the Services to withdraw the proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, protections for federally listed species.

title: Comment from Meller, Alyssa

text:
I am opposed to the proposed changes, and any changes that would weaken, limit, or undermine the Endangered Species Act or its enactment. A vast majority of Americans want a strong Endangered Species Act, want it strongly enacted, and fully funded. The proposed removal of Section 4(d) Blanket Rule would reduce protections for threatened animals and plants that are listed in the future, and therefore is counter to the intent of the ESA and the will of the majority of Americans.

Removing the blanket 4(d) rule would weaken protection for threatened species and encourage further political interference in the recovery process. By automatically applying the same prohibitions against “take” as given to endangered species (making it illegal to kill, injure, harm, or harass threatened animals), and rescinding or restricting protections when and where advisable, this regulation has helped move threatened species towards recovery for nearly 40 years. If the 4(d) rule is rescinded, I am concerned that newly listed threatened species will be afforded little to no protection. I am also concerned that political or corporate pressure may lead to more “threatened” designation of species that are truly “endangered” in order to facilitate industry and other development interests by removing requirements to minimize harm to threatened species. I urge the Services to retain the blanket 4(d) rule and maintain the existing practice of creating special rules on a case by case basis where more specific or tailored protections are needed based on scientific data. This interpretation resembles some earlier, unsuccessful legislative proposals, including the 2004 “Sound Science for Endangered Species Act Planning Act” (H.R. 1662) that sought to limit the use of predictive models in listing decisions. Such approaches directly contradict recommendations from the National Research Council’s report entitled “Science and the Endangered Species Act,” which recommended greater use of predictive modeling techniques such as population viability analysis in decision-making. In the wolverine decision, the FWS characterized the evidence of threats from loss of snow cover as “speculative,” imposing a higher level of proof for climate-driven threats. A federal court overturned this decision, concluding that “No greater level of certainty is needed to see the writing on the wall for this snow-dependent species standing squarely in the path of global climate change.” Codifying this approach through the proposed definition of “foreseeable future” would risk denying protections to many species due to perceived uncertainty. As the Court emphasized, the ESA requires “action at the earliest possible, defensible point in time to protect against the loss of biodiversity within our reach as a nation.” I urge the USFWS to withdraw the proposed definition of foreseeable future and develop one consistent with the precautionary intent of the Endangered Species Act and the best available climate science.

In addition, if enacted this would require each species to have its own rules set, and with the current administration’s staffing and funding reductions, the proposed changes would certainly result in a delay and backlog of protection decisions.
Natural solutions can combat flooding, aquifer depletion, pest control, water filtration, air filtration, soil regeneration and cleaning, and carbon sequestration far better and far far cheaper than human-based solutions can. We have to protect and invest in the species and habitats that generate this ecological capital - or the security, welfare, and wealth of all Americans will suffer. A strong ESA works to achieve that goal, and these proposed changes seem to run counter to it.

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service:

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act regulations announced on November 19, 2025. Specifically, I object to the rescission of the “Blanket Rule” under Section 4(d) and the re-introduction of economic considerations into listing decisions.

1. Restore the Blanket Rule: Removing the automatic protections for “Threatened” species creates a dangerous gap in enforcement. For species like the Tope Shark, which is currently awaiting listing decisions, this change means they could be listed as threatened but remain legally unprotected from harvest for years while species-specific rules are drafted. This delay could lead to functionally extinct populations before a single protection is enforced.

2. Science Over Profit: The ESA was designed to base extinction decisions solely on science. Re-introducing economic impact assessments into the listing and critical habitat designation process inevitably prioritizes short-term industry profits over long-term biodiversity. For highly migratory species like the Oceanic Whitetip Shark and Scalloped Hammerhead, protecting critical habitat is often inconvenient for commercial fisheries. That inconvenience is not a valid reason to allow a species to go extinct.

3. Lessons from Success: The recovery of the Eastern North Pacific (California) Gray Whale and Southern Sea Otter proves that strict, automatic protections work. The ESA has saved 99% of species listed under fifty years since the ESA was enacted. The California Gray whale population numbered only a few thousand when it was listed in 1973. The rebuilding of the population- up to 27,000 in 2016 led to the delisting of the whale in a great success story. However, a lack of food and other threats have put this whale back into peril, underscoring the need for vigilance. Weakening the ESA would ensures that other threatened species will not share in the success story shared by plants and animals protected in the past.

I urge you to withdraw these proposals and maintain the automatic protections that have prevented the extinction of 99% of listed species.

Sincerely
Kayla Jankowski
New Mexico

text:
As someone who lives in Arizona and regularly sees the effects of habitat and wildlife loss, I am concerned about weakening protections for imperiled species. Importantly, I care about science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country.

Science can tell us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both. The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality.

These are my concerns with the proposals:
1. Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
2. Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
3. Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
4. Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.

Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests; rollbacks reduce public accountability at a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections.

I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections, thus preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.

Eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract this proposed rule, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Rosenkotter, Barbara

text:
For over 50 years, as a cornerstone of US environmental law, the ESA represents a national commitment to preventing extinction and promoting recovery of imperiled species. ESA implementing regs must achieve its conservation purposes, provide regulatory clarity, and consider economic impacts. The current proposals fail on all fronts with inadequate analysis and serious legal flaws, creating uncertainty about conservation outcomes and economic impacts. These fatal flaws render the proposals unlawful for adoption. They must be withdrawn.
FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039 Courts have repeatedly held that the mandate that listing determinations be made solely on the basis of the best scientific and commercial data available requires FWS to account for future and cumulative threats where supported by science, even in the face of uncertainty, TVA v. Hill. By narrowing the interpretation of foreseeable future and restricting designation of unoccupied critical habitat, the proposal unlawfully constrains FWS’ ability to address long-term extinction risk. Nothing in the ESA authorizes FWS to discount scientifically supported future threats in favor of administrative predictability. Courts have also recognized that unoccupied habitat may be essential to conservation, Weyerhaeuser v. FWS. The proposal risks foreclosing such designations by regulation rather than science.
FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044 The duty on federal agencies to insure that their actions are not likely to jeopardize listed species or adversely modify critical habitat is institutionalized caution, requiring analysis of all effects of the action, including indirect and cumulative impacts, TVA v. Hill. The proposal unlawfully narrows the definitions of effects of the action and environmental baseline, excluding real-world stressors that courts have required agencies to consider, NWF v. NMFS. The ESA forbids FWS to redefine jeopardy analysis to reduce regulatory burden.
FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029 Courts have held that the authority to implement regulations necessary and advisable to provide for the conservation of threatened species must be exercised to advance conservation, not undermine it, Sierra Club v. Clark. Eliminating the longstanding blanket rule without ensuring immediate, enforceable protections creates regulatory gaps that expose threatened species to further decline. The ESA forbids FWS to withdraw baseline protections first, consider conservation later.
FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048 Courts have emphasized that conservation remains the paramount concern, Cape Hatteras v. DOI. By formalizing a framework that elevates economic considerations and encourages exclusions, the proposal risks converting a limited statutory exception into a default outcome, contrary to congressional intent.
An agency reversing course must acknowledge the change and provide a reasoned explanation grounded in evidence, FCC v. Fox. Across all four proposals, FWS relies on conclusory claims of restoring prior approaches without demonstrating why existing regulations are flawed or how the new rules better fulfill the ESA’s purposes. The proposals are procedurally deficient, arbitrary and capricious, and violative of the APA, by issuing several significant, complex proposals on or near the same day with only a 30-day window, these proposals are procedurally deficient because the public was not given enough time to analyze their complex interrelationships. FWS attempts to deny the public a meaningful opportunity to consider and comment on these complex proposals and their impact on reliance interests of numerous parties. FWS fails to adequately consider (1) reliance interests in existing conservation frameworks, Encino v. Navarro, (2) the cumulative effects of weakening multiple ESA provisions simultaneously, (3) scientific evidence regarding habitat fragmentation, climate stressors, and extinction risk. Ignoring these factors renders the proposals arbitrary and capricious.
FWS treats each of the four proposals in isolation, despite their cumulative effect of substantially narrowing ESA protections. The APA prohibits agencies from segmenting actions to obscure their true impact, Delaware Riverkeeper v. FERC. If multiple rules are released on the same day and are functionally dependent on one another, FWS must explain their interrelationship. FWS is hiding the ball, preventing the public from understanding the full regulatory landscape, thereby denying a meaningful opportunity to comment.
The economic analyses are deficient in several respects (1) listing decisions must be made solely on science, yet the proposals repeatedly emphasize permitting efficiency and regulatory cost savings, (2) proposals do not meaningfully quantify the economic benefits of species conservation, ecosystem services, or avoided extinction costs, agencies may not ignore benefits while highlighting costs, Michigan v. EPA, (3) proposals fail to assess the long-term economic harm of weakening protections.

title: Comment from Rahe, Abigail

text:
As someone who lives in Arizona and regularly sees the effects of habitat and wildlife loss, I am concerned about weakening protections for imperiled species. Importantly, I care about science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country.

Science can tell us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both. The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality.

These are my concerns with the proposals:
1. Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
2. Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
3. Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
4. Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.

Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests; rollbacks reduce public accountability at a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections.

I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections, thus preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
The Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule” automatically gives newly listed threatened species the same baseline protections as endangered species while the USFWS identifies species-specific safeguards. This proposed change will eliminate the “blanket rule,” which means species that could be listed in the future—like the northwestern pond turtle—may lose the standard protections vital to their recovery.

Use this sample message or write your own.
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

The ETWS act has long stood as the leading guide in the conservation world, with 99% of species it protects still surviving today. To weaken its power at the peak of its necessity is a grave error that is both unconstitutional and unethical, allowing for the slipping of more species through the cracks.

The identification and setting aside of critical habitats is a historically a mistake, as it allows for opening up and careless use of 'non-critical' habitats. Moreover, it reduces tourism opportunities instead of creates then- the industry has recently shifted towards idealizing large open natural spaces, of which the USA is currently in the top 5 with alongside Africa, Mongolia, Russia & Canada. All major countries have urban spaces and malls; America's unique landscape and creatures are becoming more of a draw and it would be short-sighted to jeopardize that.

Time is a currency that endangered species are short on but that adminstration spends a lot of, unavoidably, while making laws. In case of a fast spreading epidemic or a breeding ground under peril from a new industry, where there are only months or years suddenly left to prevent an extinction, waiting for the species-specific rule to be put in place will not save them.

Short-term planning also helps no one; to leave further space for us to miss smaller species and longer time to deal with new threats. Deliberately narrowing focus instead of constantly preventing new problems will render all efforts null down the line.

I am interested in the ESA because I understand the natural and critical connection between human health and environment from the micro to the macro scale. In 1973, when a bipartisan Congress passed the ESA, it designated two agencies to oversee promulgation of the Act: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Dept. of Interior) and National Marine Fisheries Service (NOAA - Dept. of Commerce). The combined missions of the Departments of Interior and of Commerce serve to account for economic opportunity and protection & management of "the Nation's natural resources". Not only was the ESA passed in each House of Congress, President Nixon signed the Act into law; through two co-equal branches of government, the will of the people was vicariously signed into law.

Many Acts of Congress are promulgated by a single agency. However, the 1973 legislative branch saw fit - and the executive agreed - that two administrative agencies would oversee promulgation of the ESA because the protections intended by the Act were meant to protect natural resources and allow for economic opportunity.

The Endangered Species Act protects "We the People"; the proposed alteration of the longstanding meaning of "harm" in the ESA would have the effect of reducing protections to critical, threatened, and endangered species. E.g. the California Sea Otter, listed as threatened and a keystone species to the Monterey kelp Forrests. When protections for keystone species are eliminated, the jobs of working class people are eliminated. The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.
Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.
The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.
For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from von Gohren, Abbey

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
