text:
I strongly oppose any weakening of the Endangered Species Act.

The ESA is one of the most effective environmental laws ever enacted, not only because it protects individual species, but because it safeguards entire ecosystems — systems that humans depend on for clean water, food stability, climate resilience, and planetary balance.

Extinction is irreversible. Once a species is gone, it is gone forever. No economic gain, political convenience, or short-term profit justifies that loss. The idea that we can prioritize development while treating the natural world as expendable reflects a dangerous misunderstanding of our interdependence with life on Earth.

The Endangered Species Act is not an obstacle to progress — it is progress. It represents foresight, responsibility, and respect for life. Weakening it would signal that we are willing to trade the future of the planet for immediate gain, despite overwhelming scientific evidence that biodiversity loss accelerates climate instability and ecological collapse.

I urge decision-makers to uphold and strengthen the Endangered Species Act, not dismantle it. Protecting vulnerable species is not optional or ideological — it is a moral, ecological, and human necessity.

text:
My family and I are active users of America’s public lands and waters. We have five children, and we regularly explore public lands in Utah together in our 1994 Toyota Land Cruiser. These trips are how our kids learn about conservation, responsibility, and respect for the outdoors. I’m writing in support of the Fish and Wildlife Service’s four proposed ESA regulatory updates because they move the ESA toward clearer, more practical, and more effective implementation.

For too long, ESA rules have been applied inconsistently in ways that restrict access and lawful use without actually recovering species. I support updates that focus on real, science-based results, respect multiple use and property rights, and provide more predictability for families, landowners, and local communities.

I support moving away from one-size-fits-all threatened species and 4(d) rules and toward species-specific approaches that target real threats on the ground. I also support revising ESA Section 7 consultation to be more practical and science-driven, including removing offset-style requirements that often don’t make sense for the species or habitat involved.

I support improving transparency and predictability in critical habitat designations and exclusions, as well as clearer standards for listing and delisting decisions. These changes can reduce uncertainty and litigation while keeping the focus on recovery rather than process.

These reforms matter to families like mine and to rural communities across Utah. ESA decisions affect access, local jobs, agriculture, energy, and recreation. Clearer rules reduce delays and uncertainty and make it easier for people to participate in conservation without fear of arbitrary restrictions.

They also matter for wildfire prevention. Responsible forest and rangeland management—like fuels reduction and post-fire recovery—can be slowed by overly broad ESA processes, even when projects reduce catastrophic fire risk. These reforms can help remove unnecessary barriers to work that protects habitat, watersheds, and communities.

Finally, these changes matter for recreation and access. Exploring public lands together, whether driving existing routes, camping, fishing, or just spending time outdoors, is a big part of our family life. ESA rules shouldn’t be used as a blanket justification for closures that aren’t tied to measurable recovery benefits. Conservation and access can coexist when rules are targeted, transparent, and grounded in science.

I urge the Services to finalize these reforms and refocus ESA implementation on common sense, transparency, and real recovery outcomes—using restrictions only when they are necessary, effective, and measurable.

title: Comment from McCabe, Kathryn

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act and the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) that will stop really successful strategies that have saved plants and animals from extinction that we have caused or exacerbated. We share this planet with God's creatures and have been entrusted with their care through sound and successful science and long term analysis.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Clarke , Cassie

text:
I am writing to express strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. These revisions would significantly weaken a law that exists to prevent extinction and protect the ecosystems on which both wildlife and people depend.

The Endangered Species Act was created to ensure that decisions about species protection are based on science alone. Introducing economic considerations into listing or protection decisions undermines the very foundation of the Act and shifts the focus from preventing irreversible loss to accommodating development interests. Once a species is lost, it cannot be recovered, and no economic benefit can justify that outcome.

Equally troubling is the proposal to reduce protections for critical unoccupied habitat. Many species rely on these areas for recovery, dispersal, and adaptation to changing environmental conditions. Stripping protections from habitat that may not be currently occupied ignores how wildlife actually survives and recovers, particularly in the face of climate change, habitat fragmentation, and increasing human pressures.

These changes would also weaken enforcement by narrowing how protections are applied. Requiring species to be explicitly shielded from each individual threat creates dangerous gaps in protection and exposes vulnerable wildlife to increased hunting, habitat destruction, and exploitation. Even species already listed as endangered or threatened could suffer further declines under this fragmented approach.

For decades, the Endangered Species Act has been one of the most effective conservation laws in the world. Weakening it now would jeopardize countless species, undo hard-won conservation progress, and erode the United States’ commitment to environmental responsibility. I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to reject these proposed changes and uphold the strength, intent, and scientific integrity of the Endangered Species Act.

When it comes to the existential threat that is extinction, one must act with swiftness and caution. Our government is not expert in either of these aspects. To propose these gutting revisions on the basis of improperly implemented policy is to misunderstand the function of policy. We do not have these regulations for the sake of regulating.
I grew up in an ecologically diverse wonderland. An area whose largest redeeming factor- in my eyes- is the wildlife. I've seen the pitfalls and strength of environmental policies firsthand. Our local lagoon has gone through the trials and tribulations of pollution, and with dedicated effort of our community has painstakingly worked to restore it. My whole life I have lived next to species- such as manatees- facing the threat of eradication. And my whole life I have been blessed to be around people who care enough to try and conserve the beautiful world we live in. The number of ospreys in our area used to be dismal, and I have seen in my lifetime their population skyrocket thanks to efforts bolstered by the very regulations you are proposing to repeal. The blanket rule is integral to the effectiveness of this policy- as we have seen with scientific study and our own observations. We, Humans, have such a limited understanding of our environments- of the world around us. Policy, heavy handed and ineffective as it can be, is all to eager to gloss over small interest groups and those small groups create the web of our society- and of an ecosystem. Policy makers have no business deciding which animals deserve to get resources allocated to their survival- and I anticipate a repeal of the blanket rule would exactly that. As a member of the public I also do not appreciate my share in this process being minimized if not removed. The blanket rule has proven effective for saving lives. The legal definition of harm provided has proven integral for saving species and the habitats they rely on.
My hometown would look fundamentally different than it does today without these policies. I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Hom, Patrick

text:
As a concerned citizen, I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations described in docket FWS‑HQ‑ES‑2025‑0029. After reviewing the proposal and the accompanying materials, it is clear that these changes would significantly weaken long‑standing protections for threatened species and undermine the scientific integrity and effectiveness of the ESA. The ESA has been one of the most successful conservation laws in the world, preventing the extinction of more than 99 percent of the species placed under its protection. Weakening its core regulatory framework at a time when biodiversity loss is accelerating is both scientifically unsound and contrary to the public interest.

The proposal would revise how threatened species are protected under Section 4 of the ESA, including eliminating the long‑standing “blanket 4(d) rule,” which has provided automatic, baseline protections for newly listed threatened species unless the agency adopts a species‑specific rule. According to the Federal Register summary, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is proposing to “revise our regulations concerning protections of threatened species under the Endangered Species Act”. Removing this default protection shifts the burden onto the agency to craft individualized rules for each species, a process that is time‑consuming, resource‑intensive, and vulnerable to political pressure. Historically, the blanket rule has ensured that threatened species receive immediate and meaningful safeguards during the critical period after listing, when populations are often declining most rapidly. Eliminating it would create regulatory gaps that could accelerate declines and increase the likelihood that species will require endangered status later, at far greater ecological and economic cost.

The proposed changes also occur alongside a suite of related regulatory revisions that collectively roll back protections across multiple ESA sections. As noted in public comments already submitted, the four proposals taken together “rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular”. This includes changes to listing and delisting criteria, critical habitat designation, and interagency consultation under Section 7. The cumulative effect is a regulatory environment that prioritizes administrative convenience over biological necessity, despite the ESA’s clear statutory mandate to rely on the best available science.

The agencies’ own Frequently Asked Questions document acknowledges that the revisions would “clarify and improve” processes related to listing, delisting, and critical habitat designation. However, the language of the proposed rule does not provide evidence that these changes would improve conservation outcomes. Instead, they appear designed to narrow the circumstances under which species can be listed or critical habitat designated, and to reduce the scope of federal consultation requirements. These changes would make it more difficult to protect species facing emerging threats such as climate change, habitat fragmentation, and novel diseases, all of which require precautionary and science‑driven regulatory approaches.

The ESA’s success has always depended on strong, consistent, and science‑based implementation. Weakening its regulatory backbone at a time when species are disappearing at unprecedented rates is not only irresponsible but contrary to the intent of Congress when it enacted the law. The American public overwhelmingly supports strong protections for wildlife, and the ESA remains one of the most popular environmental laws in the country. The proposed revisions do not reflect this public support, nor do they reflect the urgency of the biodiversity crisis documented by scientists worldwide.

For these reasons, I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to withdraw the proposed rule and retain the regulatory framework that has protected threatened species for decades. The ESA must remain a strong, science‑based tool capable of responding to the accelerating challenges facing our nation’s wildlife. Weakening its protections now would jeopardize irreplaceable species and ecosystems, and future generations will bear the cost of these decisions.

The Endangered Species Act is vital to protecting countless species from extinction. Wolves, for example, were wiped out of Yellowstone once. Thankfully, they were reintroduced and their numbers have increased, but they are still threatened, and therefore, need our protection. Wolves help balance the ecosystem. The prey wolves catch in the winter months help feed other species. There is a natural balance to the ecosystem when wolves are present. Allowing the hunting of wolves is a grave error and must be rectified. Threatened species, like wolves, rely on the blanket 4(d) rule for immediate protections. Another component of the current Endangered Species Act (ESA) is species-specific rules, which are necessary for long-term recovery of the species, require significant time and energy to be created so the blanket rule provides needed protections until species-specific rules are drafted. The broad baseline protections of the ESA ensure that species don’t fall prey to regulatory gaps or the influence of special-interest groups. Each of these components aids in the protection of all the species in North America.

Another notable example is the Barred Owls on the west coast. The Barred Owls are being targeted due to the decline of the Spotted Owl. The Barred Owls are not a threat to the Spotted Owl. Barred and Spotted mate with one another naturally. The deforestation on the west coast is the cause of the Spotted Owl's decline. Greedy humans have used the Barred Owl as a scapegoat. Realistically, Spotted Owls are going to be collateral due to how similar in appearance they are to Barred Owls. The sharpshooters will not necessarily know the difference. The ESA should have protected the Spotted Owl from this situation. Unfortunately, Congress used a loophole to pass the plan which will cull about 450,000 Barred Owls. This plan will inevitably kill Spotted Owls and hundreds of owlets who are orphaned after their parents are shot. Section 7 of the ESA is crucial to ensuring that other agencies’ projects (oil drilling, mining, dams, timber sales) don’t further endanger wildlife. Furthermore, the Section 7 consultation process has been significant to the Act’s success in preventing the extinction of imperiled animals and plants; 99% of species listed under the Act survive today. The new proposed regulations would greatly limit the consultation process and impact both imperiled species and the critical habitat they rely on. This proposal would make it more challenging for the US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) to prove that actions requested by other federal agencies would negatively impact listed species and critical habitat. This would exclude many indirect, cumulative, or climate-driven effects from being considered. The majority of Americans are in favor of the current rules surrounding the ESA and reject the proposed rules put forth by the Trump administration. North America is home to a variety of amazing species and we must safeguard them and their habitats. By rejecting the proposed rules, we can guarantee the species alive today will continue to live on and thrive for future generations to enjoy. If we accept the changes then there is no guarantee that species currently threatened or endangered will survive much longer. The survival of these species relies on the current ESA. We have an obligation to steward this planet in a way that allows all life to flourish. We only have one planet, which means we need to take extra care of the resources we have, including all life-forms. We have already lost too many to extinction. The current ESA is one of many laws which help us steward our planet properly. Please protect our beautiful planet by rejecting the proposals that would alter the Endangered Species Act.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I am deeply concerned about your proposals to roll back lifesaving Endangered Species Act (ESA) protections for endangered wildlife
and their habitats, and I urge you to reconsider these reckless plans.

Protections under the ESA are our most effective tool for combating the appalling decline of wildlife across the nation. Hundreds
of species were on a path to extinction until they were saved by this law's protections, including bald eagles and gray wolves. And
a million species are at risk of extinction in the coming decades, including grizzly bears, Florida panthers, and manatees. Right now,
we have a choice between bringing endangered wildlife back from the brink, or losing them forever. We must act while we still can.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted
supporter of wildlife and science-based conservation, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule, which threatens a cornerstone of
the ESA by weakening federal agency cooperation and the collaborative review of actions that jeopardize listed wildlife and their
habitats.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment not only to protecting imperiled species but also to conserving
the ecosystems that sustain them. I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and retain existing consultation
and review standards to ensure compliance with the ESA’s statutory intent and expectations of the American people.

More than four out of five Americans support the ESA. Please uphold this essential law and protect imperiled life.

Thank you.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
I’m writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed revisions to the regulations governing species listing and critical habitat designation under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

The proposed revisions flagrantly exceed the agency’s authority in a way that is entirely impermissible. Congress could not have been clearer when it directed the Secretary to make listing determinations “solely on the basis of the best scientific and commercial data available” (16 U.S.C. § 1533(b)(1)(A)). The statute does not leave room for policy preferences, economic balancing, or administrative discretion on this question. It is a mandatory, unqualified instruction. The Supreme Court has repeatedly stated that when Congress speaks with this level of clarity, agencies are bound by that command. They do not have license to revisit or dilute it.

The proposed rule attempts to do exactly that. By introducing economic considerations into the listing process, considerations Congress expressly excluded, the agency is asserting a power it does not possess. This is not a matter of interpretation or gap-filling; it is a direct contradiction of the statutory text. An agency may not override Congress because it prefers a different policy outcome, nor may it recast a prohibited factor as a permissible one through regulatory language. Doing so would effectively amend the statute by regulation, something no agency has the authority to do.

Additionally, the proposed narrowing of critical habitat designations is inconsistent with both the statutory text and longstanding judicial interpretation. Critical habitat must include both occupied and unoccupied areas essential for conservation and recovery. By imposing new constraints on unoccupied habitat, including requirements that effectively preclude designating future climate-suitable habitat, the rule undermines the recovery mandate at the heart of the ESA. The Supreme Court has affirmed that “conservation” means recovery, not mere survival. Any rule that prevents the Service from designating habitat needed for recovery is contrary to law.

The ESA is a statute whose commands are specific. The agency does not have discretion to disregard them. These proposed revisions are in defiance of the law and should be rescinded.

title: Comment from Jimenez , Shelly

text:
I urge you to withdraw this proposal. Endangered Species Act listings must be guided by science and prohibit economic considerations. Federal agencies should not be allowed to take actions that push listed species closer to extinction. The very idea that the USFWS intends to weaken the ESA in deference to commercial interests is contrary to the intent of the ESA.
 
    I urge you to withdraw this proposal. We cannot allow our environmental policy to be submissive to commercial interests at odds to the preservation of endangered or threatened species. The narrowing of the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat would be disastrous. Historic habitat is vital for the recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

    I urge you to maintain strong compliance measures for federal agencies. The proposed rule makes it easier to greenlight destructive activities, such as logging or drilling. These actions will put protected species in harm’s way. We cannot turn over our environmental regulatory framework to the very commercial interests that placed the species at risk in the first place. I urge you to withdraw this proposal. Industry should not get a “rubber stamp” for projects that put federally endangered species more at risk.

    ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Anything less than full cooperation is disorganization and willful sabotage of coherent ecological policy. 
Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law and, importantly, strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations. It is preposterous to consider enacting change without regard to cohesive, cooperative, consolidated policy. 
 
      There should be NO revision to 0 CFR part 17, subparts D and G. Section 4(d). 50 CFR 17.31 and 17.71 must remain as written. There is absolutely zero crisis that demands we change the sound policy which has worked for decades to preserve and protect species in peril. There is no "burden" on commerce. That is pure political double-speak. The ESA does not restrict commercial enterprise except in those methods which would irrevocably harm wildlife.  There should be NO consideration of "economic" impacts when proposing and executing protection of wildlife. There is no requirement to subjugate the need for environmental and species-specific protections to the interests of commercial entities. title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Greetings,

I strongly oppose the proposed rule to rescind the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Eliminating this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, which directly contradicts the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress established distinct “endangered” and “threatened” classifications to promote earlier intervention, not to postpone protections until species face severe decline. The blanket 4(d) rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents emerging threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are developed. Without this safeguards, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating the development of dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules and thereby delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I strongly urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely, consistent, and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

The Endangered Species Act is one of the most successful and important pieces of legislation in protecting the biodiversity within our country. It has protected many species from extinction, including our national symbol, the bald eagle. It is valued by the American people as 4 in 5 Americans support the Endangered Species Act. Thus, the majority of American citizens are united in support of this piece of legislation.
title: Comment from Ilg, Carissa

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Hunhoff, Lindsey

text:
I am submitting this comment because biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter deeply to me. As someone who lives in New Mexico and regularly sees the effects of habitat loss, I am concerned about weakening protections for imperiled species. I care about science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country.
The Endangered Species Act works because it centers science and the public interest—not political pressure or economic influence.
Science can tell us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both.
The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality.
Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed. Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.
Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests. These rollbacks reduce public accountability at a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections.
A democratic, science-based process requires transparency and meaningful review. I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections. Please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so states and industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife.

title: Comment from Rock, Leah

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I want the endangered species act to continue protecting wolves as they are a keystone species and responsible for the delicate balance of the ecosystem. We know that protecting wolves is a popular viewpoint with over 78% of Americans wanting to keep wolves protected. Wolves are also considered sacred to indigenous people and should be protected to honor the Indigenous way of life. In Wisconsin when there was a wolf hunt held in 2021, many wolves were slaughtered because hunters went past the quota they were supposed to hunt. I’m very concerned that this kind of slaughter could happen again as there are some very Unsportsmanlike people wanting to kill wolves because they have a negative view of them. For some reason, wolves seem particularly vulnerable to people who want to slaughter them which is incredibly sad and concerning to me. I consider wolves very much like dogs in their family habits, tenderness towards their young , and in many of their mannerisms. I would really like to see more education about wolves, and their critical importance in our ecosystem.

I’m sharing information that says the science shows we need to continue protecting wolves because they have not recovered to the extent that they used to have the same access to their habitats in the 48 states.

“For thousands of years, gray wolves shaped ecosystems across what is now the continental United States, from the deserts of the Southwest to the forests of New England, the Great Plains, and the high alpine West. They regulated prey populations, influenced how elk and deer moved and grazed, helped rivers and riparian systems recover, and strengthened ecological resilience. Their role was foundational.

Wolves did not disappear because the land stopped supporting them. They were eradicated through a deliberate, government-backed campaign of violence. Federal and state agencies paid bounties, distributed poison across public lands, and used traps, aerial gunning, and organized extermination programs to wipe wolves out across most of their historic range. By the time the Endangered Species Act passed in 1973, wolves survived only in a few isolated pockets.

The ESA was meant to correct that history, not by confining wolves to remote refuges, but by restoring them to a secure and functional role across a significant portion of their historic range. That has not happened.
Today, as Representative Lauren Boebert pushes another bill to strip protections from gray wolves, opponents of recovery are urging hunters to flood Members of Congress with trail-camera photos, claiming that the mere presence of wolves proves recovery is complete.

The courts have already rejected that logic. Just last year, WWP successfully challenged the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s refusal to protect wolves in Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho, states with the most aggressive wolf-killing policies. The court recognized that population numbers alone do not equal recovery when state management is designed to suppress, fragment, and eradicate wolves.

The real evidence is not found in selective images of wolves that survived persecution, but in photographs of absence. Of places where wolves should be. Places that remain wild and capable of supporting them, yet stand empty because recovery has been actively blocked.

The Endangered Species Act was never meant to declare victory while absence defines the map. Until wolves reclaim the lands that shaped them, recovery has not been achieved.”

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,
I am writing to express my concerns about the proposed revisions in Docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029-0001, which would remove the longstanding “blanket rule” for protecting newly listed threatened species under section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). This proposed change would end the automatic application of the broad suite of prohibitions that apply to endangered species, instead requiring the Service to develop species-specific protective regulations for each threatened species before all relevant protections take effect.
The blanket 4(d) rule has been a key component of the ESA’s effectiveness for decades. From the mid-1970s until the 2019 regulatory revision, threatened species automatically received the same prohibitions against take, harm, harassment, and other harmful activities that apply to endangered species. This default protection provided an immediate safeguard for species once listed as threatened, preventing avoidable declines while species-specific rules were developed.
Under the proposed rule, newly listed threatened species would no longer receive these automatic protections. Instead, protections would only apply once a species-specific 4(d) rule is finalized, a process that can take many months or even years. During that interim period, species newly listed as threatened could be left without full statutory protections against activities that contribute to their decline, including habitat loss, disturbance, or direct take. The ESA’s purpose is to halt species decline and promote recovery; delaying protections undermines that statutory mandate and increases the risk that species will deteriorate further before necessary safeguards are in place.
Scientific research and conservation practice show that species listed as threatened often face severe and complex threats, including habitat degradation, climate change, disease, and invasive species — threats that do not pause while new regulations are being drafted. Failure to provide immediate baseline protections increases the likelihood that populations will shrink or habitats will be degraded further, making recovery more difficult and costly, and in some cases pushing species closer to the point of no return. Congress designed section 4(d) to ensure that necessary and advisable protections are in place for threatened species, and the blanket rule was an efficient and precautionary application of that authority.
Moreover, the proposed requirement for species-specific rules could divert already limited Fish and Wildlife Service resources into extensive rulemaking processes, slowing down other critical conservation work, including listing decisions, recovery planning, and critical habitat designation. This shift in regulatory burden could diminish the Service’s capacity to respond to the ongoing biodiversity crisis, where many species are declining more rapidly than agencies can act.
For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule option or ensure that any changes to threatened species protections do not create gaps in basic statutory protections. Ensuring that threatened species are safeguarded immediately upon listing is consistent with the ESA’s core purpose of preventing extinction and fostering recovery based on the best available science.
Thank you for considering my comments.

text:
As conservation biologists, we are opposed to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act. These proposed changes are naked attempts to weaken a law that has protected species on the brink of extinction since its inception, despite numerous partisan attacks. The Act has been wildly successful in keeping thousands of species from extinction.

The argument that the ESA hinders economic growth is baseless. In the decades since the ESA was enacted, the gross national product has continued to increase. In fact, in our experience with the oil and gas industry in Wyoming, stability in the regulatory environment was their most important concern. Upending the ESA will do more economic harm than good just by removing any sense of certainty.

Eliminating the 4(d) rule for threatened species is counterproductive. The bureaucratic machinery of government is notoriously slow. That's why species that qualify for ESA protections should automatically and immediately be granted protections while listing decisions are being made.

One of the main features of the ESA when it was enacted was its recognition that species loss is chiefly tied to habitat loss. Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions would reverse these habitat protections and hasten species decline.

The real problem is that the ESA is grossly underfunded and cannot keep up with the growing threat to species from habitat loss and climate breakdown. Attempts to "fix" the Act can start by rectifying this negligence. In addition, the rationale behind the proposed changes are flimsy and not based on science. Politically-driven policies rarely produce good results.

The USFWS has forgotten that is must serve the public interest, not just industry. In this case, the public is wildly supportive of the Endangered Species Act. We encourage USFWS to abandon this foolhardy, naked attempt to weaken it.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Charlé, Suzanne

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly. It's common sense - if ecologists have cause to label a species as threatened, we must respond with immediate action rather than expensive assessments.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

Prairie Hills Audubon Society (of Western South Dakota), PO Box 788, Black Hawk, SD 57718, 605-787-6466, phas.wsd@rapidnet.com

Dear Mr. Tirpak:
Prairie Hills Audubon Society submits these comments opposing the proposed repeal of the long-standing blanket Section 4(d) rule that extends Section 9 take protections to threatened species. PHAS has signed on to the joint comment letters submitted by the Center for Biological Diversity and the Natural Resources Defense Council, and we incorporate those comments by reference. We submit this letter separately so that our organization’s name and address are clearly reflected in the administrative record.
The blanket 4(d) rule has provided efficient, predictable, and science-based protection for threatened species for decades. Eliminating automatic protections would leave many species vulnerable during lengthy delays in species-specific rulemaking, further strain already overburdened agency resources, and undermine incentives for voluntary conservation on private lands.
In South Dakota, where much imperiled species habitat occurs on non-federal land, removal of default protections would significantly weaken conservation outcomes. PHAS urges the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule and withdraw the proposed revisions.

text:
I oppose the proposal to eliminate the blanket 4(d) rule for threatened species.

The current rule provides threatened species with automatic protections equivalent to those afforded to endangered species, allowing conservation measures to take effect immediately after listing. The proposed change would replace these protections with species-specific rules, creating delays and increasing the likelihood of exemptions from the ESA’s prohibition on harm.

Scientific evidence consistently shows that early intervention is critical to preventing population collapse. Delaying protections while tailored rules are developed increases exposure to habitat loss and other threats during a period when species are already in decline.

The blanket 4(d) rule is a preventative measure that reduces extinction risk. Removing it weakens the ESA’s ability to protect species before they reach irreversible thresholds.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
What the rule does
This rule would eliminate the “blanket 4(d) rule: The long-standing policy that automatically gives newly listed threatened species the same protections as endangered species unless a species-specific rule is written. The proposal says the Fish & Wildlife Service will:
•Remove the blanket rule entirely, and
•Only issue species-specific 4(d) rules, which could reduce protections depending on what the Service chooses to include.
Until species-specific rules are written, existing blanket protections technically continue, but the direction of the rule is toward phasing them out.
Why this matters
The blanket 4(d) rule is one of the fastest and most effective tools for giving threatened species immediate protection. Removing it means:
•Threatened species will not be automatically protected from killing, harming, or habitat destruction.
•They will rely on individual 4(d) rules, which are slower, easier for industry to influence, and often weaker.
•Many species could face regulatory gaps right after listing — their most vulnerable moment.
This change comes in response to executive orders to roll back ESA protections and reduce perceived burdens on industry.
Talking points for comments
•The blanket 4(d) rule is a proven, science-based tool that gives threatened species immediate protections when they are most at risk.
•Eliminating the blanket rule will delay or weaken protections for newly listed species, putting them in harm’s way during the period when conservation actions are most critical.
•Species-specific rules are not a substitute for broad baseline protections; they are slow, resource-intensive, and increase political pressure from industries seeking exemptions.
•The ESA requires decisions to be based on the best available science, not executive orders aimed at weakening environmental safeguards.
•The Fish & Wildlife Service should retain the blanket 4(d) rule to prevent regulatory gaps that could worsen species declines.

text:
Hello my name is Natalya and I am writing to oppose removing protections for threatened species under the “blanket rule”. It is one step further to undermine conservation safeguards that the Endangered Species Act provides.

Currently, all threatened species automatically receive protections equal to endangered species and we should maintain this. I would even like to see us expand protections to include candidate species that are warranted, but precluded like the Greater Sage Grouse.

I am a birder and frequently recreate across California, Nevada, Arizona, and Utah. This summer I got to see and photograph the Greater Sage Grouse in the Inyo National Forest. Their population has declined 80% Since 1965 and yet they are not an endangered species - this is one of countless examples of species that benefit from blanket protections.

Rescinding the blanket rule is being proposed in order to narrow environmental reviews and allow different projects to move faster without considering their environmental consequences. Removing the blanket will lead to fewer protections for struggling plants and animals. We’ve lost 40% of our wildlife in North America in the last 50 years. The pressures these species face are multiple - habitat loss, degradation, invasive species, disease, and climate change. Now is the time for strengthening protections, not weakening them.

The weakening of protections only serves to benefit a select few in industries such as oil, gas, mining, and logging. This comes at a great cost to the vast majority who cherish the natural world for its intrinsic beauty, who find solace and joy in outdoor recreation, and who hold deep historical and cultural connections to these lands. Most importantly, this decision puts at risk the millions of plant and animal species that call these habitats home - species that are already struggling to survive in the face of numerous human-caused pressures. We cannot afford to lose more of our precious biodiversity; once lost, it is gone forever.

I strongly urge you to maintain the current protections for threatened species under the Endangered Species Act's "blanket rule." Our wildlife and wild places are a priceless inheritance that we must steward wisely for future generations. Prioritizing short-term economic gains over the long-term health of our ecosystems is a shortsighted and irresponsible path. We must do all we can to protect and preserve the incredible diversity of life with which we share this planet. The Endangered Species Act has proven to be a powerful tool in this effort, and we implore you to keep it strong.

Submitted via Federal eRulemaking Portal

Public Comments Processing

United States Fish and Wildlife Service
5275 Leesburg Pike
Falls Church, VA 22041-3803

Re: Comments on Proposed Rulemaking Regarding Section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act, Docket Number FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029

Dear Director Nesvik:

The Animal Welfare Institute (“AWI”), on behalf of our members and supporters nationwide, submits the following comments in strong opposition to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s (“USFWS” or “Service”) proposed rulemaking that would revoke the Service’s longstanding regulation related to implementation of section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act (“ESA”), 15 U.S.C. §§ 1531, et seq. See 90 Fed. Reg. 52,587 (Nov. 21, 2025). By eliminating the presumptive legal protections for “threatened” species, the proposed rule would significantly undermine the safeguards necessary to support the survival and recovery of threatened species.

AWI is a nonprofit organization whose mission is to alleviate animal suffering caused by people. We seek to improve the welfare of animals everywhere: in agriculture, in commerce, in our homes and communities, in research, and in the wild. Since 1951, AWI has advanced its mission through strategically crafted policy and legal advocacy, educational programs, research and analysis, litigation, and engagement with policymakers, scientists, industry, educators, other NGOs, the media, and the public. We seek scientifically-grounded protections for animals in all settings, and robust enforcement of those protections.

Section 4(d) of the ESA requires the Service to issue regulations to provide for the conservation of species listed as threatened. Id. § 1533(d). If the Service lists a species as threatened, it has concluded that special protections are necessary to halt that species’ decline toward endangerment, and therefore extinction, “within the foreseeable future.” 15 U.S.C § 1532(20). As a means of carrying out that directive, the ESA expressly allows the Service to extend the same protections to threatened species as it does to endangered species. Id. § 1533(d). To implement this section of the statute, since 1975 USFWS has relied upon what is referred to as the “blanket 4(d)” rule.

Contrary to the clear statutory mandate, the Service now proposes to leave threatened species without the legal protections required by the ESA unless and until the Service issues species-specific regulations. This shifts the presumption for threatened species from protected to unprotected, which, if such species-specific regulations are not issued, directly contravenes the ESA. The proposed rule therefore increases the risk that threatened species will be deprived of protection due to a lack of Service resources necessary to write such special rules. Given the Service’s pattern and practice of failing to issue species-specific rules, continuing to extend blanket, baseline protections to threatened species is necessary to effectuate the ESA’s mandate.

The Service proposes to rescind this 50-year-old definition based on a misinterpretation of the Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 400 (2024), and an erroneous assertion that the Service’s decades-old definition does not represent the single, best interpretation of the statute. 90 Fed. Reg. at 16,103. USFWS also purports to justify the rescission of the blanket 4(d) rule on policy grounds, yet it fails entirely to acknowledge the facts and circumstances that gave rise to the issuance of the blanket 4(d) rule. Rescission of this rule will inevitably hinder recovery and diminish the effectiveness of the ESA. AWI therefore urges USFWS to withdraw the proposed rule.

AWI specifically endorses and incorporates by reference the comments filed by the Southern Environmental Law Center (“SELC”) on behalf of itself and numerous other public interest organizations, including AWI, on USFWS’s proposed rulemakings, Docket Numbers FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, and FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048, as well as the comments filed by the Natural Resources Defense Council (“NRDC”) on behalf of itself and numerous other public interest organizations, including AWI, on USFWS’s proposed 4(d) rulemaking, Docket Number FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029.

For a full discussion of our opposition to the proposed rulemaking, please see the attached comments.

If you have any questions or if there is any additional information we can provide, please do not hesitate to contact us.

Sincerely,

Johanna Hamburger
Director and Senior Attorney
Terrestrial Wildlife Program
Animal Welfare Institute
900 Pennsylvania Ave, SE
Washington, DC 20003
