title: Comment from Steffes, Wayne

text:
I firmly oppose the plan to remove the longstanding blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For many years, this crucial rule has automatically applied most section 9 restrictions to threatened species once listed, unless specific rules were created. Eliminating this protection will lead to significant delays before threatened species receive vital conservation actions, going against the ESA’s precautionary approach.

Congress distinguished “endangered” from “threatened” categories to enable earlier intervention, not to postpone protections until situations become critical. The blanket rule offers an effective, scientifically sound method to prevent increasing threats while specific management plans are developed. Without it, newly threatened species would remain unprotected during their most vulnerable times, raising the risk of them becoming endangered or extinct.

Additionally, the proposed removal offers no proof that the blanket rule imposes undue regulatory burdens under the ESA or APA. In fact, eliminating it will heighten administrative tasks by requiring numerous species-specific 4(d) rules, hindering the delivery of urgent protections.

For these reasons, I strongly urge the Service to maintain the blanket 4(d) rule to ensure timely and scientifically backed protections for all threatened species.

text:
One of the proposed revisions to Endangered Species Act regulations would overturn the 4(d) rule, removing blanket protections for threatened species. I am writing to express my staunch opposition to this proposal, which is all but guaranteed to delay critical protections and push threatened species to the brink of endangerment.

As you know, the “blanket rule” established under the ESA automatically prohibits all threatened species from being killed, harmed, trapped, or traded. But under the proposed rule, protection would no longer be the default. Agencies would instead be required to produce species-specific rules to establish protections, making the process of listing even one threatened species an incredibly time-intensive one.

Rather than making it increasingly difficult to establish essential protections, we should be preserving the regulations that are helping threatened species recover. Please stand up for American wildlife by leaving these blanket protections in place.

Thank you.

I am against re-issuance of the 2019 revisions to the regulations in 50 CFR part 17, subparts D and G, which applies protections to a species newly listed as threatened only through issuance of a species-specific rule setting out the protective regulations that are necessary and advisable for that species. The current “blanket rule” protections allow safeguards to be more quickly put in place that can help prevent species from moving from a threatened to endangered status, while still allowing for species-specific alternatives to be approved by the federal government. The difference is that currently, species are afforded protections while those species-specific rules are under development. This proposed change would take those critical protections away, and by the time species-specific rules are implemented, the species may move from threatened to endangered or even extinct status. Development of species-specific rules for each threatened species take time, and in the time before those rules are issued, irreparable damage to species and habitats may occur. This appears to be a stalling tactic to allow plaintiffs to mount challenges against the agency and will result in reduced effectiveness of agency efforts to protect threatened species, wasted tax dollars and more opportunities for moneyed interests to mount tactics to evade Endangered Species Act requirements. I vehemently oppose this provision.
title: Comment from Prince, Tamara

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Cranmer, Julia

text:
I am writing to oppose the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s proposal to remove the longstanding blanket 4(d) rule for threatened species. Eliminating this tool weakens urgent protections at a time when wildlife across the country faces accelerating habitat loss, climate disruption, and human-caused pressures.

For decades, the blanket 4(d) rule has provided a critical safety net by ensuring that newly listed threatened species automatically receive the same core protections that prevent harm to endangered species unless and until a species-specific rule is crafted. This structure reflects the intent of the Endangered Species Act: to take precautionary action when a species is known to be declining, rather than wait for additional regulatory processes while threats continue unchecked.

Under the proposed changes, every threatened species would have to wait for a species-specific 4(d) rule before receiving clear, enforceable section 9 protections. Even with the Service’s stated intention to finalize these rules concurrently with listings, real-world delays are common due to workload, litigation, and resource constraints. Any gap in protection can result in irreversible harm to already vulnerable species.

The Service’s own past rulemakings have recognized that the blanket rule reduces administrative burdens, avoids redundant permitting processes, and focuses resources on the stressors that matter most. Removing it does the opposite: it increases regulatory complexity, increases the risk of inconsistent protections, and introduces uncertainty for species that are already in decline. The proposal cites a shift in statutory interpretation, but nothing in the text or purpose of the ESA requires the removal of essential baseline protections that have been proven to work.

Threatened species cannot withstand policy-driven delays. Immediate safeguards are essential to prevent avoidable loss of individuals, habitat damage, and further population decline. The blanket rule has been an efficient, effective mechanism to ensure those protections are in place the moment a species is listed. Replacing this with a slower, case-by-case system is a step backward for conservation.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule option and ensure that threatened species continue to receive automatic, precautionary protections upon listing. Species-specific rules can and should remain available where appropriate, but they must supplement rather than replace this vital baseline.

Protecting threatened species requires timely, science-driven action. Maintaining the blanket rule is necessary to keep protections maximized and uphold the core purpose of the Endangered Species Act.

Thank you for considering this comment.

title: Comment from LaMere, Alexis

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Yermak, Iris Patty

text:
Recently, the Trump administration proposed revisions to 4rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I STRONGLY oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings—some even before they have been named, such as some of the 80% of insect species not yet identified.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations. Loosing species can have a negative impact on humans. For instance, the loss of mosquito-eating species can mean an increase in mosquito-borne diseases such as malaria, west nile, and zika. Keeping humans healthy requires that we keep our environment healthy as well.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Pierce, Diane

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings—some even before they have been named, such as some of the 80% of insect species not yet identified.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.
title: Comment from Nogles, Tammy

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Richmond, Lonna

text:
I am firmly against the proposal to remove the longstanding blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. This blanket rule has, for years, offered vital safeguards by automatically applying most section 9 restrictions to threatened species unless specific rules are established. Eliminating these protections will lead to significant delays in providing vital conservation measures, directly opposing the ESA's precautionary principles.

Congress separated “endangered” and “threatened” categories to enable earlier action, not to postpone protections until situations worsen. The blanket rule is an effective, scientifically sound tool that prevents threats from escalating as specific management plans are developed. Without it, newly threatened species will remain unprotected during their most critical phase, heightening the risk of them moving toward endangerment or extinction.

Moreover, this proposal lacks evidence that the blanket rule imposes any regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or APA. In fact, its removal will actually increase administrative tasks by requiring multiple species-specific 4(d) rules, thus delaying essential protections.

For these reasons, I strongly encourage the Service to maintain the blanket 4(d) rule, ensuring timely, scientific protection for all threatened species.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Dow, Barbara

text:
The captains of industry appear hellbent on trampling every living thing in their path to feeding the insatiable greed of the shareholders. This leaves you the only adults in the room to save whatever is left of our stressed, overheated, abused environment. Please don’t join their extreme agenda. Just say, No.

One of the proposed revisions to Endangered Species Act regulations would overturn the 4(d) rule, removing blanket protections for threatened species. I am writing to express my staunch opposition to this proposal, which is all but guaranteed to delay critical protections and push threatened species to the brink of endangerment.

As you know, the “blanket rule” established under the ESA automatically prohibits all threatened species from being killed, harmed, trapped, or traded. But under the proposed rule, protection would no longer be the default. Agencies would instead be required to produce species-specific rules to establish protections, making the process of listing even one threatened species an incredibly time-intensive one.

Rather than making it increasingly difficult to establish essential protections, we should be preserving the regulations that are helping threatened species recover. Please stand up for American wildlife by leaving these blanket protections in place.

Thank you.
title: Comment from Williams, Donna

text: I oppose these changes as they give preference to habitat-destroying industries and cause irreversible harm to at-risk species.

title: Comment from LaRose, Yvette

text: Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule removes timely, automatic safeguards for newly listed threatened species. Requiring species-specific rules creates delays during the most vulnerable period, leaving many species exposed while rules are developed. This shift burdens agency resources, slows conservation action, and contradicts the ESA’s preventative design. Retaining the blanket rule is essential to avoid further declines.

title: Comment from Elder, Amanda

text:
To the Fish and Wildlife Service,

I’m writing because the proposal to rescind the blanket 4(d) rule genuinely terrifies me. I don’t mean that dramatically—I mean it in a practical, real-world way. I’ve spent years volunteering with local conservation groups monitoring declining species and practicing real world conservation on my 40-acre farm. I’ve seen how fragile some populations are, and how quickly things can spiral without basic protections.

Removing the blanket 4(d) rule means threatened species could go unprotected for months or years while species-specific rules get written. We all know how slow that process is. In the meantime, habitat destruction and incidental take will continue unchecked—right at the moment when those species are already showing signs of serious decline.

Congress created the “threatened” category so we wouldn’t wait until species were at the cliff’s edge. This proposal does the opposite. It’s hard to read it as anything other than an intentional delay tactic.

Please don’t do this. The blanket rule has worked for decades. It saves time, it saves money, and more importantly, it saves species that won’t survive without immediate protections. Keep it in place.

Sincerely,
A VERY Concerned Citizen of the United States of America

title: Comment from Poole, Andrea

text:

title: Comment from Zatirka, Theresa

text:
As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Shields, Janice

text:
I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings—some even before they have been named, such as some of the 80% of insect species not yet identified.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.
title: Comment from Alleman, Laura

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Green, Bryan

text:
I firmly oppose the proposed change to the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The blanket rule that automatically protects newly listed threatened species from killing, trapping and other forms of prohibited “take” must remain. Removing these protections increases the chances of species becoming endangered or extinct.

For decades the ESA has been a crucial and effective tool to support and protect wildlife on the edge of survival. It has proven successful in the recovery of Bald Eagles, Osprey, Peregrine Falcons, and many other species. As development and climate change are applying ever growing challenges for our wildlife and natural world, the US Fish & Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service should be dedicated to upholding the Endangered Species Act to its strongest-possible effectiveness in protecting animals and their crucial habitats, not weakening this law that protects our natural world.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Drabik, Bill

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings—some even before they have been named, such as some of the 80% of insect species not yet identified.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Vaz, Kimberly

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Smithwick, Doreen

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to convey my firm opposition to the four proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. Each proposal, individually and collectively, would significantly undermine the ESA's effectiveness in preventing extinction, promoting species recovery, and conserving vital ecosystems for both wildlife and human communities.

1. Eliminating default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA aims to act before species reach crisis levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule, supported by decades of scientific evidence, demonstrates that early, precautionary protections lower recovery costs and prevent further declines. Removing default protections would create unnecessary delays, necessitate case-by-case rulemaking, and expose vulnerable species to preventable harm or mortality. This contradicts the ESA's preventive intent and will incur greater ecological and financial costs over time.

2. Impeding species listing by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best available scientific data, excluding economic impacts. Introducing economic considerations undermines this objectivity and risks delaying protections until species are near extinction. Restricting the use of projected or climate-driven threats ignores conservation science, which shows that threats like habitat loss and climate change increase risk before population declines are visible. Weakening future-threat criteria reduces the likelihood of timely listings, increasing preventable extinction risks.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and narrowing the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is the primary driver of biodiversity decline globally and in the U.S. Reducing critical habitat designations, especially for unoccupied or climate-refugia areas, undermines recovery planning. Similarly, narrowing “harm” to exclude habitat degradation reverses legal and scientific precedent, as habitat destruction often indirectly kills wildlife. Weakening these definitions impairs inter-agency consultations, elevates biological risks, and contradicts the ESA’s recovery mandate.

4. Introducing new loopholes for agencies or committees to bypass ESA protections

Allowing agencies to override ESA protections, even when extinction is a foreseeable outcome, conflicts with the ESA's core mission. These loopholes encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and sideline science-based analysis. This disproportionately impacts imperiled species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, potentially accelerating their decline.

The cumulative impact of these proposals

While significant individually, collectively these rules would:
• undermine the ESA's scientific foundation,
• delay or block protections for endangered species,
• reduce habitat conservation amid accelerating climate change,
• heighten extinction risks for domestic and international species,
• undermine inter-agency cooperation,
• increase long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from extinction, ranking among the most successful conservation laws due to its basis in science, precaution, and proactive measures. These proposed changes clash with these principles.

At a time of unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the United States should strengthen—not weaken—its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes and maintain the existing regulatory framework, rooted in science, legal precedent, and decades of successful implementation.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

The proposed rule changes would weaken protections for threatened and endangered species. This would accelerate the biodiversity and extinction crises and certainly lead to more preventable extinctions, depriving our children and grandchildren of experiencing America's current wild splendor from coast to coast. These changes would also have major effects on ecosystem health, leading to agricultural problems like less-productive soil, fewer pollinators for key crops, and destabilized habitats vulnerable to increases in disease-carrying mosquitoes and ticks.

I urge the Department of Interior and US Fish and Wildlife Service to reject the proposed revisions to the ESA and retain Section 4(d) as it is. Our children and grandchildren deserve to experience the rich biodiversity that generations of Americans have enjoyed and celebrated in film and song. Thank you for your time.

title: Comment from Kent Berman, Meredith

text:
No good for the objective species can come from this change. I oppose the elimination of the longstanding “blanket 4(d) rule,” which has automatically extended endangered‑level protections to threatened species since 1978.

This rule has been foundational to the ESA’s success. The transition from “threatened” to “endangered” can happen rapidly; without default protections, species may decline irreversibly during the years‑long process of drafting species‑specific rules. Congress created the threatened category to prevent species from reaching the brink of extinction. Removing baseline safeguards defeats that purpose.

Legally, the ESA requires the Secretary to implement protective regulations “as necessary and advisable to provide for the conservation of the species” (16 U.S.C. § 1533(d)). For 45 years, administrations of both parties interpreted this to mean that threatened species generally require robust protections while individualized rules are being developed.

Removing automatic protections for newly listed threatened species creates a dangerous regulatory vacuum where industry can accelerate the very harms that triggered the listing. This is contrary to Congressional intent, which emphasized precaution, not delay.

The proposed change would lead to increased habitat destruction, population loss, and regulatory confusion. It is neither scientifically justified nor administratively efficient.

I urge the agency to withdraw the proposal and retain automatic protections that have been essential to preventing species from sliding into endangered status.
title: Comment from Fox, Roy

text: The Endangered Species Act (ESA) is crucial because it offers the strongest legal protections for vulnerable plants and animals, giving species on the brink of extinction a chance to recover. By preserving threatened wildlife, the ESA also protects entire ecosystems that are essential for human needs, such as clean air, clean water, and a stable climate. Many species saved by the ESA, including the bald eagle, gray whale, and American alligator, demonstrate that successful conservation is possible when supported by strong laws and scientific research. Maintaining the ESA also preserves the nation’s natural heritage for future generations, ensuring that biodiversity, ecological balance, and the benefits of healthy ecosystems are not permanently lost.
title: Comment from Miller, M. Barrett

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s Section 7 consultation process. These changes would narrow definitions of “effects,” ignore cumulative and indirect impacts, and dramatically lower the obligations of federal agencies to avoid jeopardizing listed species.

Section 7(a)(2) imposes an affirmative, non‑discretionary duty on federal agencies to ensure their actions are not likely to “jeopardize the continued existence” of listed species or “destroy or adversely modify” critical habitat. Courts have held that this requires a comprehensive, science‑based evaluation of direct, indirect, and cumulative impacts (see Karuk Tribe of Cal. v. U.S. Forest Serv., 681 F.3d 1006 (9th Cir. 2012)).

The proposed rule attempts to redefine away large categories of harm by excluding cumulative, long‑term, or “uncertain” impacts — which in ecology are often the most significant drivers of decline.

This is scientifically indefensible. Species are not harmed only by sudden catastrophic events; they decline through chronic habitat fragmentation, pollution, noise, climate‑driven stressors, and repeated small administrative decisions that add up to irreversible loss.

By raising the evidentiary threshold and weakening the definition of adverse modification, the rule would allow agencies to green‑light destructive federal actions — pipelines, highways, logging, mining — with virtually no accountability.

The ESA’s effectiveness depends on Section 7. Gutting consultations effectively guts the Act.

I urge the agency to withdraw this proposal.

The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Fecko, Albert

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

title: Comment from Friedman, Sarah

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Hull, Cameron

text:
I oppose the proposed revisions to the ESA’s section 4(b)(2) exclusion framework. While the ESA permits the Secretary to exclude areas from critical habitat when the benefits of exclusion outweigh the benefits of designation, Congress intended this authority to be narrow and used only when exclusion would not result in extinction. The proposed rule improperly elevates economic considerations above biological needs, requiring the agency to give de facto prioritization to economic impacts even when these impacts are speculative or secondary.

The rule also creates an impermissibly high evidentiary threshold for retaining habitat, by stating that areas should be excluded unless the agency can demonstrate that exclusion would lead to extinction. This reverses the ESA’s precautionary orientation and is inconsistent with the statute’s protective purpose. Courts have consistently held that critical habitat must be designated with recovery in mind, not merely avoidance of extinction.

Moreover, the rule appears to give disproportionate weight to non-biological actors, including private industry, by encouraging the submission of economic “concerns” without requiring equivalent scientific rigor. This threatens to transform the exclusion process into a mechanism for regulated entities to override scientific judgment — a result Congress explicitly sought to prevent when it stripped economic considerations from the listing process.

I urge the Service to abandon these revisions and maintain a 4(b)(2) framework that ensures exclusions remain rare, justified, and fully subordinate to the biological needs of listed species.

As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Khoyi Noyes, Lauren

text:
The Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule” automatically gives newly listed threatened species the same baseline protections as endangered species while the USFWS identifies species-specific safeguards. This proposed change will eliminate the “blanket rule,” which means species that could be listed in the future—like the northwestern pond turtle—may lose the standard protections vital to their recovery.

Use this sample message or write your own.
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Jones, Francesca

text: If the blanket rule is removed, it will deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly, could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings.
title: Comment from D, MG

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Wegdjie, Fhalrite

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to voice my firm opposition to the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. These changes, whether considered individually or collectively, would significantly undermine the ESA’s effectiveness in preventing extinction, aiding species recovery, and conserving the ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Repealing default protections for threatened species (the 4(d) rule)

The ESA was crafted to act before species reach crisis levels. The 4(d) rule embodies decades of scientific evidence showing early protections lower recovery costs and prevent further declines. Ending these automatic protections would cause unnecessary delays, make rule-making more cumbersome, and put vulnerable species at risk. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive nature and will lead to higher ecological and financial costs.

2. Allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

ESA listing decisions must be based solely on the best scientific data. Factoring in economic impacts would undermine objectivity and delay crucial protections. Ignoring future threats from issues like climate change dismisses vital conservation science. This weakening of criteria increases the risk of preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and narrowing the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is the top driver of biodiversity decline. Limiting habitat designations directly hampers recovery plans. Narrowing “harm” definitions disregards legal precedents recognizing habitat destruction’s indirect wildlife impacts. Weakening these definitions reduces inter-agency consultation efficacy and increases biological risk.

4. Creating loopholes to bypass ESA protections

Loopholes allowing agencies to sidestep ESA protections run counter to the Act’s purpose. These would encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and stray from science-based decision-making, disproportionately affecting imperiled species like the Florida panther, grizzly bear, and gray wolf.

Cumulative Impact

Together, these proposals would weaken the scientific base of the ESA, delay or block necessary protections, reduce habitat conservation, increase extinction risks, undermine cooperation, and raise recovery costs.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct, due to its scientific, precautionary, and proactive approach. These changes oppose those principles.

At a time of significant biodiversity loss, the U.S. should be fortifying—not weakening—this vital conservation law.

My Request:

Given these reasons, I urge the withdrawal of all four proposed rule changes and the retention of the current framework, which is rooted in science and proven success.

text:
One of the proposed revisions to Endangered Species Act regulations would overturn the 4(d) rule, removing blanket protections for threatened species. I am writing to express my staunch opposition to this proposal, which is all but guaranteed to delay critical protections and push threatened species to the brink of endangerment.

As you know, the “blanket rule” established under the ESA automatically prohibits all threatened species from being killed, harmed, trapped, or traded. Thank you.

title: Comment from Oakley, Traci

text:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act’s Section 4(d) protections. I am deeply alarmed, and frankly outraged, that this proposal would remove the automatic safeguards currently afforded to threatened species. This decision is not only scientifically unsound, but it also disregards decades of proven conservation success and exposes our most vulnerable species to irreversible harm.

Under the current framework, threatened species receive immediate, essential protections at the moment they are listed. This safety net has prevented countless declines from accelerating into full endangerment or extinction. The proposed shift to case-by-case 4(d) rules eliminates this crucial buffer and replaces it with a lengthy, bureaucratic process—one that will leave species unprotected during the most fragile, critical stages of their recovery.

The consequences of this decision are entirely foreseeable. Delayed protections mean increased habitat destruction, greater exposure to industrial impacts, and more legal “take” of species that are already struggling to survive. Many species simply cannot withstand months or years of regulatory delay; some may slip into endangerment—or disappear altogether—before a tailored rule is ever written. This is not hypothetical. It is a predictable outcome that undermines both the intent and the effectiveness of the Endangered Species Act.

This proposal also opens the door to inconsistent, politically influenced decision-making. Instead of relying on long-standing, science-based blanket protections, species fate would be determined through discretionary, case-specific rules vulnerable to lobbying and industry pressure. This fundamentally weakens the integrity of the ESA and risks turning the survival of entire species into political bargaining chips.

The environmental impacts extend far beyond individual species. When threatened species lose habitat and are pushed closer to extinction, entire ecosystems suffer. Pollinators that support our food systems, keystone species that stabilize habitats, and culturally significant wildlife all stand to be harmed. This rule does not simply affect plants and animals—it affects our clean air, clean water, agricultural systems, climate resilience, and the health of future generations.

As a member of the public who values biodiversity, environmental stability, and responsible stewardship of our natural world, I strongly urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to reject this proposal. We should be strengthening protections for struggling species—not weakening them. Removing automatic safeguards from threatened species is negligent, ecologically damaging, and contrary to the fundamental purpose of the Endangered Species Act.

I ask that the agency uphold the science-driven, precautionary principles that have guided the ESA for decades and maintain the blanket 4(d) protections that have proven effective, efficient, and essential. Our wildlife—and our environment—deserve nothing less.
