text:
The fact this is even being tossed around is just proof that all the government and those running it care about is money and making their sponsors happy. They do not care for the health and beauty of this planet, the people living on it or even their own future kids. So I’m writing to say I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.
More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.
I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.
We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.
title: Comment from Laz, Lauren

text:
I oppose the proposed changes to Section 4(d) because they would allow far broader take allowances for threatened species without adequate scientific justification. The rule shifts the default from protection to permissive use, even though threatened species often rely on early, precautionary safeguards to avoid slipping toward endangered status.

The administration frames these changes as providing “flexibility,” but the proposal gives no evidence that current 4(d) rules impede recovery or create measurable burdens. Instead, the revisions open the door for habitat destruction and lethal take before the agency has fully evaluated species-specific vulnerabilities. This contradicts decades of practice and the ESA’s intent that threatened species receive proactive, not reactive, protection.

Weakening default protections will also increase regulatory inconsistency, creating confusion for land managers and undermining recovery planning. Threatened species need clear, stable guardrails, not shifting or discretionary standards influenced by non-scientific considerations.

I urge the Fish and Wildlife Service to reject this proposal and maintain 4(d) regulations that prioritize timely, science-based safeguards for threatened species.

These categories have helped protect threatened shorebirds like the Piping Plover, a conservation-dependent species crucial to coastal diversity along the U.S. Atlantic Coast. I have personally worked with these birds during the breeding season and it has really changed my life for the better. I am inspired to pursue conservation work with plovers and other threatened species, and it would be detrimental to take their legal classifications and protections away. Before being listed as “threatened” under the ESA in 1985, Piping Plovers were in very steep decline, and very little was known about their life history and ecological importance. However, protection under the ESA has caused more research and conservation work to be directed towards restoring Piping Plover populations, and it is crucial that this work continues, otherwise Piping Plovers and other threatened species could be at risk of disappearing again. Many people may not know about these species now, but we will feel the impact of their population decline and extinction if they are not continually protected.

title: Comment from Sendilkumar, Akhil

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings—some even before they have been named, such as some of the 80% of insect species not yet identified.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.
title: Comment from Yarbrough, Jim

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to express my deep opposition to the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA). These changes represent a serious threat to the integrity and effectiveness of one of our nation’s most important environmental protections. For decades, the ESA has served as a critical safeguard for species on the brink of extinction, ensuring that vulnerable wildlife and the habitats they depend on are given the chance to recover and thrive. Weakening its provisions would not only jeopardize the survival of countless species but also undermine the ecological balance that sustains healthy environments for future generations.

The proposed revisions appear to prioritize short-term economic or political interests over the long-term health of our ecosystems. Such an approach disregards the interconnected nature of biodiversity, where the loss of even a single species can have cascading effects on entire habitats, water systems, and human communities. While concerning individually, together these rules would:
- undermine the scientific foundation of the ESA,
- delay or obstruct protections for at-risk species,
- reduce habitat conservation amidst accelerating climate change,
- heighten extinction risk for both domestic and internationally threatened species,
- undermine inter-agency cooperation,
- and escalate long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA is not merely a legal framework — it is a moral commitment to protect the natural heritage we have inherited and to pass it on intact to those who come after us. The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct, making it one of the most effective conservation laws due to its foundation in science, precaution, and early action. These proposed changes contradict those principles.

During this time of massive global biodiversity loss, the United States should be strengthening, not weakening, its most effective wildlife protection law.

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed changes and instead strengthen the ESA’s protections, ensuring that it continues to serve as a beacon of responsible stewardship and environmental responsibility.

Thank you for considering this comment.

title: Comment from Boyle, Jeff

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from BAKER, TRACI

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings—some even before they have been named, such as some of the 80% of insect species not yet identified.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

title: Comment from Tisdale , A

text:
I am submitting this comment because biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter deeply to me. I hold a Master's Degree in Geology and value biodiversity, scientific review of policy and protection of the environment. I care about science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country. The Endangered Species Act works because it centers science and the public interest—not political pressure or economic influence.
Science can tell us what species need to survive; values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both.
The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality. Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.
Federal oversight is often the only check on state wildlife systems that are already heavily shaped by industry interests. These rollbacks reduce public accountability at a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections.
I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections.
Please strengthen, not weaken, federal safeguards so states and industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife.
I ask you to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.
Thank you, Stacey Lane

I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you
to withdraw it.

This would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when
deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or on a

title: Comment from Jamulla, John

text: Biodiversity is one of the most beautiful things about the United States. We have such a variety of habitats that support a wide range of species that have taken major hits at the hands of humans. Throughout our history Americans have had to grapple with these immense amounts of loss by our hand. From the decimation of beaver populations during the fur trade, to the clearcutting of old growth forest during the industrial revolution. These events had profound impacts on the shape of our landscapes, in the case of beavers our environment became drier and altered the fire regime. In the case of forests, today in america there is less than 10% remaining. Old growth forests are prime habitat for many species particularly birds such as the spotted owl. I say this to point to the importance of preserving our remaining species and habitats. We have in our history experienced what decimation can do, not just to our landscape but to our future. Every species fills a niche that keeps our planet healthy and functioning, without them I would argue that we’d be leaving the Earth “immunocompromised.” Without this layer of resilience, we in the United States will experience the impacts of climate change in a way we never have before. We will see even more intense wildfires, flooding, landslides, heat waves and more. I feel so honored to live in a country with such a variety of habitat and species, it would be a shame to lose them due to this bill. If anything regulations for endangered species and their habitats should be more intense not less. I urge you to reconsider this proposal, for the love of this country that many species of residents call home.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

title: Comment from Hillmann, Tamara

text:
As a docent at Woodland Park Zoo in Seattle, I am profoundly aware that threatened species often soon become endangered species. If we are to act to save them, the best chance is before they become critically endangered.

The Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule” automatically gives newly listed threatened species the same baseline protections as endangered species while the USFWS identifies species-specific safeguards. This proposed change will eliminate the “blanket rule,” which means species that could be listed in the future—like the northwestern pond turtle—may lose the standard protections vital to their recovery.

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Kendall, Dean

text:
Subject: Opposition to Proposed Changes to ESA Regulations

---

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am compelled to voice my firm opposition to the four proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. These changes, both individually and collectively, pose a serious threat to the ESA’s capacity to avert extinction, aid species recovery, and protect the crucial ecosystems that both wildlife and human populations rely on.

**1. Repeal of Default Protections for Threatened Species**

The ESA’s intent is to act before species become critically endangered. The established 4(d) rule has proven, through years of scientific research, that early precautionary measures reduce recovery costs and curb further declines. Eliminating automatic protections would lead to unnecessary delays, requiring case-by-case rule-making and exposing threatened species to preventable harm. This move is counter to the ESA’s preventive purpose and is likely to escalate ecological and financial burdens over time.

**2. Economic Considerations in Listing Decisions**

It's essential that the ESA decisions are grounded solely in scientific evidence, not economic impacts. Introducing economic factors undermines statutory language and scientific integrity, delaying crucial protections until species are near extinction. Furthermore, downplaying future threats ignores vital conservation science, which highlights that long-term pressures like habitat loss and climate change already endanger species before population declines are evident. Weakening these criteria threatens timely listings and increases preventable extinctions.

**3. Reducing Critical Habitat Protections and Limiting “Harm” Definition**

Habitat loss is a primary contributor to biodiversity decline globally. Curtailing critical habitat designations undermines recovery efforts, and narrowing the “harm” definition to exclude habitat degradation reverses decades of legal and scientific practice. This weakens inter-agency consultations, increases biological risk, and contradicts the ESA’s recovery objectives.

**4. Loopholes that Undermine ESA Protections**

By enabling agencies to bypass ESA safeguards, even when extinction is likely, these proposals contradict the ESA’s core objectives. Such loopholes encourage exemptions, decrease transparency, and divert decisions from science-based analysis, disproportionately affecting species like the Florida panther, grizzly bear, and gray wolf, which are already under severe threat.

**Cumulative Impact**

When considered collectively, these proposals would:
- Erode the scientific basis of the ESA,
- Delay or obstruct essential species protections,
- Diminish habitat conservation amidst escalating climate change,
- Heighten extinction risks for both local and global species,
- Undermine inter-agency collaboration,
- Inflate long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from extinction, thanks to its foundation in science, caution, and proactive efforts. These suggested changes oppose these foundational principles.

In this era of unprecedented biodiversity loss, the U.S. should be enhancing, not weakening, its most effective wildlife protection law.

**Conclusion**

Given the reasons detailed above, I urge the agencies to reject all four proposed rule changes entirely and retain the current regulatory framework, which is anchored in science, legal precedence, and decades of proven success.

Sincerely,

Emma

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I request that you reject the proposed rules, which would:

**Deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings.

**Narrow the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

**Loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

**Violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

Thank you.

text:
I am submitting this comment in strong opposition to the Services’ proposal to roll back critical portions of the 2024 Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations and revert to the less protective 2019 framework.

The ESA is one of the most successful conservation laws in history precisely because Congress designed it to rely on scientific judgment, precaution, and a clear legislative mandate to conserve ecosystems and prevent extinction. Nothing in the statute authorizes weakening protections to satisfy the deregulatory impulses of Executive Orders focused on short-term energy expansion or administrative convenience. The ESA’s text is explicit: listing, delisting, and critical habitat decisions must prioritize the best available scientific and commercial data. They are not economic balancing tests, nor are they meant to bend to non-scientific policy goals.

This proposed rule does three especially damaging things:

1. It narrows the definition of “foreseeable future,” inviting underestimation of climate-driven threats that are, by their nature, probabilistic yet well-supported by peer-reviewed science.

2. It reinstates constraints on designating unoccupied critical habitat, precisely at the moment when species require adaptive range expansion to survive accelerating habitat loss, drought, wildfire, invasive species, and warming.

3. It broadens the circumstances for “not prudent” habitat designations, which risks transforming what Congress intended as a rare exception into a discretionary loophole.

Each of these changes reduces the government’s ability to protect species under real ecological conditions. Climate disruption does not wait for “reasonable certainty.” Species on the brink cannot survive habitat definitions that ignore future viability. And the ESA cannot function when its mandatory duties are carved into discretionary options.

The Services cite recent litigation and Executive Orders as justification. But neither litigation nor executive preference overrides statutory purpose. The ESA’s directive is unambiguous: Federal agencies shall seek to conserve endangered and threatened species. That means the precautionary principle must govern, not political expediency or narrow readings that discount emerging science.

I urge the Services to withdraw this proposal and preserve the 2024 regulations, which more faithfully reflect congressional intent, current ecological realities, and the plain meaning of the Act. We do not get a second chance with extinction. Regulatory frameworks must reflect that irreversible fact.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

title: Comment from Geiser, Rosann

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings—some even before they have been named, such as some of the 80% of insect species not yet identified.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

title: Comment from Pellman, Julie

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to strongly oppose the four suggested changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently being considered. These proposals, whether individually or collectively, would significantly undermine the ESA’s capacity to prevent extinctions, aid species recovery, and protect the ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Eliminating default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA was created to act before species reach critical danger levels. The 4(d) rule has long shown that early, precautionary actions reduce recovery costs and prevent further declines. Ending such automatic protections would cause unnecessary delays, require individual rulemaking, and expose species to avoidable threats. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive purpose and will lead to greater ecological and financial consequences over time.

2. Complicating species listing by considering economic factors and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions rely solely on the best scientific data, excluding economic impacts. Allowing economic considerations would contradict this, erode scientific objectivity, and risk delaying protections until species face extinction. Ignoring projections of threats like habitat loss and climate change neglects current science, making preventive actions less likely and increasing the risk of preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and redefining “harm”

Habitat destruction is the main driver of biodiversity decline. Limiting critical habitat designations undermines recovery efforts. Similarly, narrowing “harm” definitions to exclude habitat degradation reverses years of legal and scientific understanding. These changes would weaken inter-agency consultations and increase risks, contrasting with the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. Creating loopholes for agencies to bypass ESA protections

Allowing agencies to override ESA protections, even when extinction is foreseeable, conflicts with the ESA’s core mission. These loopholes would encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and shift decisions away from science. This would disproportionately affect imperiled species like Florida panthers and gray wolves, accelerating their decline.

Cumulative Impact

Together, these rules would:
• Weaken ESA’s scientific foundation,
• Delay or block necessary protections,
• Reduce habitat conservation amid climate change,
• Increase extinction risks,
• Undermine agency cooperation,
• Raise long-term taxpayer costs.

The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from extinction due to its science-based, precautionary approach. Weakening these protections contradicts its successful history.

In an era of significant global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should bolster—not dilute—its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes entirely and maintain the existing, scientifically grounded regulatory framework.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings—some even before they have been named, such as some of the 80% of insect species not yet identified.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.
title: Comment from Ramos, J

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.
More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.
I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.
We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.
title: Comment from LENKER, V

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.
title: Comment from Derasary, Lara

text:
As a concerned citizen and supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule.”

The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and repealing it means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline.

I urge the Administration to recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance of survival.

Prioritizing economic factors may be temporarily expedient, but will dilute the principles of the ESA. The resulting loss of habitat and the species living there will be irreversible and ultimately endanger the survival of all species including humans.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Sprenger, Keri

text:
One of the proposed revisions to Endangered Species Act regulations would overturn the 4(d) rule, removing blanket protections for threatened species. I am writing to express my staunch opposition to this proposal, which is all but guaranteed to delay critical protections and push threatened species to the brink of endangerment.

As you know, the “blanket rule” established under the ESA automatically prohibits all threatened species from being killed, harmed, trapped, or traded. But under the proposed rule, protection would no longer be the default. Agencies would instead be required to produce species-specific rules to establish protections, making the process of listing even one threatened species an incredibly time-intensive one.

Rather than making it increasingly difficult to establish essential protections, we should be preserving the regulations that are helping threatened species recover. Please stand up for American wildlife by leaving these blanket protections in place.

Thank you.
title: Comment from Prestien, James

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to express my firm opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. These changes would significantly undermine the ESA’s mission to prevent extinction, aid species recovery, and conserve vital ecosystems for wildlife and human communities alike.

1. **Removing default protections for threatened species**
The repeal of the 4(d) rule would lead to unnecessary delays and expose vulnerable species to harm. The ESA was designed to provide early protections, which have proven essential in reducing recovery costs and preventing species declines.

2. **Incorporating economic considerations in listing decisions**
Decisions should be based solely on scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic factors would conflict with the ESA’s intent and compromise scientific objectivity, delaying crucial protections.

3. **Reducing critical habitat protections**
Limiting habitat designations and narrowing the definition of “harm” would directly impair recovery efforts. Habitat destruction is a leading threat to biodiversity, and weakening these protections contradicts ecological science and legal precedent.

4. **Creating loopholes to bypass ESA protections**
Allowing agencies to override protections would conflict with the ESA's purpose. These loopholes would reduce transparency and harm wide-ranging and imperiled species like the Florida panther and gray wolf.

**Cumulative Impact**
Taken together, these proposals would weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation, delay protections, reduce habitat conservation during a climate crisis, and increase extinction risks. The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct due to its grounding in science and early action.

**Request**
I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed changes and maintain the current regulatory framework, which is based on science, legal precedent, and decades of success.

Thank you for your attention.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

Thank you.
title: Comment from Hallead, Gerald

text:
Subject: Protect Our Wildlife—Do Not Weaken the Endangered Species Act

To Secretary Doug Burgum and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,

As a concerned citizen, urge you to maintain the Endangered Species Act (ESA) exactly as it is written and to reject the currently proposed amendments that threaten to dismantle America’s most effective wildlife protection law. For over 50 years, (and signed into law by a Republican) the ESA has prevented the extinction of 99% of the species under its care. We ask that you stand by science and conservation, rather than corporate interests, to ensure this legacy continues.

I staunchly oppose the following proposed changes to the ESA:

Removing the “Blanket Rule” for Threatened Species: I oppose ending the automatic protections for species listed as “threatened.” forcing them to wait for species-specific rules leaves them vulnerable to exploitation and hunting when they need help the most.
Prioritizing Profit Over Extinction: I reject the proposal to allow economic impacts to be weighed when deciding if a species should be listed. A species’ right to exist should be determined by biological science, not by the cost to industry.
Redefining “Harm” to Exclude Habitat Destruction: I oppose the proposal to rescind the definition of “harm” that includes habitat degradation. Destroying a wild animal’s home is the same as destroying the animal itself.
Limiting Critical Habitat Designations: I oppose rules that make it easier to exclude areas from “critical habitat” protection based on economic or national security claims, which will shrink the safe havens our wildlife desperately needs.
These changes will have devastating, real-world consequences for this country's iconic species.

I call on you to uphold your duty to steward our nation’s natural heritage. Please keep the Endangered Species Act strong, science-based, and free from economic loopholes.

Signed,
Brett Ochs, Boulder, CO

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings—some even before they have been named, such as some of the 80% of insect species not yet identified.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

title: Comment from Shoaf, Cindy

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

I am writing to express my staunch opposition to this proposal, which is all but guaranteed to delay critical protections and push threatened species to the brink of endangerment.

title: Comment from Phillips, Betsy

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. These changes would significantly undermine the ESA's ability to prevent extinction, support species recovery, and conserve ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. **Removing default protections for threatened species**: Ending the blanket 4(d) rule goes against the ESA’s preventive nature, increasing ecological and financial costs by creating unnecessary delays and exposing vulnerable species to harm.

2. **Considering economic impacts in listing decisions**: The ESA mandates decisions based solely on scientific data. Introducing economic factors compromises scientific objectivity and risks delayed protections, which could lead to species extinction.

3. **Reducing critical habitat protections**: Cutting back on habitat designations undermines recovery efforts and weakens the ESA's recovery goals. Narrowing the definition of "harm" reverses established legal and scientific understanding, increasing biological risks.

4. **Bypassing ESA protections**: Allowing agencies to override protections conflicts with the ESA's core mission. These loopholes reduce transparency and could accelerate declines in imperiled species.

**Cumulative impact**: Collectively, these proposals weaken the ESA's scientific foundation, delay protections, reduce habitat conservation, and increase extinction risks and recovery costs. The ESA has a proven track record of success based on science and precaution. These changes contradict its principles at a time when strengthening conservation laws is critical.

**Request**: I urge the agencies to withdraw these proposed changes and maintain the current framework, which has been effective due to its grounding in science and legal precedent.

title: Comment from Camden, Michelle

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to firmly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. Each change would considerably undermine the ESA’s ability to prevent extinction, aid species recovery, and protect ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. **Removing default protections for threatened species**

The longstanding 4(d) rule, based on decades of scientific evidence, wisely provides early protections to prevent species from reaching crisis levels, reducing recovery costs and preventing further declines. Removing these automatic protections would lead to unnecessary delays and expose vulnerable species to avoidable harm, contradicting the ESA's preventive purpose and increasing long-term ecological and financial costs.

2. **Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis**

Listing should rely solely on the best scientific data, not economic factors. Introducing these considerations undermines the ESA’s basis, potentially delaying protections. Ignoring projected threats such as habitat loss and climate change disregards current science, increasing the likelihood of preventable extinctions.

3. **Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”**

As habitat loss is a leading driver of biodiversity decline, reducing habitat protection undermines recovery efforts. Narrowing the definition of “harm” dismisses the indirect impacts of habitat degradation, diminishing the effectiveness of legal protections and increasing biological risks.

4. **Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections**

Allowing agencies to override ESA protections conflicts with its core purpose. These loopholes risk increasing exemption incentives, reducing transparency, and shifting decisions away from science, threatening species like the Florida panther and gray wolf.

**Cumulative Impact**

Collectively, these proposals would weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation, delay protections, reduce habitat conservation, increase extinction risks, undermine cooperation, and raise taxpayer recovery costs. The ESA’s success in preventing 99% of listed species from extinction is due to its scientific and precautionary basis.

In light of growing biodiversity loss, the United States should reinforce, not weaken, its effective wildlife protection law.

**Request**

For these reasons, I urge the withdrawal of all four proposed rule changes and the retention of the current regulatory framework, rooted in science and successful implementation.

As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. I am writing to express my staunch opposition to this proposal, which is all but guaranteed to delay critical protections and push threatened species to the brink of endangerment.

As you know, the “blanket rule” established under the ESA automatically prohibits all threatened species from being killed, harmed, trapped, or traded. But under the proposed rule, protection would no longer be the default. Agencies would instead be required to produce species-specific rules to establish protections, making the process of listing even one threatened species an incredibly time-intensive one.

Rather than making it increasingly difficult to establish essential protections, we should be preserving the regulations that are helping threatened species recover. Please stand up for American wildlife by leaving these blanket protections in place.

Thank you.

Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings—some even before they have been named, such as some of the 80% of insect species not yet identified.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

title: Comment from Keller, Janis

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029
Searching
Subject:
Opposition to Proposed Rule Rescinding the "Blanket 4(d) Rule" for Threatened Species (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029)
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries,
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule that would remove the "blanket rule" option for applying standard protections to newly listed threatened species under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029).
My opposition is rooted firmly in conservation biology and statistical analysis regarding species recovery rates. The best available science indicates that robust, immediate protections are essential to prevent species listed as threatened from reaching the brink of extinction.
Arguments & Analysis: The Necessity of the "Blanket 4(d) Rule"
The core of my scientific argument rests on three main points: the preventative function of the ESA, the statistical correlation between timely protection and recovery, and the administrative risk of implementation delays.

Preventing Extinction Requires Precaution: A species is listed as "threatened" when it is "likely to become endangered within the foreseeable future". This status is a critical warning sign that the species' population trajectory is already negative. Automatically extending the full take prohibitions (which include significant habitat modification) of Section 9 provides immediate, necessary conservation measures to stabilize populations before they decline further. Removing this default protection is a gamble with a species' survival, substituting a precautionary scientific approach with regulatory uncertainty.
Statistical Evidence Supports Robust Protections: Research has consistently shown that the ESA is highly effective at preventing extinction, with estimates suggesting over 99% of listed species have avoided extinction. A significant factor in successful recovery is the timely implementation of comprehensive protections. Studies have found that species with recovery plans and designated critical habitat for several years are significantly more likely to have improving population trends. The "blanket rule" ensures these protections are in place by default, providing a safety net that species-by-species rules may delay.
Species-Specific Rules Cause Delays and Gaps: Requiring tailored, species-specific 4(d) rules for every new threatened listing is administratively burdensome. The current proposal requires the Service to develop bespoke regulations for each species, a time-intensive process that risks regulatory gaps. During the potentially lengthy period required to craft and implement a species-specific rule, threatened species would lack crucial "take" prohibitions, potentially suffering irreversible population declines. This administrative delay undermines the scientific urgency implied by a "threatened" status.

Conclusion & Recommendation
The proposed change is contrary to the best available science regarding the dynamics of species decline and recovery. The existing "blanket 4(d) rule" is a scientifically sound, effective, and efficient mechanism for stemming the slide of threatened species toward extinction and facilitating their recovery.
I urge you to consider the robust scientific data supporting the effectiveness of comprehensive, immediate protections. I respectfully request that you withdraw the proposed rule (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029) and maintain the established "blanket rule" to ensure a precautionary and effective approach to species conservation.
Sincerely,
Lisa Conner
Concerned Citizen and Conservationist
Gig Harbor, WA
