text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Bush, Ken

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.
Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.
The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.
For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Johnston, Heidi

text:
To Whom It May Concern:

I am submitting this comment because healthy ecosystems and strong wildlife protections matter deeply to me. The continued decline in genetic diversity among Mexican gray wolves is only one example of how urgently imperiled species need science-based safeguards.

The proposed rule changes weaken the Endangered Species Act by undermining the scientific standards and democratic accountability that have made the law effective. The ESA works because decisions are grounded in evidence and insulated from political or economic pressure. These proposals shift decision-making away from that foundation.

Removing automatic protections for newly listed species would leave vulnerable wildlife exposed at the moment they most need support. Ending the blanket 4(d) rule risks inconsistent and delayed protections for threatened species. Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to outweigh biological necessity, putting entire ecosystems at risk. Weakening Section 7 consultation would make it easier for harmful projects to advance without full evaluation of their impacts on endangered species.

These changes also reduce transparency and limit opportunities for public oversight, even though most Americans support strong conservation protections.

I urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s science-based framework. Please strengthen—not weaken—federal safeguards so that imperiled species can recover and future generations inherit healthy, resilient ecosystems. The impact if you don't is either not possible and/or incredibly expensive to reverse the impact. The decisions made today will impact unknown future generations. This short comment period right before the holidays is an example of not showing care or respect for the type of decision-making needed to protect the biodiversity now or for generations to come. I again urge the agency to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s science-based framework.

The disappearance of a species disrupts ecosystems, weakens ecological resilience, and can further contribute to climate instability.

Overall, endangered species should remain under the protection of the blanket rule while new regulations are crafted, and their survival must take precedence over short-term economic concerns.

As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings—some even before they have been named, such as some of the 80% of insect species not yet identified.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.
title: Comment from Frohn, Joyce

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule (Docket No. FWS–HQ–ES–2025-0039) that revises the regulations for listing, delisting, reclassification, and critical habitat designations under Section 4. By reintroducing economic considerations into listing decisions and narrowing the definition of “foreseeable future,” this rule undermines the very purpose of the Endangered Species Act: preventing extinction. The ESA has successfully kept 99% of listed species from disappearing, proving that strong, science-based protections save lives and ecosystems. I urge the agencies to retain rigorous, science-driven standards that prioritize species recovery, not industry interests.
____

I oppose the proposed rule (Docket No. FWS–HQ–ES–2025-0044) concerning interagency cooperation under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act. Weakening the consultation process between federal agencies would open the door to harmful actions on critical habitat without meaningful review. The ESA’s collaborative framework has been essential to preventing extinction for hundreds of species, and these changes would undercut that successful model. Please withdraw this proposal and uphold a robust Section 7 process.
____

I object to the proposed rule (Docket No. FWS–HQ–ES–2025-0029) that would eliminate the “blanket” protections for threatened species under Section 4(d) and require case-by-case regulations. This rollback will create gaps in protection for newly listed threatened species and delay recovery. The ESA has a decades-long track record of successfully stabilizing species when protections are applied early and consistently. The Act must provide full, dependable protections—not create loopholes.
____

I strongly oppose the proposed rule (Docket No. FWS–HQ–ES–2025-0048) regarding exclusions from critical habitat designations under Section 4(b)(2). Allowing economic or other non-conservation factors to outweigh species’ survival puts wildlife in peril and contradicts the ESA’s recovery mission. Critical habitat protections have played a central role in the ESA’s 99% success rate in preventing extinction, and weakening them would reverse decades of progress. Please reject this harmful proposal.

text:
One of the proposed revisions to Endangered Species Act regulations would overturn the 4(d) rule, removing blanket protections for threatened species. I am writing to express my staunch opposition to this proposal, which is all but guaranteed to delay critical protections and push threatened species to the brink of endangerment.

As you know, the “blanket rule” established under the ESA automatically prohibits all threatened species from being killed, harmed, trapped, or traded. But under the proposed rule, protection would no longer be the default. Agencies would instead be required to produce species-specific rules to establish protections, making the process of listing even one threatened species an incredibly time-intensive one.

Rather than making it increasingly difficult to establish essential protections, we should be preserving the regulations that are helping threatened species recover. Please stand up for American wildlife by leaving these blanket protections in place.

Thank you.

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA). These changes would significantly weaken protections for endangered and threatened species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA created strong, science-based safeguards, including the prohibition on “take,” the requirement that federal agencies ensure their actions do not jeopardize listed species, and the development of recovery plans for at-risk species.

Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum has stated that these revisions “restore the Endangered Species Act to its original intent” by providing “clear, consistent and lawful standards” that respect the livelihoods of Americans. However, the purposes of the ESA, as written in the statute, do not support weakening core protections. Congress explicitly stated that the Act exists to conserve ecosystems upon which species depend; to provide programs for the conservation of endangered and threatened species; and to implement relevant treaties for species protection.

Congress also made clear findings when passing the ESA:

Many species in the United States have already been rendered extinct due to economic growth and development carried out without adequate conservation;

Other species have been so depleted that they are now endangered or threatened; and

These species hold esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value for the nation.

The original legislative intent was not to lessen regulatory burdens on industries whose activities jeopardize biodiversity. Instead, it was to ensure that economic activity is tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” The proposed rules contradict this intent by undermining basic protections for threatened and endangered species and by narrowing the definition and use of critical habitat.

I oppose these rule changes, which would deprive newly listed threatened species of automatic protections against killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species currently being considered for listing—such as the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage-grouse, and Monarch butterfly—could remain unprotected for years even after federal listing decisions. The impacts extend to species not yet identified, including the roughly 80% of insect species still unnamed.

The Earth is experiencing an accelerating extinction crisis. Addressing this crisis requires strong, science-based ESA regulations, not weakened ones. I urge the agency to withdraw the proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s longstanding, effective protections.

title: Comment from Schaef, Dennis

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Sayre, Emma

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. title: Comment from Fiesler, Laurie

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

Positive conservation and recovery outcomes are more likely to be attained if measures are put in place before a species is on the brink, experiencing reduced genetic diversity and limited habitat in which to forage, shelter, migrate and reproduce. It’s also a lot cheaper to protect an existing wetland, for example, than it is restore one to provide habitat to an endangered plant, insect, or animal.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.
For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.
title: Comment from Wells, K.A.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Olsen, Pamela

text:
To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, I am submitting this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule, Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, which seeks to remove the "blanket rule" (the automatic extension of Section 9 prohibitions to newly listed threatened species) under 50 CFR 17.31 and 17.71. This proposed revision fundamentally misunderstands the protective intent and precautionary principle underpinning the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and creates unnecessary risk for vulnerable wildlife. The blanket rule is an essential, immediate conservation measure, acting as a vital safety net that ensures threatened species—defined as those "likely to become an endangered species within the foreseeable future"—receive robust, baseline protections the moment they are listed. Its removal would immediately compromise the conservation status of newly listed species by creating a dangerous regulatory void.

The primary flaw in this proposal is the failure to guarantee the continuation of immediate protections. By requiring a complex, legally defensible, species-specific 4(d) rule to be finalized concurrently with the final listing determination, the Service exponentially increases the potential for regulatory gaps and conservation delay. The listing process itself is often lengthy and vulnerable to administrative hurdles; adding the mandate to propose, review, solicit comment on, and finalize a highly detailed rule—which now must explicitly consider and justify both conservation and economic impacts—significantly burdens the limited resources of the FWS. If a final listing rule is published before its corresponding 4(d) rule, the threatened species will be left with only minimal, if any, federal protection against "take," habitat destruction, and other adverse actions. This gap directly undermines the ESA's precautionary mandate, allowing irreparable harm to occur during the precise period when a species is most acutely at risk of decline.

Furthermore, the Service's justification that species-specific rules are superior from a policy perspective because they improve efficiency and reduce burdens is highly questionable when considering the aggregate administrative cost. The FWS's staff and budget should be focused on executing crucial recovery actions—including monitoring, habitat restoration, and enforcement—not on the massive, continuous undertaking of drafting, reviewing, and defending a separate, bespoke 4(d) rule for every single threatened species listing. For the majority of listings, the resulting species-specific 4(d) rule will likely mirror the basic protections currently afforded by the blanket rule, rendering the extensive administrative effort a profound waste of limited personnel and fiscal resources. The current system provides the flexibility to issue less restrictive rules only when necessary for specific conservation benefits, thereby focusing limited resources on the few situations that genuinely require regulatory tailoring, a far more efficient and effective approach than the blanket mandate proposed here.

Finally, the shift away from the blanket rule compromises the precautionary principle by fundamentally altering the regulatory burden. The blanket rule reflects the "necessary and advisable" determination that all threatened species need the baseline protections offered to endangered species unless proven otherwise. The proposed rule shifts this burden, forcing the Service to justify why a species already determined to be facing imminent threat requires any protections at all, thereby exposing the rulemaking process to greater political and economic pressure to minimize safeguards. This approach prioritizes administrative and commercial convenience over the robust, proactive conservation mandated by the ESA. I strongly urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to recognize the fundamental conservation value of the automatic protections and to withdraw this proposed rule immediately, thereby retaining the vital, effective safety net provided by the blanket 4(d) rule.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to strongly oppose the four proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. Collectively and individually, these proposals would undermine the ESA's critical role in preventing extinction, aiding species recovery, and conserving ecosystems vital to both wildlife and human communities.

1. Repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule
The ESA is designed to act before species reach critical endangerment levels. The 4(d) rule has shown that early protections reduce recovery costs and prevent further declines. Removing default protections would lead to unnecessary delays and expose species to harm, contrary to the ESA’s preventive aim.

2. Economic considerations and weakened threat analysis
Listing decisions should be based solely on scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic factors contradicts the ESA and risks delaying essential protections. Weakening future-threat criteria will make timely listing less likely and increase preventable extinctions.

3. Reduced habitat protections
Habitat loss is a major driver of biodiversity decline. Reducing critical habitat designations undermines recovery efforts, and narrowing the definition of “harm” reverses longstanding precedents. These changes would weaken agency consultations and increase biological risks.

4. Loopholes for bypassing ESA protections
Expanding mechanisms that allow agencies to override ESA protections goes against the core purpose of the ESA. Such loopholes reduce transparency and rely less on science, affecting species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves.

Cumulative impact
Together, these rules would weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation, delay protections, reduce habitat conservation, increase extinction risk, undermine cooperation, and raise recovery costs.

The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct. In light of global biodiversity loss, we should strengthen protection laws, not weaken them.

Request

I urge the agencies to withdraw these proposals and maintain the current framework, founded on science and successful precedents.
title: Comment from Forrest, Hunter

text: Please do your best to protect the animals from harm. And please place the protection and well-being of animals high on your list of priorities, Fish and Wildlife Service. Animals are all precious and they need protection and safe havens desperately. Thank you for your time. Please protect the animals.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am firmly against the proposed rule that seeks to remove the established blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. These protections have been crucial for decades, automatically applying most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon their listing, unless specific rules are developed for them. Eliminating these safeguards will lead to significant delays in implementing necessary conservation efforts, directly opposing the ESA’s precautionary approach.

Congress intentionally created separate categories for “endangered” and “threatened” species to allow for prompt intervention, not to postpone protection until conditions worsen. The blanket rule serves as an effective and scientifically justified method to prevent threats from escalating while tailored management plans are developed. Doing away with it would leave newly threatened species unprotected during their most crucial time, increasing the risk of them becoming endangered or extinct.

Additionally, the proposed rule fails to demonstrate that the blanket rule imposes any undue regulatory burdens under the ESA or the APA. In fact, removing the rule would increase administrative challenges by requiring numerous species-specific 4(d) rules, thereby delaying essential protections.

Therefore, I strongly urge the Service to maintain the blanket 4(d) rule, ensuring timely and science-based protection for all threatened species.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Cerniglia, Grace

text:
I am submitting this comment because our environment is extremely important. Health ecosystems and biodiversity matter deeply to me. It is our duty to protect all living creatures. The Endangered Species Act works because it is science based and it centers around those scientific findings and public interest. The proposed changes would be detrimental and it would allow considerations to outweigh biological need and scientific reality.
Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin. Newly listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed.
Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide.
Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species.
Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.
I urge to to please withdraw these proposed rules. We need to maintain the ESA's strong, science-based protections. Those protections need to be strengthen so federal safeguards will not allow states and industries to sidestep responsibility to protect imperiled wildlife.
Science must guide the decisions that are made about our wildlife. Corporations have to abide to those regulations and should not be allowed to influence.
title: Comment from Roman, Azucena

text:
It is much more difficult to rescue a species that has become endangered than it is to prevent it becoming endangered in the first place. By removing the blanket protections, you will end up having an unintended impact, where more species will require listing as endangered, due to lack of protection when threatened, and they will remain covered under the ESA for longer, and may never be removed.

Using the blanket rule for threatened species increases the chances that the species will recover, and never require listing as endangered, and may actually decrease the amount of time they need to have the blanket protections, which is actually a net benefit to industry, rather than having many more endangered species that are perpetually on the list.

Rescinding is a terrible idea.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Repensek, Frank

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As an avid supporter of America’s wildlife (wildlife that makes our country healthy, beautiful, and magnificent), I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people. Our wild spaces and wildlife are what make our country so incredible. We must protect both!

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Simmons, Patricia

text:
I am submitting these comments because healthy and well-balanced biodiversity and ecosystems matter deeply to me. I live in the beautiful state of Montana and regularly see the effects of habitat loss, and I am extremely concerned about weakening protections for imperiled species. This is the time to incorporate science-informed stewardship of the wildlife in this country and not allow your politics to drive the decisions.
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) works because it centers both science and the public interest, as it should, and NOT political pressure or economic influence. The science tells us what species need to survive, and values determine whether we choose to protect them. These rules shift decision-making away from both. The proposed changes would allow industry considerations to outweigh both biological need and scientific reality.
Proposals:
1)Proposed Classification Rule (Section 4): Removing automatic protections from newly-listed species places vulnerable wildlife at risk before recovery efforts even begin; newly-listed species could go unprotected while recovery is delayed;
2)Proposed 4(d) Rule (Section 4(d)): Eliminating the blanket rule for threatened species allows inconsistent protections and delays recovery for imperiled wildlife at a time when they need the fullest protection we can provide;
3)Proposed Exclusion Rule (Section 4(b)(2)): Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. If economic interests weigh more than essential habitat, entire ecosystems are at risk, not just wildlife species; and
4)Proposed Consultation Rule (Section 7): Limiting federal review of agency actions would make it easier for destructive projects to proceed without fully assessing impacts on endangered wildlife.

The only check on state wildlife systems is, oftentimes, on the federal level, which is already heavily shaped by industry interests. At a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections, which is evident in my state of Montana, these rollbacks reduce public accountability. Transparency is required for a science-backed and democratic science-based process, on which the ESA is founded.

In closing, I fervently encourage you to withdraw these proposed rules and maintain the ESA’s strong, science-based protections, post haste. It is my strong hope you will strengthen and not weaken the federal safeguards so states and the industry cannot sidestep responsibility to protect endangered wildlife. Please uphold the intent of the ESA, which is to prevent extinction and ensure future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Thompson, Sandra

text: In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades

The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.

We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Carver, Heather

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. text:
I am submitting this comment in strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and the 4(d) Blanket Rule under 50 CFR 17.31. The ESA has a long and proven history as one of our nation’s most effective conservation laws, preventing the extinction of hundreds of species and enabling many to recover. Weakening the protections provided through the Blanket Rule would undermine the very framework that makes the ESA successful.

The Blanket Rule ensures that species listed as “threatened” automatically receive essential protections unless a species-specific 4(d) rule is created. Removing or narrowing this standard safety net exposes newly listed species—often already experiencing rapid declines—to harmful activities during the period when they are most vulnerable. Without these default protections, species may face unnecessary delays in receiving safeguards critical for preventing their further decline toward extinction.

Furthermore, the proposed changes risk creating inconsistencies, increasing administrative burdens, and shifting the conservation process away from science-based decisions. A piecemeal approach to threatened species protections could leave some species underprotected simply because a tailored rule has not yet been completed, not because they do not need the protection.

The ESA’s success relies on maintaining strong, proactive, and science-driven measures. The Blanket Rule is a cornerstone of that approach, ensuring that threatened species receive timely and meaningful protection while recovery plans and species-specific rules are developed.

For these reasons, I firmly oppose the proposed changes to the ESA and the Blanket Rule at 50 CFR 17.31. Maintaining strong, consistent protections is essential for safeguarding biodiversity, supporting healthy ecosystems, and honoring our national commitment to conservation.

text:
To whom it may concern,

I’m writing to firmly oppose the four proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations. Each proposal, both individually and collectively, threatens to weaken the ESA’s crucial role in preventing extinction, aiding species recovery, and conserving ecosystems vital to both human and wildlife communities.

1. Removing Default Protections for Threatened Species
The ESA aims to act before species reach critical levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule is underpinned by scientific evidence showing that early protections reduce recovery costs and prevent declines. Eliminating automatic protections would lead to delays, necessitate case-by-case rules currently automatic, and expose at-risk species to unnecessary risks, contradicting the ESA’s preventive intent and incurring greater ecological and financial costs over time.

2. Introducing Economic Considerations in Listing Species
The ESA mandates listing decisions be based on the best scientific data, not economic impacts. Factoring in economic considerations undermines scientific rigor and risks delaying protections until species are near extinction. Limiting future-threat analyses ignores conservation science, which shows habitat loss and climate impacts already threaten species before population declines become visible. Weakening these criteria increases the likelihood of preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing Critical Habitat Protections
Habitat loss is the leading cause of biodiversity decline. Limiting critical habitat designations undermines recovery efforts, while narrowing the harm definition reverses legal precedent and ignores how habitat destruction indirectly harms wildlife. These changes would weaken agency consultations and increase biological risks, opposing the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. Allowing Agencies to Bypass ESA Protections
New loopholes enabling agencies to override ESA protections threaten its core purpose. They encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and move decisions away from science, affecting species like the Florida panther and gray wolf, accelerating declines among already pressured species.

Cumulative Impact
Individually and collectively, these proposals:
- Weaken the ESA’s scientific basis,
- Delay protections for species,
- Reduce habitat conservation amid climate change,
- Raise extinction risks,
- Undermine agency cooperation,
- Increase taxpayer recovery costs.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct, making it a historically successful conservation law due to its scientific foundation and proactive approach. These changes oppose those principles. Amid a biodiversity crisis, strengthening—not weakening—our key wildlife protection law is vital.

Request
I urge the withdrawal of all proposed rule changes and the retention of the current framework, rooted in science and successful implementation.

title: Comment from Norton, Gina

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings—some even before they have been named, such as some of the 80% of insect species not yet identified.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you.

For years, this rule has been crucial, automatically applying most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species, unless specific rules are created. Getting rid of it would cause significant delays before these species receive the conservation efforts they require, directly opposing the ESA’s precautionary intent.

Congress crafted the “endangered” and “threatened” categories to enable early intervention, not to postpone action until the situation worsens. The blanket rule is an effective, scientifically sound approach that mitigates risks while tailored management plans are developed. Without it, newly threatened species would remain unprotected during their most critical time, increasing the risk of them becoming endangered or extinct.

Moreover, there’s no evidence showing that this rule imposes regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or APA. In fact, removing it would increase administrative tasks with the need for multiple species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying crucial protections.

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
STOP THE ABUSES!!! NOW!!!
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.

text:
Greetings! I am a young person who cares deeply about wildlife protection. I strongly oppose any rollbacks to endangered species protections.
Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would narrow the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

Thank you for your time and consideration!
Take care, Rebecca
