title: Comment from Hurd, Pamela

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. title: Comment from Hurd, Pamela

text:
I am writing to oppose the proposed elimination of the blanket 4(d) rule, which has provided automatic protections to newly listed threatened species for decades.
The blanket 4(d) rule is a proven, science-based tool that delivers immediate protections to threatened species at their most vulnerable moment—right after listing. By automatically extending the same safeguards given to endangered species, this rule ensures that threatened species receive urgent protection from killing, harassment, and habitat destruction without delay.
Eliminating the blanket rule in favor of species-specific 4(d) rules will create dangerous regulatory gaps precisely when conservation action is most critical. Species-specific rules are time-consuming and resource-intensive to develop, meaning newly listed species could remain unprotected for months or even years while awaiting tailored regulations. During this vulnerable period, populations could suffer irreversible declines.
Furthermore, species-specific rules are far more susceptible to political and industry pressure. Rather than relying on consistent, science-based baseline protections, each rule becomes a negotiation that may prioritize economic considerations over species recovery. This piecemeal approach increases opportunities for industry to lobby for exemptions and weaker standards, undermining the ESA's conservation mission.
The Endangered Species Act mandates that listing and protection decisions be based on the best available scientific evidence—not executive orders designed to reduce regulatory requirements for industry. The blanket 4(d) rule embodies this scientific approach by ensuring all threatened species receive comprehensive protection as a starting point.
I urge the Fish & Wildlife Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule. Removing this safeguard will delay protections, create inconsistent standards, and place threatened species at greater risk during the critical early stages of their recovery. Science-based, immediate protections are essential to preventing further population declines and achieving the ESA's goal of species conservation and recovery.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Regarding the proposed rule changes for changes to endangered and threatened species, you need to keep these points in mind:

● The blanket 4(d) rule is a proven, science-based tool that gives threatened species
immediate protections when they are most at risk.
● Eliminating the blanket rule will delay or weaken protections for newly listed species, putting them in harm’s way during the period when conservation actions are most critical. This is simply wrong.
● Species-specific rules are not a substitute for broad baseline protections; they are slow, resource-intensive, and increase political pressure from industries seeking exemptions.
● The ESA requires decisions to be based on the best available science, not executive
orders aimed at weakening environmental safeguards. Follow the science, not politics.
● The Fish & Wildlife Service should retain the blanket 4(d) rule to prevent regulatory gaps that could worsen species declines.

text:
Below is a well-structured, formal public comment opposing proposed changes to the **Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants**. It avoids targeted political persuasion and focuses on policy, science, and procedural concerns.

---

**Public Comment Opposing Proposed Changes to the Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants Regulations**

To Whom It May Concern:

I am submitting this comment to express my strong opposition to the proposed changes to the regulations implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) for endangered and threatened wildlife and plants. The ESA is one of the most effective and respected conservation laws in the world, and weakening its regulatory framework poses significant risks to imperiled species, ecosystems, and the long-term health of our natural heritage.

**1. The proposed changes reduce science-based protections.**
Several provisions would allow economic or non-scientific considerations to influence listing decisions and recovery planning. The ESA was intentionally designed so that decisions about whether a species is endangered or threatened rely solely on the best available scientific and commercial data. Introducing additional considerations undermines the objectivity and integrity of this process and increases the likelihood that species will continue to decline unnoticed or unprotected.

**2. These changes could delay or dilute critical protections.**
Modifying standards for listing, delisting, and reclassifying species may create additional procedural hurdles or subjective criteria that slow down conservation actions. Many species already face rapid declines due to habitat loss, climate change, pollution, and invasive species. Any delay in protection can mean the difference between recovery and extinction.

**3. Habitat protections would be weakened at a time when they are most needed.**
Restrictions or narrowed definitions related to “critical habitat” would make it more difficult to designate and protect the areas essential for species survival. Habitat loss is a primary driver of biodiversity decline, and reducing the scope or strength of habitat-related protections would severely compromise recovery efforts.

**4. Long-term environmental and economic impacts are not adequately addressed.**
Healthy ecosystems provide measurable public benefits—including water purification, pollination, climate resilience, and recreational value. Weakening ESA regulations threatens these benefits and may lead to significant future costs for communities, industries, and taxpayers. The proposal does not sufficiently evaluate these long-term risks.

**5. The changes are inconsistent with the ESA’s core intent.**
Congress enacted the ESA to prevent extinction “whatever the cost,” recognizing the irreplaceable value of biodiversity. The proposed regulatory changes shift away from this foundational principle and prioritize short-term administrative flexibility over the conservation outcomes the law was designed to achieve.

**Conclusion**
For these reasons, I respectfully urge the agency to withdraw the proposed rule changes. Instead, efforts should focus on strengthening science-based decision-making, restoring degraded habitat, improving interagency cooperation, and ensuring that the ESA continues to function as an effective safeguard for species at risk of extinction.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

title: Comment from Buquicchio, Joseph

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.
More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.
I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.
We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.

title: Comment from Mendoza, Tony

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Al meqdad, Elaine

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Rosen, Ronald

text:
It is vital that the Fish & Wildlife Service and the entire Federal Government NOT weaken in any way, the Endangered Species Act. Stick to the saying, "If it's not broken, don't fix it". And, the ESA is NOT broken and is in fact more important than ever - just as it is.

The blanket 4(d) rule is a proven, science-based tool that gives threatened species
immediate protections when they are most at risk.
Eliminating the blanket rule will delay or weaken protections for newly listed species,
putting them in harm’s way during the period when conservation actions are most critical.

Species-specific rules are not a substitute for broad baseline protections; they are slow, resource-intensive, and increase political pressure from industries seeking exemptions.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. title: Comment from Flynn, Debbie

text:
Hello. I am a mother writing to ask you to please uphold all endangered species protections. This is a historically successful law that has safeguarded many incredible plant and animal species.
Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would narrow the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

title: Comment from Vallero, Daniel

text:
Last month, the Trump administration proposed revisions to four rules implementing the Endangered Species Act (ESA) that will severely weaken endangered species. Passed with bipartisan support in 1973, the ESA establishes “a prohibition on 'take' of a species, the requirement that all federal agencies ensure that the actions they carry out will not jeopardize the continued existence of a threatened or endangered species, and the drafting and implementation of recovery plans for at risk species,” according to the National Agricultural Law Center.

Secretary of DOI Doug Burgum describes the action: “This administration is restoring the Endangered Species Act to its original intent, protecting species through clear, consistent and lawful standards that also respect the livelihoods of Americans who depend on our land and resources.” However, the purposes of the ESA, as laid out in the statute, are inconsistent with the proposed rules: “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of the treaties and conventions set forth in subsection (a) of this section.”

Among the findings stated by Congress in passing ESA are the following:

(1) various species of fish, wildlife, and plants in the United States have been rendered extinct as a consequence of economic growth and development untempered by adequate concern and conservation;
(2) other species of fish, wildlife, and plants have been so depleted in numbers that they are in danger of or threatened with extinction; AND
(3) these species of fish, wildlife, and plants are of esthetic, ecological, educational, historical, recreational, and scientific value to the Nation and its people; . . .

Thus, the original intent was not to relieve burdens on industries whose actions threaten biodiversity, but to ensure that such actions are tempered by “adequate concern and conservation.” Thus, the proposals undermine the basic protections provided threatened and endangered species and narrow the definition of critical habitats.

I oppose the rule changes in this docket, which would deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings—some even before they have been named, such as some of the 80% of insect species not yet identified.

The Earth is facing an extinction crisis, which must be addressed by strong ESA regulations.

text:
I am writing with grave urgency AS AN AMERICAN TAXPAYER to urge FWS to uphold and defend the Endangered Species Act. Protecting our wildlife is MUCH MORE IMPORTANT TO ME than the interests behind this attack. PLEASE PROTECT OUR NATURAL RESOURCES. THIS IS WHAT THE AMERICAN PUBLIC WANTS!

The blanket 4(d) rule is a proven, science-based tool that gives threatened species
immediate protections when they are most at risk.

putting them in harm’s way during the period when conservation actions are most critical.

resource-intensive, and increase political pressure from industries seeking exemptions.

orders aimed at weakening environmental safeguards.

risk.

scientific evidence and allow harmful actions to proceed without full review.
● The rollback reinstates 2019 rules that courts and scientists criticized as inconsistent
with the ESA’s conservation mandate.
● Climate impacts, cumulative habitat loss, and landscape-scale consequences must be
included in consultations as they are essential to understanding jeopardy.
● The rule should be withdrawn; the Service should restore the stronger 2024 protections
instead of narrowing them.

The 2020 rule improperly elevated economic and political considerations over the
biological needs of species.
Reinstating it contradicts the ESA’s purpose: to conserve ecosystems and recover
species, not to reduce protections for industry convenience.
● The Service must base exclusions on clear scientific evidence, not speculative economic
concerns.

harms recovery prospects.

framework.

listing criteria undermines that legal standard.

restricting unoccupied critical habitat contradicts the purpose of the ESA.

outdated language.

THANK YOU

title: Comment from Diggle, Gloria

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.
title: Comment from Julian, Stacy

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a citizen and devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change, which abandons decades of legal precedent, overrides the best available science and erodes the original intent of Congress by creating loopholes allowing the Administration to exclude critical habitat for recovering species.

Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

The Endangered Species Act reflects our commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation we must not weaken. This rule change will accelerate species decline and harm the ESA’s fundamental purpose.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the ESA’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from hazzard, sandra

text:
The blanket 4(d) rule is a proven, science-based tool that gives threatened species
immediate protections when they are most at risk.
Eliminating the blanket rule will delay or weaken protections for newly listed species,
putting them in harm’s way during the period when conservation actions are most critical.
Species-specific rules are not a substitute for broad baseline protections; they are slow,
resource-intensive, and increase political pressure from industries seeking exemptions.
The ESA requires decisions to be based on the best available science, not executive
orders aimed at weakening environmental safeguards.
The Fish & Wildlife Service should retain the blanket 4(d) rule to prevent regulatory gaps
that could worsen species declines.

title: Comment from Mitchell, Stephen

text:
In the 51 years since its passage, the Endangered Species Act has prevented the extinctions of 99% of its listed species, making it very successful. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the federal government to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
I strongly oppose this proposed rule change. This change would leave newly listed species vulnerable to killing, trapping, and other forms of "take." text:
I am submitting this comment because biodiversity and healthy ecosystems matter very deeply to me. As someone who lives in Maryland and regularly sees both the negative effects of habitat loss, and very positive benefits of habitat restoration, I am concerned about weakening protections for vulnerable species. Healthy and protected ecosystems not only benefit the endangered species we are trying to save, but the health and longevity of the human race. It is only a matter of time before the destruction of many intact ecosystems, which require the presence of all species to be balanced and healthy, starts to very negatively impact the ability for humans to survive on this planet. We were designed to walk alongside the natural world, not topple over it. We depend on it for survival.

The Endangered Species Act works because it centers science and the public interest, not political pressure or economic influence. Narrowing criteria for critical habitat exclusions could allow economic interests to override habitat protection, threatening ecosystem health. This is very irresponsible. These rollbacks reduce public accountability at a time when most Americans support stronger environmental conservation protections.

I ask you to uphold the intent of the ESA: preventing extinction and ensuring future generations inherit thriving, resilient ecosystems.

title: Comment from Velasquez, Aldo

text:
Section 7 consultation is the ESA’s last line of defense, the moment when a federal agency must stop, look at the land, and ask whether its actions will push a species closer to extinction. This rule weakens that safeguard by narrowing definitions, erasing indirect impacts, and removing tools that help offset harm. The law commands federal agencies to ensure their actions are not likely to jeopardize listed species. That mandate becomes hollow if the analysis is allowed to ignore the very forces driving species toward decline.

But beyond the legal failings, this proposal speaks to a diminished view of our responsibility. It suggests that the consequences of our actions — the long, cumulative pressures of fragmentation, drought, climate disruption, and habitat loss — are somehow theoretical unless they manifest immediately. Nothing in the natural world works that way. Decline is incremental, disappearance is quiet before it’s final. The nation that once proudly wrote the ESA to prevent such losses now seeks to normalize them. This is not the wish of the American people.

Aldo Leopold wrote that “a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community.” Consultation is where the government decides whether it will act in accordance with that ethic or against it. Weakening that process is not simply a regulatory change, it’s a statement of values, a declaration that we are willing to look away.

I urge the USFWS to preserve a consultation process that honors the law, the science, and our duty to the living world.

title: Comment from Bode, Liz

text: Dear USFWS and administration officials, Please understand and consider that the blanket 4(d) rule is a proven, science-based tool that gives threatened species immediate protections when they are most at risk. Eliminating the blanket rule would delay or weaken protections for newly listed species, putting them in harm’s way during the period when conservation actions are most critical. Species-specific rules are not a valid substitute for broad baseline protections; they are slow, resource-intensive, and are subject to political pressure from industries seeking exemptions. Further, the ESA requires decisions to be based on the best available science, not executive orders aimed at weakening environmental safeguards. The Fish & Wildlife Service should retain the blanket 4(d) rule to prevent regulatory gaps that could worsen species declines. Please reconsider your proposal based on these points.

title: Comment from Miller, Melissa

text:
The blanket rule has, for decades, served as a bridge between threat and survival — giving newly listed species the basic protections they need while more tailored plans are developed. Rescinding it abandons that principle of early intervention. It will leave threatened species exposed precisely when they are most vulnerable, forcing them to wait for individualized rules that are likely to arrive too late.

This proposal moves us away from prevention toward delay, from prudence toward negligence or worse. It assumes that species on the brink can withstand additional pressure while agencies work through lengthy processes. Many cannot. And once a population tips, the slide toward endangered status is often swift and irreversible.

There is also a deeper betrayal here, a departure from the national character that led Congress to pass the ESA with overwhelming bipartisan support. They did so because they believed saving species was an expression of our moral identity, a reflection of the kind of nation we aspired to be. The blanket rule embodies that spirit: act early, act responsibly, act with humility before the complexity of the natural world.

To remove it is to turn our backs on that legacy. I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) protections and uphold the law’s essential purpose: to conserve species before they are lost forever.

title: Comment from Wheeler, Colleen

text:
I strongly urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) to carefully consider the broader ecological and long-term consequences before finalizing these changes. The changes included in 2025-20552 will be devastating to the United States. My key concerns are included below:
1. Removing the "blanket rule" undermines protections during a critical window. The proposal would eliminate the automatic protections for newly listed threatened species under the "blanket rule". Until the government can create and implement species-specific regulations, this in-between period can leave many vulnerable species exposed. As we are already undergoing a mass-extinction event, this could result in a catastrophic changes to our ecosystem and economy.
2. Risk of fragmented, inconsistent protections across species. By requiring species-specific rules for each threatened species, this approach may lead to uneven protection standards. Some species may get robust protections quickly while others may languish under weak or delayed rules. This undermines the goal of equal protection under the Act.
3. Potential for weakened Conservation outcomes overall. When biodiversity loss, habitat destruction, and climate-related threats are accelerating, weakening the regulatory safety net is counter-productive to conservation objections.
4. Public trust and transparency demand strong protections, not weakening them. The Endangered Species Act represents a commitment to preserve natural heritage, biodiversity, and ecosystem resilience that is one of the most highly supported policies across the political aisle from the people. You are not listening to the public and removing our lands from us and the animals that live here. Removing or weakening fundamental protections (even temporarily) risks undermining public confidence in the law and the agencies charged with upholding it.

The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text: I object to the proposed rule (Docket No. FWS–HQ–ES–2025-0029) that would eliminate the “blanket” protections for threatened species under Section 4(d) and require case-by-case regulations. title: Comment from Fontaine, Raymond

text: I am writing to let you know that I strongly oppose the changes to the Endangered Species Act.  These changes would corrupt science-based decision-making with considerations that favor habitat-destroying industries. These proposals would cause irreparable harm to at-risk species and essential habitat and worsen the biodiversity and extinction crisis. I strongly encourage you to uphold the ESA’s mission by rejecting these changes.
title: Comment from HARRIS, KRISTI

text:
To Whom It May Concern,
It is critical to continue to protecting species who are endangered, including those listed such as the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly. If the blanket rule is removed, it will deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings. Thank you for your time. Allison Sykes

title: Comment from Naples, Jean

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Reichert, Robyn

text: I am writing to urge the FWS to withdraw its proposal to eliminate the "blanket rule" providing interim protection for threatened species.  The ESA has been one of our nation's most effective conservation and environmental protection laws, precisely because it provides strong protection not only for the species in question, but also the habitat needed for species survival.  This proposed rule would critically weaken the protection provided to newly listed theatened species.  Scientists need time to develop a longer-term plan to protect those species; getting rid of the blanket rule withdraws protections during this critical period.  There are eight billion people on this planet; we have a responsibility to preserve as best we can the diversity of the other species with which we share the earth.  Please withdraw this proposal and recommit the FWS and its sister agencies to the original purpose of the ESA -- protecting our fellow creatures who are in trouble.

title: Comment from Boden, Kimberly

text:
I strongly urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) to carefully consider the broader ecological and long-term consequences before finalizing these changes. The changes included in 2025-20552 will be devastating to the United States. My key concerns are included below:
1. Removing the "blanket rule" undermines protections during a critical window. The proposal would eliminate the automatic protections for newly listed threatened species under the "blanket rule". Until the government can create and implement species-specific regulations, this in-between period can leave many vulnerable species exposed. As we are already undergoing a mass-extinction event, this could result in a catastrophic changes to our ecosystem and economy.
2. Risk of fragmented, inconsistent protections across species. By requiring species-specific rules for each threatened species, this approach may lead to uneven protection standards. Some species may get robust protections quickly while others may languish under weak or delayed rules. This undermines the goal of equal protection under the Act.
3. Potential for weakened Conservation outcomes overall. When biodiversity loss, habitat destruction, and climate-related threats are accelerating, weakening the regulatory safety net is counter-productive to conservation objections.
4. Public trust and transparency demand strong protections, not weakening them. The Endangered Species Act represents a commitment to preserve natural heritage, biodiversity, and ecosystem resilience that is one of the most highly supported policies across the political aisle from the people. You are not listening to the public and removing our lands from us and the animals that live here. Removing or weakening fundamental protections (even temporarily) risks undermining public confidence in the law and the agencies charged with upholding it.

title: Comment from Foley, Diane

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Brake, Susan

text: I am strongly opposed to the proposed Endangered species Act Rule changes. I spend considerable time in the mountains as a recreationalist and citizen scientist. I live in the North Cascades and have witnessed the impact of climate change on the wildlife and plants in our area. The proposed changes  make it easier for federal agencies and industry to avoid or narrow protections for at‑risk species and their habitats, especially in ways that downplay climate change and economic impacts on regulated parties. In practice, they shift the balance of ESA implementation away from precautionary, science‑driven conservation and toward accommodating development. From a conservation perspective, the“certainty”  which is created by the changes largely accrues to regulated interests (oil and gas, timber, infrastructure) rather than to species whose long‑term survival depends on protecting future habitat and anticipating climate‑driven threats.That is not the intent of the law. These changes to the ESP should not be implemented.

title: Comment from M, J

text:
I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) to withdraw the proposed rescission of the Blanket 4d rule as an option for extending Section 9 protections to newly listed species under Section 4d of the Act.
While I recognize the purpose of species-specific rules are to provide “tailored” protections, the proposed framework introduces significant ecological risks and administrative burdens that were not adequately addressed in this rulemaking. Without a binding requirement to issue species-specific rules concurrently with listings, conservation efforts are dependent on agency discretion. Therefore, I cannot support this regulatory change unless the final ruling requires agencies to have species-specific rules finalized at the time of listing.
Opposition: removal of the blanket rule
Since 1973, the Act has remained one of the most effective federal environmental protection laws, saving 99 percent of listed species from extinction. The Blanket rule has protected countless species from extinction by immediately granting endangered-level protection to newly listed species. The proposed removal of the blanket rule represents a significant departure from the Act’s foundational goal of recovery through conservation efforts. The Act defines a threatened species as “one that is likely to become endangered in the foreseeable future.” Eliminating the blanket rule jeopardizes newly listed species by removing the immediate safeguard that prevents their further decline to endangered status. Conserving threatened species requires prompt intervention to prevent populations declining to low levels that the population cannot recover. Once a species is listed as endangered, it is defined as “in danger of extinction” and all Section 9 prohibitions apply. At that point, the resources expended to develop species-specific rules would be rendered unnecessary and therefore used inefficiently. Therefore, I recommend that FWS retain the blanket rule to provide the necessary, immediate protection for newly listed species while species-specific regulations are developed. These regulatory approaches should be used in conjunction with one another to maximize conservation efforts.

Under the current administration, staffing, funds, and resources within the conservation sector are limited. While the FWS argues that species-specific rules will maximize “limited personnel and fiscal resources”, in practice it creates administrative hurdles that delay conservation efforts. The proposed process is redundant and time-consuming, as each newly listed species requires separate, “necessary and advisable” determination, public comment period, and economic impact analysis. This process is a repetition of procedures already undertaken in order to list a species under the Act. Adding the economic review does not contribute to conservation efforts as it creates unnecessary barriers with no clear benefit to species recovery. Given that federal level protections already take 2-5 years to implement, the addition of redundant procedures further delays the process. The stated “intention” to issue concurrent species-specific rules lacks both regulatory accountability and any form of enforceable timeline. Without legal obligation to finalize species-specific rules, the timeline for their issuance remains at the discretion of the FWS. This reliance on agency discretion undermines the theoretical value of tailoring species-specific rules.
Recommendations and requested actions
Publish finalized species-specific regulations concurrently with listing - The FWS should be legally required to conduct their ‘necessary, advisable’ determinations, and economic review within the year-long status review process included in the Act. The proposed comment period should be combined with the comment period already required under the Act. These measures reduce redundant procedures and ensure efficient use of scarce resources.
Utilize the best available science as the primary basis for species-specific rules - Regulatory decisions must prioritize biological and ecological considerations over economic impacts. While an economic impact analysis highlights opportunity costs tied to protecting threatened species, it does little to support or improve conservation efforts. Protections for threatened species must be rooted in ecological considerations such as life history traits, reproductive rates, and habitat requirements to maximize conservation outcomes.
Evaluate administrative feasibility of implementation at the state and local level - The FWS should collaborate with state and local agencies in developing species-specific rules to ensure feasibility. If administrative resources and staffing are deemed insufficient, the FWS must support state and local agencies in enforcement and permit issuance. The final ruling should include guidance for implementation at the state and local level.

The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Yerden, Carol

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.
Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.
The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.
For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

title: Comment from Mullen, John

text:
Phasing out existing blanket safeguards and reducing protections that have kept countless species from sliding toward extinction are the goals of this proposal as-written. It's a terrible idea for these reasons and more:

● The blanket 4(d) rule is a proven, science-based tool that gives threatened species
immediate protections when they are most at risk.

● Eliminating the blanket rule will delay or weaken protections for newly listed species, putting them in harm’s way during the period when conservation actions are most critical.

● Species-specific rules are not a substitute for broad baseline protections; they are slow, resource-intensive, and increase political pressure from industries seeking exemptions.

● The ESA requires decisions to be based on the best available science, not executive
orders aimed at weakening environmental safeguards.

● The Fish & Wildlife Service should retain the blanket 4(d) rule to prevent regulatory gaps that could worsen species declines.
title: Comment from Lang, Katarina

text: I am against re-issuance of the 2019 revisions to the regulations in 50 CFR part 17, subparts D and G, which applies protections to a species newly listed as threatened only through issuance of a species-specific rule setting out the protective regulations that are necessary and advisable for that species. The current “blanket rule” protections allow safeguards to be more quickly put in place that can help prevent species from moving from a threatened to endangered status, while still allowing for species-specific alternatives to be approved by the federal government. The difference is that currently, species are afforded protections while those species-specific rules are under development. This proposed change would take those critical protections away, and by the time species-specific rules are implemented, the species may move from threatened to endangered or even extinct status. Development of species-specific rules for each threatened species take time, and in the time before those rules are issued, irreparable damage to species and habitats may occur. This appears to be a stalling tactic to allow plaintiffs to mount challenges against the agency and will result in reduced effectiveness of agency efforts to protect threatened species, wasted tax dollars and more opportunities for moneyed interests to mount tactics to evade Endangered Species Act requirements. I vehemently oppose this provision.

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.

We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Steele, Stephanie

text:
One of the proposed revisions to Endangered Species Act regulations would overturn the 4(d) rule, removing blanket protections for threatened species. I am writing to express my staunch opposition to this proposal, which is all but guaranteed to delay critical protections and push threatened species to the brink of endangerment.

As you know, the “blanket rule” established under the ESA automatically prohibits all threatened species from being killed, harmed, trapped, or traded. But under the proposed rule, protection would no longer be the default. Agencies would instead be required to produce species-specific rules to establish protections, making the process of listing even one threatened species an incredibly time-intensive one.

Rather than making it increasingly difficult to establish essential protections, we should be preserving the regulations that are helping threatened species recover. Please stand up for American wildlife by leaving these blanket protections in place.

Thank you.
