title: Comment from Hoffman , Megan

text:
To whom it may concern,

I wish to convey my firm opposition to the four proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. Each of these proposals, individually and collectively, would significantly diminish the ESA’s capacity to prevent extinctions, aid species recovery, and protect vital ecosystems for both wildlife and human communities.

1. Removing default protections for threatened species (repeal of the blanket 4(d) rule)

The ESA was crafted to act before species reach crisis levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule embodies decades of scientific evidence demonstrating that early, precautionary measures reduce overall recovery costs and curb further declines. Eliminating default protections will create unnecessary delays, demand case-by-case rulemaking for currently automatic protections, and expose vulnerable species to preventable harm or death. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive purpose and will lead to heightened ecological and financial costs in the long term.

2. Making it harder to list species by allowing economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis

The ESA mandates that listing decisions be based exclusively on the best available scientific data, not economic impacts. Introducing economic factors would contradict statutory language, compromise scientific integrity, and risk delaying protections until species reach critical levels. Furthermore, restricting the use of future-threat analysis disregards current conservation science, which shows slow-burn pressures like habitat loss and climate change already threaten species long before declines appear in population counts. Weakening future-threat criteria decreases the likelihood of timely listings, increasing preventable extinction risks.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and limiting the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss drives global and U.S. biodiversity declines. Reducing critical habitat designations, especially those essential for long-term recovery, weakens recovery planning. Similarly, narrowing “harm” definitions to exclude habitat degradation would reverse decades of legal and scientific precedent. Habitat destruction often indirectly kills wildlife, a fact long recognized by law. Weakening these definitions undermines inter-agency consultations, elevates biological risks, and creates inconsistency with the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. Opening new loopholes that allow agencies or special committees to bypass ESA protections

Establishing or expanding loopholes for agencies to override ESA protections, even when extinction is foreseeable, conflicts with the ESA’s core mission. These loopholes would encourage exemptions, decrease transparency, and move decision-making away from science-based analysis. This would particularly affect wide-ranging and imperiled species like Florida panthers, grizzly bears, and gray wolves, accelerating declines in species already under severe stress.

The collective impact of these proposals

Each rule is concerning on its own, but together, they would:
• weaken the ESA’s scientific foundation,
• delay or block necessary species protections,
• reduce habitat conservation amid escalating climate change,
• elevate extinction risks for both domestic and internationally threatened species,
• undermine inter-agency cooperation, and
• increase long-term recovery costs for taxpayers.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct and remains one of the most successful conservation laws due to its grounding in science, precaution, and proactive measures. These proposed changes oppose these principles.

Amid unprecedented global biodiversity loss, the United States should be reinforcing—not weakening—its most effective wildlife protection law.

Request

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed rule changes in full and maintain the current regulatory framework, which is rooted in science, legal precedent, and a history of successful implementation.

text:
Hello,

My name is Derick Dietrich and I am submitting this comment in response to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s (FWS) proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) of 1973.

I believe that the changes proposed to remove the “blanket rule” option from 50 CFR 17.31 and 17.71 of the ESA is a mistake that will systematically weaken the ESA. Removing the blanket rule option could threaten endangered species by slowing the process of conservation efforts and limiting the ability to provide proactive measures to protect vulnerable species.

As an environmental regulator, the wording of regulations must be done in a way that strengthens the goal and/or purpose of the regulation. These proposed changes create obstacles that reduce the efficiency of the ESA and limit proactive conservation efforts for threatened or endangered species. The blanket rule allows for conservationists/biologists to provide baseline conservation measures to species that are added to the endangered species list while the species-specific plans are developed. This process would become longer and slower with the proposed changes and delaying conservation efforts would negatively affect vulnerable species, which would be the opposite of the goal of the ESA. The more tools that are available to protect endangered species support the overall goal of the ESA and the blanket rule option is a tool that should be utilized to help conservation efforts.

Thank you for taking the time to review my comments and I urge you to rescind this proposed change.
title: Comment from Dietrich, Derick

text:
Since it was signed into law in 1973, the Endangered Species Act has been credited with saving 99 percent of the species it protects, including the Endangered Whooping Crane, which was part of the very first cohort protected by the law.

Birds—and cranes as umbrella species—are among the most visible indicators of ecosystem health, and their continued declines demand stronger, not weaker, protections. These proposed rule changes would erode safeguards essential to preventing extinctions, recovering imperiled species, and conserving the habitats on which birds and other wildlife depend.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the Endangered Species Act’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

title: Comment from Ariosta, Cynthia

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text: Species-specific rules would be great in theory, but seem to underestimate just how many species fall under such protections. That's not even to mention the ongoing debates about where species end and subspecies begin. This suggested change in this proposed rule in particular will add far more work, far more time, and far more precarious periods of inactivity than the currently instated rule. There's already budget cuts, department gutting, and contract terminations in the mix - must we add this much back and forth, especially as points-of-contacts potentially continuously change (or even fall through the cracks)? I would certainly hope that this is just an oversight that wasn't considered, and not a purposeful attempt at stopping important movements that will secure a sustainable world. Because history has proven time and time again, the loss of a species can have surprising significance to the food web, the ecosystem, the surrounding economies, and even scientific progress. If we lose species due to the limbo that these proposed rules create, it won't just be other animals that suffer the oft irreparable consequences, but we will too.

title: Comment from Dina, Chrysa

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.
title: Comment from Gilmore, Susan

text: Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed changes to the ESA, an important piece of legislation that has served the American public and saved hundreds of species from extinction. I urge you to withdraw the proposal to remove the blanket rule. The removal of this rule would weaken protections for endangered species and leave them vulnerable to increased "take."

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.

We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.

Victoria Brown
Brunswick County, NC

title: Comment from Richardson , Ashleigh

text:
Subject: Strong Opposition to Proposed Rules Regarding the Listing of Endangered and Threatened Species and Designation of Critical Habitat
I am writing to express my strong, unequivocal opposition to the suite of proposed rules that seek to dismantle and weaken the foundational strength of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) of 1973. This Act is one of the most successful, essential, and universally supported conservation laws in the United States, and these proposed rollbacks directly undermine its core mission.
The Endangered Species Act Works
Since its passage in 1973, the ESA has been incredibly effective, having prevented the extinction of approximately 99% of the species placed under its protection. Iconic American species like the Bald Eagle, American Alligator, and Gray Whale serve as powerful testaments to the Act's success. The proposed changes—which are framed as providing "certainty" but will result in increased habitat destruction and species vulnerability—are an affront to decades of successful conservation policy.
Specific Opposition to Key Proposed Revisions
I urge the Services to immediately withdraw the proposals and maintain the strongest possible protections for threatened and endangered wildlife. My opposition is centered on the following proposals:
* Elimination of the "Blanket Rule" for Threatened Species:
* The proposal to eliminate the automatic extension of "endangered" protections to newly listed "threatened" species is a dangerous regulatory delay tactic.
* Requiring species-specific Section 4(d) rules for every threatened species will inevitably leave vulnerable species exposed to harm for months or years while the rule-making process is underway. This administrative burden will create conservation gaps and increase the risk of extinction for species at a critical point in their recovery.
* Restoring Consideration of Economic Impacts in Listing and Critical Habitat Decisions:
* The ESA clearly mandates that listing and delisting decisions must be based solely on the best available scientific and commercial data.
* Reintroducing language that allows for the transparent consideration of economic impacts, while technically not the basis for the final decision, injects political and financial motives into a process that must remain scientifically objective. This invites litigation and creates a chilling effect that prioritizes profits over biological facts.
* Restricting Critical Habitat Designation and Defining "Foreseeable Future":
* The proposal to reinstate a restrictive two-step process for designating unoccupied critical habitat is short-sighted and fundamentally undermines long-term recovery efforts. For species facing the existential threat of climate change, protecting future, currently unoccupied habitat is scientifically essential for survival and climate migration.
* Restoring a narrow definition of "foreseeable future" limits the Services' ability to consider long-term, predictable threats, particularly climate change, in listing decisions. This is an unscientific approach that ignores the most significant driver of species decline in the 21st century.
Conclusion and Demand
The proposed rollbacks will strip vital protections from our nation's most vulnerable species and pave the way for widespread habitat destruction. The true intent of the ESA is to use the full weight of the federal government to conserve endangered and threatened species and the ecosystems upon which they depend.
I stand with the majority of Americans in strong support of the current protections under the Endangered Species Act. I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries to cease this destructive attempt to weaken the Act by withdrawing all proposed rules immediately.
Sincerely,
Greg Haworth
Portland Oregon 97215

text:
As a nation, we shpuld not prioritize energy use -- and susbsequent deforestation, strip mining, destruction of land and habitat for all organisms that occupy this planet and ensure the survival of ecosystems and humanity -- over cpnservation and environmental protection.

I srongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

This legislation has had support across the country since 1973 because safeguarding America’s wildlife is not only a responsibility, but a proud part of our nation’s history.Thank you for your time.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
Re: Opposition to Proposed Rule Rescinding the "Blanket Rule" for Threatened Species Protections FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029-0001

To Whom It May Concern:

I submit the following comments in strong opposition to the proposed rule rescinding the "blanket rule" that provides automatic baseline protections for threatened species under the Endangered Species Act.
The proposed rule is fundamentally flawed for the following reasons:

1. Eliminates Critical Baseline Protections: The blanket rule ensures that vital prohibitions—including restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife—are automatically applied upon listing. Rescinding this rule removes the essential safety net that threatened species have relied on for decades.

2. Creates Dangerous Protection Gaps: Without automatic protections, threatened species could remain unprotected for months or years during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. This administrative delay will accelerate species loss at the precise moment intervention is most critical.

3. Increases Administrative Burden: The blanket rule is an efficient mechanism that has provided clarity and consistency for both agencies and landowners. Requiring case-by-case determinations will strain already limited agency capacity and create regulatory uncertainty.

4. Contradicts Scientific Best Practices: The blanket rule represents a scientifically sound approach to conservation, ensuring immediate protection while species-specific regulations are developed. Removing this safeguard ignores conservation biology principles regarding timely intervention.

5. Undermines ESA Success: For 51 years, the ESA has prevented extinction for 99% of listed species. The blanket rule has been integral to this success by ensuring no threatened species falls through regulatory gaps during the listing process.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety. The blanket rule reflects Congress's mandate that the federal government act swiftly and comprehensively to protect imperiled species and the ecosystems they depend on. Rescinding it directly undermines the ESA's core objective and the conservation principles the American people expect their government to uphold.

Sincerely,
Tara Shade
Kenilworth, IL
title: Comment from Shade, Tara

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Cummings, Linda

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Sellers, Martha

text:
As a voter who values life and living places, I write in support of preservation of endangered animals, plants, and habitats. Extinction events are irreversible.

Since it was signed into law in 1973, the Endangered Species Act has been credited with saving 99 percent of the species it protects, including the Endangered Whooping Crane, which was part of the very first cohort protected by the law.

Birds—and cranes as umbrella species—are among the most visible indicators of ecosystem health, and their continued declines demand stronger, not weaker, protections. These proposed rule changes would erode safeguards essential to preventing extinctions, recovering imperiled species, and conserving the habitats on which birds and other wildlife depend.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the Endangered Species Act’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

title: Comment from Becker, Elaine

text: There is no good reason for this proposal. Endangered species provide necessary links in the lives of the flora and fauna of our shared earth. We cannot, in good conscience, or with any good sense, allow species to die off. Every loss of a species weakens the environment in ways that may not be felt immediately, but will have lasting effects that will impact our population.
title: Comment from Harris, Karen

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Merljak, Julija

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. The blanket rule is why we still have piping plovers on Atlantic shorelines and sea otters in California. It is an effective and efficient rule that should remain in place.

Species currently proposed to be listed as "threatened" - like the monarch butterfly and California spotted owl - can't afford delay.

title: Comment from MacLagan, Lynette

text:
For over fifty years, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has played a major role in protecting wildlife, preventing nearly 99% of listed species from becoming extinct. This legislation has had support across the country since 1973 because safeguarding America’s wildlife is not only a responsibility, but a proud part of our nation’s history.

The proposed change to remove the ESA’s Blanket 4(d) Rule will result in fewer protections for threatened species and compromise the ESA’s mission. It is imperative to maintain our commitment to protecting endangered species and their habitats.

I encourage the Administration to withdraw all proposed changes to the ESA in order to ensure our country’s wildlife will continue to be protected for generations to come.

title: Comment from Serra, Ragen

text:
As someone who cares deeply about wildlife and the future of our planet, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule that would undermine wildlife protections granted by the Endangered Species Act. This change would go against decades of conservation progress and weaken one of our nation’s most important environmental laws.

The “blanket rule” gives essential baseline protection to threatened species until species-specific safeguards can be established. Removing the “blanket rule” may make them more vulnerable to extinction, in opposition to the intent of this legislation.

I urge you to uphold the mission of the Endangered Species Act and maintain the “blanket rule.” Our wildlife, wild places, and future generations are counting on it.

title: Comment from Jones, Jennifer

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife and science-based conservation, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Pelletier, Sarah

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am submitting this comment in strong support of maintaining and strengthening the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and its implementing regulations, including provisions that ensure species receive timely and effective protections.

The ESA is the United States’ most successful and enduring wildlife conservation law—providing essential protections to species on the brink of extinction and contributing to dramatic recoveries of wildlife such as the bald eagle, American alligator, peregrine falcon, gray wolf, and hundreds of other plants and animals. Its central purpose—to prevent extinction and promote recovery—has been affirmed by decades of conservation progress rooted in science-based decision-making. ￼

Organizations like the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, which actively work to conserve imperiled wildlife including Mexican wolves, polar bears, Texas ocelots, and American burying beetles, emphasize the importance of the ESA’s long-standing protections. Removing or weakening foundational elements of the ESA—including baseline safeguards that automatically apply to newly listed species until species-specific rules are developed—will undermine decades of conservation gains and may delay essential protections when they are most needed. Without these baseline protections, vulnerable species could be left exposed to increased threats from habitat loss, harmful take, and other pressures during critical periods of recovery. ￼

For these reasons, I strongly urge the Services to:
1.Retain and uphold the “blanket rule” and baseline protective standards that ensure newly listed species receive immediate safeguards as intended under the ESA; and
2.Ensure that any regulatory changes continue to prioritize the best available science and meaningful conservation outcomes.

The future of America’s wildlife and the ecological, educational, cultural, and intrinsic values they represent depend on robust, science-based implementation of the ESA. Weakening the Act’s protections places imperiled species and the ecosystems they support at greater risk of decline and extinction.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. title: Comment from Ford, Natalie

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Rivers, Kat

text:
To Whomever it May Concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.

The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.

Humans seem to think that we are separate from the environment, when in truth we play just as critical a role in these ecosystems as other organisms. Endangered species are the “canaries in the coal mine”; what harms them harms us just as much. We should take care to protect endangered species because what causes their demise will come for us too, sooner or later.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,

Audrae Seladi Roberts
Water Quality Manager
Mystic Aquarium
title: Comment from Mystic Aquarium

text:
To the US Department of the Interior - Fish and Wildlife Service:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Jones, Linda

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Liberty Miller

I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from hof, annette

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Leung, Eda

text:
International Crane Foundation
North America
News
Whooping Crane
Stand up for Endangered Species
Stand up for endangered species, like the Whooping Crane, and submit your comment(s) on the proposed rule changes to the Endangered Species Act by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on December 22, 2025.

Share
Last month, the Trump Administration proposed four new rule changes that would profoundly weaken the Endangered Species Act (ESA), the most important law for protecting and conserving threatened plants and animals in our country. We believe these changes would be catastrophic for Endangered Whooping Cranes, as well as countless other species, and their habitats.

Birds—and cranes as umbrella species—are among the most visible indicators of ecosystem health, and their continued declines demand stronger, not weaker, protections. These proposed rule changes would erode safeguards essential to preventing extinctions, recovering imperiled species, and conserving the habitats on which birds and other wildlife depend.

Signed into law in 1973—the same year as the International Crane Foundation was established—the ESA is a keystone of conservation success. It is credited with saving 99 percent of the species it protects, such as the Endangered Whooping Crane, which was part of the first cohort protected by the law.

Despite its overwhelming success and public support, the ESA has been sharply criticized by those who want to increase mining, drilling, and other land- and water-resource development that could negatively impact the habitat requirements of endangered species.

Stand up for endangered species, like the Whooping Crane, and submit your public comment(s) by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on December 22, 2025.
Click on the four proposed rule changes below to find the unique link for each to submit a comment. You may submit a comment for one or all four rule changes.

Following is an example comment you may copy and edit:

Since it was signed into law in 1973, the Endangered Species Act has been credited with saving 99 percent of the species it protects, including the Endangered Whooping Crane, which was part of the very first cohort protected by the law.

Birds—and cranes as umbrella species—are among the most visible indicators of ecosystem health, and their continued declines demand stronger, not weaker, protections. These proposed rule changes would erode safeguards essential to preventing extinctions, recovering imperiled species, and conserving the habitats on which birds and other wildlife depend.

I urge the Administration to withdraw its proposed rule and recommit to the Endangered Species Act’s original mandate: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on. Strong, science-based habitat protections are crucial for giving imperiled wildlife a real chance at recovery.

title: Comment from Rider, Carissa

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted

title: Comment from Clark, Chloe

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I urge the Administration to withdraw the proposed rule that would rescind the Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule” for threatened species.

The “blanket rule” has been a critical and effective safeguard, ensuring that newly listed threatened species receive baseline protections while species-specific management measures are developed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Removing this rule would create dangerous gaps in protection at precisely the time when species are most vulnerable to further decline.

This concern is particularly relevant for ocelots (Leopardus pardalis) in Texas, one of the most imperiled wild cat populations in North America. With fewer than 100 individuals remaining in the United States, Texas ocelots face ongoing threats from habitat fragmentation, vehicle collisions, and development pressures. These small, isolated populations depend on timely and consistent federal protections to prevent additional mortality and habitat loss. Any delay or weakening of safeguards during listing or re-evaluation periods could have irreversible consequences for their survival.

For more than five decades, the Endangered Species Act has successfully prevented extinction for 99% of listed species by providing clear, enforceable protections grounded in science. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported mechanism that ensures threatened species are not left unprotected while administrative processes unfold. Eliminating it would increase uncertainty for conservation practitioners, landowners, and agencies alike, while placing additional strain on already limited agency resources.

The Endangered Species Act reflects a clear congressional mandate to conserve imperiled species and the ecosystems upon which they depend. Weakening this framework by repealing the “blanket rule” runs counter to both the intent of the law and decades of conservation success.

I respectfully urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and maintain the “blanket rule” to ensure that species such as the ocelot—and many others facing similar risks—receive the timely, consistent protections necessary for recovery.

To whomever it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.

The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.

Protecting the Endangered Species Act is important because it prevents the extinction of plants and animals that are vital to healthy ecosystems. By preserving biodiversity, the ESA also supports clean air and water, food security, and a balanced environment for future generations.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,

Megan Cole
Mystic Aquarium

title: Comment from Chase, Mary Kay

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Friends of Manatees

title: Comment from Findley, A

text:
The Endangered Species Act (ESA) of 1973 can, without employing hyperbole or relying on exaggeration, be considered to be one of, if not the, the most durable, meaningful, and effective pieces of bipartisan supported environmental legislation in the history of the United States.

The ESA has an astounding track record of success, making possible the recovery of iconic species throughout the United States including the bald eagle, American alligator, black-footed ferret, Florida manatee, gray wolf, California condor, peregrine falcon, and grizzly bear; just to list a few of the estimated 291 species that the ESA has buffered from extinction. In fact, 99% of the species that have been listed to the ESA have avoided that fate.

At a time when global biodiversity is decreasing and species are disappearing at many times the normal background rate, weakening or hamstringing the ESA is a profoundly shortsighted and irresponsible maneuver on the part of the administration and as both a wildlife professional and an American citizen I wholeheartedly oppose the changes proposed by the Trump administration.

Included in these proposed rule changes are ones that would eliminate the “blanket rule”, which automatically extends endangered species protections to species newly listed as threatened. It can be easily argued that the blanket rule employs the Precautionary Principle, that is, the taking of preventive action against potential harm to, in this case, the environment even when the specific science surrounding risk to that entity may be lacking. Stripping the blanket rule from the ESA in the manner in which the administration seeks to do it exposes newly listed threatened species to further risk, harm, habitat loss, and population degradation while species-specific plans are hammered into place. It also increases the burden on already beleaguered wildlife professionals to rush to form these plans before further species loss can occur which may in turn lead to plans that are incomplete or less effective at reaching conservation goals. While it is tempting to leverage the idea that species-specific goals are ideal and the blanket rule is overreach, that is an ineffective argument since most conservation professionals, myself included, would agree that species-specific protections are preferrable but threatened species need temporary safeguards until effective plans for each can be formed.

The Endangered Species Act is extremely popular among Americans, with numbers from polls running from 2023 to 2025 showing consistent levels of support around 84% and some reports as high as 95%. That support is bipartisan, with the ESA receiving accolades from both conservative as well as liberals. To complement those statistics, the vast majority of those polled (up to 92%) believe that ESA listing decisions should be made by scientists and be based in science.

Given these verifiable facts, the increasing fragility of biodiversity both locally and globally, and the ever mounting impacts of human-precipitated shifts in climate regimes, now is the time to seize opportunities to increase safeguards for wildlife, to act before small problems become large crises, to bolster protections for imperiled species and take steps to limit new threats, and to act on behalf of the wishes of the American people and not pave the way for development and extraction interests to realize increased profits using our wildlife, America’s shared natural heritage, as aggregate to lay the road.

I will close with a quote from Aldo Leopold, the preeminent writer, ecologist, and forester:

"A thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community. It is wrong when it tends otherwise."

This proposed action from the administration falls squarely in the latter camp.

text:
