text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.

The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.

Once a species becomes imperiled, it is much harder to safeguard them, so it is our job as stewards of the land to ensure we protect these species while we can.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Stacie Cole
Supervisor of Belugas- Mystic Aquarium

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Lauren Smith

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Grause, jerry

text:
Sophia Laxton
11 December 2025
Against the Removal of Blanket Protections for Threatened Species
I am a sixteen year old high school student and I oppose this removal of blanket protections on behalf of the future. My generation, and the generations after us will look to the past for an explanation when the world that we treasure is either safe or ruined. You have the opportunity to be the people that protect our wildlife before it becomes endangered.
I’m strongly opposed to removing the blanket protections that are currently in place to protect threatened species. By waiting for animals to become endangered before granting protections, you make it far more likely for more to become endangered. Secretary Doug Bergum wrote that "these revisions end years of legal confusion and regulatory overreach, delivering certainty to states, tribes, landowners and businesses while ensuring conservation efforts remain grounded in sound science and common sense," (US Fish & Wildlife Service). I’d like to address all parts of this statement. He first discusses a problem of legal confusion. I believe this should be rephrased into an opportunity to think seriously about taking actions that could harm animals, ecosystems, and the people living in and around them. By remaining open to legal debates, the government can ensure all voices are heard. He then talks about regulatory overreach. This isn’t a problem that we’re facing because the Fish and Wildlife and the National Marine Fisheries services are well within their rights to make regulations protecting threatened animals under the Endangered Species Act because congress has delegated them power. “Under the ESA, it is the policy of Congress that all federal agencies shall seek to conserve threatened and endangered species, use their authorities in furtherance of the ESA, and cooperate with state and local agencies to resolve water resource issues in concert with conserving endangered species,” (Congress). Finally, he argues that the blanket rule lacks a basis in sound science and common sense. This is an incredibly illogical argument as protecting threatened species is inherently important. By protecting our wildlife, we keep our country usable for future generations, valuable for ecotourism, and healthy for our people.
We must keep the current protections for threatened species and consult with specialists in their wellbeing to ensure our natural wealth is protected. By keeping these blanket protections, we ensure people think critically before doing potentially dangerous actions, follow congress’ directive to protect these animals, and help to keep our country beautiful. I truly hope you don’t make this grievous error. God bless America.

Works Cited
Congress. “The Endangered Species Act: Overview and Implementation | Congress.gov | Library of Congress.” Congress, 3 April 2021, https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R46677. Accessed 12 December 2025.
US Fish & Wildlife Service. “Administration Revises Endangered Species Act Regulations to Strengthen Certainty, Reduce Burdens and Uphold the Law.” US Fish & Wildlife Service, 19 November 2025, https://www.fws.gov/press-release/2025-11/administration-revises-endangered-species-act-regulations-strengthen. Accessed 12 December 2025.

text:
My name is Ty. I am writing to oppose your proposal to rid of the “blanket rule.” I am a High School student (11th Grade, Junior) from North Carolina, who has been learning about environmental processes and how they affect us. For years, I have been in love with Sloths, I care about them so deeply. They provide nutrients to the grounds of mangroves and forests, they carry whole ecosystems on their backs with their special fur algae by providing energy to others like moths and beetles, indicating healthy ecosystems.
The Pygmy Three-Toed Sloth is currently being proposed to be threatened under the FWS. Yet, under the IUCN Red List, they are Critically Endangered, with anywhere from 100-2,000 of these beautiful creatures left struggling to exist in the entire world.
Proposing to take away this blanket rule is utterly abhorrent when you cannot even admit a species as endangered as this one to your threatened species list. If the Pygmy Three-toed Sloth were to be added to your threatened species list, and you take from threatened species protections, neither I, nor any scientist, could whole-heartedly believe that you intend to do good by evaluating each species individually due to your lack of awareness and understanding of certain Critically Endangered species that continue to contribute to our planet even at their dangerously low numbers.
According to the National Library of Medicine, peer reviewed by the Canadian Medical Association Journal, bears are a very important species to humans because research is underway to understand how they prevent bone density loss, to help humans fight osteoporosis. These bears are being over-hunted for their parts and bodies as a whole, for human economic gain.
Bears are listed as threatened with the FWS. Currently, under the blanket rule, they have almost the same amount of protections as endangered species, helping to keep their numbers up in the wild. Bears are a species that has been overlooked in the past due to recovery plans being difficult surrounding bears, so they do not have as easy a time recovering from over-hunting as species like wolves do. Again, this blanket rule ensures that bears and other threatened species that are slower at regeneration have a fair chance at surviving and being protected as any other species, even if they are not currently endangered, because they deserve our help too.
(Chivian E. Environment and health: 7. Species loss and ecosystem disruption--the implications for human health. CMAJ. 2001 Jan 9;164(1):66-9. PMID: 11202670; PMCID: PMC80637.)
I advise you to look at this from the perspective of not just these animals, but from my perspective. From the perspective of so many other teenagers and young adults who will be leading this world in the upcoming decades. We care about our animals, we care about how every soul on this planet matters to our lives, to our survival. These species bring so much life to our lives, and I am sure you understand that, but, what I need you to understand is that these species cannot save themselves. We, humans, cause this harm to them, and we, humans, HAVE to be the ones to save them from endangerment or extinction. There is no other way out. In 30 years from now, 2055, I will be in my late 40s, in 50 years from now, 2075, I will be in my 60s. I want my grandkids born in 2065 to see a pygmy sloth, and learn about how they help our environment currently, not about how they HELPED before they went extinct. I want them to go camping and see tens of hundreds of types of birds, not one singular species. I want my future generations to frolic in the diversity of our world, learning everything there is to know about our beautiful animals, their survival means our survival.
Thank you,
Ty Runheim

Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Barnes, Jeannette

text:
I’m writing this letter as a concerned citizen, but also as a teenager who would love to be outlived by most of the species of plants and animals that currently inhabit this planet. The Endangered Species Act is the first line of defense for many threatened and endangered species, and to alter the protections it gives to threatened species would be devastating for thousands of plants and animals.

The ESA states that “The purposes of this Act are to provide a means whereby the ecosystems upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species,” (Section 2b of the ESA). The wording of the Act itself doesn’t draw a distinction between endangered and threatened species, and neither should we. Threatened species may not be in immediate danger of going extinct, but they’re still heading in that direction, and often rapidly. Instead of waiting until a species is critical and almost gone, we need to start conservation earlier to never let the species get to that point. As we continue to urbanize and destroy habitats, the threatened list just keeps getting longer, and so is the endangered list. Conservation takes time, money, and effort, but it's a whole lot easier to regenerate a population of a thousand than a population of fourteen. By the time a species is declared endangered, it's often too late for a full population recovery. A threatened designation is a different story. Protecting threatened species is a way to be proactive about extinction, and it gives species of plants and animals a fighting chance to get off the list entirely.

We’re always told that children are the future, but it would be nice if the adults left a future for us to shape. The Earth is a habitat to around 8.7 million species of organisms, but current projections from Tufts University show that between 30 and 50 percent of species could go extinct by 2050. That's 4 million species gone in the next 30 years. This isn’t a fluke, and it's not a normal occurrence. The earth is entering its 6th mass extinction event, the anthropocene extinction, and its humanities fault. It’s not as dramatic as the asteroid that took out the dinosaurs, but it doesn’t need to be dramatic to be damaging. We have torn down forests and polluted rivers; we’re melting the ice caps and raising ocean temperatures. In the 1900s, we took drastic measures to destroy wildlife and urbanize, and we have to take drastic measures now if we want to make it right.

As a concerned citizen, I implore you to rethink the proposed revisions to the section 4(d) “blanket rule” of the Endangered Species Act because threatened species deserve the same protections as endangered species do. The clock to save our wildlife is ticking, but we have the power to stop it. Protecting our wildlife until it is no longer under threat of extinction is the only way to save it. By leaving the “blanket rule” protections of threatened species in place, we can give our endangered species a chance to come back and no longer need protection.
title: Comment from Shearburn, Brice

text:
As a teenager in the United States, and as someone who is environmentally conscious and values the natural world, I have a vested interest in the existence of threatened and endangered species. If laws and regulations are enacted that harm already threatened species, myself, my generation, and future generations may be robbed of the opportunity to see some species threatened with extinction.

This proposal removes the blanket rule on habitat protections, lessening protections on the habitats of threatened species so that they are not as protected as designated endangered species. Under this proposal, habitats will be reviewed to exclude “areas from critical habitat if the benefits of excluding the area outweigh the benefits of designating it as a critical habitat.” (U.S Fish and Wildlife Service)

According to professors at NC State University, reducing protections for the habitats of threatened and endangered species has the potential to exacerbate the main cause of population decline, which is habitat loss. Because habitat is species specific, already threatened species rely on the specific conditions of their ecosystem and habitat. Removing this habitat would remove the conditions required for survival. One example that professors reference is the red-cockaded woodpecker, which requires open pine forests for nesting and foraging. The birds nest within the pine trees, usually choosing older trees that contain a specific fungus, which softens the wood. Habitat loss already threatens this species and has led to population decline, and the modification to the law could further threaten their species if their habitats did not receive protection. The cutting down of these trees would be detrimental to the woodpeckers. This situation is applicable to all threatened species, which should all receive adequate protections so that they do not become endangered or extinct. (Moore)

I recommend that instead of creating species-specific 4(d) rules that have the potential to harm threatened species and drastically increase stakeholder influence, the FWS keeps the blanket 4(d) rule that automatically gives threatened species the same protections as endangered species. This would help ensure the survival of species already threatened by habitat loss and human activities.

In summary, the species-specific 4(d) rule proposal removes essential automatic protections for threatened species regarding “takes” and habitat use. According to experts in conservation, this proposal could be very detrimental to species that require specific habitats and conditions. Also, all young people deserve to live in a world where iconic species do not become extinct due to preventable human interference and interaction. Because of this, the FWS should keep the blanket rule that provides threatened species the same protections as endangered species.

Works Cited
Moore, Andrew. “Endangered Species Act Revision Could Weaken Habitat Protections for At-Risk Wildlife, Experts Say.” College of Natural Resources News, June 11, 2025, https://cnr.ncsu.edu/news/2025/06/endangered-species-act-revision-could-weaken-habitat-protections/.
U.S Fish and Wildlife Service, “Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat.” Federal Register, November 21, 2025, https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/11/21/2025-20550/endangered-and-threatened-wildlife-and-plants-regulations-for-designating-critical-habitat.

o whomever it may concern,



I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.



The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.



As a disabled veteran and dedicated conservationist, I strongly believe that safeguarding America’s natural beauty and biodiversity for future generations is of utmost importance.



I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.



Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.



Sincerely,

Jonathan Kellner

Mystic Aquarium

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Pamela Hansen
Elkhorn, NE

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Deal, Abigail

text:
I am writing to oppose your proposal to remove the “blanket rule” option for protecting newly listed threatened species.

My name is Sophie and I am eighteen years old. I am a North Carolina resident and I have spent countless hours enjoying our local forests. However, removing the “blanket rule” puts these very forests at risk for exploitation and degradation.

Under the existing rule, threatened species are protected from “harm,” which includes the damage to their respective habitat. Removing this rule to have an instead “tailored” conservation plan would allow room for the exploitation of their habitat. A species-specific approach would leave too much power up to the discretion of those at the USFWS and NMFS. While there are numerous experts and life-long civil servants who take conservation very seriously, it does not mean that the politically appointed executives of these agencies have to as well. Under this rule, you say that “the Secretary shall issue regulations that are necessary and advisable to provide for the conservation of the species.” The words “necessary and advisable” are quite ambiguous. These words directly give power to political appointees to alter regulations to meet their personal objectives, not what is actually best for the species at risk.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted, S. B.

Protecting Wildlife: Why the Endangered Species Act MattersEmpty heading
Posted December 15, 2025 by David Jenike
The Endangered Species Act, enacted in 1973, currently serves as the most effective wildlife legislation ever enacted to preserve biodiversity. Species such as the California condor, gray wolf, American alligator, and bald eagle are all here today as a result of this legislation. Here at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, we work to conserve numerous species listed under the Endangered Species Act, including Mexican wolves, Polar bear, sihek, Texas ocelots, and American burying beetles.

One of the most concerning proposals would eliminate the Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule.” This rule automatically provides basic protections for species listed as threatened , such as prohibitions on harming or harassing that wildlife, while species-specific rules are developed.

Without the blanket rule, newly listed species could go months or even years without specific protections, and this delaying of safeguards increases the risk of further population decline.

text:
Subject: Comment Opposing Removal of ESA “Blanket 4(d) Rule” Protections
Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029

To the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,

I am writing to express strong concern with the Service’s proposal to remove the long-standing option to apply the ESA’s “blanket 4(d) rule” to newly listed threatened species (Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029).

The blanket rule has always struck me as a straightforward, practical safeguard. It ensures that when a species is formally recognized as threatened, it immediately receives basic protections against harm and harassment while species-specific 4(d) rules are developed. Removing this default creates an unnecessary gap in protections at precisely the moment a species is acknowledged to be at risk.

A threatened listing is not a casual designation—it reflects a scientific determination that a species is likely to become endangered in the foreseeable future. Allowing protections to lag behind that determination runs counter to the preventative intent of the Endangered Species Act. Delays at this stage increase the likelihood of further decline and make recovery more difficult, more uncertain, and more expensive.

The proposed rule notes the Service’s intent to finalize species-specific 4(d) rules at the time of listing. While that goal is understandable, intent alone does not ensure timely outcomes. In practice, rulemakings are often complex and resource-intensive, and even short delays can leave newly listed species vulnerable to the very pressures that led to their decline.

For more than fifty years, the ESA has been one of the most effective conservation tools in the United States because it prioritizes timely, enforceable protections. Weakening immediate safeguards for threatened species risks eroding that effectiveness and undermining the Act’s core purpose.

I respectfully urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule as the default minimum level of protection for newly listed threatened species, using species-specific 4(d) rules to refine or strengthen protections where appropriate—not to postpone or reduce them.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this comment and for considering these concerns.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act regulations announced on November 19, 2025. Specifically, I object to the rescission of the “Blanket Rule” under Section 4(d) and the re-introduction of economic considerations into listing decisions. Additionally, removing language that would reduce critical habitat protection will cause irreparable harm to threatened and endangered species.

1. Restore the Blanket Rule: Removing the automatic protections for “Threatened” species creates a dangerous gap in enforcement. For species like the Tope Shark, which is currently awaiting listing decisions, this change means they could be listed as threatened but remain legally unprotected from harvest for years while species-specific rules are drafted. This delay could lead to functionally extinct populations before a single protection is enforced.

2. Maintain Critical Habitat Protection: The ESA was designed to base extinction decisions solely on science. Re-introducing economic impact assessments into the listing and critical habitat designation process inevitably prioritizes short-term industry profits over long-term biodiversity. For highly migratory species like the Oceanic Whitetip Shark and Scalloped Hammerhead, protecting critical habitat is often inconvenient for commercial fisheries. That inconvenience is not a valid reason to allow a species to go extinct.

3. Lessons from Success: The recovery of the Eastern North Pacific (California) Gray Whale and Southern Sea Otter proves that strict, automatic protections work. The ESA has saved 99% of species listed under fifty years since the ESA was enacted. The California Gray whale population numbered only a few thousand when it was listed in 1973. The rebuilding of the population- up to 27,000 in 2016 led to the delisting of the whale in a great success story. However, a lack of food and other threats have put this whale back into peril, underscoring the need for vigilance. Weakening the ESA would ensures that other threatened species will not share in the success story shared by plants and animals protected in the past.

I urge you to withdraw these proposals and maintain the automatic protections that have prevented the extinction of 99% of listed species.

Sincerely, Carley Ochs (Cincinnati, Ohio)

text:
I strongly oppose any effort to weaken or change the Endangered Species Act. This law has been the foundation of species recovery in the United States for more than 50 years and has helped bring back iconic animals like the bald eagle, American alligator, California condor, and gray wolf from the brink of extinction. In my area, we are now seeing bald eagles regularly, and they are thriving! Back in 1996, I traveled across the country to visit Yellowstone National Park to see the wildlife firsthand. One of the key species I wanted to see in the wild was a bald eagle, and now they are are in my own backyard thanks to the protections they’ve received over the past decades.

The proposed gutting of key protections — including rules that automatically protect newly listed threatened species — would leave vulnerable wildlife exposed for months or years without safeguards. Delaying protections increases the risk that populations will decline even further or never recover. Tearing down and destroying natural spaces and the extinction of species is forever; you cannot just bring them back. Have we learned nothing from our past history of allowing, or even causing, the extinction of species on this planet?

Scientists and conservation groups point out that the ESA works based on science and habitat protection, not economics, and that weakening it would put hundreds of species at greater risk of extinction. We are already facing a global biodiversity crisis driven by habitat loss, climate change, and pollution — now is not the time to roll back protections that have been proven to work.

Our wildlife and wild places are part of America’s natural heritage and worth protecting for future generations, not to mention the need to maintain the balance of nature. Please preserve the strength of the Endangered Species Act and reject changes that would undermine species recovery and conservation.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife and science-based conservation, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,
Concerned Individual

text:
I urge fish and wildlife to do its government duty to uphold the endangered species act and maintain the “blanket rule.” This is important and a minimum duty for us humans to protect wildlife from the destructive of humans and our capitalist behavior.

Maintaining the Endangered Species Act's 'blanket rule' for threatened species is essential for effective, timely, and efficient conservation. Once a species is scientifically determined to be 'threatened', meaning it is likely to become endangered in the foreseeable future, it requires immediate and robust regulatory safeguards to prevent its decline into the more severe 'endangered' status.

The blanket rule achieves this by automatically applying the strong protections of endangered species (such as prohibitions on 'take' or harm) the moment a species is listed. Without this default protection, the process of developing a complex, species-specific rule for every newly threatened species creates a perilous administrative gap. This gap is often caused by limited agency funding and personnel. Without the blanket rule, this will allow ongoing habitat destruction and other threats to continue unchecked, pushing vulnerable species closer to extinction while bureaucrats draft tailored regulations.

The blanket rule is not a barrier to flexibility; it is a safety net. It provides the necessary breathing room for the species to stabilize while the Fish and Wildlife Service can then choose to develop species specific rules that carve out appropriate exceptions to encourage proactive conservation and collaboration with stakeholders. The burden must remain on regulators to demonstrate that an activity is safe for a species, not on the species to wait for protections. Therefore, the blanket rule is the most practical, protective, and preventative approach to ensure the survival and eventual recovery of America's most vulnerable wildlife.

Posted December 15, 2025 by David Jenike
The Endangered Species Act, enacted in 1973, currently serves as the most effective wildlife legislation ever enacted to preserve biodiversity. Species such as the California condor, gray wolf, American alligator, and bald eagle are all here today as a result of this legislation. Here at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, we work to conserve numerous species listed under the Endangered Species Act, including Mexican wolves, Polar bear, sihek, Texas ocelots, and American burying beetles.

One of the most concerning proposals would eliminate the Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule.” This rule automatically provides basic protections for species listed as threatened , such as prohibitions on harming or harassing that wildlife, while species-specific rules are developed.

Without the blanket rule, newly listed species could go months or even years without specific protections, and this delaying of safeguards increases the risk of further population decline.

title: Comment from Moseley, Alice

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Thompson, William

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Garera, Brittany

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

Protecting Wildlife: Why the Endangered Species Act MattersEmpty heading
Posted December 15, 2025 by David Jenike
The Endangered Species Act, enacted in 1973, currently serves as the most effective wildlife legislation ever enacted to preserve biodiversity. Species such as the California condor, gray wolf, American alligator, and bald eagle are all here today as a result of this legislation. Here at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, we work to conserve numerous species listed under the Endangered Species Act, including Mexican wolves, Polar bear, sihek, Texas ocelots, and American burying beetles.

One of the most concerning proposals would eliminate the Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule.” This rule automatically provides basic protections for species listed as threatened , such as prohibitions on harming or harassing that wildlife, while species-specific rules are developed.

Without the blanket rule, newly listed species could go months or even years without specific protections, and this delaying of safeguards increases the risk of further population decline.

text:
To whomever it may concern,

I am writing to express my strong support for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and to urge you to maintain its protections for endangered and threatened species.

The ESA is important to me because I care deeply about the species Mystic Aquarium works with, including marine mammals, sea turtles, and other coastal and marine wildlife. These animals play vital roles in their ecosystems, inspire people through education and outreach, and are central to our research, rescue, and conservation programs. Protecting them helps preserve the biodiversity and health of our oceans and coasts, and ensures that future generations can experience and learn from these remarkable species.

For over 25 years, the ESA has used science-based decision-making to assist in the recovery of many species, including sea otters and manatees. In today’s world, I believe we should be focused on increasing protections for the natural resources (both landscapes and species) we still have and not tearing down existing protections.

I am concerned that the proposed changes—such as removing recovery as a basis for delisting, allowing agencies to limit critical habitat protections, reducing mitigation requirements, and eliminating default protections for threatened species—could weaken safeguards for vulnerable wildlife. These changes could slow recovery efforts, increase stress on wild populations, and place additional pressure on the programs Mystic Aquarium supports.

Maintaining strong, science-based protections under the ESA is essential for giving these species a chance to recover and thrive, for supporting healthy ecosystems, and for ensuring that our shared natural heritage is preserved. I urge you to preserve the ESA’s current protections and continue to rely on science-driven decision-making.

Thank you for your attention to this important issue and for considering my comments.

Sincerely,
Danielle R. Lavoie, MS

Protecting Wildlife: Why the Endangered Species Act MattersEmpty heading
Posted December 15, 2025 by David Jenike
The Endangered Species Act, enacted in 1973, currently serves as the most effective wildlife legislation ever enacted to preserve biodiversity. Species such as the California condor, gray wolf, American alligator, and bald eagle are all here today as a result of this legislation. Here at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, we work to conserve numerous species listed under the Endangered Species Act, including Mexican wolves, Polar bear, sihek, Texas ocelots, and American burying beetles.

One of the most concerning proposals would eliminate the Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule.” This rule automatically provides basic protections for species listed as threatened , such as prohibitions on harming or harassing that wildlife, while species-specific rules are developed.

Without the blanket rule, newly listed species could go months or even years without specific protections, and this delaying of safeguards increases the risk of further population decline.

title: Comment from Hanafin, Jacqlyn

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Liband, Hillary

text:
For more than 50 years, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction, a remarkable track record of success that Americans should be proud of. As someone who values America's wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

As someone who cares deeply about wildlife and the future of our planet, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule that would undermine wildlife protections granted by the Endangered Species Act. This change would go against decades of conservation progress and weaken one of our nation’s most important environmental laws.

The “blanket rule” gives essential baseline protection to threatened species until species-specific safeguards can be established. Removing the “blanket rule” may make them more vulnerable to extinction, in opposition to the intent of this legislation.

I urge you to uphold the mission of the Endangered Species Act and maintain the “blanket rule.” Our wildlife, wild places, and future generations are counting on it.

It is incredibly important we protect those who cannot protect themselves and that includes the other animals of this earth. Humans have the power to destroy so easily, that we must push back and curb that power so this planet and it's inhabitants can be protected. We can't rely on people to do the "right" thing always so we must ensure these protections stand. Please think of the future and not some immediate cash grab that could help cooperations be able to just bypass things and the continued destruction they can impose. We need laws like this to make people stop, look, listen and help the community, world and future.
