I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

title: Comment from corsaut, william

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.
title: Comment from Cass, Reed

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Scism, Ashley

text:
I’m writing to ask the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to keep strong protections in place for endangered and threatened species under the Endangered Species Act.

The Endangered Species Act has protected America’s wildlife for more than 50 years. It was signed into law by President Richard Nixon with broad bipartisan support, reflecting a shared belief that preventing extinction and caring for our natural heritage is a responsibility we all share.

Strong, science-based ESA protections help safeguard wildlife and the habitats they depend on, while also supporting hunting, fishing, outdoor recreation, and responsible land management on public lands. These protections matter not just for wildlife, but for the communities and traditions connected to healthy ecosystems.

Weakening how the law is implemented would make it harder to protect species already under stress and could undermine long-term conservation efforts. I urge the Service to uphold the intent of the Endangered Species Act and maintain clear, effective protections grounded in science.

Thank you for considering my comment and for the work you do to protect America’s wildlife for future generations.
title: Comment from Wilbanks, Tom

title: Comment from Fishburn, Adam

text:
I am writing to formally oppose the proposed change under docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029.

I hold a master’s degree in Fisheries and Wildlife Resources and currently work as a conservation professional. My education and professional experience involve applying the Endangered Species Act in practical, on-the-ground conservation and recovery efforts. Based on that experience, I am deeply concerned that the proposed change would weaken the effectiveness of the ESA and undermine its core purpose.

The strength of the Endangered Species Act lies in its clear, science-based standards and precautionary approach to species protection. The proposed change introduces increased ambiguity and discretion that could reduce consistency in decision-making, delay conservation action, and increase the likelihood that species decline further before meaningful protections are applied. In practice, this shifts the Act away from prevention and recovery and toward reactive management, which is both less effective and more costly over time.

As a working conservation professional, I have seen firsthand how early, decisive protections improve outcomes for species and habitats. Weakening these safeguards risks placing additional strain on already limited conservation resources while increasing uncertainty for agencies, partners, and the public. The ESA has a long record of success when implemented as intended, and altering its foundational protections without clear biological justification is not supported by the best available science.

I respectfully urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to withdraw this proposed change and retain the existing standards of the Endangered Species Act. Any revisions to ESA implementation should strengthen, not erode, our ability to conserve imperiled species and the ecosystems upon which they depend.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment and for considering the perspectives of conservation professionals working directly with threatened and endangered species.

title: Comment from Lawson, Shara

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
At a time like this!? Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Regretfully submitted, Ms. Smith

text:

Irreparable damage to the health of our marine life is not an option to be good stewards of our Earth!

Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.
title: Comment from Ardohain, Beatrice

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Reynier, Delphine

text:
I strongly oppose all four proposed changes to ESA regulations. These changes would undermine science-based protections that have prevented 99% of listed species from extinction.
Removing default 4(d) protections contradicts preventive conservation principles. Allowing economic considerations in listing violates Congressional intent established in TVA v. Hill and ignores climate threats. Narrowing "harm" definitions reverses Babbitt v. Sweet Home precedent—habitat destruction kills wildlife indirectly but certainly. For example, the loss of sea turtle nesting beaches and inwater habitat results in the loss of sea turtles that are already killed by pollution (death by plastic ingestion and/or entanglement), recreational and commercial fisheries, and boat strikes. Agency exemption loopholes would fragment protections for wide-ranging species like panthers and grizzlies.
At a time of global biodiversity crisis, we should strengthen, not weaken, our most effective conservation law.
I urge immediate withdrawal of these proposals.

text:
Dear Director Nesvik and Acting Director Menashes,

I am writing in opposition to the four proposed rules regarding the Endangered Species Act found in the following dockets:

FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048
FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029
FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044
FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039

As someone concerned with the protection of birds across the United States, and someone who believes in the power and importance of the Endangered Species Act as a tool to boost recovery and prevent extinction, I request that these proposed rules be withdrawn and the current statutory language stay in place.

Species like the Hawaiian Coot, Nene, Marbled Murrelet, and Eastern Black Rail are facing high pressure from invasive species, habitat loss, and climate change. Threatened species such as the Florida Scrub-Jay have long escaped being designated as “endangered” because of crucial protections in the blanket 4(d) rule. Additionally, birds such as the Whooping Crane and Streaked Horned Lark could be harmed by federal projects from other agencies, making clear inter-agency communication important.

I believe that the proposed rules would weaken the Endangered Species Act for birds, making important tools such as critical habitat designations, inclusion of historical baselines in listing decisions, and blanket protections for threatened species inaccessible.

Please withdraw the proposed rules in dockets FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044, and FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039. Given the ongoing declines of birds confirmed by scientific studies, now is not the time to weaken ESA protections. As a scientist who directly works to inform effective conservation and management strategies for animals protected by the Endangered Species Act, I must emphasize how important it is that the ESA remains unaltered. Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely, Josh

title: Comment from Dunkelberger, Lori

text:
I oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, specifically the FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029 (Section 4(d)) revision. This change would make protecting species less efficient and more error-prone in conservation efforts.
A key aspect of the change to Section 4(d) is the abolition of the “blanket rule.” The blanket rule extends many protections granted to endangered species to threatened species as well. FWS.gov notes that these include prohibitions on selling, transporting, and exporting these listed species (Section 4(D) Rules: Frequently Asked Questions | U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, 2021). These provisions are essential for both endangered and threatened species. Treating threatened species on a case-by-case basis would inherently reduce these protections and create more work to ensure them for species that need them.
A less efficient system of determining protections will occur as a result of these proposed changes. The Wildlife Organization states, “Each species-specific rule would evaluate conservation needs, consider economic impacts and be subject to public comment” (Zipp, 2025). Ensuring a thorough understanding of each species’s situation and creating guidelines specific for each is unrealistic when so many of the species exist. Additionally, many periods of public comment would delay responses. Instead, the blanket rule should be kept to avoid the inefficiency that these changes cause.
Finally, the FWS’s own experience with the success of the blanket rule speaks to its effectiveness. It reports, “This approach will result in less confusion, less duplication of regulatory text in the Code of Federal Regulations, a lower risk of error in transposing regulatory text, and reduced administrative costs associated with developing and publishing a rule in the Federal Register and Code of Federal Regulations” (Section 4(D) Rules: Frequently Asked Questions | U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, 2021). Eliminating the blanket rule would incur these additional costs and make conservation less effective, more costly, and less appealing for the government. In order to keep conservation a practical and efficient tool of the government to ensure biodiversity, simpler laws that keep conservation more efficient are essential.
To keep conservation a process that efficiently and effectively protects all threatened species, I oppose these proposed changes, and urge the agencies to retract them. If we keep the blanket rule, we can keep America on the path of biodiversity and ecological health.

References
Section 4(d) Rules: Frequently Asked Questions | U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service. (2021, October 1). Www.fws.gov. https://www.fws.gov/node/267756
Zipp, K. (2025, December 15). How will ESA rollback impact threatened species? The Wildlife Society. https://wildlife.org/how-will-esa-rollback-impact-threatened-species/
title: Comment from Josef, Asher

text:
As an American, I’m writing to ask the government of the United States of America to oppose any efforts to diminish the strength and coverage of the Endangered Species Act. This landmark law has protected Hawaiian monk seals, Guadalupe fur seals, southern sea otters and other vital animals and their ecosystems for more than 50 years. The proposed changes would seriously undermine these protections for extremely vulnerable wildlife and would threaten decades of progress that has been made in protecting these animal populations.
Sea otters reside in kelp forests and are a keystone species in our environment. They already exist in incredibly small numbers. Without them, it will further unbalance our fragile ocean ecosystem. They feed on sea urchins which, left unchecked, eat and destroy the kelp forests which are the sea otters’ habitat - the places sea otters wrap themselves in kelp when resting so they are not swept away by currents, and the places they leave their baby otters to float safely while the mother sea otters dive for the large amounts of food they must consume to feed their babies. Sea otters have already disappeared from their ancestral homes along the Oregon Coast.
As a pro-life mother, and a person who has learned about the important role of these animals while watching livestreams and videos of them from aquariums along the Pacific Ocean (Monterey Bay Aquarium, Oregon Coast Aquarium, Vancouver Aquarium, Port Defiance Zoo & Aquarium), I have also learned, along with my own children, how difficult it is to care for these animals in captivity and how difficult it is to regrow their populations in the wild.
Please reject these reckless changes and stand up for endangered species and the ecosystems we all depend on.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from A Jennings, Linda

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am writing to convey my strong disagreement with the four proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) currently under review. Individually and collectively, these changes would significantly weaken the ESA's capacity to prevent extinction, aid species recovery, and protect ecosystems vital to both wildlife and humans. Public health is dependent on ecosystem health.

1. Repealing default protections for threatened species is just weakening a law for no reason other than to please the oil and gas industry. (4(d) rule)

The ESA was designed to act before species reach critical levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule is built on decades of scientific evidence demonstrating that early protective measures lower recovery costs and prevent further declines. Ending default protections would cause unnecessary delays, force case-by-case rulemaking, and expose vulnerable species to harm. This contradicts the ESA’s preventive mission and will result in higher ecological and financial costs in the long run.

2. Including economic considerations and weakening future-threat analysis for listings

The ESA mandates that listing decisions be based solely on scientific data, not economic impacts. Allowing economic factors would contradict legal statutes, undermine scientific integrity, and risk delaying protections until species face extinction. Ignoring future threats like climate change contradicts current conservation science, which shows that these pressures pose significant risks. Weakening future-threat criteria hinders timely listings and increases preventable extinctions.

3. Reducing critical habitat protections and altering the definition of “harm”

Habitat loss is the primary threat to biodiversity worldwide. Limiting critical habitat designation directly undermines recovery efforts. Similarly, narrowing the definition of “harm” would reverse established legal and scientific standards. Habitat degradation often indirectly harms wildlife, a fact long recognized by law. These changes would make consultations less effective, increase biological risks, and conflict with recovery mandates.

4. Creating loopholes for bypassing ESA protections

Allowing agencies to override ESA protections when extinction is foreseeable contradicts the ESA’s purpose. These loopholes would promote project-based exemptions, reduce transparency, and deviate from science-based decision-making. This disproportionately impacts species like the Florida panther, grizzly bear, and gray wolf, accelerating declines in already pressured species.

Collectively, these proposed rules would:

- Undermine the scientific basis of the ESA,
- Delay or prevent necessary protections,
- Reduce habitat conservation amid climate change,
- Increase extinction risks,
- Undermine inter-agency cooperation,
- Raise recovery costs.

The ESA has prevented 99% of listed species from going extinct and is successful because it is based on science, precaution, and early action. These changes oppose those principles. At a time of global biodiversity loss, the U.S. should strengthen its wildlife protection law, not weaken it.

For these reasons, I urge the agencies to withdraw all four proposed changes and maintain the current regulatory framework rooted in science, law, and proven success.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

Removing the blanket rule's protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design. Given the urgency with which we must address species declines, delays in protection will prove costly in terms of money needed to study and enact conservation programs to reverse species declines, and in terms of biodiversity loss as species reach unrecoverable population tipping points.

While species-specific rules could better align regulations with conservation needs, the anticipated increase in workload combined with ongoing loss of agency capacity raises concerns about the feasibility of developing and implementing such rules effectively. The work of USFWS has long been impacted by funding and personnel cuts that may limit its ability to develop timely and effective species-specific rules for every threatened species.

title: Comment from Van Tatenhove, Aimee

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Tigner, Anastasia

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule to rescind the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has ensured that most Section 9 prohibitions automatically apply to threatened species upon listing, unless and until species-specific rules are developed. Removing this safeguard will create significant delays before threatened species receive meaningful protection, undermining the Endangered Species Act’s precautionary and preventative framework.

Congress established separate “endangered” and “threatened” classifications to allow for earlier intervention—not to postpone protections until species face imminent extinction. The blanket 4(d) rule is an efficient, science-based tool that prevents threats from escalating during the critical period when a species is first listed and recovery strategies are still being developed. Eliminating it leaves newly listed threatened species exposed during their most vulnerable phase, increasing the risk that they decline further and require endangered status.

The proposed rule also fails to demonstrate that the blanket 4(d) protections impose regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the Administrative Procedure Act. In fact, rescinding the rule is likely to increase administrative complexity by requiring numerous species-specific 4(d) rules, slowing implementation and delaying urgently needed conservation measures.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule, which provides timely, effective, and scientifically grounded protections essential to preventing further biodiversity loss.

Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.
title: Comment from Asteinza, Maria

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I am writing to express strong support for robust endangered species protections and to urge elected officials to continue defending and strengthening these laws. Protecting endangered species is not a special interest, it is a public responsibility with ecological, economic, and moral implications that directly affect our communities and future generations.

Endangered species protections exist because ecosystems are interconnected. When one species declines or disappears, it often signals broader environmental instability (declining water quality, loss of habitat, and weakened resilience to climate change and extreme weather). Healthy ecosystems provide services that humans depend on every day, including clean drinking water, flood mitigation, pollination, fisheries, and tourism. Protecting species at risk helps preserve these systems before they reach irreversible tipping points, saving both environmental and taxpayer costs in the long run.

These protections also reflect sound, science-based governance. The Endangered Species Act and similar laws rely on biological data and expert review, not political convenience. When elected officials uphold science-driven conservation policy, they reinforce public trust in government decision-making. Weakening protections for short-term gain undermines that trust and often leads to costly restoration efforts later, after damage has already been done.

From an economic perspective, endangered species protections support jobs and local economies. Outdoor recreation, fishing, wildlife tourism, and coastal and watershed-based industries depend on intact habitats and healthy species populations. In many regions, conservation investments create more stable, long-term economic benefits than extractive or development practices that degrade land and water and require expensive remediation. Protecting species is not an obstacle to prosperity, it is part of sustainable economic planning.

There is also a moral dimension that should not be overlooked. Many endangered species are at risk because of human activity resulting in habitat destruction, pollution, overexploitation, and climate change. Having caused much of the problem, we have an ethical obligation to be part of the solution. Allowing species to go extinct when recovery is still possible reflects a failure of stewardship and responsibility.

Elected officials should care about endangered species protections because voters care about clean water, resilient communities, and leaving a livable world for their children. Conservation is not a partisan issue; it is a shared value rooted in foresight, accountability, and respect for the natural systems that sustain life. Strong protections demonstrate leadership that looks beyond election cycles and prioritizes long-term public interest.

I urge decision-makers to maintain and strengthen endangered species protections, fully fund conservation programs, and resist efforts to weaken environmental laws. Doing so protects not only wildlife, but also the health, safety, and economic well-being of the people you serve.

Thank you for considering this comment and for your commitment to responsible environmental stewardship.

title: Comment from Nair, Krishna

text:
This rule has automatically provided threatened species with protections against harm until a tailored plan can be finalized. For decades, it has helped species like the piping plover, southern sea otter, and Florida manatee gain immediate safeguards upon listing (FWS, 2019).
Without this automatic protection, newly listed threatened species could be killed, captured, or harassed without legal consequence while they await a species-specific rule. This exposes species to preventable harm during their most vulnerable period.
Habitat loss is the number one driver of extinction. The ESA already allows exclusions, but only when they will not lead to extinction. Broadening this power increases risk to species that already live on the edge. For example, habitat loss contributed to the extinction of the ivory-billed woodpecker, Little Mariana fruit bat, and multiple freshwater mussel species (FWS, 2021)

text:
I am writing to respectfully express my strong concern regarding all four of the proposed regulatory revisions to the Endangered Species Act (ESA). As a constituent and as someone deeply committed to the protection of our nation’s wildlife and ecosystems, I believe these changes would significantly weaken one of the most successful conservation laws in American history. The four proposed changes to the ESA —particularly those affecting the listing process, critical habitat designations, interagency consultations, and default protections for threatened species—appear to diminish the scientific and precautionary framework that has made the Act effective.
At a time when biodiversity loss is accelerating nationally and globally, it is essential that we strengthen, rather than dilute, the mechanisms that safeguard vulnerable species and the ecosystems upon which they depend. Weakening the ESA not only jeopardizes imperiled wildlife but also undermines the environmental stability, cultural heritage, and long-term ecological health that benefit all Americans. In addition, I feel that it is our responsibility as thoughtful citizens to protect those who cannot protect themselves, this is our job as stewards of our wildlife. Lastly, I understand that the ESA significantly affects people in rural communities more than urban ones, and in a state where I live, Montana, the ESA can be a tremendous burden. Supporting people who are most affected by the ESA is a better solution than changing the ESA to this watered down legislation. The ESA actually works, and has for a long time - the bald eagles I saw on the way to work this morning is a clear sign of its success. Please reconsider this proposal.
title: Comment from Galloway, Julia

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

text:
The proposed rule here is arbitrary and capricious at least because the agency relied on factors Congress did not intend it to rely on (State Farm) and because it is based on a legally incorrect reading of Loper Bright.

First, Congress clearly stated its purpose in passing the Endangered Species Act. In the ESA Congress said "It is further declared to be the policy of Congress that all Federal departments and agencies shall seek to conserve endangered species and threatened
species and shall utilize their authorities in furtherance of the purposes of this Act." (ESA Section 2(c)(1)). The ESA does not allow any agency to rely on the effect of the ESA on "the development energy resources." In fact, in TVA v. Hill, the ESA was the basis of enjoining the construction of the Tellico Dam. If anything the ESA is specifically about promoting biodiversity at the expense of economic development based on a policy decision made by Congress. To rely on the executive order cited in the NPRM is to rely on a factor Congress did not intend which violates 5 USC 706 as interpreted by the Supreme Court in State Farm.

Second, the agency misreads and misapplies Loper Bright. The first mistake the agency makes is applying the "best reading" standard to its own reading of the statute. The best reading is a judicial question, not an agency question. Even ignoring this mistake, Loper Bright itself makes it a point to say that cases decided under Chevron are not overruled. Rather, a special justification is required to overturn settled precedent.

Finally, the agency's reading of Loper Bright is not the best reading even if it were possible to reach that issue. In the context of the ESA, the blanket rule is not meant to replace species specific rules. The blanket rule is intended to provide protection for a species that has been listed as endangered during the period of rulemaking for a species specific rule. Even accepting the agency's reasoning that species specific rules are better policy, the blanket rule does nothing to limit those better rules. Removing it simply delays protection.

For at least these reasons the current rule should be left as is and the proposed amendment should be cancelled.

Protecting Wildlife: Why the Endangered Species Act MattersEmpty heading
Posted December 15, 2025 by David Jenike
The Endangered Species Act, enacted in 1973, currently serves as the most effective wildlife legislation ever enacted to preserve biodiversity. Species such as the California condor, gray wolf, American alligator, and bald eagle are all here today as a result of this legislation. Here at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, we work to conserve numerous species listed under the Endangered Species Act, including Mexican wolves, Polar bear, sihek, Texas ocelots, and American burying beetles.

One of the most concerning proposals would eliminate the Endangered Species Act’s long-standing “blanket rule.” This rule automatically provides basic protections for species listed as threatened , such as prohibitions on harming or harassing that wildlife, while species-specific rules are developed.

Without the blanket rule, newly listed species could go months or even years without specific protections, and this delaying of safeguards increases the risk of further population decline.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.
Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.
The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.
For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.

text:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration,

Since its bipartisan passage in 1973, the Endangered Species Act (ESA) has been one of our bedrock environmental laws, providing protections to over 1,600 species across the last five decades. That includes numerous listed species important to the Long Island Sound region, such as the Roseate tern, Piping Plover, Northern Long-Eared Bat, and Hawksbill sea turtle. But the proposed revisions to the ESA regulations threaten to reverse much of what the Act has accomplished, ignoring science and the law. I oppose these efforts which would severely weaken the ESA and further fuel the ongoing biodiversity crisis toward catastrophic consequences.

The proposed rules would:

Allow purported economic impacts to influence decisions regarding a species' status as "threatened" or "endangered"—despite the Act plainly prohibiting such considerations. Where the best science shows a species is at risk of extinction, a corporation's desire to build a new data center or shopping mall on its habitat should not stop that species from receiving the Act's necessary protections;

Effectively prohibit currently unoccupied, yet essential, habitat from designation as "critical habitat." This proposal is particularly alarming in a time when the effects of climate change and biodiversity loss are forcing species to shift their ranges to survive;

Deprive newly-listed threatened species of critical tools needed to support their recovery by removing the Rule 4(d) "blanket rule." Since the earliest days of the ESA the "blanket rule" has been crucial to jump-starting threatened species' path toward recovery, automatically extending to threatened species most of the same protections provided to endangered species. Now is not the time to lose this important tool in the fight against the biodiversity crisis;

Raise the bar dangerously high for species to be listed as "threatened" by redefining "foreseeable future" to require that both the future threats and the species' responses to those threats are "likely." Requiring such a high level of certainty is scientifically unsound and threatens to impede protections for species threatened by emerging issues such as the worsening impacts of climate change and toxics chemicals in the environment;

Unduly amplify industry and polluter interests in decisions regarding areas to be excluded from critical habitat designation; and

Weaken interagency consultation, allowing destructive activities to proceed with less oversight or mitigation of harms to listed species and their habitat.

If finalized, the damaging effects of these rules will not be isolated to listed species, but rather will have cascading effects across ecosystems, harming many other species, including humans and our communities. Please revoke all four proposed rules.

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

For decades, it has helped species like the piping plover, southern sea otter, and Florida manatee gain immediate safeguards upon listing (FWS, 2019).

Without automatic protections, any newly listed species can still be damaged, killed, harassed, and more without any legal repercussions while they wait for the species-specific guidelines to be put in place.

The ESA already has language in place that allows exclusions, provided that the habitat's alterations will not lead to the extinction of species. Broadening the power already given further increases the risk of species loss. We've seen the results of habitat destruction and its harm to various mammals, birds, reptiles and fish species, all of which once contributed to their local ecosystems. I urge you to reconsider the revisions, or add in language that ensures the safety of newly-listed species against companies that do not see their value.
