text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,

Eryn Rogers

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Diaz, Breanna

text:
I am writing to formally oppose the proposed rule by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to remove the “blanket rule” option for protecting newly listed threatened species under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). This proposed revision not only undermines the effectiveness of the ESA but also jeopardizes conservation efforts that are crucial for the survival of many threatened species.

The blanket rule has historically provided immediate and much-needed protections for newly listed species without needing lengthy and potentially bureaucratic processes to establish species-specific rules. By removing this option, the Service risks creating significant delays in the implementation of essential protections during a critical time when many species face rapidly worsening threats due to climate change, habitat loss, and other environmental pressures.

Furthermore, while the argument is made that species-specific rules allow for more tailored protections, this approach could lead to inconsistent applications of the ESA, leaving vulnerable species at greater risk. The process of developing individual rules can be time-consuming and may result in some species remaining unprotected for extended periods, effectively leaving them without the immediate safeguards they need.

The decision to revert to a species-specific rule-by-rule approach disregards the intent of the ESA, which aims to provide broad protections to ensure the conservation of our nation’s biodiversity. It is imperative that the Service maintains the flexibility of the blanket rule, which ensures that protections are in place as soon as a species is listed, allowing for timely conservation actions that can make a significant difference in recovery efforts.

I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to reconsider this proposed rule and prioritize the immediate and effective protections afforded by the blanket rule for threatened species. Our wildlife and ecosystems depend on it!!

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

title: Comment from Hanks, Laura

text:
Protecting wildlife is not just about saving individual species, it is about safeguarding the health, balance, and resilience of the ecosystems we all depend on. The Endangered Species Act (ESA) is one of the most effective conservation laws in the world, and a key reason for its success is the blanket rule, which provides immediate, consistent protection for threatened species before it is too late.

The blanket rule ensures that species listed as threatened receive the same core protections as endangered species, unless science clearly shows otherwise. This proactive approach matters because ecosystems do not collapse overnight—they unravel gradually. Waiting until a species is on the brink of extinction often means waiting too long.

Healthy ecosystems are interconnected systems, where plants, animals, water, and land rely on one another. When a species begins to disappear, the impacts ripple outward, affecting vegetation, waterways, soil stability, and other wildlife. The blanket rule helps stop this cascade early, preserving not only the species itself but the larger environmental landscape it supports.

Protecting threatened species early is also more effective and less costly than emergency recovery efforts after severe decline. It allows ecosystems the time and space to self-correct, maintaining balance rather than attempting to rebuild it after damage has already occurred.

Preserving wildlife benefits people, too. Strong ecosystems provide cleaner water, healthier soil, natural flood control, and greater resilience to climate change. By maintaining consistent protections through the blanket rule, the ESA helps ensure that conservation decisions are guided by science, not delayed by uncertainty or politics.

The Endangered Species Act, and the blanket rule in particular, reflect a commitment to prevention, stewardship, and responsibility. By protecting species before they reach the point of no return, we protect the natural systems that sustain all life, including our own.

Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.
title: Comment from Christian, Jesper

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
As someone who cares deeply about wildlife and the future of our planet, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule that would undermine wildlife protections granted by the Endangered Species Act. This change would go against decades of conservation progress and weaken one of our nation’s most important environmental laws.

The “blanket rule” gives essential baseline protection to threatened species until species-specific safeguards can be established. Removing the “blanket rule” may make them more vulnerable to extinction, in opposition to the intent of this legislation.

I urge you to uphold the mission of the Endangered Species Act and maintain the “blanket rule.” Our wildlife, wild places, and future generations are counting on it.

title: Comment from Martelle, Eva

text:
One of the proposed revisions to Endangered Species Act regulations would overturn the 4(d) rule, removing blanket protections for threatened species. I am writing to express my staunch opposition to this proposal, which is all but guaranteed to delay critical protections and push threatened species to the brink of endangerment.

Rather than making it increasingly difficult to establish essential protections, we should be preserving the regulations that are helping threatened species recover. Please stand up for American wildlife by leaving these blanket protections in place.

Thank you.

title: Comment from Richards, Jarri

text:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to firmly oppose the four proposed amendments to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations currently under review. These proposals, both individually and collectively, threaten to significantly undermine the ESA’s crucial role in preventing extinctions, aiding species recovery, and preserving vital ecosystems for both wildlife and human communities.

1. **Repealing Default Protections (4(d) Rule)**

The ESA’s proactive approach is key to preventing species from reaching critical endangerment levels. The longstanding 4(d) rule, supported by extensive scientific research, shows that early protective measures reduce recovery costs and prevent species decline. Ending these automatic protections introduces unnecessary delays and risks to vulnerable species, contradicting the ESA’s preventive objectives. This change will likely increase long-term ecological and financial costs.

2. **Considering Economic Factors in Listing Decisions**

The ESA mandates that species listing decisions be based solely on scientific data, not economic impacts. Allowing economic considerations would violate statutory language, compromise scientific integrity, and delay urgent protections. Additionally, ignoring projected climate threats disregards current conservation science, which reveals that gradual pressures like habitat loss and climate change already endanger species. Weakening these criteria will increase preventable extinctions.

3. **Reducing Habitat Protections and Redefining “Harm”**

Habitat loss is the leading cause of biodiversity decline globally. Reducing critical habitat designations undermines recovery efforts, while redefining “harm” to exclude habitat degradation contradicts legal and scientific precedents. These changes would make consultations less effective, heighten biological risk, and conflict with the ESA’s recovery goals.

4. **Loopholes Allowing Bypassing of ESA Protections**

Creating mechanisms for agencies to override ESA protections, even with foreseeable extinction risks, undermines the ESA’s core mission. These loopholes encourage exemptions, reduce transparency, and sideline science-based decision-making, disproportionately impacting species like the Florida panther and grizzly bear.

**Combined Impact**

Together, these proposals would weaken the scientific foundation of the ESA, delay protections, reduce habitat conservation, increase extinction risks, undermine inter-agency cooperation, and elevate taxpayer recovery costs. The ESA has successfully prevented 99% of listed species from extinction due to its scientific, precautionary, and proactive principles. At a time of unprecedented biodiversity loss, the United States should strengthen, not weaken, this vital conservation law.

**Request**

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

title: Comment from Fergeson, Cheryl

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act. The ESA is a successful bipartisan piece of legislation that has saved hundreds of species from extinction and its current format provides optimum protections.

As a citizen of this beautiful country I would request that you withdraw the proposed rule change that would remove the blanket rule.

• Removing this rule would once again put threatened species at risk and leave them open to things like environmental disturbances and killing.
title: Comment from Rust, Christine

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Swanson, Robin

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Stringer, Kelly

text:
As someone who cares deeply about wildlife and the future of our planet, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule that would undermine wildlife protections granted by the Endangered Species Act. This change would go against decades of conservation progress and weaken one of our nation’s most important environmental laws.

The “blanket rule” gives essential baseline protection to threatened species until species-specific safeguards can be established. Removing the “blanket rule” may make them more vulnerable to extinction, in opposition to the intent of this legislation.

I urge you to uphold the mission of the Endangered Species Act and maintain the “blanket rule.” Our wildlife, wild places, and future generations are counting on it.

I love animals and I want them around for future generations to enjoy!!!

title: Comment from Richardson , Spencer

text:
I oppose this proposal to rewrite Endangered Species Act rules, and I urge you to withdraw it. This proposal would reverse a longstanding rule prohibiting consideration of economic impacts when deciding whether to list a species as endangered or threatened.

More than 99% of species under the ESA's care have been saved or are on the path to recovery. The ESA has protected millions of acres of natural habitat, including forests, mountains, rivers, deserts, beaches, and oceans. To achieve this success, ESA listings must be guided by science and be free of economic considerations, and projects must be held accountable for taxpayer-funded actions that would harm listed species.

I am also concerned that the administration's proposal is opposed by the majority of Americans. A recent peer-reviewed paper, "Support for the US Endangered Species Act Is High and Steady Over the Past Three Decades," authored by Professor Vucetich, shows that 84% of Americans support the Endangered Species Act. This support for the ESA is consistent among people living in urban, suburban, and rural environments.

We should strengthen the ESA to protect manatees, monarch butterflies, red knots, wolverines, and other species that need to be recovered. This proposal puts our wildlife at even greater risk of extinction.

title: Comment from Jones, Israel

text:
I strongly oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. As an avid hunter, outdoorswoman, and photographer, I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is one of the environmental laws that I'm most proud of as an American: it protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against the loss of our nation's natural heritage.

Fish and Wildlife should retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species. This should be especially relevant for Fish and Wildlife, given the nearly 20% reduction in your workforce over the last year.

Additionally, I believe you should keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I hope it goes without saying, but I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

Please, focus your efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and the looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Help protect this incredible part of our legacy as Americans --- our wildlife and wild spaces. Thank you.
title: Comment from Hobson, Lauren

text:
Rolling back protections under the Endangered Species Act directly contradicts established scientific evidence and places already vulnerable species, including the Florida manatee, at serious risk. Manatees remain threatened due to habitat loss, watercraft strikes, cold stress, and starvation caused by seagrass decline driven by water pollution and coastal development (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; NOAA).

Extinction and ecosystem collapse are irreversible. Scientific research shows that the loss of keystone and indicator species such as manatees signals broader ecosystem failure, particularly in coastal and freshwater systems. Once these systems are degraded beyond a threshold, restoration is often impossible within human timescales (IPBES; National Academy of Sciences).

The natural ecosystems of this state evolved over millions of years and do not operate on economic or political timelines. Short term economic considerations fail to account for the long term ecological costs, including the loss of biodiversity, diminished water quality, increased vulnerability to climate impacts, and the permanent erosion of natural heritage. These costs are borne by communities and future generations, not by short term development interests.

Manatees are protected because science has demonstrated that without strong, enforceable safeguards, population declines accelerate rapidly. Weakening the Endangered Species Act undermines science based conservation, ignores evolutionary and ecological realities, and risks irreversible environmental damage. The value of this state is inseparable from its natural life. Protecting endangered species is not optional. It is a responsibility grounded in evidence, stewardship, and long term public interest.

References:
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Manatee Recovery Program)
NOAA Fisheries
IPBES Global Assessment on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
National Academy of Sciences
title: Comment from Travieso, Nancy

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.

I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted, Thanh Lam

text:
To whom it may concern,

I am a first-year student currently studying at Georgetown University, where scientific reasoning, critical thinking, and policy engagement has been heavily emphasized. This past semester, my science course has delved heavily into the Endangered Species Act and other policies and factors surrounding species conservation, including habitat destruction, species prioritization, economic values, and impact of human activities. My final project analyzed the threats posed to New Zealand’s endangered yellow-eyed penguins and how conditions can be improved through human involvement. Though I am not a scientific expert by any means, I write from the perspective of a young student hoping to preserve our world and urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to repeal its proposed change to 50 CFR part 17, Section 4(d).

This proposed change, which “proposes to eliminate the ‘blanket rule’ option and require species-specific 4(d) rules tailored to each threatened species,” has devastating implications for threatened species (Administration Revises Endangered Species Act Regulations to Strengthen Certainty, Reduce Burdens and Uphold the Law | U.S. Department of the Interior, 2025). Currently, while species listed as “endangered” receive full protections, threatened species do not have full recovery plans and only receive protection that could prevent it from becoming endangered. However, removing this layer of protection simply because threatened species are less at risk would only serve to put more strain on conservation efforts in the long run. If the blanket rule is blocking threatened species from worsening conditions, removing it would mean allowing threatened species to continue on their track of becoming endangered, thus creating the need for more recovery plans and more high-risk species to worry about. If endangered species is the core issue, the blanket rule prevents that issue from developing in the first place, nipping it in the bud as best as possible.

“Almost all U.S. threatened animal species are sensitive to climate change,” claims a study by Weber et. al assessing their climate sensitivity, defined as responses to “temperature, precipitation, fire regimes, or other key processes” (Weber et al., 2023). With global warming rapidly increasing, already having irreversibly altered entire ecosystems past their tipping points, it’s only safe to say that it gets worse from here. While specification in protection plans is at times vital, the generalization of the blanket rule decreases the risk of further species endangerment in that preventative measures can be taken without the long and tedious process of continuous back and forth between classification and evaluation that would only delay conservation.

In short, as the American Bird Conservancy states, “[r]escinding this part of the ESA could push more species towards extinction, ultimately requiring more time, resources, and funds to pull a species back from the brink” (Proposed Endangered Species Act Rule Changes Pose Major Risks to Birds - American Bird Conservancy, 2025). This proposed change will only strain the agency’s resources in the long run by removing the dam blocking a streaming river. For the sake of the future world, I once again urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to repeal its proposed change to Section 4(d) and thank you for your time.
References

Administration Revises Endangered Species Act Regulations to Strengthen Certainty, Reduce Burdens and Uphold the Law | U.S. Department of the Interior. (2025, November 19). U.S. Department of the Interior. https://www.doi.gov/pressreleases/administration-revises-endangered-species-act-regulations-strengthen-certainty
Chaney, R. (2025, August 21). Is “Blanket Rule” Protecting Threatened Species Under ESA Doomed? Mountain Journal. https://mountainjournal.org/is-blanket-rule-protecting-threatened-species-under-endangered-species-act-doomed/
Proposed Endangered Species Act Rule Changes Pose Major Risks to Birds - American Bird Conservancy. (2025, November 20). American Bird Conservancy. https://abcbirds.org/news/esa-proposed-rules-2025/
Weber, T., Delach, A., Albrecht, R., & Niederman, T. E. (2023). Agency management plans also fail to address threatened species vulnerability to climate change in the US. Biological Conservation, 284, 110184. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocon.2023.110184

text:
December 19, 2025



Via Regulations.gov Docket



 

Dear Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service  



Attached please find the names of 24,729 individuals who are opposed to any effort by this administration to weaken the Endangered Species Act. Inserted below is the letter that Earthjustice supporters signed, and attached to this docket submission is the file containing their names.



RE: FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039 (Section 4), FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044 (Section 7),FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029 (Section 4(d)), FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048 (Section 4(b)(2))

Dear Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service,



The Endangered Species Act is the essential tool for stopping the extinction crisis in its tracks. We cannot guarantee species survival and recovery without the strong backstop of a fully protective ESA.

I oppose any effort by this administration to weaken the Endangered Species Act. The proposed rules are yet another in a series of attacks on imperiled species and the places they live that ignore science and prioritize destruction over conservation. The proposed rules:

Deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, greater sage grouse, and monarch butterfly could be left unprotected even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings.

Narrow the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat. Historic habitat is vital for recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss.

Loosen compliance measures for federal agencies to make it easier to greenlight destructive actions, like logging or drilling, that put a protected species in harm's way.

Violate the letter of the law by allowing “economic considerations” in decisions about whether to protect species that are scientifically shown to be at risk of extinction. With this rule, the federal government could decide against protecting an endangered species after considering lost revenue from prohibiting a golf course or hotel development to be built where the species lives.

Alter the criteria for designating critical habitat to make it easier to exclude areas from protections by giving more weight to industry claims of economic impact.

With greater threats facing species than ever before, these attempts to weaken the ESA are dangerous.

More than a million of the Earth’s species face the possibility of extinction due to climate change, pollution, habitat loss, and exploitation. Even species that are not yet on the brink will face huge population declines. This extinction crisis is depleting fisheries, wiping out the pollinators that support our food supply, and making our rivers, wetlands, and forests disappear.

Humans are not isolated from the natural environment, and what happens to other creatures affects our existence, too.

At a time when we must be redoubling our commitment to protect biodiversity and stop extinction, this administration’s proposals are dangerous and will delay the progress we must make to address the alarming rate of extinction our planet now faces.

Sincerely,  

[undersigned] 



Please let me know if you need more information. Thank you for your attention to this matter.  



Sincerely,  



Swetha Pottam  

Digital Advocacy Associate, Earthjustice

Spottam@earthjustice.org

Dear Fisheries and Wildlife Service,

I am writing today as an American wife, mother, and Christian that cares deeply about the health of our children and our country’s natural heritage. By removing blanket protections, the effectiveness is weakened. The ESA protects species before they get to the point of critical endangerment. The wildlife that we hunt and the natural spaces we camp and swim in also belong to the wildlife. text:
I urge you to withdraw this proposal. The longstanding policy, known as the blanket rule, is critical to protecting threatened species during the period before species-specific rules are enacted. Species-specific rules are subjected to the bureaucracies, road blocks, and the glacial speed of government progress, putting these species at risk. Threatened species are not listed under ESA but require protections to prevent further erosion of the status. The blanket rule affords these protections, which are critical to prevent intentional harm, killing, taking, or habitat destruction of species that are at risk of becoming endangered.

Two examples can be seen with the polar bear and West Indian manatee, both currently classified as threatened under the ESA. Both species experience sensitivities to habitat loss and ecological impacts due to climate change. The West Indian manatee has experienced many Unusual Mortality Events (1996, 2002, 2003, 2006, 2007, 2010, 2011, 2013, 2021) across their range, due to biotoxin exposure and/or ecological impacts from warming oceans. Without protections under the blanket rule, like vessel speed restriction zones, this species could also face unsustainable mortality rates due to human interaction. They could be left unprotected for years as the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes their species-specific rule and future ESA listings.

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Beckwith, Wayne

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:
Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):
* Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
* Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
* Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
* Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.
Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment.  Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.
Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.
Respectfully submitted,
Rita Jackson

Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

title: Comment from McGeary, Jessica

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I strongly oppose the proposed revisions to Section 4 of the Endangered Species Act. These changes would weaken how species are listed and how critical habitat is protected, putting already vulnerable wildlife at even greater risk. Species like the West Indian manatee depend on healthy habitats, especially seagrass meadows, for food and survival. Manatees have already experienced severe population losses due to declining water quality, habitat destruction, and seagrass die-offs, including the recent mass starvation events in Florida, where more than 1,100 manatees died in a single year. I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service to reject this proposal and uphold the Endangered Species Act's science-based mission to conserve wildlife and the habitats we all depend on.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

text:
Subject: FWS Rulemaking Dockets: FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044; FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048

I’m writing to oppose key adverse changes to Endangered Species Act rules that would reduce protections for wildlife facing extinction. I care deeply for our nation’s wildlife and am a strong supporter of the Endangered Species Act. It is a bedrock American environmental law that protects our most vulnerable wildlife, providing a backstop against irretrievable loss of the nation’s natural heritage.

Retain blanket protections for species listed as “threatened” under the Act, because removing the automatic 4(d) rule could cause imperiled wildlife to endure habitat loss and other threats. Requiring rule-making from scratch in lieu of allowing blanket protections until more tailored rules are developed will also place a large burden on overworked staff, further delaying key protections for species.

Keep listing decisions scientifically focused on biology, not economics, to ensure an accurate account of which species most need care and attention. Even though the rule is saying that economic information won’t be part of the listing decision, including it as part of a listing package will be confusing, and add yet another cost to the process.

I am opposed to any weakening of habitat protections that will be harmful to vulnerable wildlife, including around unoccupied habitat for recovery, where agency consultation is required, or resulting from climate change.

Finally, I am opposed to weakening the Section 7 consultation process by changing the definition and practice of what is considered an “effect” of an agency action. In the complex world we live in with many interacting reasons for species decline, I am concerned proposed changes will reduce the effectiveness of this crucial part of the ESA.

I encourage you to focus efforts on strengthening the Endangered Species Act’s rules by focusing on improving wildlife recovery efforts. With all the pressure on wildlife from population growth and development, and looming threat of climate change, we need a strong and effective Endangered Species Act now more than ever. Thank you.

title: Comment from Pinque, Meryl

text:
This proposal to weaken default protections for threatened species is not categorically excludable and cannot lawfully be evaluated apart from the other ESA rulemakings issued concurrently. The ESA’s threatened-species framework is inherently preventative; dismantling it foreseeably accelerates species decline. Segmenting this rule from companion ESA rollbacks conceals their combined environmental impact, undermining NEPA’s prohibition on segmentation and the APA’s requirement for reasoned decision-making. The rushed comment period and restrictive character limits further frustrate meaningful public participation.

The agency errs in treating the consequences of removing automatic protections as uncertain or speculative. When legal standards change such that previously prohibited conduct becomes permissible, the predictable increase in that conduct is neither hypothetical nor remote—it is the intended effect of the rule. Courts do not accept the argument that repealing safety protections has no foreseeable consequences simply because the government itself does not directly commit the ensuing harm.

A regulatory framework stating “if a species is no longer protected absent a species-specific rule, then habitat destruction may proceed” necessarily entails increased habitat loss. NEPA requires analysis of indirect and cumulative effects; dismissing them because they occur after rule implementation violates NEPA and the APA’s mandate to provide a reasoned explanation. Regardless of judicial interpretations or executive guidance, the agency must consider the foreseeable consequences of weakened protections, including cumulative, indirect, and downstream impacts, and may not avoid its statutory obligations under NEPA or the ESA by citing executive orders or selective case law.

The proposed changes to Section 4(d) protections represent a fundamental departure from the ESA’s preventive purpose. Framed as regulatory flexibility, this proposal — in combination with the other three ESA rulemakings — effectively dismantles the early-intervention framework that has made the Act successful. Threatened species are, by definition, on a trajectory toward endangerment; eliminating default protections shifts the ESA from a preventive to a reactive statute, intervening only after species reach crisis levels. This approach directly increases extinction risk and contradicts congressional intent.

The ESA’s historic success — protecting over 99 percent of listed species from extinction — reflects early, robust protections. Species-by-species discretionary rules are often delayed, underfunded, or never finalized. The foreseeable result is regulatory gaps during which habitat destruction and population decline continue unchecked, undermining both statutory purpose and the agency’s duty under the ESA.

These harms extend beyond wildlife. Loss of species and ecosystems degrades critical ecosystem services — flood control, water filtration, pollination, pest control, and climate regulation. The economic and social costs — disaster recovery, insurance losses, agricultural decline, public health impacts — are borne by states, tribes, and taxpayers, not the industries benefiting from weakened protections.

Weakening default protections for threatened species also foreseeably interferes with Indigenous religious practices that depend on continued access to specific animals, plants, and ecological relationships. Regulatory changes permitting species decline impose a tangible burden on religious exercise, implicating the American Indian Religious Freedom Act and the federal trust responsibility. These impacts are a predictable consequence of the rule’s design, not speculative downstream effects.

Conclusion: By failing to analyze cumulative impacts alongside narrower habitat definitions, reduced consultation, and expanded exclusions, the agency violates NEPA’s requirement to consider indirect and cumulative effects and fails to provide a reasoned explanation as required under the APA. The predictable ecological, economic, and cultural consequences demand a comprehensive, science-based review. This proposal should be withdrawn.
title: Comment from Murphy, Amanda

text:
I am writing to formally oppose the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s proposed revision to remove the blanket 4(d) rule protections for newly listed threatened species under the Endangered Species Act.

The blanket 4(d) rule has long served as a critical, science-based safeguard that ensures threatened species receive immediate and consistent protections at the moment they are listed. Removing this default protection creates an unnecessary and dangerous gap between listing and the implementation of species-specific rules—during which time vulnerable populations may face irreversible habitat loss, exploitation, or disturbance.

While the proposal states that existing protections would remain in place until species-specific rules are finalized, history demonstrates that rulemaking can take years. Threatened species do not have the luxury of administrative delay. For some, that delay will mean the difference between recovery and extinction.

If this proposal moves forward, it is not an abstract policy shift—it will have permanent biological consequences. Species that could have been protected may instead disappear entirely. Future generations may never experience these animals in the wild, learning about them only through books, photographs, or online archives as examples of what was lost due to inaction.

Requiring species-specific rules for every threatened species also introduces uncertainty, inconsistency, and increased political pressure into what should remain a science-driven process. The blanket 4(d) rule provides clarity for landowners, agencies, and conservation partners while ensuring baseline protections are applied uniformly and efficiently.

At a time when biodiversity loss and climate-related stressors are accelerating, weakening default protections under the Endangered Species Act moves policy in the wrong direction. The Act was designed to be precautionary—to prevent species from slipping closer to extinction—not to introduce procedural hurdles that delay meaningful protection.

I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule and continue to uphold the Endangered Species Act’s core purpose: protecting imperiled species before they are lost forever.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this critical issue.

title: Comment from Garcia, Madeline

text:
Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick:

Out of grave concern for manatees, I urge you to withdraw the following proposed regulations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA):

Regulations for Listing Endangered and Threatened Species and Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0039;
Regulations Pertaining to Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029;
Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Interagency Cooperation, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0044;
Regulations for Designating Critical Habitat, FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0048.
I oppose these proposed regulations because they would eviscerate the protections available to manatees and all other imperiled species under the ESA. Manatees are a strong example of why the ESA matters, as well as a stark reminder of why its protections are needed now more than ever. Since the species’ 1967 federal listing, the manatee population has increased—thanks in large part to ESA-based protections—but so have its threats. The 2020-2022 Unusual Mortality Event (UME), which claimed the lives of over 1,200 manatees from seagrass loss-driven starvation, showcased that manatees remain extremely vulnerable. Additionally, over 60% of Florida’s manatees rely on warm water outfalls from power plants to survive the cold winter months. As facilities transition their technology to configurations that no longer discharge warm water, manatees urgently need access to alternative warm-water winter habitat to ensure their continued survival. Other threats, such as watercraft and water control structures (dams, locks, etc.), continue to injure and kill many manatees every year. These ongoing challenges to manatee recovery highlight why it is essential to maintain or strengthen the ESA’s regulations—not weaken them.

Manatees, Florida’s beloved state marine mammal and an important driver of economic activity (e.g., manatee viewing tourism), depend greatly on the protections afforded by the ESA. Manatees are particularly vulnerable to the proposed regulatory changes due to their urgent habitat protection and restoration needs and their being listed as “threatened” under the ESA. One of the proposed regulations would remove the “blanket 4(d)” rule, which currently ensures that newly listed threatened animal species, such as the Florida manatee, automatically receive protections from harmful behaviors such as killing, trapping, and harassment. Further, by placing additional hurdles to designating “critical habitat” and allowing economic impacts to influence listing and critical habitat decisions, the proposed regulations would let the federal government deny needed protections for imperiled species. With manatees’ many habitat-based threats, including the looming threat from power plant transition, it is important that the government has all possible habitat protection options available under the ESA.

Please withdraw these terrible proposed regulations. Without the foundational protections afforded by the ESA, manatees will be more vulnerable than ever at a time when forward-looking conservation—not regression—is urgently needed.
