title: Comment from Loveland, Jim

text: For decades, “harm” has included actions that degrade habitats and threaten the survival of endangered species. This protection has been crucial for species like the Hawaiian monk seal and Florida manatee. Without it, gillnetting, overfishing, ocean mining and blasting, logging, wetland development, and other human activities could wipe out vital ecosystems and the species the Endangered Species Act was meant to protect.
title: Comment from Arce, Stephanie

text: The Endangered Species Act is a key component for effective conservation. It not only protects imperiled species across the country, it also works to provide invaluable protection to the habitats that they (and countless other species) need to thrive into the future. The short term “benefits” of extraction and degradation of our natural resources are not nearly worth the cost to the benefits to ecosystem health, outdoor recreation, and the proper functioning of responsible stewardship. Do not push forth any legislation that would threaten our, and future generations, rights to live in an intact world that strives for the greater good of all. This includes the dismantling of the Endangered Species Act.
title: Comment from Ryan, Tate

text: Request to deny proposed changes to blanket protection rule under 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act. Under the current rule, Threatened species receive the blanket 4(d) rule and are automatically placed under a blanket protection that is the same as endangered species. This protects the Threatened species from also being "taken" via harassment, harm, wound, hunting, etc. Threatened species rely on the blanket 4(d) protection rule to ensure immediate protections. Under the proposed regulation, this blanket protection would end and species would only be granted this protection when species-specific rules are created. While species-specific rules are necessary for long-term recovery of a species, it requires significant time and energy to be created - the blanket rule provides the needed protections until such rules can be drafted. Furthermore, broad baseline protections ensure that species don't fall prey to regulatory gaps or the influence of special-interest groups. A Threatened species is characterized as a plant, animal or fungus at high risk of extinction in the near future due to factors such as habitat loss, poaching, climate change, and invasive species. This act safeguards the survivability of a species during the interim period in which a species-specific protective measure can be created and implemented.

title: Comment from DeGerolamo, Jennifer

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

The “blanket rule” gives essential baseline protection to threatened species until species-specific safeguards can be established. Removing the “blanket rule” may make them more vulnerable to extinction, in opposition to the intent of this legislation.

I urge you to uphold the mission of the Endangered Species Act and maintain the “blanket rule.” Our wildlife, wild places, and future generations are counting on it.

title: Comment from Cowan, Gerald

text:
Virtually no one would say that the world needs fewer birds, less fish, or fewer animals. Ensuring that populations continue, or in some cases, rebound to a sustainable level just makes sense in a world where all species are interconnected - often in ways we don't fully understand. Sometimes that seemingly insignificant insect turns out to be really important after all.

Lest we think they will do just fine on their own, we might consider the seemingly inexhaustible populations of passenger pigeons, American bison, or the North Carolina parakeet. Humans can be frighteningly efficient in wiping out vast numbers. Animals of all sorts need our protection, and the Endangered Species Act has proven itself to be very effective for over five decades.

Please protect this vital legislation going forward - it matters greatly.

title: Comment from Makedonsky, Brian

text:
The Port Gamble S’Klallam Tribe opposes the changes to the Endangered Species Act in – Docket Number: FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029. The Tribe opposes the weakening of automatic protections for threatened species, which leaves them vulnerable to harm. Elimination of the blanket rule under section 4(d) leaves threatened species without protection until species specific plans are in place, which may be subject to delays, loopholes, and inconsistencies. Removing this safeguard undermines the ESA’s intent by removing safety measures for threatened species and exposing threatened species to harm, which may place them on an extinction trajectory. Understudied species may be especially vulnerable to harm, particularly invertebrates that play important roles in ecosystems and food webs. This may have a cumulative effect on an ecosystem.
Creating species specific protections increases administrative burdens and delays, during which time a threatened species could become endangered. It also risks inconsistencies based on staffing, political pressures, and stakeholder influence that may not be in line with best available science. Immediate protection is critical for safeguarding species and ensuring recovery, especially for species with small populations, long generational times, or rapid habitat loss, where delay increases threats. The blanket rule provided this immediate application of Section 9. Elimination means species will lack equivalent take protection during the period required to develop an individualized rule, which can stress species to the point of near extinction. Gaps in protection and delays can impact Tribal treaty rights, as well, regarding species that are important to subsistence, ceremony, cultural identity, and treaty obligations. The blanket rule supports Tribal treaty rights by immediately implementing protections once a species is threatened, which does not place undue burdens on Tribal communities to manage threatened species without proper federal protection and support. The Tribe notes that this has not gone through proper government-to-government consultation, which are necessary for changes that impact Tribal rights.

title: Comment from keyser, diana

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule rescinding the long-standing blanket 4(d) protections for threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has provided essential safeguards by automatically extending most section 9 prohibitions to threatened species upon listing, unless species-specific rules were developed. Removing this protection will result in long delays before threatened species receive necessary conservation measures, directly contradicting the ESA’s precautionary design.

Congress created distinct “endangered” and “threatened” categories to allow for earlier intervention, not to defer protections until decline becomes severe. The blanket rule is an efficient, scientifically defensible mechanism that prevents threats from escalating while species-specific management plans are crafted. Without it, newly threatened species will be left unprotected during their most vulnerable period, increasing the likelihood that they progress toward endangered status or extinction.

The proposed rule also provides no evidence that the blanket rule creates regulatory burdens inconsistent with the ESA or the APA. On the contrary, eliminating the rule will increase administrative workload by necessitating dozens of species-specific 4(d) rules, delaying urgently needed protections.

For these reasons, I urge the Service to retain the blanket 4(d) rule that ensures timely and scientifically grounded protections for all threatened species.
title: Comment from Peterson, William

text:
The purposes of the Endangered Species Act of 1973, as amended (16 U.S.C. 1531

et seq.

(the Act)), are to provide a means to conserve the ecosystems upon which listed species depend, develop a program for the conservation of listed species, and achieve the purposes of certain treaties and conventions (16 U.S.C. 1531(b)). Moreover, it is the policy of Congress that the Federal Government will seek to conserve endangered and threatened species and use its authorities to further the purposes of the Act (16 U.S.C. 1531(c)(1)). Please honor nature and the environment by protecting these laws.
Animals and plants are important for our world.
title: Comment from Zweig, Julie

text:
To whom it may concern,

In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.

For more than five decades, the Endangered Species Act has successfully prevented extinction for 99% of the species placed under its protection. As a strong supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule that would eliminate the long-standing “blanket rule.” This rule ensures that critical protections—such as prohibitions on killing, harming, or harassing wildlife—automatically take effect when a species is listed. Removing it would strip threatened species of the basic safeguards they have depended on for decades.
The ESA represents the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only at-risk species, but also the ecosystems that sustain them, a responsibility that must not be weakened. Repealing the “blanket rule” would leave threatened species without protection for months or even years during the most vulnerable stage of their decline. The “blanket rule” has long served as a practical, science-backed safety net, allowing protections to be applied quickly and consistently. Eliminating it would create unnecessary administrative delays, overwhelm agency resources, and increase risks to species already on the brink.
In addition, the “blanket rule” has provided clear, consistent guidance for both landowners and agencies, while ensuring that essential protections are put in place efficiently and uniformly. I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule and reaffirm the Endangered Species Act’s original purpose: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as mandated by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Sit , Samantha

text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to the Endangered Species Act, which would undermine the law's original intent and expose threatened and endangered wildlife to a heightened risk of extinction. Taken together, the four proposals (FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0029, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0044, FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0048) rescind longstanding conservation regulations that have proven to be both effective and popular.

First, eliminating the "blanket 4(d) rule" increases the risk that populations of threatened species will further decline, and removes a clear, legally defensible, and effective conservation tool that has contributed to the success of the ESA. The existing rule already allows the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to issue special rules for each listed species to provide exemptions in its implementation of protections. Eliminating the blanket 4(d) rule places a greater burden on the agency, as it would then be compelled to issue specific 4(d) rules for every species listed as threatened to comply with the ESA's requirements.

Second, the proposed alterations to critical habitat regulations significantly weaken the process of listing species and designating their critical habitat. Under this rule, habitat on federal public land could be excluded from protection if development of the land would produce greater economic benefits than protecting it for wildlife. This would allow energy development, grazing, logging, and other commercial uses on land that threatened and endangered species need to survive and recover as they face increasing habitat loss due to land conversion, pollution, and climate change. Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. Drastically shrinking the requirements for designating critical habitat is a clear giveaway to industry, to the enormous detriment of both short- and long-term species recovery.

Third, introducing economic considerations into the process of deciding whether to list a species as threatened or endangered undermines one of the key tenets of the ESA: that species listing decisions be based only on the best available scientific and commercial data. This change opens the door to burdensome and inappropriate cost-benefit analyses that risk politicizing a process that should be wholly science-based.

Fourth, undercutting the process of interagency consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and National Marine Fisheries Service will allow federal agencies to ignore development's impact on imperiled species. The push to "streamline" the interagency consultation process is misleading--what it could mean is that the federal agencies tasked with implementing the ESA would have little or no input in determining a project's harm to listed species.

These drastic revisions, among others in the ESA proposed rules, revive many of the same attacks on wildlife that were put in place during the first Trump term. However, these actions are neither aligned with the law's record of success nor with public sentiment. Since it was enacted, 99 percent of ESA-protected species have been spared from extinction. Furthermore, according to a 2025 poll, the ESA enjoys the support of more than four out of five Americans across political and geographic boundaries.

Today, most imperiled species occupy small fractions of their historical range. The need for species protections has not decreased over the decades since the ESA was enacted. Rather, increased threats from development and a changing climate necessitate strong and full implementation and enforcement of the ESA--now more than ever.

I urge the agencies to retract these regulatory changes, for the sake of America's imperiled wildlife and the habitat they depend upon for their survival.

title: Comment from Allen, Cynthia

text:
In the 51 years since its creation, the Endangered Species Act has saved 99% of the listed species from extinction. As a devoted supporter of America’s wildlife, I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule change to rescind the “blanket rule,” which provides uniform safeguards to ensure that vital prohibitions, like restrictions on killing, harming, and harassing wildlife, are automatically applied upon a species listing. This proposal will remove the essential baseline protections that threatened species have relied on for decades.

The Endangered Species Act reflects the federal government’s commitment to protecting not only imperiled species but the ecosystems that sustain them, an obligation that must not be weakened. Repealing the long-standing “blanket rule” means that threatened species could go months or even years without protections during the most vulnerable phase of their decline. The “blanket rule” is a proven, efficient, and scientifically supported safety net, and removing it creates administrative delay that will strain agency capacity and put already-imperiled species at greater risk at a critical time. The “blanket rule” has provided clarity and consistency for landowners and agencies while ensuring that baseline protections are established quickly and uniformly.

I urge the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule that directly undermines the ESA’s original objective: conserving endangered species and the ecosystems they depend on, as required by Congress and expected by the American people.
title: Comment from Byrnes, Samantha

text: Sea turtles need continued protection if they are downlisted under the ESA in the future. The “blanket rule” ensures that species are protected when they are at their most vulnerable – before they are considered “endangered” of becoming extinct. I encourage USFWS and NOAA to keep the “blanket rule” under the ESA as it stands now.
title: Comment from Porfiri, Dave

text:
If the blanket rule is removed, it will deprive newly listed threatened animal and plant species from automatically receiving protections from killing, trapping, and other forms of prohibited “take.” Species now proposed for listing, like the Florida manatee, California spotted owl, Greater sage grouse, and Monarch butterfly, could be left unprotected for years even after the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service finalizes the listings. Endangered Species Act listings must be guided by science and prohibit economic considerations. Federal agencies should not be allowed to take actions that push listed species closer to extinction. The narrowing of the definition of “critical habitat” to exclude currently unoccupied but historic habitat would be disastrous. Historic habitat is vital for the recovery of imperiled species, especially as the areas where they currently live shrink due to the rapidly changing climate and the chain effects of ongoing biodiversity loss. Critical habitat protections should be strengthened, but this proposal does the very opposite by making it harder to designate critical habitat and allowing destruction to designated critical habitat. The proposed rule makes it easier to greenlight destructive activities, such as logging or drilling. These actions will put protected species in harm’s way.
ESA Section 7 calls for interagency cooperation. When federal agencies coordinate, share information, and carefully evaluate the impacts of their actions, they help prevent avoidable harm and promote long-term conservation. Strong interagency collaboration upholds the law and, importantly, strengthens transparency, improves decision-making, and reflects our shared responsibility to safeguard biodiversity for future generations. I urge you to keep the analysis method for determining critical habitat, habitat that are essential to species recovery; science-based critical habitat designations are essential to truly recover endangered species.
title: Comment from Goldberg, Susan

text:
This rule has automatically provided threatened species with protections against harm until a tailored plan can be finalized. For decades, it has helped species like the piping plover, southern sea otter, and Florida manatee gain immediate safeguards upon listing (FWS, 2019).
Without this automatic protection, newly listed threatened species could be killed, captured, or harassed without legal consequence while they await a species-specific rule. This exposes species to preventable harm during their most vulnerable period.
Habitat loss is the number one driver of extinction. The ESA already allows exclusions, but only when they will not lead to extinction. Broadening this power increases risk to species that already live on the edge. For example, habitat loss contributed to the extinction of the ivory-billed woodpecker, Little Mariana fruit bat, and multiple freshwater mussel species (FWS, 2021)

title: Comment from Anonymous

text:
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s proposal to eliminate the Endangered Species Act (ESA) “blanket rule” for threatened species under section 4(d) is inconsistent with the statute’s text, purpose, and long-standing judicial interpretation. The ESA is a precautionary law designed to prevent extinction before species become endangered, and its structure supports immediate baseline protections for species listed as threatened.

Section 4(d) authorizes the Service to promulgate regulations “necessary and advisable to provide for the conservation” of threatened species. For decades, the blanket rule has lawfully implemented this authority by extending core section 9 prohibitions to newly listed threatened species unless and until species-specific rules are developed. This approach ensures regulatory continuity and avoids protection gaps during the often lengthy rulemaking process.

Removing the blanket rule undermines the ESA’s conservation mandate by shifting risk from regulated activities to imperiled species. Newly listed threatened species would face delayed or uncertain protections at precisely the stage when early intervention is most effective. Given persistent agency resource constraints, reliance on species-specific 4(d) rules is likely to result in prolonged periods of diminished protection, contrary to Congress’s intent that the ESA “halt and reverse the trend toward species extinction.”

The proposal also raises concerns under the Administrative Procedure Act by increasing discretionary, species-by-species decision-making without a consistent protective baseline, heightening the risk of arbitrary or inconsistent outcomes. The blanket rule provides a lawful, efficient, and scientifically defensible default that aligns with the ESA’s precautionary framework.

Accordingly, the Service should retain the blanket 4(d) rule as the default mechanism for threatened species protections while continuing to develop species-specific rules where scientifically justified.
